Guidelines require that the clinician weigh tumor characteristics against the patient's health status and anticipated life expectancy before recommending surveillance, surgery, or radiation, because men with limited life expectancy are unlikely to benefit from aggressive therapy while those with long life expectancy may be harmed by undertreatment. Bone scan and CT have a negligible yield in low- and intermediate-risk disease and are not indicated. Genomic testing may refine risk in selected cases but is not a required step, and urodynamics do not inform cancer management.
learning_point: For clinically localized (low or intermediate risk) prostate cancer, an assessment of life expectancy and overall health status is required before treatment counseling; staging CT, bone scan, and urodynamics are not indicated at this risk level.
key_facts: Life expectancy, not chronologic age, determines whether a man is likely to benefit from definitive treatment.
Bone scan and CT have very low yield in low- and intermediate-risk localized disease and are not routinely recommended.
Urodynamics play no role in cancer treatment decisions; molecular tests are optional adjuncts, not prerequisites.

question: Two years after radical cystectomy and ileal orthotopic neobladder, a 66-year-old man is completely dry during the day but wets the bed two or three nights a week. The most likely explanation is:

options.B: loss of the afferent-mediated reflex increase in urethral sphincter tone during filling.
options.C: poor compliance of the intestinal reservoir.
options.D: injury to the pelvic autonomic plexus.

rationale: With a native bladder, stretch afferents during filling drive a spinal guarding reflex that raises urethral sphincter tone, which persists even during sleep. An intestinal neobladder has no such afferent connection to the central nervous system, so sphincter tone falls with sleep and leakage occurs at night despite normal daytime continence; this is why isolated nocturnal incontinence is common after neobladder but rare after radical prostatectomy, where the afferent reflex is intact. Rhabdosphincter damage, a noncompliant reservoir, or high-pressure reservoir contractions would all cause leakage during the day as well. Pelvic plexus injury contributes to overall continence and erectile outcomes but does not produce a purely nocturnal pattern.
learning_point: Isolated nocturnal incontinence after orthotopic neobladder results from loss of the bladder afferent pathway that normally produces a reflex rise in urethral sphincter tone during filling; sphincter injury or a poorly compliant or contractile reservoir would cause both day and night leakage.
key_facts: Nighttime enuresis is common after neobladder (reported in roughly a quarter or more of patients) even with good daytime control.
Native bladder afferents trigger a guarding reflex that increases urethral pressure with filling; the intestinal reservoir lacks this input.
Rhabdosphincter damage, low compliance, or high-pressure reservoir contractions cause incontinence day and night.
Timed nighttime voiding (alarm) is the usual management.

question: A 30-year-old woman with a complete T6 spinal cord injury performs CIC every four hours and takes maximal-dose solifenacin, yet remains incontinent between catheterizations. Urodynamics show phasic detrusor contractions reaching 60 cm H2O with leakage and no stress-related leakage. Six weeks ago her physiatrist injected 300 units of onabotulinumtoxinA into her lower extremities for spasticity. She wants to be dry. The next step is:

options.B: immediate injection of 200 units of intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA.
options.D: intradetrusor injection of 200 units of onabotulinumtoxinA in about six weeks.

rationale: Her incontinence is from neurogenic detrusor overactivity that has failed conservative therapy, so intradetrusor botulinum toxin is the appropriate next step, with 200 units as the standard starting dose. Because she received 300 units six weeks ago for spasticity, injecting 200 more now would push her well past the recommended ceiling of about 360 units per 12 weeks and raise the risk of systemic weakness and antibody development; waiting until 12 weeks have elapsed from the prior dose is the safe approach, coordinated with her physiatrist. Augmentation is a major operation reserved for failure of less invasive options. Sacral neuromodulation is not established for complete spinal cord injury, and an artificial sphincter addresses sphincteric incompetence, which her study did not show.
learning_point: Intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (200 units) is the next step for neurogenic detrusor overactivity refractory to CIC and antimuscarinics, but the cumulative dose from all indications should not exceed about 360 units within any 12-week period, so injection must be timed around recent spasticity dosing.
key_facts: Starting intradetrusor dose for neurogenic detrusor overactivity is 200 units; 300 units may be used for refractory cases.
Total onabotulinumtoxinA from all body sites should stay at or below roughly 360 units per 3 months to limit systemic toxicity and antibody formation.
Coordinate dosing with physiatry when the patient also receives toxin for spasticity.
At the time of the source item, sacral neuromodulation lacked an FDA indication for neurogenic bladder, and an artificial sphincter treats stress incontinence, not detrusor overactivity.

question: A 58-year-old healthy woman undergoes complete resection of a 3.5 cm posterior wall bladder tumor. Pathology shows urothelial carcinoma with extensive micropapillary features invading the lamina propria with lymphovascular invasion; muscularis propria is present in the specimen and uninvolved. The next step is:

options.A: repeat transurethral resection in four weeks.
options.C: radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection.
options.E: neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by cystectomy.

rationale: Micropapillary histology, tumor size over 3 cm, and lymphovascular invasion each mark T1 disease at very high risk of understaging and progression, and micropapillary tumors in particular respond poorly to intravesical therapy. Because early radical cystectomy cures most patients with disease still confined to the bladder, immediate cystectomy with lymphadenectomy is the recommended approach in a fit patient. Restaging TUR is appropriate for conventional T1 disease before BCG but should not delay definitive therapy here; BCG itself is unreliable for this variant. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy has established benefit only for muscle-invasive disease, and partial cystectomy leaves a bladder prone to multifocal recurrence.
learning_point: T1 bladder cancer with aggressive features such as micropapillary histology, size over 3 cm, or lymphovascular invasion has a high risk of progression and responds poorly to intravesical therapy; upfront radical cystectomy is recommended rather than BCG, partial cystectomy, or neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
key_facts: Micropapillary variant is associated with understaging and early progression; intravesical BCG is unreliable.
Early cystectomy for high-risk T1 disease yields excellent cancer-specific survival.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is proven for muscle-invasive disease, not for non-muscle-invasive tumors.
Partial cystectomy risks multifocal recurrence in the retained bladder.

question: A 68-year-old woman is two years out from radical cystectomy and an ileal orthotopic neobladder constructed from approximately 55 cm of ileum. She reports five to six watery stools daily for the past four months. Stool studies are negative, serum B12 is normal, and the ileocecal valve was preserved. The best initial management is:
rationale: Removing a long ileal segment while sparing the ileocecal valve impairs bile salt reabsorption; unabsorbed bile salts reach the colon, stimulate secretion of water and bicarbonate, and produce a chronic secretory diarrhea. Binding bile salts with cholestyramine, together with a low-fat diet to lower the bile acid load, is the first-line treatment. Loperamide and bulking fiber are appropriate for the rapid-transit osmotic diarrhea that follows loss of the ileocecal valve or colon, which is not the case here. B12 replacement corrects anemia and neuropathy after terminal ileal loss but does not affect stool frequency, and pancreatic insufficiency is not a consequence of urinary diversion.
learning_point: Chronic diarrhea after an ileal urinary diversion that removed a substantial segment of ileum (but spared the ileocecal valve) is a bile salt-induced secretory diarrhea, best treated initially with dietary fat reduction and cholestyramine; bulking agents and loperamide suit the osmotic/rapid-transit diarrhea seen after ileocecal or colonic resection.
key_facts: Resection of roughly 40-100 cm of ileum reduces bile salt reabsorption; excess bile salts irritate the colon and cause secretory diarrhea.
Cholestyramine binds bile salts; a low-fat diet reduces the stimulus.
Loss of the ileocecal valve or colon causes rapid transit and osmotic diarrhea, treated with bulking agents and loperamide.
Vitamin B12 deficiency develops after terminal ileal resection but does not cause diarrhea; fluid restriction is harmful with a diversion.

question: A 70-year-old man with stage 3 chronic kidney disease undergoes ureteroscopy for a filling defect, and a solitary 1 cm papillary tumor in the distal left ureter is biopsied and completely ablated with a holmium laser. Pathology shows low-grade, non-invasive (Ta) urothelial carcinoma. The next step is:

options.B: ureteral stent placement with retrograde BCG instillations.
options.D: scheduled surveillance ureteroscopy or imaging with cystoscopy and urine cytology.

rationale: A single, small, low-grade, non-invasive ureteral tumor that has been completely ablated is a classic indication for kidney-sparing endoscopic management, which is especially attractive in a patient with impaired renal function. The ablation itself is the definitive treatment; what remains is a rigorous surveillance program that evaluates the treated ureter (ureteroscopy or imaging), the bladder (cystoscopy, because intravesical recurrence is common), and urine cytology. Nephroureterectomy or segmental ureterectomy would sacrifice nephrons for negligible additional cancer control in low-risk disease. Topical BCG, whether antegrade or retrograde, is considered for high-grade disease or CIS and is unnecessary for a low-grade Ta lesion.
learning_point: A solitary, small, low-grade, non-invasive (Ta) ureteral tumor completely ablated endoscopically is adequately treated by the ablation; management then consists of close surveillance of the upper tract, bladder (cystoscopy), and urine cytology, not ureterectomy or upper tract BCG.
key_facts: Low-grade, low-volume upper tract urothelial carcinoma is appropriate for kidney-sparing endoscopic management.
Surveillance must include the bladder because of a high rate of subsequent intravesical recurrence.
Upper tract BCG is reserved for high-grade disease or CIS, typically in imperative (solitary kidney) situations, with limited supporting data.
Segmental ureterectomy adds surgical morbidity with minimal oncologic gain for low-risk disease.

question: A 66-year-old woman with high-grade muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma has multifocal tumors, diffuse CIS, a trigonal tumor that extends onto the bladder neck, and mild left hydronephrosis. She strongly prefers an orthotopic neobladder. The finding that is the strongest relative contraindication to orthotopic diversion is:

options.E: tumor extension onto the bladder neck.

rationale: In women, the urethra is short and tumor at the bladder neck is the strongest predictor of urethral involvement; roughly half of women with bladder neck tumor have disease in the urethra, compared with about 12% overall. It remains a relative rather than absolute contraindication because a negative intraoperative full-thickness frozen section of the proximal urethral margin allows the neobladder to proceed safely. CIS and multifocality raise the risk of urethral disease modestly but far less than bladder neck involvement. Unilateral hydronephrosis reflects local tumor extent and does not itself bar orthotopic diversion, and chronologic age is not a contraindication in a fit patient.
learning_point: In women considered for orthotopic neobladder, tumor involvement of the bladder neck is the strongest relative contraindication because it predicts urethral involvement; it is not absolute if intraoperative frozen section of the proximal urethral margin is negative. Age, CIS, and multifocality are lesser risk factors.
key_facts: Urethral tumor involvement occurs in about 12% of women undergoing cystectomy; bladder neck tumor is present in about 22% and about half of those have urethral disease.
Urethral recurrence after properly selected orthotopic diversion in women is under 4%.
A negative full-thickness frozen section of the distal (urethral) margin permits neobladder even with bladder neck tumor.
Age, grade, stage, and unilateral hydronephrosis are not contraindications by themselves.

question: During open repair of an inguinal hernia in a 2-year-old boy, after the external oblique aponeurosis is opened, the ilioinguinal nerve can be reliably separated from the vas and vessels by opening the:
rationale: The ilioinguinal nerve courses along the cord within the cremasteric layer. When the surgeon opens the cremaster and sweeps it off the cord, the nerve stays with the cremasteric fibers and is carried away from the vas, testicular vessels, and processus vaginalis, so it need not be dissected separately. The external spermatic fascia lies superficial to the cremaster and is traversed before the nerve is encountered, while the internal spermatic fascia lies deep to it and directly surrounds the cord elements. The transversalis fascia forms the canal floor and the tunica vaginalis surrounds the testis, neither of which contains the nerve.
learning_point: During inguinal surgery the ilioinguinal nerve travels within the cremasteric layer of the cord; opening the cremaster and sweeping it away from the cord structures protects the nerve without needing to dissect it individually.
key_facts: The ilioinguinal nerve enters the inguinal canal through the internal ring region and runs on the cord within the cremasteric fibers to exit at the external ring.
Separating the cremaster from the cord isolates the nerve with the cremaster, away from the hernia sac and vas.
Injury causes numbness of the upper medial thigh, scrotum, or labia.

question: A 29-year-old man is evaluated for azoospermia. Testes are 20 mL bilaterally, the vasa are not palpable on either side, and serum FSH and testosterone are normal. The finding most likely to be present is:

options.B: AZFc microdeletion of the Y chromosome.

rationale: Nonpalpable vasa with normal testicular volume and normal gonadotropins define congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, which is a Wolffian duct anomaly linked to CFTR mutations. Because the seminal vesicles share this developmental origin they are absent or hypoplastic, and the resulting ejaculate is consistently small in volume, acidic, and fructose-negative. Spermatogenesis is intact, so FSH is normal and biopsy would show normal sperm production rather than maturation arrest. Renal agenesis occurs in only a minority, mostly CFTR-negative men, and Y chromosome microdeletions are not associated with this condition.
learning_point: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens is associated with CFTR mutations in most men and with absent or hypoplastic seminal vesicles, so the ejaculate is almost always low volume and acidic; spermatogenesis is normal, renal agenesis is uncommon, and there is no link to Y microdeletions.
key_facts: About 85% of men with CBAVD carry at least one CFTR mutation; partner CFTR testing is essential before IVF/ICSI.
Seminal vesicle hypoplasia produces low-volume (often under 1 mL), acidic, fructose-negative ejaculate.
Unilateral renal agenesis occurs in only 10-15%, mostly in men without CFTR mutations.
Testicular size and FSH are usually normal; sperm can be retrieved for ICSI.

question: A five-month-old boy who underwent valve ablation at two weeks of age for posterior urethral valves presents with fever. The nurse is unable to pass an 8 Fr feeding tube into the bladder; it advances easily through the anterior urethra but meets resistance proximally. The most likely cause is:

options.C: a false passage from the prior instrumentation.

rationale: Longstanding outlet obstruction in a valve bladder produces marked hypertrophy of the detrusor and bladder neck, and the poorly muscled prostatic urethra elongates and dilates behind it. The elevated bladder neck sits anteriorly, so a catheter advancing along the floor of the dilated posterior urethra is deflected; directing the tip anteriorly, as one does with the cystoscope in these boys, usually solves the problem. A stricture would typically impede passage in the anterior or bulbar urethra, residual valve leaflets rarely stop a small catheter, and a false passage or sphincter spasm are possible but far less common explanations in this setting.
learning_point: After posterior urethral valve ablation, difficulty passing a urethral catheter is most often due to the hypertrophied, high-riding bladder neck and elongated posterior urethra, which deflect the catheter; the scope or catheter must be angled anteriorly to enter the bladder.
key_facts: Chronic outlet obstruction from PUV causes detrusor and bladder neck hypertrophy with dilation and elongation of the prostatic urethra.
The elevated bladder neck creates an anterior angulation that catches catheters; a coude tip or anterior angulation helps.
Strictures, residual leaflets, and false passages can also impede catheterization but are much less common.

question: A 42-year-old man with a seizure disorder controlled by topiramate has formed two calcium phosphate stones. His 24-hour urine shows pH 6.9, citrate 110 mg, calcium 320 mg, and normal uric acid; serum bicarbonate is 19 mEq/L. His neurologist does not want to change his anticonvulsant. The best treatment to reduce further stone formation is:
rationale: Topiramate's carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes a chronic metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine, severe hypocitraturia, and hypercalciuria, creating ideal conditions for calcium phosphate stones. Because the drug cannot be stopped, potassium citrate is the treatment of choice: it corrects the systemic acidosis, restores urinary citrate (a potent inhibitor of calcium crystallization), and lowers urinary calcium. Acetazolamide is itself a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor and would compound the defect. Allopurinol treats hyperuricosuria, which is absent, and calcium carbonate has no therapeutic role. Amiloride is used only as an adjunct to thiazides to limit potassium loss.
learning_point: Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase and produces a distal RTA-like picture (systemic acidosis, high urine pH, profound hypocitraturia, hypercalciuria) that promotes calcium phosphate stones; management is to stop the drug if possible or give potassium citrate.
key_facts: Topiramate (and zonisamide, acetazolamide) cause metabolic acidosis, urine pH above 6.5, and very low urinary citrate.
Potassium citrate corrects acidosis and hypocitraturia and reduces calcium phosphate supersaturation.
Adding another carbonic anhydrase inhibitor would worsen the problem; allopurinol targets hyperuricosuria; calcium carbonate has no role.
Amiloride is an adjunct to thiazides for hypercalciuria, not a primary therapy here.

question: A 41-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents with a 60-hour erection. Corporal aspiration and repeated phenylephrine injections fail, and a distal T-shunt followed by a proximal corpora-spongiosum shunt leave the penis firm and indurated. The next step is:

options.B: selective embolization of the cavernous artery.
options.D: penile duplex Doppler ultrasound and corporal blood gas analysis.
options.E: immediate placement of a penile prosthesis.

rationale: After more than two days of ischemia and failure of both distal and proximal shunts, the firm penis may reflect ongoing ischemia or merely postoperative edema in corpora that have already been irreversibly damaged. Before committing to an irreversible operation, persistent ischemia should be documented with duplex Doppler (absent cavernous arterial flow) and corporal blood gas (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis). If ischemia is confirmed, early insertion of a penile prosthesis is recommended because later implantation into fibrotic corpora is technically difficult and complication-prone, but the diagnostic confirmation comes first. Embolization is reserved for high-flow priapism, terbutaline is ineffective at this duration, and another shunt is unlikely to succeed where two have failed.
learning_point: When prolonged ischemic priapism remains rigid and indurated after distal and proximal shunting, penile duplex Doppler ultrasound and corporal blood gas should be obtained to confirm persistent ischemia; if confirmed, early penile prosthesis placement is advocated because delayed implantation into fibrotic corpora is far more difficult.
key_facts: Ischemic priapism beyond 48-72 hours rarely responds to aspiration, sympathomimetics, or shunts and predictably causes erectile dysfunction.
Persistent induration after shunting may represent ongoing ischemia or simply edema; Doppler flow and blood gas distinguish them.
Early prosthesis in refractory ischemic priapism avoids the high complication rate of implantation into scarred corpora.
Arterial embolization is for high-flow (nonischemic) priapism.

question: A 57-year-old woman has a 3.5 cm right adrenal mass found on a CT performed for abdominal pain. The unenhanced attenuation of the mass is 24 Hounsfield units. Biochemical evaluation for pheochromocytoma, hypercortisolism, and hyperaldosteronism is negative. The study most likely to distinguish a benign from a malignant lesion is:

options.E: adrenal protocol CT with and without contrast and delayed washout.

rationale: An indeterminate mass with unenhanced density above 10 HU could be a lipid-poor adenoma or a malignancy, and the discriminating test is contrast-enhanced CT with delayed imaging to calculate washout: adenomas enhance and then wash out rapidly, whereas carcinomas and metastases retain contrast. Chemical-shift MRI is useful for lipid-rich lesions but is less helpful once the lesion has proven lipid-poor on CT. FDG-PET can suggest malignancy but is less specific and generally reserved for patients with a known extra-adrenal cancer, and MIBG is a functional study for pheochromocytoma, which has already been excluded. Needle biopsy is avoided in the adrenal because it is poor at distinguishing adenoma from carcinoma and risks tumor spillage.
learning_point: For a hormonally inactive adrenal incidentaloma, dedicated adrenal CT without and with contrast including delayed washout is the most reliable imaging method to separate benign adenoma from malignancy: unenhanced density under 10 HU indicates a lipid-rich adenoma, and lipid-poor adenomas show rapid contrast washout while malignant lesions retain contrast.
key_facts: Size is the single strongest clinical predictor: masses under 4 cm are malignant in about 2% of cases.
Unenhanced attenuation below 10 HU is diagnostic of a lipid-rich adenoma.
Absolute washout above 60% (relative above 40%) at 10-15 minutes indicates adenoma; malignant and pheochromocytoma lesions wash out slowly.
MRI chemical shift is an alternative; FDG-PET and MIBG are adjuncts for specific questions; biopsy is rarely appropriate.

question: A two-month-old girl has intermittent clear fluid draining from the umbilicus but is feeding well and voids normally. A sinogram performed by injecting contrast into the umbilical opening shows a tract extending to and filling the dome of the bladder. The next step is:

options.A: silver nitrate cauterization of the umbilical tract.
options.B: prompt excision of the urachal remnant with a bladder cuff.
options.D: observation, with excision if drainage persists at six months of age.

rationale: The sinogram establishes the diagnosis of a patent urachus. Because about half of these tracts close spontaneously during the first six months of life, an asymptomatic infant without infection or voiding difficulty is best observed, with surgical excision reserved for persistent drainage or complications. Silver nitrate is contraindicated when the tract communicates with the bladder because the caustic agent can injure the bladder mucosa. A VCUG is reserved for infants whose history suggests bladder outlet obstruction as the driver of urachal patency, and a CT adds nothing once the sinogram has demonstrated the communication.
learning_point: A radiographically confirmed patent urachus in an otherwise well infant can be observed, because about half close spontaneously within the first six months; excision is reserved for persistence or complications, and silver nitrate is contraindicated when a true tract to the bladder exists.
key_facts: Patent urachus presents with clear fluid draining from the umbilicus; a sinogram showing contrast entering the bladder confirms it.
Roughly 50% close by six months of age; surgery is deferred unless infection, persistent drainage, or outlet obstruction is present.
Silver nitrate is acceptable for small umbilical granulomas or cysts but risks bladder or bowel injury with a patent urachus or omphalomesenteric duct.
VCUG is indicated only if bladder outlet obstruction is suspected as the cause; CT is unnecessary once a sinogram shows the tract.

question: A 50-year-old man with recurrent calcium oxalate stones has a 24-hour urinary uric acid excretion of 950 mg with a normal serum uric acid level and no history of gout or hematologic disease. The most likely cause of his hyperuricosuria is:

options.E: high dietary intake of purine-rich animal protein.

rationale: Most hyperuricosuria in stone formers is dietary, driven by generous intake of meat, fish, and other purine-rich foods, and it commonly occurs with a normal serum urate. Gout and myeloproliferative states are genuine but much less common causes and are not suggested by his history. Vitamin C excess is metabolized to oxalate and is a cause of hyperoxaluria, not hyperuricosuria. A low urine volume concentrates urate but does not increase the 24-hour quantity excreted.
learning_point: Excessive dietary purine intake (animal protein) is by far the most common cause of hyperuricosuria; gout, metabolic syndrome, and myeloproliferative disorders are less frequent contributors, and vitamin C excess causes hyperoxaluria rather than hyperuricosuria.
key_facts: Hyperuricosuria is defined as more than about 800 mg/day in men and 750 mg/day in women.
Hyperuricosuria promotes calcium oxalate stones via heterogeneous nucleation and salting out, even with normal serum urate.
Dietary purine restriction is first-line; allopurinol is used for persistent hyperuricosuria with calcium oxalate stones.
Low urine volume raises concentration but not total daily uric acid excretion.

question: A 64-year-old man has a 2.5 cm squamous cell carcinoma of the pendulous urethra and a firm, mobile 2 cm left inguinal lymph node. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no other disease. In addition to partial penectomy, management should include:

options.E: observation of the inguinal regions with repeat examination in six weeks.

rationale: Distal urethral carcinoma is excised with partial penectomy and an adequate margin. The anterior urethra drains to the inguinal nodes, and a palpable node in urethral cancer almost always contains tumor, so there is no role for a trial of antibiotics or observation as is sometimes done in penile cancer. Therapeutic lymphadenectomy of the involved groin is indicated, but, in contrast to penile cancer, prophylactic dissection of the clinically negative contralateral groin has not been shown to improve outcomes. Squamous urethral tumors respond poorly to cisplatin-based regimens, and radiation is generally reserved for early lesions in patients who decline surgery.
learning_point: Squamous carcinoma of the distal (pendulous) male urethra is treated with partial penectomy, and a palpable inguinal node almost always represents metastasis, so ipsilateral inguinal lymphadenectomy is indicated; unlike penile cancer, prophylactic contralateral dissection or groin radiation has no proven benefit.
key_facts: Anterior urethral lymphatics drain to superficial and deep inguinal nodes (occasionally external iliac).
Palpable nodes occur in about 20% of urethral cancers and, unlike penile cancer, are rarely inflammatory.
Surgery is the mainstay; squamous urethral tumors respond poorly to MVAC-type chemotherapy, and radiation is reserved for early lesions in patients refusing surgery.

question: A seven-year-old girl develops painless gross hematuria an hour after falling off her bicycle at low speed onto grass. She is hemodynamically normal, her abdomen is soft and nontender, and there are no external marks. The next step is:

options.A: admission for serial examinations and hematocrits.
options.C: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
options.E: observation and repeat urinalysis in one week.

rationale: Gross hematuria after a minor mechanism in a child is a recognized warning sign of an underlying structural abnormality such as hydronephrosis from UPJ obstruction, a multicystic or horseshoe kidney, or a renal mass, all of which are far more prevalent in pediatric trauma patients than in adults. Ultrasound detects these conditions without radiation and determines whether further imaging is needed. CT is appropriate when the mechanism is significant or the ultrasound is abnormal. Admission with serial hematocrits is for documented renal injury, and cystoscopy is not part of the initial evaluation of hematuria in children.
learning_point: Gross hematuria after trivial trauma in a child raises concern for a pre-existing renal anomaly (hydronephrosis, UPJ obstruction, multicystic kidney, Wilms tumor, fusion anomaly), so renal and bladder ultrasound is the appropriate first imaging study; CT is reserved for significant mechanisms or abnormal ultrasound.
key_facts: Underlying GU abnormalities are at least three times more common in children than adults evaluated for trauma.
Hematuria disproportionate to the mechanism is the classic clue to an occult anomaly.
Ultrasound avoids radiation and screens for hydronephrosis, cystic disease, or mass; CT follows if abnormal or if the injury mechanism is severe.
Cystoscopy has no role in the initial workup of pediatric hematuria.

question: An eight-year-old girl with myelomeningocele underwent bladder neck reconstruction and creation of a continent catheterizable channel nine months ago. She has since had two febrile UTIs. Renal ultrasound is normal, but a VCUG now shows new grade III right vesicoureteral reflux that was absent preoperatively. The next step is:

options.B: endoscopic bulking agent injection for the reflux.
options.D: increase the dose of her antimuscarinic.

rationale: Increasing outlet resistance in a neurogenic bladder can unmask or induce poor compliance, and the appearance of new reflux with febrile infections suggests that storage pressures have risen or that the bladder is being overdistended between catheterizations. Urodynamics distinguish between these possibilities and direct therapy: if compliance has deteriorated, intensified antimuscarinics or augmentation is required, whereas if the bladder is unchanged, catheterization technique and frequency are addressed. Treating the reflux endoscopically without knowing the bladder pressures is likely to fail. Empirically adjusting medication or CIC frequency without data is guesswork, and a spinal MRI is a later consideration if urodynamic changes cannot be explained by the surgery.
learning_point: New vesicoureteral reflux and febrile UTIs after a bladder outlet procedure in a child with neurogenic bladder signal possible loss of compliance or inadequate emptying; urodynamics must be obtained first to assess storage pressures before any reflux correction or empiric change in therapy.
key_facts: About 15% of neurogenic bladders deteriorate (reduced compliance) after outlet resistance is increased surgically.
New reflux may stem from high storage pressures or from overdistension due to inadequate CIC frequency.
Correcting reflux in a hostile bladder fails; treatment is directed at pressures (CIC frequency, antimuscarinics, augmentation).
Spinal MRI is considered only if urodynamic change cannot be explained by the outlet procedure.

question: Ten weeks after a retropubic mid-urethral sling, a 68-year-old woman is dry but reports a slow stream and a sensation of incomplete emptying. Her PVR is 280 mL, and urinalysis shows many red cells and white cells; she is given antibiotics. In addition to teaching clean intermittent catheterization, the next step is:
rationale: Her new obstruction clearly dates to the sling, so release of the sling will almost certainly be needed, but hematuria and pyuria in this setting must prompt endoscopic evaluation to look for mesh that has perforated the urethra or bladder, as well as for over-suspension or other pathology. The findings determine whether a simple incision or a more extensive excision is required, so cystoscopy precedes any revision. Urethral dilation is ineffective and potentially harmful once the mesh has scarred in place, and an alpha-blocker will not relieve a fixed anatomic obstruction. Urodynamics are optional when the temporal relationship to surgery is this clear.
learning_point: A woman with voiding dysfunction and hematuria/pyuria weeks after a mid-urethral sling needs cystourethroscopy before sling incision to exclude mesh perforation of the urethra or bladder; office urethral dilation and alpha-blockers are not appropriate for a fixed iatrogenic obstruction.
key_facts: Obstruction after a synthetic sling that begins immediately postoperatively generally requires sling incision regardless of urodynamic findings.
Hematuria or persistent irritative symptoms after sling raise concern for intravesical or intraurethral mesh, which must be identified before any revision.
Urethral dilation is not recommended once the mesh has scarred in (weeks after surgery).
CIC manages retention in the interim.

question: A 52-year-old man with a 38 mL prostate and no median lobe has bothersome LUTS despite tamsulosin and finasteride. Pressure-flow urodynamics show a detrusor pressure at maximum flow of 95 cm H2O with a maximum flow rate of 8 mL/s. He states that preserving antegrade ejaculation is his highest priority. The best treatment is:

options.E: holmium laser enucleation of the prostate.

rationale: His urodynamics confirm high-pressure, low-flow bladder outlet obstruction, so any of the listed procedures would address the obstruction. The deciding factor is ejaculatory preservation: the prostatic urethral lift mechanically retracts the lateral lobes without cutting or ablating tissue near the bladder neck, and clinical trials have not reported retrograde ejaculation or new erectile dysfunction. TUIP, HoLEP, PVP, and TUMT each disrupt bladder neck or prostatic tissue and carry retrograde ejaculation rates ranging from roughly 9% to over 60%. His prostate size and absence of a median lobe make him a suitable candidate for the lift.
learning_point: Among surgical treatments for urodynamically proven bladder outlet obstruction, the prostatic urethral lift is the option that preserves antegrade ejaculation; TUIP, TUMT, laser vaporization, and enucleation all carry a meaningful risk of retrograde ejaculation.
key_facts: Prostatic urethral lift uses permanent implants to retract the lateral lobes without resecting tissue; it is suited to prostates under about 80 mL without an obstructing median lobe.
Reported rates of retrograde ejaculation range widely (roughly 9-67%) for TUIP, TUMT, PVP, and HoLEP.
Urethral lift has not been associated with new erectile dysfunction or retrograde ejaculation in trials.
Urodynamic obstruction is defined by high detrusor pressure with low flow (e.g., Pdet at Qmax around 100 cm H2O with Qmax under 10 mL/s).

question: A 60-year-old woman with a solitary right kidney underwent cystectomy with ileal conduit four years ago. Surveillance imaging and ureteroscopy now reveal multifocal high-grade papillary tumors of the renal pelvis invading the lamina propria and biopsy-proven CIS in the mid-ureter. She is otherwise healthy. The next step is:

options.B: nephroureterectomy, leaving the ileal conduit in place.
options.C: retrograde BCG instillation through the conduit.
options.D: percutaneous resection followed by antegrade BCG.
options.E: nephroureterectomy with excision of the ileal conduit.

rationale: Multifocal high-grade T1 disease with ureteral CIS in a solitary kidney leaves no reliable organ-sparing option: endoscopic or percutaneous resection cannot control multifocal high-grade tumors plus CIS, and BCG delivered through or into a system draining via an ileal conduit is absorbed across intestinal mucosa with a substantial risk of BCG sepsis. Partial nephrectomy likewise fails with multifocality. Cisplatin would be poorly tolerated in a solitary kidney and does not eradicate CIS. Nephroureterectomy with planned hemodialysis offers the best cancer control, and the conduit should be retained because it can serve as the drainage conduit for a future renal transplant.
learning_point: Multifocal high-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma with CIS in a solitary kidney after ileal conduit diversion is best treated by nephroureterectomy (accepting dialysis), because topical BCG via a conduit risks systemic absorption and sepsis and partial nephrectomy fails with multifocality; the conduit is left in place for possible future transplantation.
key_facts: BCG instilled into a system draining through an ileal conduit carries up to a 10% risk of BCG sepsis from absorption.
Multifocal high-grade disease and CIS are not controlled by partial nephrectomy or endoscopic ablation.
Systemic chemotherapy is poorly tolerated with a solitary kidney and does not eradicate CIS.
Leaving the conduit in situ preserves a drainage option if the patient later receives a renal transplant.

question: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with scrotal pain, crepitus, and necrotic skin extending to the perineum, and Fournier gangrene is diagnosed. Along with early diagnosis and aggressive surgical debridement, the intervention demonstrated to improve survival is:

options.B: immediate transfer to a tertiary center.

rationale: Fournier gangrene is a rapidly progressive polymicrobial necrotizing infection, and the only measures consistently shown to lower mortality are rapid diagnosis, wide surgical excision of all necrotic tissue, and broad-spectrum antibiotics covering aerobic gram-positive and gram-negative organisms as well as anaerobes. Hyperbaric oxygen has theoretical appeal and may reduce tissue loss but has not improved survival in controlled data. Fecal or urinary diversion facilitates wound care and reduces local complications without affecting mortality. Transferring a septic patient before stabilization and initial debridement can delay the life-saving steps.
learning_point: Survival in Fournier gangrene depends on early recognition, prompt aggressive surgical debridement, and broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics; hyperbaric oxygen, urinary or fecal diversion, glycemic control, and transfer have not been shown to reduce mortality.
key_facts: Fournier gangrene is a polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia with mortality historically 20-40%.
Antibiotics should cover gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms (e.g., carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin, with MRSA coverage as needed).
Diversion of urine or stool reduces wound complications but not mortality; hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive and unproven for survival.
Transfer should occur only after stabilization and initial debridement.

question: A 31-year-old woman with a complete T5 spinal cord injury managed with CIC has had several episodes of pounding headache, facial flushing, and profuse sweating, with a blood pressure of 190/110 mm Hg recorded during one episode. Non-contrast CT shows a 10 mm proximal left ureteral stone with a density of 350 Hounsfield units and moderate hydronephrosis. Urinalysis shows pH 5.0, moderate blood, and no bacteria or pyuria. The next step is:
rationale: Her episodic headaches, flushing, and severe hypertension are autonomic dysreflexia, which in a lesion above T6 can cause stroke, seizure, or death, and the obstructing stone is the noxious stimulus driving it. The immediate priority is to remove the trigger by decompressing the kidney, and a ureteral stent accomplishes that rapidly and reliably. The low attenuation and acidic urine suggest a uric acid stone that may dissolve with alkalinization, but this takes weeks and must not be attempted with the obstruction and dysreflexia unaddressed; medical expulsive therapy is similarly too slow. Definitive lithotripsy by ureteroscopy or PCNL can be planned once the patient is stented and stabilized if dissolution fails.
learning_point: In a patient with a high (above T6) spinal cord injury, an obstructing ureteral stone triggering autonomic dysreflexia is a life-threatening emergency; the first step is immediate decompression with a ureteral stent, after which alkalinization or definitive stone treatment can follow.
key_facts: Autonomic dysreflexia presents with pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the lesion, and severe hypertension in response to noxious stimuli below the injury.
Obstruction and distension of the urinary tract are among the most common triggers; relieving the stimulus is the treatment.
A radiolucent stone with urine pH around 5 suggests uric acid; dissolution with alkalinization is reasonable only after drainage is secured.
Definitive ureteroscopy or PCNL can be undertaken electively once the patient is stabilized.

question: A 59-year-old woman who had a hysterectomy years ago underwent a transobturator mid-urethral sling five months ago. She now reports intermittent blood-tinged vaginal discharge. Examination shows a small area of granulation tissue in the anterior vaginal sulcus without palpable or visible mesh, and urinalysis is normal. The next step is:

options.A: topical vaginal estrogen with reexamination in several weeks.
options.D: reassurance and follow-up in six months.

rationale: Persistent bloody discharge with granulation tissue along the sling track months after surgery almost certainly reflects a small mesh exposure that has not yet become visible, particularly since the uterus has been removed as an alternative source. A small exposure in an atrophic vagina may epithelialize with local estrogen, so a trial of vaginal estrogen with close reexamination is reasonable; if the exposure persists or enlarges, partial sling excision with reapproximation of the vaginal edges is the next step. Complete sling removal is reserved for extensive exposure, infection, or pain and is excessive here. Antibiotics do not treat an extrusion, cystoscopy is indicated when hematuria or new urinary symptoms suggest urethral or bladder mesh, and waiting six months allows a correctable problem to progress.
learning_point: Bloody vaginal discharge months after a synthetic mid-urethral sling in a woman without a uterus should be presumed to indicate a small mesh extrusion even if mesh is not visible; a trial of vaginal estrogen with reexamination is appropriate, with partial excision if it fails, whereas complete sling removal is unnecessary for a small exposure.
key_facts: Vaginal mesh exposure after mid-urethral sling occurs in roughly 1-2% and may present with discharge, spotting, or partner dyspareunia.
Small exposures may heal with topical estrogen; persistent exposure is treated with partial excision and closure of vaginal epithelium.
Prior hysterectomy removes uterine causes of bleeding; otherwise gynecologic evaluation is needed.
Cystoscopy is indicated if there is hematuria or new severe urinary symptoms suggesting urethral or bladder perforation.

question: A ten-month-old boy has a temperature of 38.8 degrees C without a clear source. A bagged urine specimen shows trace leukocyte esterase and negative nitrite, and the culture shows no growth at 48 hours. The next step is:

options.B: obtain a catheterized urine specimen for repeat culture.
options.E: no further urinary evaluation; look for another source of fever.

rationale: A bagged specimen is prone to false-positive results because it collects skin and perineal organisms, but a culture that grows nothing is highly reliable evidence against urinary infection, with a negative predictive value exceeding 99%. Trace leukocyte esterase is nonspecific and merely indicates contact with inflamed tissue, and a negative nitrite further lowers the likelihood of a typical Enterobacteriaceae UTI. Repeating the culture by catheter or suprapubic aspiration adds cost and discomfort without changing the conclusion, and empiric antibiotics would treat an infection that is not present. Imaging is indicated only after a confirmed febrile UTI, so the appropriate action is to pursue other causes of the fever.
learning_point: A bagged urine culture that shows no growth effectively excludes UTI in a febrile infant (negative predictive value above 99%) even if leukocyte esterase is positive, so no further urinary testing or antibiotics are needed and another source of fever should be sought; a positive bagged culture, by contrast, is unreliable and must be confirmed by catheter specimen.
key_facts: Bagged specimens are contaminated by perineal flora; up to 80% of positive bagged cultures are false positives compared with catheterized samples.
A negative bagged culture is reliable for excluding infection.
Leukocyte esterase alone is nonspecific; nitrite reflects Enterobacteriaceae and is negative in most non-Enterobacteriaceae infections.
Imaging is reserved for confirmed febrile UTI.

question: A 64-year-old man with bothersome LUTS performs a noninvasive uroflow: voided volume 220 mL, maximum flow rate 9 mL/s, with a prolonged, flattened curve, and a PVR of 90 mL. Which of the following is the correct interpretation?

options.A: the low flow could result from outlet obstruction, impaired detrusor contractility, or both.
options.B: the study is invalid because the voided volume is too low.
options.C: the flattened curve is diagnostic of a urethral stricture.
options.D: his maximum flow rate predicts a severe AUA Symptom Score.
options.E: he will have less symptom improvement after TURP than a man with a maximum flow above 15 mL/s.

rationale: Uroflowmetry measures the output of the voiding system as a whole, so a low peak flow can be produced by increased outlet resistance, by a weak detrusor, or by both together; separating these requires simultaneous measurement of detrusor pressure in a pressure-flow study. A voided volume of 220 mL exceeds the 125-150 mL threshold for a valid study. Peak flow correlates poorly with symptom scores, and medical therapy often improves symptoms without changing flow. Men with Qmax below 15 mL/s obtain greater, not smaller, symptomatic benefit from TURP. A flattened plateau raises suspicion for stricture but is not diagnostic; obstruction from any cause and poor contractility can produce similar tracings.
learning_point: A reduced peak flow on noninvasive uroflowmetry reflects the combined effect of outlet resistance and detrusor contractility and therefore cannot distinguish obstruction from an underactive detrusor; only pressure-flow studies can make that distinction. Flow rate correlates poorly with symptom scores, and men with Qmax under 15 mL/s actually improve more after TURP.
key_facts: Uroflow is interpretable once voided volume exceeds about 125-150 mL.
Average Qmax in men falls with age: about 21 mL/s under 45, 12 mL/s at 46-65, and 9 mL/s at 66-80.
Low Qmax may result from obstruction, impaired contractility, or both.
There is little correlation between Qmax and IPSS; Qmax under 15 mL/s predicts a better symptomatic response to TURP than Qmax over 15.

question: A four-year-old boy who recently emigrated from a rural region of Southeast Asia, where his diet consisted largely of rice and other cereals with little animal protein, presents with dysuria and a 2 cm bladder stone. Analysis shows ammonium acid urate. The urinary abnormality most responsible for this stone is:

options.A: high ammonium excretion with low urinary phosphate.

rationale: Endemic bladder calculi of childhood arise from a diet lacking animal protein, which leads to phosphate deficiency; the kidney responds with low urinary phosphate and high ammonium excretion, favoring precipitation of ammonium acid urate. This dietary mechanism distinguishes endemic stones from the calcium oxalate stones seen in well-nourished children. Hypercalciuria and hyperoxaluria drive calcium stones, high sodium intake increases calcium excretion but is not the mechanism here, and urinary phosphate is low rather than high in these children.
learning_point: Endemic pediatric bladder stones in developing regions are ammonium acid urate stones that form because a cereal-based, animal-protein-poor diet causes dietary phosphate deficiency, low urinary phosphate, and high urinary ammonium excretion.
key_facts: Seen in children from North Africa, the Middle East, and South and Southeast Asia, often in boys from rural areas.
Low protein and phosphate intake increases urinary ammonia; the stones are ammonium acid urate, sometimes mixed with calcium oxalate.
Hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, and high urinary sodium are not the drivers of these stones.
Dietary improvement with animal protein and phosphate prevents recurrence.

question: A 44-year-old woman with MEN 2A has a 4 cm left adrenal pheochromocytoma confirmed by elevated plasma metanephrines. After two weeks of phenoxybenzamine titrated to the maximum tolerated dose, she continues to have paroxysms of palpitations and diaphoresis with blood pressures as high as 200/110 mm Hg. The next step is:
rationale: Adequate preoperative control of catecholamine effects is essential to avoid intraoperative hypertensive crisis and postoperative collapse. When maximal alpha blockade with phenoxybenzamine fails to control paroxysms, metyrosine, which inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase and thereby lowers catecholamine production, is the recommended addition to achieve stability before anesthesia. Adding a beta-blocker in the face of inadequate alpha blockade removes beta-mediated vasodilation and can precipitate severe hypertension. Switching to doxazosin, a less potent competitive alpha-1 blocker, is unlikely to improve control. Operating on an unprepared patient is hazardous, and clonidine is not part of pheochromocytoma preparation.
learning_point: When a pheochromocytoma patient remains hypertensive with paroxysms despite maximal phenoxybenzamine, metyrosine (a tyrosine hydroxylase inhibitor that reduces catecholamine synthesis) should be added before surgery; adding a beta-blocker with incomplete alpha blockade can worsen hypertension, and operating without control is dangerous.
key_facts: Preoperative alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine or a selective alpha-1 blocker) for 10-14 days is mandatory before pheochromocytoma resection.
Metyrosine depletes catecholamine stores and is added when alpha blockade alone fails.
Beta-blockers are added only after adequate alpha blockade, mainly for tachyarrhythmia; unopposed beta blockade risks hypertensive crisis.
Clonidine and metyrapone have no role; MEN2 patients should also have calcitonin and calcium assessed.

question: A 72-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer begins abiraterone acetate with low-dose prednisone. Of the following adverse effects, the one most likely to require dose reduction or interruption of abiraterone is:
rationale: Abiraterone inhibits CYP17, suppressing androgen synthesis but also cortisol production, which drives a compensatory rise in ACTH and mineralocorticoid excess; the resulting hypertension, fluid retention, and hypokalemia are common but are usually controlled with prednisone, potassium, and antihypertensives without altering the abiraterone dose. Hepatotoxicity, in contrast, can be severe and potentially fatal, which is why liver function is monitored every two weeks for the first three months and significant transaminase elevation requires holding the drug and resuming at a reduced dose or stopping it. Abiraterone has no recognized renal toxicity.
learning_point: Abiraterone, a CYP17 inhibitor given with prednisone for castration-resistant prostate cancer, commonly causes mineralocorticoid excess effects (hypertension, hypokalemia, edema) that are usually managed without dose change; hepatotoxicity is the adverse effect that most often requires dose reduction or discontinuation and mandates frequent liver enzyme monitoring.
key_facts: CYP17 blockade raises ACTH and mineralocorticoid precursors, causing hypertension, fluid retention, and hypokalemia; prednisone blunts this.
Liver enzymes should be checked every two weeks for the first three months, then monthly.
Marked transaminase elevation requires holding the drug and restarting at a lower dose or discontinuing.
Abiraterone is not nephrotoxic.

question: A 30-year-old man with clinical stage I nonseminomatous germ cell tumor elects a laparoscopic retroperitoneal lymph node dissection. The most common complication reported with the laparoscopic approach is:
rationale: Laparoscopic RPLND requires meticulous dissection along the aorta, vena cava, and lumbar vessels, and injury to these structures with intraoperative bleeding is the complication most often reported in published series; it is more frequent than with open RPLND and occurs predominantly early in a surgeon's experience. Oncologic adequacy in experienced hands is equivalent to open surgery. Chylous ascites, retrograde ejaculation, bowel injury, and ileus all occur but at rates no higher than those seen with the open approach, so none is the leading complication.
learning_point: The most frequently reported complication of laparoscopic RPLND is intraoperative hemorrhage, which exceeds rates seen with open RPLND and is strongly linked to surgeon experience; rates of retrograde ejaculation, chylous ascites, bowel injury, and ileus are similar to the open approach.
key_facts: Vascular injury during dissection around the great vessels and lumbar veins is the leading complication of laparoscopic RPLND.
Bleeding complications decline with experience and are most common on the learning curve.
In experienced hands node yield and recurrence rates match open surgery.
Other complications (chylous ascites, ejaculatory dysfunction, ileus) occur at rates comparable to open RPLND.

question: A four-month-old boy has a temperature of 39.2 degrees C, irritability, and vomiting. A catheterized urine specimen shows 2+ leukocyte esterase, positive nitrite, and bacteria on microscopy; culture is sent. The next step is:

options.A: obtain a renal and bladder ultrasound before starting antibiotics.
options.C: withhold antibiotics until the culture result is available.

rationale: A febrile, vomiting infant with pyuria, nitrite positivity, and bacteriuria on a catheterized specimen almost certainly has pyelonephritis, and treatment must begin promptly to prevent renal scarring and sepsis rather than waiting 24-48 hours for culture confirmation. Because he is vomiting and systemically ill, parenteral therapy with an agent such as ceftriaxone or cefotaxime is appropriate. Nitrofurantoin concentrates only in the bladder and does not achieve adequate serum or renal parenchymal levels, making it unsuitable for febrile UTI at any age. Ultrasound is part of the evaluation after a first febrile UTI but should not delay antibiotics, and a DMSA scan is not indicated before treatment.
learning_point: An ill-appearing febrile infant whose catheterized urinalysis shows pyuria, positive nitrite, and bacteriuria has a presumptive UTI and should receive empiric parenteral broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., a third-generation cephalosporin) without waiting for culture; nitrofurantoin is inappropriate for febrile UTI, and imaging follows treatment.
key_facts: Positive leukocyte esterase plus nitrite predicts a positive culture in about 75% of cases; bacteria on a catheterized specimen is about 70% sensitive.
Nitrofurantoin achieves poor serum and renal tissue levels and should not be used for pyelonephritis.
Renal and bladder ultrasound is obtained after a first febrile UTI, urgently only if the child fails to improve within 48-72 hours.
DMSA is not performed before initiating treatment.

question: A six-year-old boy with spina bifida on clean intermittent catheterization leaks between catheterizations. Urodynamics show a detrusor leak point pressure of 45 cm H2O and a Valsalva leak point pressure of 65 cm H2O. He is started on oxybutynin. Compared with the baseline study, repeat urodynamics on treatment would be expected to show:

options.A: unchanged detrusor LPP; unchanged Valsalva LPP.
options.B: decreased detrusor LPP; decreased Valsalva LPP.
options.C: increased detrusor LPP; unchanged Valsalva LPP.
options.D: decreased detrusor LPP; unchanged Valsalva LPP.
options.E: unchanged detrusor LPP; increased Valsalva LPP.

rationale: Both leak point pressures are measures of how much pressure the outlet can resist before urine escapes, and that resistance is provided by the striated external sphincter and bladder neck, which have no muscarinic dependence. Oxybutynin works on detrusor smooth muscle: it blunts overactive contractions and increases compliance, so the bladder holds a larger volume before reaching any given pressure, enlarging functional capacity and improving continence between catheterizations. The pressure at which leakage ultimately occurs, however, is set by the sphincter and does not change. Any option predicting a rise or fall in either LPP misattributes a sphincteric property to a detrusor drug.
learning_point: Detrusor and Valsalva leak point pressures are determined by outlet (external sphincter) resistance, which is striated muscle unaffected by antimuscarinics; starting oxybutynin therefore improves compliance and capacity but leaves both leak point pressures unchanged.
key_facts: Detrusor LPP is the detrusor pressure at which leakage occurs in the absence of a contraction or strain; it reflects outlet resistance and is a marker of upper tract risk when above 40 cm H2O.
Valsalva LPP measures the abdominal pressure needed to overcome the sphincter and reflects sphincteric competence.
Antimuscarinics act on detrusor smooth muscle, increasing the volume stored at a given pressure (compliance and capacity).
Neither LPP changes because sphincter function is unaltered; outlet procedures are what raise LPP.

question: A 57-year-old woman who smokes one pack per day is scheduled for elective radical cystectomy with ileal conduit. She asks how long before surgery she must stop smoking so that her risk of postoperative pulmonary complications approaches that of a nonsmoker. The minimum duration of abstinence is:
rationale: Epidemiologic data show that smokers carry substantially higher pulmonary morbidity after major surgery, and that the excess risk is not eliminated until smoking has been stopped for about two months. Two or four weeks of abstinence improves oxygen carrying capacity and some ciliary function but has not been shown to normalize pulmonary complication rates. Six or twelve months are not required to reach the nonsmoker baseline for pulmonary outcomes, so they are not the minimum. The correct counseling is a minimum of roughly eight weeks.
learning_point: Smokers have markedly higher postoperative pulmonary morbidity and mortality; abstinence for at least two months (about eight weeks) before surgery is needed to bring pulmonary complication rates down to the level of nonsmokers.
key_facts: Postoperative morbidity is several-fold and mortality up to tenfold higher in active smokers undergoing major urologic surgery.
Pulmonary complication risk falls to nonsmoker levels only after roughly eight weeks of cessation.
Shorter periods of cessation (days to a few weeks) reduce carboxyhemoglobin but do not normalize pulmonary risk.

question: A 72-year-old woman with multifocal CIS of the bladder completes a six-week induction course of intravesical BCG. At her three-month evaluation, cystoscopy shows no lesions and voided cytology is negative. The next step is:

options.A: a single BCG instillation each month for twelve months.
options.B: a second six-week induction course of BCG.
options.C: three weekly BCG instillations now, repeated at six months and then every six months.
options.D: random bladder biopsies to document complete response.
options.E: surveillance cystoscopy and cytology every three months with no further BCG.

rationale: Carcinoma in situ is high-risk disease, and the proven way to sustain the complete response achieved with induction BCG is maintenance therapy on the SWOG schedule, which begins with three weekly instillations at the three-month mark. Random biopsies add nothing when cystoscopy and cytology are both negative. Surveillance without maintenance leaves the patient with a substantially higher recurrence risk and is reserved for those who cannot tolerate BCG. A second full induction course is used for incomplete responders, not for complete responders, and monthly single-dose maintenance lacks comparable evidence.
learning_point: A patient with CIS who has a complete response to induction BCG should receive maintenance BCG using the SWOG schedule: three weekly instillations at 3 and 6 months and then every 6 months for 3 years. Biopsy is unnecessary when cystoscopy and cytology are negative.
key_facts: SWOG 8507 maintenance schedule: 6-week induction, then 3 weekly doses at months 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36.
Maintenance roughly doubled median recurrence-free survival compared with induction alone.
Negative cystoscopy plus negative cytology at the 3-month check is sufficient to declare complete response; routine biopsy is not required.
Monthly single-dose BCG has not been validated against the SWOG schedule.

question: A 61-year-old woman sustains a posterior bladder wall laceration during abdominoperineal resection for rectal adenocarcinoma. The injury is closed in two layers and a urethral catheter is left in place. Cystograms at 3, 6, and 10 weeks each show persistent extraperitoneal extravasation from the repair site; the catheter drains well and CT shows no pelvic fluid collection or ureteral injury. The next step is:

options.A: continue catheter drainage and repeat the cystogram in four weeks.
options.E: cystoscopy with biopsy of the leaking area.

rationale: A bladder repair that has not healed after ten weeks of adequate catheter drainage is unlikely to heal with more time, and in a patient operated on for pelvic cancer the most important possibility to exclude is persistent or recurrent malignancy at the site. Cystoscopy with biopsy answers that question and determines whether definitive reconstruction is appropriate. Repeating the cystogram only delays the diagnosis. Fulguration or formal re-repair with omentum would be premature without first excluding tumor, and an added suprapubic tube does not drain better than a functioning urethral catheter.
learning_point: A repaired bladder injury that still leaks on cystogram many weeks later in a patient operated on for pelvic malignancy should be evaluated by cystoscopy and biopsy to exclude persistent or recurrent cancer before any definitive repair.
key_facts: Most repaired bladder injuries seal with 2-3 weeks of catheter drainage; failure after 8-9 weeks implies a cause such as foreign body, poor drainage, or tumor.
In a cancer patient, malignancy at the leak site must be excluded histologically before surgical repair.
Fulguration or fibrin glue is only an option for very small (under 5 mm) tracts, and only after tumor is excluded.
Added suprapubic drainage does not improve healing if the urethral catheter already drains well.

question: A 44-year-old woman has a 14 mm lower-pole renal calculus measured on noncontrast CT. If the same stone is measured on renal ultrasound and on a plain abdominal radiograph (KUB), the expected size estimates relative to CT are, respectively:
rationale: For a stone larger than 10 mm, ultrasound measurement agrees with CT in most cases, so it is considered reasonably accurate in this size range, whereas its tendency to overestimate applies mainly to stones smaller than 10 mm. KUB, by contrast, underestimates the size of well over 90% of stones larger than 10 mm because a single projection cannot capture the true three-dimensional extent of the calculus. Options suggesting that KUB is accurate or overestimates are therefore incorrect, as is the suggestion that ultrasound systematically overestimates a 14 mm stone.
learning_point: Ultrasound correlates with CT stone size about two-thirds of the time and is reasonably accurate for stones larger than 10 mm (it tends to overestimate small stones), whereas KUB underestimates the size of more than 90% of stones larger than 10 mm.
key_facts: Ultrasound overestimates about one-third of stones under 10 mm and underestimates about one-third of stones over 10 mm; overall it matches CT roughly two-thirds of the time.
KUB cannot measure in three dimensions and underestimates the great majority of stones over 10 mm.
Ultrasound is attractive for follow-up because it avoids ionizing radiation, but its measurement limits should be understood.

question: A 56-year-old woman performs clean intermittent catheterization four times daily for urinary retention that began after decompressive surgery for a lumbar disc herniation nine months ago. She has no leakage between catheterizations. Urodynamics show frequent sharp deflections in the subtracted detrusor pressure that mirror spikes in the abdominal pressure tracing, while the vesical pressure remains flat to a filled volume of 950 ml with no leakage and no voluntary contraction. The next step is:
rationale: The apparent detrusor activity on this study is artifact: every deflection in Pdet is matched by a spike in Pabd while Pves stays flat, which means the bladder itself is acontractile with normal compliance to a large volume. A continent patient with such a bladder is already ideally managed on CIC and needs no change. Antimuscarinics and onabotulinumtoxinA lower detrusor pressure, which is not elevated. An alpha-blocker cannot restore emptying in an areflexic bladder, and neuromodulation has not been shown to restore voiding in retention after lumbar surgery.
learning_point: In a patient with an areflexic, large-capacity bladder after lumbar spine surgery who is continent on CIC, a urodynamic study whose Pdet activity is artifact from the rectal catheter (flat Pves) indicates no need for pressure-lowering therapy; the correct management is to continue CIC.
key_facts: Always read all tracings: artifactual deflections in Pdet with a flat Pves and active Pabd reflect rectal catheter activity, not detrusor contraction.
An acontractile bladder with normal compliance and no leakage is safely managed by CIC alone.
Antimuscarinics and onabotulinumtoxinA treat detrusor overactivity or poor compliance, which are absent here.
Alpha-blockers do not help an areflexic bladder empty; nerve rerouting procedures lack evidence for this population.

question: A 27-year-old man has a complete spinal cord injury at the T12-L1 level sustained in a motorcycle crash. Six months later, with no treatment, his expected sexual function is:

options.A: no erections, emission absent, ejaculation absent.
options.B: psychogenic erections preserved, emission and ejaculation absent.
options.C: reflex erections preserved, emission normal, ejaculation retrograde.
options.D: no erections, emission normal, ejaculation antegrade.
options.E: reflex erections preserved, emission absent, ejaculation absent.

rationale: A complete thoracolumbar lesion destroys the sympathetic outflow responsible for seminal emission and bladder neck closure, so neither emission nor the subsequent somatic ejaculatory reflex can occur. The sacral cord below the lesion is intact, so penile stimulation still produces reflex erections, although psychogenic erections, which depend on descending pathways from the cortex, are lost. Options describing preserved emission or retrograde ejaculation misplace the lesion in the sacral or infrasacral region, and options with no erections at all would require sacral cord or cauda equina damage.
learning_point: A complete spinal cord lesion at T12-L2 interrupts the sympathetic outflow needed for emission and bladder neck closure, so emission and ejaculation are lost, while reflex erections persist because the S2-S4 parasympathetic and sensory arcs remain intact.
key_facts: Sympathetic T10-L2 fibers drive emission and bladder neck closure; parasympathetic S2-S4 fibers drive erection; somatic S2-S4 (Onuf nucleus) drives rhythmic ejaculation.
Reflex erections survive when the sacral cord is intact and isolated from the brain; psychogenic erections require intact spinal pathways from the cortex.
Without emission there is no bulbar urethral distension and therefore no ejaculatory reflex.

question: A 71-year-old man receiving maintenance intravesical BCG for high-grade Ta bladder cancer has a rise in PSA from 1.9 to 4.4 ng/ml and a new firm area in the right prostate lobe on rectal examination. He has no fever, dysuria, or systemic symptoms. Transrectal biopsy shows caseating granulomas without carcinoma. The next step is:

options.B: stop BCG and begin isoniazid plus rifampin for six months.
options.C: no specific treatment; continue scheduled BCG maintenance.
options.E: repeat prostate biopsy in three months.

rationale: The biopsy establishes granulomatous prostatitis caused by BCG, a frequent and self-limited local reaction. Because the patient is asymptomatic, there is nothing to treat, and the finding does not require interruption of his maintenance schedule. Antituberculous regimens are indicated for systemic BCG toxicity such as persistent high fever, sepsis, or hepatitis, none of which is present. Repeat biopsy is unnecessary now that the nodule and PSA rise are explained, and resection of the prostate has no role.
learning_point: Granulomatous prostatitis is a common, benign consequence of intravesical BCG; in an asymptomatic patient it needs no antituberculous therapy, and planned BCG may continue.
key_facts: BCG granulomatous prostatitis can cause a firm nodule and a PSA rise, mimicking cancer.
Asymptomatic granulomatous prostatitis requires no treatment and is not a contraindication to continuing BCG.
Isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol are reserved for systemic BCG infection (persistent high fever, sepsis, hepatitis, pneumonitis).

question: A seven-year-old boy whose posterior urethral valves were ablated in infancy has progressive bilateral hydroureteronephrosis on surveillance ultrasound. Serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dl and his daily urine output is about 3 liters. He voids 350-450 ml every three hours by schedule and is dry day and night. Videourodynamics show no urethral obstruction or reflux; detrusor pressure is 35 cm H2O at 450 ml and rises to 55 cm H2O at 650 ml, and he empties by abdominal straining to a residual of 180 ml. The next step is:

options.B: limit fluid intake to 1.5 liters per day.
options.E: clean intermittent catheterization every three hours.

rationale: This boy has valve bladder syndrome: high obligatory urine output from a concentrating defect, a bladder whose compliance falls once volume exceeds about 500 ml, and a significant residual that keeps him in the high-pressure range. Catheterizing every three hours empties the bladder before it reaches the poorly compliant volume and removes the residual, protecting the upper tracts; overnight catheter drainage can be added if hydronephrosis persists. Fluid restriction cannot overcome nephrogenic polyuria and risks dehydration and renal injury. Anticholinergic or botulinum toxin therapy without catheterization would increase an already large residual, and augmentation is premature before a full trial of medical management.
learning_point: Valve bladder syndrome combines obligatory polyuria from nephrogenic concentrating defect with a poorly compliant bladder at large volumes and incomplete emptying; instituting CIC on a schedule that keeps the bladder in a low-pressure volume range (with overnight catheter drainage if needed) is the first step before augmentation.
key_facts: Post-PUV kidneys often cannot concentrate urine, producing high hourly urine output that fluid restriction cannot and should not correct.
Compliance is typically acceptable at moderate volumes but deteriorates at high volumes; keeping the bladder below that threshold protects the upper tracts.
Anticholinergics or onabotulinumtoxinA alone worsen emptying when the residual is already large.
Augmentation is reserved for failure of maximal medical and catheterization management.

question: A 29-year-old man undergoing evaluation for primary infertility has bilateral diagnostic testicular biopsies. The right testis shows intratubular germ cell neoplasia; the left shows hypospermatogenesis without neoplasia. Scrotal ultrasound shows no testicular mass and a small right varicocele. He and his partner strongly desire biological children. The next step is:

options.A: 20 Gy external beam radiation to the right testis.
options.C: two cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin.
options.D: surveillance with scrotal ultrasound every six months.

rationale: ITGCN is a premalignant lesion with a high rate of progression to invasive germ cell tumor, so definitive treatment is warranted. Because this man has a neoplasia-free contralateral testis and wants children, radical orchiectomy of the affected testis removes the risk while sparing the other testis entirely. Low-dose radiation controls ITGCN but inevitably scatters to the contralateral testis and would compromise the spermatogenesis he is relying on. Systemic chemotherapy has no established role in isolated ITGCN, and varicocelectomy does nothing about the neoplasia. Surveillance is reasonable only in selected men who are actively pursuing conception with usable sperm and accept deferred treatment.
learning_point: Germ cell neoplasia in situ (ITGCN) discovered on infertility biopsy carries about a 50% risk of invasive tumor; in a man with a normal contralateral testis who wants future paternity, radical orchiectomy is preferred because low-dose radiation would scatter to the other testis and impair spermatogenesis.
key_facts: ITGCN progresses to invasive germ cell tumor in roughly half of patients within 5 years.
Treatment choices: orchiectomy, low-dose (about 20 Gy) radiation, or close surveillance; choice depends on the contralateral testis and fertility goals.
Radiation preserves Leydig cell function but destroys germ cells and scatters to the contralateral testis, so it is favored only when paternity is not desired or the contralateral testis is absent.
Carboplatin is for stage I seminoma, not ITGCN; varicocele repair does not address the neoplasia.

question: A 35-year-old man reports a snapping sound and rapid loss of erection during intercourse six hours earlier. On examination the penis is mildly swollen with slight tenderness along the right shaft, no ecchymosis, no palpable tunical defect, and no blood at the meatus. Urinalysis is normal. The next step is:
rationale: The history is typical of penile fracture, but the examination lacks the hematoma, ecchymosis, and palpable defect that normally make the diagnosis clinical, raising the possibility of a false fracture from a superficial vein rupture. MRI directly images the tunica albuginea and is the most accurate way to determine whether a tear is present, sparing the patient an unnecessary operation if it is not. Doppler ultrasound and cavernosography both miss a substantial proportion of tunical tears. Immediate exploration is appropriate when the exam is classic, and a urethrogram is indicated once fracture is confirmed or if hematuria or blood at the meatus suggests urethral injury, neither of which is present.
learning_point: When the history suggests penile fracture but the examination is not classic (little swelling, no ecchymosis or palpable defect), penile MRI is the most accurate study to confirm or exclude a tunical tear and avoid unnecessary exploration; Doppler ultrasound and cavernosography have high false-negative rates.
key_facts: Classic penile fracture (pop, detumescence, eggplant deformity) is a clinical diagnosis that goes directly to surgical repair.
False fracture from a ruptured superficial vein can mimic the history; MRI distinguishes an intact from a torn tunica albuginea.
Urethral injury accompanies 10-20% of fractures; urinalysis is mandatory and urethral imaging is needed before exploration if a fracture is confirmed.

question: A 62-year-old man with urgency, frequency, and a weak stream undergoes pressure-flow urodynamics. During filling there are several involuntary detrusor contractions, each accompanied by a short burst of external sphincter EMG activity that subsides when the contraction ends. When he is given permission to void, the EMG becomes silent, detrusor pressure at maximum flow is 78 cm H2O, maximum flow rate is 8 ml/s, and the postvoid residual is 20 ml. The most likely cause of his symptoms is:

options.C: neurogenic detrusor overactivity from multiple sclerosis.
options.D: prostatic enlargement with secondary detrusor overactivity.

rationale: The EMG bursts during filling coincide with involuntary contractions and represent the normal guarding response, and the sphincter relaxes appropriately once he is allowed to void. A voiding pressure of 78 cm H2O with a flow of only 8 ml/s and a urethral resistance factor near 0.5 meets urodynamic criteria for outlet obstruction, and in a 62-year-old man with complete emptying this points to benign prostatic enlargement with secondary detrusor overactivity. Dyssynergia, dysfunctional voiding, and Hinman-type patterns require sphincter activity during the void, which is absent here. Detrusor underactivity would show low voiding pressures, and multiple sclerosis would be expected to produce persistent EMG activity during voiding rather than normal relaxation.
learning_point: Detrusor overactivity accompanied by brief sphincter EMG bursts during filling (a normal guarding reflex) that silence when voiding is permitted, together with high detrusor pressure at low flow and no residual, indicates bladder outlet obstruction from prostatic enlargement with secondary detrusor overactivity, not a neurogenic or dysfunctional voiding pattern.
key_facts: A guarding reflex is normal: sphincter EMG increases during an involuntary detrusor contraction and quiets once voiding is permitted.
DESD, dysfunctional voiding, and Hinman syndrome all show sphincter activity during the voiding phase itself.
