She also has a 3 cm firm, painful eschar on the right labium majus. She is afebrile with a normal white blood cell count. The next step is:

options.B: skin biopsy of the labial lesion.
options.C: supportive care without debridement or biopsy.

rationale: The combination of dialysis dependence, obesity, diabetes, and painful retiform purpura progressing to necrotic eschars is characteristic of calciphylaxis, a diagnosis that is made clinically. Debridement is approached with great caution because the ischemic tissue heals poorly and debridement does not relieve pain; biopsy is similarly discouraged because it can trigger further necrosis. Corticosteroids have not shown benefit, and because infection is not the underlying process, antifungal or antibacterial therapy is not indicated in the absence of secondary infection.
learning_point: Painful necrotic skin eschars on the trunk, thighs, or genitalia in a dialysis patient with obesity and diabetes represent calciphylaxis; management is supportive, avoiding debridement and biopsy, since neither steroids nor antimicrobials help.
key_facts: Calciphylaxis is an obliterative small-vessel vasculopathy with medial calcification causing ischemic skin necrosis.
Debrided wounds heal poorly and pain is not improved; biopsy can precipitate new ulceration.
Infection is not part of the pathophysiology, so antibiotics and antifungals are not indicated.

question: A 26-year-old man receiving BEP for a good-prognosis non-seminomatous germ cell tumor develops a dry cough after his second cycle. Pulmonary function testing shows a 30% decline in DLCO from baseline, and chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities. Before the third cycle, the next step is:

options.A: reduce the bleomycin dose by half.
options.B: delay the cycle until repeat pulmonary function tests normalize.
options.C: start prophylactic prednisone and continue BEP unchanged.
options.D: switch to vinblastine, ifosfamide, and cisplatin (VIP).
options.E: omit bleomycin and continue etoposide and cisplatin.

rationale: A falling DLCO with new ground-glass changes during BEP is bleomycin pneumonitis, and the standard response is to discontinue bleomycin for the remaining cycles while continuing cisplatin and etoposide on schedule. Halving the dose still exposes an already injured lung and has no demonstrated equivalent efficacy. Prophylactic steroids do not prevent further bleomycin injury. Switching to an ifosfamide-based regimen is unnecessary when simply removing bleomycin suffices, and delaying treatment pending repeat PFTs compromises chemotherapy dose intensity without changing the decision.
learning_point: Evidence of bleomycin pneumonitis (declining DLCO, ground-glass opacities) during BEP mandates dropping bleomycin from subsequent cycles; dose reduction, prophylactic steroids, and changing to a different regimen are not indicated.
key_facts: Bleomycin pulmonary toxicity occurs in roughly 10% and is dose-dependent; fatal toxicity is < 1% after three cycles and 1-2% after four.
Cisplatin's main toxicity is neuropathy; etoposide's is myelosuppression.
G-CSF and repeat PFTs do not alter management once pneumonitis is recognized.

question: A 15-year-old girl with known cystinuria has a right staghorn calculus and undergoes percutaneous nephrolithotomy. In addition to counseling on high fluid intake, the most appropriate initial medical therapy to prevent recurrence is:

options.A: hemiacidrin irrigation of the collecting system.
options.D: restriction of fluid intake to 1.5 L daily.

rationale: Cystine is far more soluble in alkaline urine, so potassium citrate to raise urinary pH, combined with a fluid intake of 3-4 L per day including nighttime hydration, forms the foundation of cystine stone prevention. Chelating agents such as tiopronin (preferred over penicillamine for fewer side effects) are reserved for patients who continue to form stones despite hydration and alkalinization. Acetohydroxamic acid is a urease inhibitor used for infection stones, and hemiacidrin irrigation dissolves struvite or apatite, not cystine. Limiting fluids would be counterproductive.
learning_point: After surgical clearance of a cystine staghorn calculus, first-line medical prevention is high fluid intake (3-4 L/day) and urinary alkalinization with potassium citrate; chelating agents (tiopronin, penicillamine) are added only if these measures fail.
key_facts: Cystinuria is autosomal recessive; average age at first stone is about 12 years.
Cystine solubility rises sharply at urine pH above 7.0-7.5.
Acetohydroxamic acid and hemiacidrin irrigation are for struvite/apatite stones, not cystine.

question: A 19-year-old woman with myelomeningocele and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt underwent ileocystoplasty six months ago and catheterizes every four hours. She presents with 12 hours of vomiting, generalized abdominal pain, and a temperature of 38.3 C; her catheterized volumes have fallen to about 100 mL. The abdomen is distended and diffusely tender, and a catheterized urinalysis shows 5-10 WBC/hpf. The next step is:
rationale: Peritoneal signs, fever, vomiting, and a drop in catheterized volume after bladder augmentation are the classic picture of augment perforation, which is life-threatening and must be excluded first. A CT cystogram fills the bladder under pressure and reliably shows intraperitoneal contrast; it also delineates fluid around a shunt catheter or an alternative source if the bladder is intact. Ultrasound may show free fluid but cannot tell a ruptured augment from an infected shunt pseudocyst. Cystoscopy adds little diagnostic accuracy and can worsen sepsis by irrigating through a perforation. Antibiotics alone, or a shunt tap first, would delay recognition of a surgical emergency.
learning_point: Acute abdominal pain, fever, and vomiting after enterocystoplasty in a patient with myelomeningocele must be assumed to be spontaneous augment perforation until proven otherwise; a CT cystogram is the diagnostic test of choice. Ultrasound cannot distinguish rupture from a VP shunt-related collection, and cystoscopy risks sepsis.
key_facts: Augmented bladder perforation presents with peritonitis-type pain, fever, nausea/vomiting, and often reduced catheterized volumes; sensory deficits can blunt the exam.
CT cystogram (retrograde filling under pressure) is the most accurate study; plain cystography may miss small leaks.
Differential includes infected VP shunt with peritoneal pseudocyst, appendicitis, and cystitis; the CT also helps evaluate these.
Treatment of confirmed rupture is usually open repair, though selected stable patients may be managed with catheter drainage and antibiotics.

question: A 16-year-old boy has passed three radiolucent stones over two years; stone analysis shows 100% uric acid. He has increased his fluid intake, reduced red meat, and takes allopurinol 100 mg daily. A 24-hour urine shows a pH of 5.3 with normal calcium and oxalate. The next step is:

options.B: sodium restriction to less than 2 g/day.

rationale: The urine remains acidic despite dietary measures and xanthine oxidase inhibition, and low urine pH is the dominant risk factor for uric acid crystallization. Alkalinizing the urine with potassium citrate to a pH above 6 dissolves and prevents uric acid stones and is the first-line pharmacologic step. Raising allopurinol is a second-line move once alkalinization has been tried. Tiopronin is a cystine-binding drug with no role here, thiazides treat hypercalciuria, and sodium restriction primarily lowers urinary calcium rather than altering pH.
learning_point: For recurrent uric acid stones, first-line therapy is fluid intake, reduced animal protein, and urinary alkalinization with potassium citrate to a pH above 6; allopurinol dose escalation is reserved for failure of alkalinization or documented hyperuricosuria.
key_facts: Uric acid solubility rises sharply as urine pH exceeds 6.0; persistently acidic urine is the main driver of uric acid stones.
Potassium citrate is preferred over sodium alkali because sodium load increases calciuria.
Tiopronin (alpha-mercaptopropionylglycine) is for cystinuria; sodium restriction targets hypercalciuria.
Allopurinol (100-300 mg/day in adults) is added when alkalinization fails or urinary uric acid remains elevated.

question: During cavernosometry in an animal model, the end of a pharmacologically induced erection is recorded. The earliest change in intracavernosal pressure that marks the onset of detumescence is:

options.A: oscillating pressure synchronous with the pulse.
options.C: no change until arterial inflow ceases.
options.D: a gradual fall as venous channels reopen.
options.E: a brief rise above the erect plateau.

rationale: Detumescence is triggered by contraction of the trabecular and arteriolar smooth muscle; because venous outflow is still compressed at that instant, the contraction transiently increases intracavernosal pressure above the plateau. Only afterward do the subtunical venules reopen, producing a slow pressure decline, and finally a rapid drop to flaccidity. Options describing a gradual or abrupt fall are later phases, not the initiating event. Pulse-synchronous oscillation and waiting for arterial inflow to stop do not describe the physiology.
learning_point: Detumescence begins with contraction of cavernosal smooth muscle, which produces a brief transient rise in intracavernosal pressure before venous channels reopen; it is followed by a slow and then a rapid pressure decline to flaccidity.
key_facts: Erection is initiated by smooth muscle relaxation (NO/cGMP); detumescence is initiated by smooth muscle contraction (sympathetic, endothelin, RhoA/Rho-kinase).
Three detumescence phases: transient pressure rise, slow pressure decrease as venous outflow resumes, then rapid pressure fall.
Endothelial relaxation is part of tumescence, not detumescence.

question: A nine-year-old girl underwent left dismembered pyeloplasty at age one. An ultrasound eight months ago showed only trace left pelviectasis. She now has acute left flank pain with emesis, and CT shows an 8 mm stone lodged at the left UPJ with new moderate hydronephrosis. The best treatment is:

options.A: tamsulosin and repeat imaging in two weeks.

rationale: The hydronephrosis is new and attributable to the obstructing stone, and recent imaging showed a well-draining repair, so there is no indication to revise the pyeloplasty. Ureteroscopy with laser fragmentation offers excellent clearance for an 8 mm stone with minimal morbidity and is the preferred option in a reconstructed system. SWL fragments clear poorly across a surgically altered UPJ. Medical expulsive therapy has little chance of passing a stone of this size that has not entered the ureter, and PCNL is more invasive than needed for this stone burden.
learning_point: A symptomatic 7 mm stone impacted at the UPJ in a child with a prior pyeloplasty is best treated with ureteroscopic laser lithotripsy; SWL has poor results after reconstruction, medical expulsive therapy is unlikely to work for a renal pelvic stone, and revision pyeloplasty is unwarranted when recent imaging showed no obstruction.
key_facts: Pediatric ureteroscopy achieves high stone-free rates for stones under 15 mm and is less invasive than PCNL.
SWL is acceptable for pediatric stones up to about 15 mm but performs poorly with anatomic abnormality or prior reconstruction.
Alpha-blockers help passage of distal ureteral stones in children but not stones still in the pelvis/UPJ.
Minimal hydronephrosis on recent imaging argues against recurrent UPJ obstruction.

question: A 48-year-old man with a BMI of 44 kg/m2 and type 2 diabetes reports erectile dysfunction and low libido. Which pattern is most likely on his morning serum hormone panel?

options.A: low total testosterone, high estradiol, low SHBG.
options.B: normal total testosterone, low estradiol, low SHBG.
options.C: low total testosterone, low estradiol, high SHBG.
options.D: high total testosterone, low estradiol, high SHBG.
options.E: high total testosterone, high estradiol, low SHBG.

rationale: Visceral adiposity and hyperinsulinemia suppress hepatic SHBG synthesis, so the bound fraction and therefore total testosterone fall even when free testosterone is near normal. Fat-rich aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol, raising estradiol and adding negative feedback on the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. Patterns with high SHBG reflect aging or liver disease rather than obesity, and high total testosterone is not expected in morbid obesity. Low estradiol is inconsistent with increased peripheral aromatization.
learning_point: Obesity lowers hepatic SHBG production and increases aromatase activity in adipose tissue, so the typical profile is low total testosterone, elevated estradiol, and low SHBG with free testosterone relatively preserved.
key_facts: Most circulating testosterone is bound to SHBG; only 1-3% is free.
SHBG falls with obesity, insulin resistance, and nephrotic syndrome; it rises with aging, hyperthyroidism, and liver disease.
Adipose aromatase converts testosterone to estradiol, further lowering total T and suppressing gonadotropins.
Free or bioavailable testosterone should be measured when SHBG is likely abnormal.

question: During a left laparoscopic nephrectomy, the surgeon places an 11 mm umbilical trocar blindly after Veress insufflation. When the obturator is withdrawn, bright red pulsatile blood pours from the cannula; the heart rate rises to 135 and blood pressure falls to 78/45 mmHg. Anesthesia begins resuscitation and vascular surgery is paged. The next step is:

options.A: place a second trocar and clip the bleeding vessel laparoscopically.
options.B: convert to hand-assisted laparoscopy for repair.
options.C: insufflate to 25 mmHg and insert the laparoscope.
options.D: close the trocar valve, leave it in place, and perform immediate laparotomy.
options.E: remove the trocar and apply pressure while opening.

rationale: The trocar is probably sitting in the aorta or a common iliac artery; keeping it in situ partially occludes the defect and marks the exact injury site for the open surgeon. The patient is hemodynamically collapsing, so the fastest route to control is a midline laparotomy with the trocar left as a guide. Pulling the trocar removes tamponade and loses pneumoperitoneum, risking rapid exsanguination. Attempts at laparoscopic or hand-assisted repair and simply raising insufflation pressure consume time and cannot control a major arterial injury in an unstable patient.
learning_point: Pulsatile bleeding from a blindly placed trocar with hemodynamic collapse indicates a major vascular (aorta/iliac) injury; leave the trocar in place with its valve closed to tamponade and localize the injury, and convert immediately to open laparotomy with vascular surgery assistance.
key_facts: Great vessel injury occurs most often during blind Veress or primary trocar insertion at the umbilicus.
Removing the trocar can release tamponade and cause exsanguination.
Laparoscopic repair or hand-assist conversion is reasonable only in a stable patient with appropriate expertise.
Raising insufflation pressure does not control arterial hemorrhage.

question: A 58-year-old man completed four cycles of intralesional collagenase for a 55 degree dorsal curvature. Fourteen months later his curvature is 30 degrees, and he can no longer achieve erections sufficient for penetration despite maximal-dose tadalafil. He wants definitive treatment. The next step is:

options.B: vacuum erection device and traction therapy.

rationale: He now has two problems, residual curvature and PDE5-refractory erectile dysfunction, and only a penile prosthesis addresses both. Plication straightens the penis but does nothing for erections and is contraindicated with meaningful ED. Collagenase has already been given to its labeled maximum of eight injections, and his curvature is now at the lower threshold for treatment, so more cycles are off-label and unlikely to help his main complaint. Interferon and vacuum/traction do not restore erectile function in a man who has failed oral therapy.
learning_point: A man with residual Peyronie's curvature and moderate-to-severe erectile dysfunction that does not respond to PDE5 inhibitors is best treated with a penile prosthesis; collagenase is limited to eight injections and curvature over 30 degrees, and plication is avoided when ED is significant.
key_facts: Collagenase clostridium histolyticum is labeled for stable dorsal/lateral curvature of 30-90 degrees, maximum four cycles (eight injections).
Plication or grafting is appropriate only for men with adequate erectile function.
Prosthesis (with modeling if needed) corrects both curvature and ED.
Intralesional verapamil is off-label with weaker evidence.

question: Three weeks after a transobturator mid-urethral sling, a 38-year-old triathlete with a slender build reports aching pain in both groins that worsens with adduction and running. She voids well with a PVR of 15 mL and a normal urinalysis. Oral analgesics give partial relief. The next step is:

options.A: trigger point injection by a pain specialist.
options.B: pelvic MRI to evaluate for abscess.

rationale: Adductor-region pain after transobturator sling placement is a recognized, usually self-limited complication, and three weeks is early in the expected course. Without voiding dysfunction, infection, or signs of mesh complication, continued analgesia, activity modification, and time are appropriate. Referral for trigger point injections or physical therapy is the next tier if pain persists past about six to eight weeks, and sling removal is reserved for pain that fails those measures. Urethrolysis treats obstruction, which her normal PVR excludes, and imaging for abscess is not warranted without fever or wound findings.
learning_point: Groin and medial thigh pain in the first weeks after a transobturator sling, especially in thin athletic women, usually resolves with time and conservative measures; pain management or physical therapy referral is considered only if pain persists beyond six to eight weeks, and sling excision is reserved for refractory cases.
key_facts: Transobturator tapes traverse the adductor compartment, producing groin/thigh pain in a minority, more often in slim, muscular patients.
Most pain resolves spontaneously within weeks; NSAIDs and activity modification are first-line.
Some experts favor a retropubic approach in thin athletic women to avoid this complication.
Normal voiding (low PVR) argues against obstruction, so urethrolysis is not indicated.

question: A 61-year-old woman had a low anterior resection with neoadjuvant chemoradiation for rectal adenocarcinoma three years ago. She now reports passing gas and stool-colored material in her urine. Cystoscopy demonstrates an indurated, nodular area with surrounding erythema on the posterior bladder wall. The next step is:
rationale: Her history of rectal cancer and pelvic radiation puts her at risk for both radiation-induced fistula and local recurrence invading the bladder, and the nodular cystoscopic appearance raises concern for malignancy. Tissue diagnosis dictates the entire treatment plan, from simple fistula repair to multivisceral resection, so biopsy is the required first step. Fulguration would obliterate diagnostic tissue and does not close a fistula. Committing to partial cystectomy, diversion, or exenteration before confirming or excluding recurrence is premature.
learning_point: A colovesical fistula developing years after resection and pelvic radiation for colorectal cancer may represent local tumor recurrence; the fistulous area must be biopsied to establish a diagnosis before any definitive or radical surgery.
key_facts: Fistulas after pelvic radiation can be benign (radiation injury) or malignant (recurrent cancer); management differs completely.
Fulguration destroys tissue without providing a diagnosis.
Partial cystectomy, en bloc resection, or exenteration are planned only after histology is known.
Pneumaturia and fecaluria are classic symptoms of enterovesical fistula.

question: A 31-year-old woman sustains a burst fracture of L3 in a fall and, one year later, has a stable pattern of urinary retention managed with catheterization. A multichannel urodynamic study with needle sphincter EMG is performed. The expected findings are:

options.A: poorly compliant bladder with sphincter dyssynergia.
options.B: acontractile detrusor with normal voluntary sphincter recruitment.
options.C: detrusor overactivity with detrusor-external sphincter dyssynergia.
options.D: acontractile detrusor with denervation potentials in the external sphincter.
options.E: detrusor overactivity with synergic sphincter relaxation.

rationale: A fracture at L3 lies well below the conus and injures the cauda equina, which carries the sacral roots that supply both the detrusor and the external urethral sphincter. Interruption of these roots eliminates the sacral reflex arc, so the detrusor is areflexic, and the striated sphincter shows denervation activity on EMG rather than normal recruitment. Dyssynergia and detrusor overactivity are hallmarks of suprasacral cord lesions where the sacral cord is intact but disconnected from the brainstem. Normal voluntary sphincter recruitment would imply intact sacral roots, which is inconsistent with the injury.
learning_point: A cauda equina injury at the lumbar vertebral level damages sacral nerve roots, producing detrusor areflexia together with denervation of the external sphincter (denervation potentials on EMG); true detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia requires an intact sacral cord with a suprasacral lesion.
key_facts: Spinal cord ends at about L1-L2; injuries below this damage roots (lower motor neuron), not cord.
Lower motor neuron lesions cause acontractile detrusor and a denervated, often incompetent striated sphincter with fibrillation/denervation potentials.
DSD arises from suprasacral spinal cord lesions that disconnect the pontine micturition center from the sacral cord.
The smooth muscle internal sphincter may remain closed (fixed) but is not dyssynergic.

question: A 47-year-old man noticed a dorsal penile bend of about 50 degrees developing over the past four months, and erections are now painful. Examination shows a tender dorsal plaque. The best treatment is:
rationale: Pain with erections and a curvature that is still changing define the active inflammatory phase of Peyronie's disease, during which NSAIDs are the appropriate guideline-endorsed therapy for symptom relief. Intralesional collagenase and surgical correction are indicated only once the deformity has stabilized for several months. Vitamin E and colchicine have not shown efficacy and are specifically not recommended. Plication in the active phase risks recurrence as the plaque continues to evolve.
learning_point: In the active (acute) phase of Peyronie's disease marked by pain with erections, NSAIDs are the guideline-supported treatment; intralesional collagenase and surgery are reserved for the stable phase, and vitamin E and other oral agents are not recommended.
key_facts: Active phase: evolving curvature and painful erections, typically the first 6-18 months.
AUA guideline: offer NSAIDs for pain in the active phase; do not offer vitamin E, tamoxifen, procarbazine, or omega-3.
Pentoxifylline and traction are off-label with limited evidence.
Collagenase requires a stable curvature of 30-90 degrees.

question: During a robotic right partial nephrectomy, the bedside assistant swaps a fenestrated bipolar for a needle driver. As the needle driver is advanced it travels beyond the expected depth and punctures the liver edge, although the console surgeon had not moved the arm. The most likely explanation is:

options.A: loss of pneumoperitoneum shifted the liver toward the port.
options.B: the assistant inserted the instrument too slowly.
options.C: the instrument was not seated on the faceplate.
options.D: the arm clutch was pressed, erasing the stored instrument position.
options.E: the needle driver was a defective instrument.

rationale: The robotic system's guided exchange feature memorizes the depth and path of the removed instrument so a replacement stops just proximal to the former tip; overshoot therefore means the memory was lost. The clutch button on the arm releases the joints and clears that stored position, after which the instrument slides freely and must be guided manually under vision. An unseated or defective instrument would fail to engage and could not be advanced through the system at all. Insertion speed and transient pressure changes do not override the depth stop.
learning_point: Robotic guided instrument exchange automatically returns a new instrument to just short of the prior instrument's tip position; pressing the arm clutch resets this memory, so a subsequent exchange can overshoot into adjacent organs unless advanced under direct vision.
key_facts: Guided instrument exchange stores the trajectory and depth of the removed instrument and stops the new one about 1 mm short.
Activating the clutch button on the robotic arm clears the stored position, requiring manual insertion under vision.
A defective instrument or dislodged faceplate prevents engagement and advancement rather than causing overshoot.
All instruments should still be inserted under laparoscopic visualization.

question: A 67-year-old woman with hypertension controlled on a single ACE inhibitor undergoes CT angiography for a small infrarenal aortic aneurysm, which incidentally shows a 55% narrowing at the origin of the right renal artery without post-stenotic dilatation. Her creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL, plasma renin activity is normal, and renal artery duplex shows normal velocities bilaterally. The next step is:

options.D: periodic blood pressure and renal function monitoring.
options.E: switch the ACE inhibitor to a calcium channel blocker.

rationale: A moderate ostial stenosis is only clinically important if it is hemodynamically significant, and her normal duplex velocities, normal renin, preserved renal function, and controlled pressure all indicate it is not. In that setting, revascularization offers no benefit and carries procedural risk, as confirmed by randomized trials of stenting versus medical therapy. Observation with serial blood pressure and creatinine checks, with reimaging if either deteriorates, is appropriate. Renin sampling and captopril scintigraphy would not change management in an asymptomatic, well-controlled patient, and there is no reason to abandon an effective ACE inhibitor when renal function is normal.
learning_point: An incidentally found moderate renal artery stenosis in a patient with well-controlled hypertension, normal renal function, normal renin, and a normal duplex study is not hemodynamically significant; management is serial monitoring of blood pressure and renal function rather than revascularization.
key_facts: Renovascular hypertension accounts for under 1% of all hypertension and 10-20% of refractory cases.
Stenosis is usually considered functionally significant above about 75%, or above 50% with post-stenotic dilatation; duplex Doppler is a sensitive, specific noninvasive screen.
Randomized trials (ASTRAL, CORAL) showed no benefit of stenting over medical therapy in most atherosclerotic RAS.
Renal vein renin sampling is rarely used today because of invasiveness and limited predictive value.

question: A patient with hemorrhagic shock maintains a near-normal glomerular filtration rate despite a marked fall in renal blood flow. The principal renal hemodynamic action of angiotensin II responsible for this is:

options.D: constriction of the main renal artery.
options.E: stimulation of active sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct.

rationale: Angiotensin II constricts both glomerular arterioles but acts preferentially on the efferent side; narrowing the outflow raises hydrostatic pressure within the glomerular capillaries and sustains filtration even as total renal plasma flow declines. Afferent dilation during hypovolemia is mediated by prostaglandins, not angiotensin II. Angiotensin II reduces rather than increases medullary blood flow, and while it does promote sodium reabsorption through aldosterone, that is a tubular effect that does not maintain GFR. Renal artery constriction would reduce, not protect, filtration.
learning_point: Angiotensin II preserves GFR during volume depletion mainly by constricting the efferent arteriole more than the afferent, which raises glomerular capillary pressure despite reduced renal plasma flow.
key_facts: Efferent constriction increases filtration fraction and maintains GFR as renal blood flow falls.
ACE inhibitors or ARBs blunt this response and can precipitate acute kidney injury in hypovolemia or bilateral RAS.
Angiotensin II also stimulates aldosterone, proximal sodium reabsorption, and reduces medullary blood flow.
Prostaglandins dilate the afferent arteriole in the same setting; NSAIDs remove this protection.

question: A two-year-old boy develops a pinpoint urethrocutaneous fistula at the penoscrotal junction eight months after a tubularized incised plate repair. He is scheduled for fistula closure. The step most critical to preventing recurrence is:

options.A: covering the repair with a tunica vaginalis flap.
options.B: use of 7-0 polyglactin suture for the urethral layer.
options.C: leaving a urethral stent for seven days.
options.D: closing the fistula in three separate layers.
options.E: calibrating the urethra to exclude distal stricture.

rationale: A fistula is frequently a pressure vent for urine that cannot exit a stenotic meatus or strictured distal neourethra; if that obstruction is not identified and corrected, the repair will break down regardless of technique. Intraoperative calibration or endoscopy of the distal urethra is therefore the essential first step. Fine sutures, multilayer closure, and vascularized flap coverage all help but are secondary to relieving distal obstruction. Stenting has not been shown to improve outcomes of simple fistula repair.
learning_point: Before repairing a urethrocutaneous fistula after hypospadias surgery, the urethra must be calibrated to exclude distal stricture or meatal stenosis, because unrecognized distal obstruction is the main cause of fistula recurrence.
key_facts: Fistula repair should wait at least six months after the original surgery for tissue maturation.
Steps: exclude distal obstruction, excise tract, close urethra, cover with a well-vascularized intermediate layer (dartos or tunica vaginalis).
Postoperative stenting adds little for simple fistula repairs.
Healthy surrounding skin and avoidance of overlapping suture lines reduce recurrence.

question: A 39-year-old woman who flies commercial aircraft is found to have 2-5 RBC/hpf on a flight physical. Non-contrast CT reveals four nonobstructing calyceal stones, 3-4 mm each, in both kidneys. Cystoscopy is planned. The additional next step is:

options.A: SWL to the larger kidney first.

rationale: Although small nonobstructing calyceal stones are often observed in the general population, a pilot can be grounded until stone-free because of the risk of incapacitating colic in flight, creating a vocational indication for removal. Ureteroscopy can address both kidneys in one anesthetic and allows direct visualization of complete clearance, which is what aviation authorities require for return to duty. SWL would need staged sessions and offers no immediate proof of clearance. Alpha-blockers do not expel renal stones, and citrate therapy should await a metabolic workup and does not remove existing stones.
learning_point: Patients with occupational restrictions, such as pilots, have a vocational indication to clear even small asymptomatic renal stones; ureteroscopy is preferred because it can treat both sides in one session and provides immediate confirmation of stone-free status.
key_facts: Occupational indications for stone removal include pilots, military deployment, and remote travel.
SWL does not permit same-session bilateral treatment and leaves fragments that may pass unpredictably.
Medical expulsive therapy applies only to ureteral stones.
Metabolic evaluation precedes preventive medication such as potassium citrate.

question: A 55-year-old man undergoes a right retroperitoneoscopic adrenalectomy. After balloon dissection, a conventional 12 mm port is placed and sutured to the fascia. Forty minutes into the case the anesthesiologist notes end-tidal CO2 rising from 36 to 52 mmHg, and crepitus is palpable across the flank and chest wall. The most likely cause is:

options.A: CO2 escaping around the trocar into the subcutaneous tissue.
options.C: complete dislodgement of the trocar into the subcutaneous space.
options.D: gas embolism through a lumbar vein.

rationale: The fascial incision made for balloon dissection is usually wider than a standard trocar, so even a secured port allows CO2 to track into the subcutaneous plane; the retroperitoneum also absorbs CO2 readily, so hypercarbia follows. Palpable crepitus with progressive end-tidal CO2 elevation is the signature of this leak. A ruptured bleb would present as pneumothorax with hypoxia and falling, not rising, end-tidal CO2. Gas embolism causes an abrupt drop in end-tidal CO2 and hemodynamic collapse. Entering the peritoneum reduces working space but does not produce flank crepitus, and a fully dislodged trocar would be evident to the surgeon with immediate loss of the working space.
learning_point: In retroperitoneoscopy, a standard trocar placed through a fascial incision larger than the cannula leaks CO2 into the subcutaneous tissue, causing subcutaneous emphysema and rising end-tidal CO2; balloon-tipped access trocars minimize this leak.
key_facts: Retroperitoneal CO2 absorbs faster than intraperitoneal CO2 and hypercarbia is more common.
Subcutaneous emphysema results from gas tracking around a loosely sealed port, not from pulmonary bleb rupture (which causes pneumothorax).
Peritoneal entry during retroperitoneoscopy reduces working space but does not by itself cause crepitus.
Management: lower insufflation pressure, increase ventilation, secure or replace the trocar.

question: A 38-year-old woman with end-stage renal disease from IgA nephropathy is being evaluated for a deceased-donor kidney transplant. Pre-transplant CT shows a 1.5 cm nonobstructing stone in the lower pole of her right native kidney; she has never had colic or urinary infections. The next step is:

options.A: right native nephrectomy at the time of transplant.
options.E: proceed with transplantation without treating the stone.

rationale: Stones in a native, nonfunctioning kidney that have caused no symptoms or infection are clinically irrelevant to transplantation and do not threaten the allograft. Intervening with SWL, ureteroscopy, or PCNL in a dialysis-dependent patient adds procedural risk and delays listing without any demonstrated benefit. Native nephrectomy is reserved for specific indications such as recurrent pyelonephritis, uncontrolled hypertension, or large polycystic kidneys occupying the iliac fossa. The correct approach is to proceed with the transplant and simply monitor the native stone.
learning_point: An asymptomatic stone in a native kidney does not need to be treated before renal transplantation; the patient should proceed with the transplant.
key_facts: Native kidneys are left in situ at transplant unless there is a specific indication (recurrent infection, refractory hypertension, massive polycystic kidneys, suspected malignancy).
Asymptomatic native stones rarely cause problems post-transplant and do not increase graft risk.
Donor kidney stones, by contrast, are usually removed before implantation.
Treating native stones would add morbidity and delay transplantation without benefit.

question: A 23-year-old woman with polycystic ovarian syndrome and no prior surgery presents with two days of suprapubic discomfort and inability to void; she denies any urge to urinate. Catheterization yields 1500 mL. Neurologic examination and spine MRI are normal. On urodynamics, the finding that most specifically supports the diagnosis is:

options.A: complex repetitive discharges on urethral sphincter needle EMG.
options.D: reduced compliance with end-fill pressure above 40 cm H2O.
options.E: high detrusor pressure with low flow.

rationale: The presentation of a young woman with painless, urgency-free retention of a very large volume, a normal neurologic workup, and coexisting polycystic ovaries is classic for Fowler's syndrome. Its defining feature is an abnormal striated sphincter EMG with complex repetitive discharges and decelerating bursts that prevent sphincter relaxation. The bladder is typically acontractile with excellent compliance, so reduced compliance, detrusor overactivity, and dyssynergia are not expected. High-pressure low-flow voiding indicates an obstructed but contractile bladder, which is not the case here.
learning_point: Fowler's syndrome is painless-urgency-free urinary retention in young women without neurologic disease, often with polycystic ovaries; the diagnostic urodynamic hallmark is abnormal external urethral sphincter EMG (complex repetitive discharges and decelerating bursts) with a large-capacity acontractile bladder.
key_facts: Typical patient: woman under 30, retention over 1 L, lack of urgency, normal neurologic exam.
About half have polycystic ovarian syndrome.
The EMG abnormality impairs sphincter relaxation; detrusor is acontractile with excellent compliance, so true DSD is not seen.
Sacral neuromodulation is the most effective treatment.

question: A 69-year-old man presents with hip pain. PSA is 210 ng/mL and biopsy shows Gleason 4+5 adenocarcinoma. Bone scan demonstrates six lesions involving the thoracic spine, pelvis, left femur, and two ribs, and CT shows retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy. He has never received hormonal therapy. In addition to androgen deprivation, the next step is:
rationale: Multiple bone metastases extending beyond the axial skeleton and pelvis define high-volume hormone-sensitive disease, the group that gained the largest survival benefit from adding six cycles of docetaxel to ADT in the CHAARTED and STAMPEDE trials. Waiting for castration resistance forfeits that survival advantage. Sipuleucel-T and radium-223 are indicated for castration-resistant disease, the latter for symptomatic bone-predominant disease without visceral metastases. Ketoconazole lowers androgens but has no demonstrated survival benefit in this setting.
learning_point: For newly diagnosed high-volume metastatic hormone-sensitive prostate cancer, adding docetaxel to androgen deprivation therapy improves overall survival (CHAARTED, STAMPEDE); at the time of this item, enzalutamide, abiraterone, and sipuleucel-T were approved only for castration-resistant disease.
key_facts: High volume (CHAARTED): visceral metastases or at least four bone lesions with at least one beyond the pelvis and spine.
CHAARTED: median OS improved from about 44 to 58 months overall with ADT plus docetaxel; greatest benefit in high-volume disease.
Ketoconazole is a secondary hormonal agent, not standard first-line intensification.
Later trials (LATITUDE, STAMPEDE arm G) also support ADT plus abiraterone for high-risk mHSPC; current guidelines accept several intensification options.

question: A patient with sepsis mounts an appropriate ACTH-driven surge in serum cortisol. The adrenal layer responsible for this glucocorticoid output is the:
rationale: Glucocorticoid synthesis, including the stress-induced cortisol rise stimulated by ACTH, occurs in the zona fasciculata, the thick middle zone of the cortex rich in lipid-laden cells. The outer zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone under renin-angiotensin control, and the inner zona reticularis produces DHEA and other weak androgens. The medulla is a chromaffin tissue producing catecholamines, and the capsule is connective tissue with no hormonal function.
learning_point: Cortisol is synthesized in the zona fasciculata, the middle and largest layer of the adrenal cortex; the zona glomerulosa produces aldosterone, the zona reticularis produces adrenal androgens, and the medulla secretes catecholamines.
key_facts: Cortex layers from outside in: glomerulosa (mineralocorticoids), fasciculata (glucocorticoids), reticularis (androgens/estrogens).
ACTH drives the fasciculata and reticularis; angiotensin II and potassium drive the glomerulosa.
The medulla is neuroectodermal and releases epinephrine and norepinephrine.

question: A five-year-old girl's brother, age nine, is brought in three hours after a neighbor's dog bit his scrotum. There are two puncture wounds and a 2 cm laceration of the left hemiscrotum extending through dartos; both testes are normal on palpation and there is no blood at the meatus. Tetanus is up to date and the dog is vaccinated. After starting amoxicillin-clavulanate, the next step is:

options.C: operative exploration, irrigation, debridement, and primary closure.
options.D: bedside irrigation and dressing with delayed closure.
options.E: scrotal ultrasound to assess the testis.

rationale: A dog bite that penetrates the dartos is a penetrating scrotal injury and warrants formal exploration to irrigate, debride devitalized tissue, and inspect the testis and cord. Unlike human bites, dog bites may be closed primarily after thorough debridement under antibiotic coverage with acceptable infection rates. Ultrasound adds little when the testes are normal on examination, and a urethrogram is reserved for signs of urethral involvement such as meatal blood or penile injury. Leaving the wound open or performing delayed closure is appropriate for human bites, not canine bites.
learning_point: Dog bites to the scrotum are treated as penetrating scrotal trauma: broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Pasteurella, tetanus prophylaxis, operative exploration with irrigation and debridement, and primary closure; human bites are not closed primarily.
key_facts: Antibiotic coverage: amoxicillin-clavulanate covers Pasteurella, Streptococcus, and Staphylococcus.
Confirm rabies status of the animal; give tetanus prophylaxis.
Scrotal ultrasound and urethrography are only needed when exam suggests testicular or urethral injury.
Human bites: debride and leave open or delayed closure due to higher infection risk.

question: A 70-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes and neuropathy has frequency, urgency incontinence, and a weak stream despite alfuzosin. His prostate is 30 g on ultrasound. Urodynamics show first sensation at 450 mL, capacity of 900 mL, terminal detrusor overactivity, Qmax of 7 mL/sec at a detrusor pressure of 92 cm H2O, and PVR of 400 mL. Cystoscopy shows an occlusive median lobe without stricture. The best treatment is:
rationale: The pressure-flow data (high detrusor pressure with very low flow) establish bladder outlet obstruction, and cystoscopy localizes it to the prostate while excluding a stricture. Relieving the obstruction with TURP addresses the primary pathology and often improves the secondary storage symptoms and residual urine, even in a patient with underlying diabetic cystopathy. A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor is ineffective for a 30 g gland, and sacral neuromodulation is not appropriate in the presence of obstruction. CIC or a beta-3 agonist may help symptoms but leaves the obstruction untreated.
learning_point: In a diabetic man with storage symptoms and a high-capacity bladder, urodynamically proven bladder outlet obstruction (high pressure, low flow) with a cystoscopically confirmed prostatic cause should be treated by relieving the obstruction with TURP, even with a small prostate; neuromodulation and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors are not indicated.
key_facts: Diabetic cystopathy: impaired sensation, large capacity, reduced contractility, elevated PVR; detrusor overactivity may coexist.
Pressure-flow study is the key to distinguishing obstruction from underactivity in men with high PVR.
5-ARIs benefit only prostates over about 30-40 g.
Sacral neuromodulation is contraindicated when obstruction is present; CIC treats emptying but not the cause.

question: A 71-year-old man received induction and one year of maintenance BCG for bladder CIS four years ago and has had negative cystoscopies since. He undergoes TURP for retention; pathology shows nodular hyperplasia and urothelial CIS limited to the prostatic urethral epithelium, with no involvement of ducts or stroma. Upper tract imaging is normal. The next step is:

options.A: repeat transurethral resection of the prostate.
options.D: surveillance cystoscopy and cytology at three months.

rationale: Mucosal CIS of the prostatic urethra without ductal or stromal invasion is non-invasive disease that is largely removed by the TURP and is accessible to intravesical BCG once the prostatic urethra has been opened. BCG remains the most effective agent for CIS, and treating after resection reduces recurrence compared with observation alone. Radical surgery is appropriate if the disease involves ducts or stroma or fails BCG, but is excessive here. Repeat resection adds nothing after a complete TURP, and gemcitabine is inferior to BCG for CIS as first-line therapy in a BCG-naive-equivalent setting.
learning_point: Carcinoma in situ confined to the prostatic urethral mucosa (no ductal or stromal invasion) found after TURP in a patient with prior bladder CIS/NMIBC is treated with a course of intravesical BCG, which reaches the resected prostatic urethra; cystectomy is reserved for BCG failure.
key_facts: Prostatic urethral involvement is common after intravesical therapy for bladder CIS; TURP both stages and treats mucosal disease.
BCG is more effective than mitomycin for CIS.
Ductal or stromal invasion of the prostate mandates radical cystoprostatectomy.
Surveillance alone has higher recurrence than BCG after resection.

question: A transplanted kidney maintains a nearly constant blood flow when the recipient's mean arterial pressure fluctuates between 90 and 150 mmHg. The mechanism primarily responsible for this constancy is:

options.A: sympathetic innervation of the renal vasculature.
options.E: antidiuretic hormone acting on the collecting duct.

rationale: Autoregulation is an intrinsic property of the kidney mediated by the afferent arteriole, which constricts as perfusion pressure rises and dilates as it falls through both a myogenic reflex and tubuloglomerular feedback from the macula densa. Because the response is intrinsic, a denervated allograft autoregulates just as a native kidney does, which excludes sympathetic innervation as the primary mechanism. Efferent constriction by angiotensin II helps preserve GFR during hypoperfusion but is not the main regulator of total renal blood flow. Endothelin and ADH are not the principal autoregulatory mediators.
learning_point: Renal blood flow and GFR are autoregulated across a wide range of perfusion pressures chiefly by changes in afferent arteriolar resistance (myogenic response and tubuloglomerular feedback); this persists in denervated kidneys.
key_facts: Autoregulation holds RBF and GFR nearly constant between roughly 80 and 180 mmHg mean arterial pressure.
Tubuloglomerular feedback: macula densa senses distal tubular flow and signals the afferent arteriole; the macula densa is the sensor, the afferent arteriole is the effector.
Efferent tone is modulated mainly by angiotensin II and fine-tunes GFR rather than autoregulating flow.
A transplanted (denervated) kidney autoregulates normally.

question: A 49-year-old man has vague abdominal discomfort and a normal blood pressure. CT shows a 4 cm right adrenal mass measuring 38 HU on unenhanced images with avid heterogeneous enhancement. On MRI the lesion is isointense to liver on T1 and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, without signal loss on out-of-phase imaging. The imaging is most consistent with:
rationale: An unenhanced attenuation well above 10 HU with no chemical-shift signal loss excludes a lipid-rich adenoma, and avid enhancement with striking T2 hyperintensity is the characteristic appearance of a pheochromocytoma. A myelolipoma would contain fat, giving negative attenuation on CT and high T1 signal. A simple cyst would be near water density and would not enhance. Hemorrhage is typically hyperdense acutely but does not enhance and shows variable T1 signal rather than this pattern. Normotension does not exclude pheochromocytoma, so biochemical testing should follow.
learning_point: An adrenal mass that is dense on unenhanced CT (greater than 10 HU) and markedly hyperintense on T2-weighted MRI (the 'light bulb' sign) is most consistent with pheochromocytoma; adenomas are low-density and lose signal on chemical shift, myelolipomas contain macroscopic fat (bright on T1), and cysts are water density.
key_facts: Lipid-rich adenoma: unenhanced CT under 10 HU, rapid contrast washout, signal drop on out-of-phase MRI.
Pheochromocytoma: usually over 10 HU, avid heterogeneous enhancement, slow washout, very bright T2 signal (not pathognomonic; carcinoma and metastases can also be bright).
Myelolipoma: macroscopic fat, negative HU, bright on T1.
Biochemical confirmation (plasma or urine metanephrines) is required before surgery.

question: A 70 kg man submits a 24-hour urine for creatinine clearance as part of a stone evaluation. Before interpreting the clearance value, the laboratory parameter that best confirms the collection was complete is the:
rationale: Daily creatinine production is a function of muscle mass and varies little from day to day, so a 70 kg man should excrete roughly 1.4-1.7 g of creatinine per 24 hours; a value far below that indicates missed voids and an invalid clearance. Urine volume varies with fluid intake and cannot distinguish a complete dilute collection from an incomplete concentrated one. Urea excretion depends on protein intake and catabolic state, and sodium and specific gravity reflect diet and hydration rather than completeness.
learning_point: The adequacy of a 24-hour urine collection for creatinine clearance is judged by the total creatinine excreted, which is roughly constant for a given muscle mass (about 1.0 mg/kg/hr, or 20-25 mg/kg/day in men and 15-20 mg/kg/day in women).
key_facts: Creatinine production depends on muscle mass and is relatively constant day to day.
Total creatinine well below the expected amount suggests an incomplete collection; well above suggests over-collection.
Urine volume, sodium, urea, and osmolality vary with diet and hydration and do not validate completeness.

question: A 22-year-old woman has headaches and blood pressure of 175/110 mmHg. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L, plasma renin activity is markedly elevated, and aldosterone is high. CT shows a 2.5 cm well-circumscribed hypoenhancing mass in the cortex of the left kidney with normal adrenal glands and no renal artery stenosis. The most likely diagnosis is:
rationale: The triad of severe hypertension, hypokalemia, and high renin with high aldosterone indicates secondary hyperaldosteronism driven by autonomous renin secretion, and in a young patient with a small renal cortical mass the source is a juxtaglomerular cell tumor. An aldosterone-producing adenoma would present with suppressed renin and an adrenal, not renal, lesion. Pheochromocytoma produces catecholamine excess without hypokalemia. Fibromuscular dysplasia causes renin-mediated hypertension but there is no arterial stenosis and it does not produce a mass. Renal cell carcinoma rarely secretes renin and would be an unusual explanation at this age.
learning_point: A young patient with severe hypertension, hypokalemia, elevated plasma renin, and a small renal cortical mass most likely has a juxtaglomerular cell tumor (reninoma), a benign renin-secreting tumor cured by excision; aldosteronomas suppress renin and pheochromocytomas do not cause hypokalemia.
key_facts: Reninoma: rare, usually under age 20-30, female predominance, causes secondary hyperaldosteronism (high renin, high aldosterone, low potassium).
Primary aldosteronism (adrenal adenoma) has suppressed renin.
Pheochromocytoma causes catecholamine-driven hypertension without hypokalemia.
Treatment is partial nephrectomy or enucleation; hypertension typically resolves.

question: A patient develops complete unilateral ureteral obstruction from a stone. Among the nephron functions listed, the one that becomes impaired first is:

options.B: hydrogen ion secretion in the distal nephron.
options.E: chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb.

rationale: Obstruction rapidly reduces expression of aquaporin water channels in the collecting duct and washes out the medullary gradient, so the ability to concentrate urine is lost early. This is why post-obstructive diuresis is characteristically hypotonic. Impairment of distal hydrogen and potassium secretion, producing a hyperkalemic type 4-like acidosis, and defects in proximal bicarbonate or loop chloride handling occur later with more prolonged or severe obstruction.
learning_point: The earliest tubular defect caused by ureteral obstruction is impaired water reabsorption (a urinary concentrating defect) due to downregulation of collecting duct aquaporin channels; defects in acid, potassium, and electrolyte handling develop later.
key_facts: Obstruction reduces aquaporin-2 expression and medullary tonicity, impairing concentration.
Post-obstructive diuresis reflects this concentrating defect plus solute load.
Distal acidification and potassium secretion defects (hyperkalemic distal RTA) appear with more prolonged obstruction.

question: Sixteen days after a deceased-donor renal transplant, a 55-year-old woman notes her wound soaking the dressing. Creatinine has risen from 1.3 to 2.4 mg/dL, and ultrasound shows an 8 cm fluid collection with mild allograft hydronephrosis. Fluid analysis shows creatinine 14 mg/dL and no organisms. The most likely cause is:

options.B: early technical failure of the ureteroneocystostomy.
options.D: lymph leak from recipient iliac dissection.
options.E: ischemic necrosis of the distal transplant ureter.

rationale: Drain fluid creatinine several times the serum value proves the collection is urine, excluding a lymphocele of either donor or recipient origin. A technically faulty anastomosis leaks almost immediately after surgery, whereas a leak appearing in the second or third postoperative week is the classic timing of distal ureteral ischemia, because the transplant ureter relies on fragile hilar vessels and the distal segment necroses and sloughs. Edema at the anastomosis would produce obstruction with hydronephrosis but no extravasation.
learning_point: A urine leak presenting one to three weeks after kidney transplantation (drain fluid creatinine far above serum) is most often due to ischemic necrosis of the distal donor ureter, which depends on a tenuous blood supply from the renal artery branches; immediate leaks suggest anastomotic technical failure, and low-creatinine fluid suggests lymphocele.
key_facts: Distal transplant ureter is supplied only by periureteral branches from the renal hilum; excess dissection or long ureter risks necrosis.
Drain fluid creatinine much higher than serum confirms urine; lymph has creatinine equal to serum.
Technical anastomotic leaks appear within the first days; ischemic necrosis appears at 1-3 weeks.
Management: stent and nephrostomy decompression, with open ureteral reimplantation or native ureteropyelostomy if it fails.

question: A 41-year-old woman with Cushing syndrome undergoes right adrenalectomy for a 2 cm adenoma. Six weeks later she remains cushingoid with elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol; plasma ACTH is suppressed and pituitary MRI is unremarkable. Repeat imaging suggests nodularity of the remaining left adrenal. The next step is:
rationale: Suppressed ACTH with ongoing hypercortisolism after removing one gland means the remaining adrenal is autonomously producing cortisol, most likely bilateral nodular disease. Medical control with metyrapone, which blocks the final step of cortisol synthesis, is effective, well tolerated, and preserves the option of later definitive surgery. Ketoconazole lowers cortisol but carries a serious hepatotoxicity warning, and mitotane is adrenolytic and reserved mainly for adrenocortical carcinoma. Immediate contralateral adrenalectomy would leave her with no adrenal tissue and permanent dependence on steroid replacement, while pasireotide targets pituitary ACTH secretion and is irrelevant in ACTH-independent disease.
learning_point: Persistent ACTH-independent hypercortisolism after unilateral adrenalectomy for a presumed adenoma points to a contralateral or bilateral adrenal source; metyrapone, an 11-beta-hydroxylase inhibitor, is the preferred medical agent to control cortisol, while ketoconazole carries hepatotoxicity warnings and bilateral adrenalectomy commits the patient to lifelong steroid replacement.
key_facts: Low ACTH with high cortisol = adrenal (ACTH-independent) Cushing syndrome.
Metyrapone blocks 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol; it rarely causes salt wasting because deoxycorticosterone rises.
Aminoglutethimide is no longer available; mitotane is mainly for adrenocortical carcinoma.
Oral ketoconazole has an FDA boxed warning for hepatotoxicity.

question: A 34-year-old woman with recurrent Proteus urinary infections has had six months of dull right flank pain, low-grade fevers, and 7 kg weight loss. Non-contrast CT shows an enlarged right kidney with a staghorn calculus in a contracted pelvis and multiple low-attenuation areas replacing the parenchyma; the left kidney is normal. Antibiotics are started. The next step is:
rationale: The combination of chronic infection with a urease-splitting organism, constitutional symptoms, and a CT picture of a reniform-enlarged kidney with a central stone and hypodense parenchymal replacement is characteristic of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. Although nephrectomy is the usual outcome, the differential function of the affected kidney must be established first; a functioning kidney might be drained and treated rather than removed. Endoscopic stone procedures are ineffective and hazardous in the inflamed, fibrotic XGP kidney. Retrograde pyelography adds little anatomic information beyond the CT and does not quantify function.
learning_point: A chronically infected, enlarged kidney with a central stone and surrounding low-density parenchyma (xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis) usually requires nephrectomy, but a DMSA scan should first document the degree of residual function, since a kidney with meaningful function may warrant drainage or partial nephrectomy instead.
key_facts: XGP: chronic obstruction plus infection (Proteus, E. coli) producing lipid-laden macrophages; CT shows reniform enlargement, staghorn stone, 'bear paw' hypodense areas.
Nephrectomy is definitive for a nonfunctioning kidney; preoperative antibiotics are mandatory.
PCNL and ureteroscopy are not appropriate for XGP; stone burden and tissue friability make them futile.
If function is preserved, nephrostomy drainage and antibiotics may allow salvage or partial nephrectomy.

question: A 31-year-old woman at eight weeks of gestation has a routine prenatal urine culture growing more than 100,000 CFU/mL of pan-sensitive E. coli. She has no urinary symptoms and no prior infections. The next step is:

options.C: nitrofurantoin prophylaxis for the remainder of pregnancy.
options.E: repeat the culture in two weeks before treating.

rationale: Pregnancy is the one setting in which asymptomatic bacteriuria is always treated, because physiologic ureteral dilation and stasis allow a high proportion of untreated cases to progress to pyelonephritis with associated preterm labor and low birth weight. A 3-7 day course of a safe agent such as cephalexin or amoxicillin is appropriate, followed by a test of cure. Observation or waiting for symptoms is inappropriate. Fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy, and continuous prophylaxis is reserved for women with recurrent infections, not a first episode.
learning_point: Asymptomatic bacteriuria detected on screening in pregnancy must be treated with a short (3-7 day) course of a pregnancy-safe antibiotic such as an aminopenicillin or cephalosporin, because untreated bacteriuria substantially increases the risk of pyelonephritis and adverse pregnancy outcomes.
key_facts: Untreated bacteriuria in pregnancy progresses to pyelonephritis in 20-40% of cases.
Safe agents: amoxicillin, cephalexin, nitrofurantoin (avoid near term), fosfomycin; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines, use sulfonamides with caution.
Prophylaxis is reserved for recurrent bacteriuria/UTI during pregnancy.
A catheterized specimen is unnecessary unless contamination is suspected.

question: A 52-year-old man underwent abdominoperineal resection for low rectal cancer 15 months ago. He has persistent difficulty emptying, straining to void, and leakage with coughing. Videourodynamics are most likely to demonstrate:

options.A: normal compliance, open bladder neck, and normal sphincter relaxation.
options.B: normal compliance, closed bladder neck, and normal sphincter relaxation.
options.C: reduced compliance, open bladder neck, and fixed non-relaxing external sphincter.
options.D: reduced compliance, closed bladder neck, and normal sphincter relaxation.
options.E: detrusor overactivity, closed bladder neck, and sphincter dyssynergia.

rationale: Extensive rectal surgery damages the pelvic plexus, removing both autonomic limbs to the lower urinary tract. Without sympathetic tone the bladder neck remains open at rest, which explains stress leakage; without parasympathetic input the detrusor is acontractile, and over time the decentralized bladder frequently develops poor compliance. The striated sphincter, supplied by the pudendal nerve, retains fixed tone that does not relax with attempted voiding, producing retention and straining. Detrusor overactivity with dyssynergia is a suprasacral cord pattern, not a peripheral plexus injury pattern, and a closed bladder neck would not explain his leakage.
learning_point: Pelvic plexus injury after radical pelvic surgery (APR, low anterior resection, radical hysterectomy) produces a parasympathetically and sympathetically denervated bladder: detrusor areflexia with reduced compliance, an open (incompetent) bladder neck, and a fixed, non-relaxing external sphincter.
key_facts: The inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus lies lateral to the rectum and vagina and is vulnerable in rectal and gynecologic surgery.
Loss of sympathetic input leaves the bladder neck open; loss of parasympathetic input leaves the detrusor acontractile and often poorly compliant.
Fixed striated sphincter tone maintains outlet resistance, leading to retention with overflow or stress leakage.
Management usually involves CIC; persistent dysfunction beyond 6-12 months is often permanent.

question: A six-year-old boy who underwent valve ablation as a neonate wets the bed nightly and has occasional daytime dampness. Serum creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL. A 24-hour urine volume is 2200 mL with a morning urine osmolality of 180 mOsm/kg. Ultrasound shows a thick-walled bladder with a small residual. The best treatment is:

options.A: scheduled frequent voiding including a nighttime void.

rationale: A very large daily urine output with dilute morning urine in a boy with prior valves indicates a renal concentrating defect, essentially nephrogenic diabetes insipidus from early obstructive nephropathy. Because the kidney cannot respond to vasopressin, desmopressin is ineffective, and restricting fluids will not meaningfully reduce the obligate output and risks dehydration. The only way to stay dry is to empty the bladder more often, including waking to void at night, which also protects the upper tracts from high-volume storage. Anticholinergics do not address polyuria and may worsen emptying; salt restriction has little effect on urine volume in this setting.
learning_point: Boys with a history of posterior urethral valves often have a nephrogenic concentrating defect producing polyuria; their enuresis and daytime wetting do not respond to desmopressin or fluid restriction, so management relies on more frequent voiding (including nocturnal voids) to match the obligatory urine output.
key_facts: Valve bladder syndrome: polyuria from tubular damage, large-capacity poorly sensate bladder, high residuals.
Nephrogenic DI does not respond to DDAVP; fluid restriction risks dehydration and does not lower output substantially.
Timed and double voiding, with overnight voiding or catheterization, are the mainstays.
Assess for incomplete emptying; CIC is added if residuals are high.

question: A 34-year-old man with untreated bipolar disorder amputates his penis at the mid-shaft during a psychotic episode. He arrives 90 minutes later; the severed segment was wrapped in a wet cloth and kept cool without ice. After suprapubic tube placement and wound debridement, the next step is:

options.A: closure of the stump with spatulated urethral meatoplasty.
options.C: dressing changes and healing by secondary intention.

rationale: A viable amputated segment presenting well within the window of acceptable warm ischemia should be replanted, as outcomes for erectile function, sensation, and voiding are far superior to any reconstructive alternative. Microsurgical anastomosis of the dorsal arteries, deep dorsal vein, and dorsal nerves reduces complications such as skin necrosis, urethral stricture, and anesthesia. Stump closure, perineal urethrostomy, or leaving the wound open abandon the salvageable organ, and phalloplasty is a complex secondary option for cases where replantation is not possible. Psychiatric management must accompany surgical care.
learning_point: A traumatically amputated penis should be replanted whenever the segment is available and the ischemia time is acceptable (up to about 6 hours warm or 16 hours cold), with microsurgical repair of the dorsal vessels and nerves when possible; stump closure or neophallus creation is reserved for cases where replantation is impossible.
key_facts: Preserve the amputated part wrapped in saline gauze in a bag on ice, avoiding direct contact to prevent frost injury.
Replant with suprapubic diversion, debridement, urethral and corporal reapproximation, and microvascular anastomosis of dorsal arteries, vein, and nerves.
Microsurgical technique reduces skin loss, stricture, and sensory loss.
Most self-amputation patients are psychotic; psychiatric care is essential.

question: Cytogenetic analysis of a resected renal tumor demonstrates loss of the short arm of chromosome 3 with a somatic VHL mutation. The histologic subtype most consistent with this finding is:
rationale: Deletion of 3p and inactivation of the VHL tumor suppressor are the defining molecular events of clear cell RCC, resulting in constitutive hypoxia-inducible factor signaling and VEGF-driven angiogenesis, which is why antiangiogenic therapy targets this subtype. Papillary tumors are characterized by trisomies of chromosomes 7 and 17 rather than 3p loss. Chromophobe carcinomas show widespread monosomies of other chromosomes. Medullary and collecting duct carcinomas have their own distinct alterations and do not typically involve VHL.
learning_point: Loss or mutation of chromosome 3p, including the VHL gene at 3p25, is the characteristic genetic alteration of clear cell renal cell carcinoma; other subtypes have distinct signatures (papillary: trisomy 7 and 17, MET; chromophobe: multiple chromosomal losses).
key_facts: VHL inactivation in about 50-90% of sporadic clear cell RCC leads to HIF accumulation and VEGF overexpression.
Papillary type 1 RCC: gains of chromosomes 7 and 17, loss of Y, MET mutations.
Chromophobe RCC: losses of chromosomes 1, 2, 6, 10, 13, 17, 21.
Renal medullary carcinoma: SMARCB1 loss, associated with sickle cell trait.

question: Four months after an Indiana pouch for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, a 63-year-old man reports two episodes of low-grade fever with aching over the reservoir. Creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL, ultrasound shows a full pouch with mild bilateral hydronephrosis, and culture grows a sensitive Klebsiella. After antibiotic treatment, the next step is:

options.B: a schedule of routine pouch irrigation.
options.C: change to a larger catheter for drainage.

rationale: Recurrent low-grade pouch infections in the early months after continent diversion reflect mucus accumulation and stasis, and the finding of a distended reservoir with mild hydronephrosis suggests incomplete emptying through mucus plugging. Establishing regular saline irrigation clears the mucus, improves emptying, and lowers the infection rate. Prophylactic antibiotics or urinary acidification are second-line if infections continue despite irrigation. A larger catheter drains urine but not thick mucus, and imaging or endoscopy is reserved for suspicion of stones, stricture, or structural leak rather than as the initial step.
learning_point: Early pouchitis in a continent cutaneous reservoir is usually driven by retained mucus and incomplete emptying; after treating the infection, instituting a program of regular pouch irrigation is the appropriate next step, with prophylactic antibiotics or acidification reserved for persistent infection and pouchogram or endoscopy only if structural problems are suspected.
key_facts: Intestinal segments secrete mucus that pools and promotes bacterial growth, especially in the first months.
Routine saline irrigation reduces symptomatic infections though colonization often persists.
A larger catheter improves urine drainage but does not clear mucus effectively.
Persistent symptoms despite irrigation prompt evaluation for stones, retained mucus plugs, or stomal stenosis.

question: A six-year-old girl falls from a trampoline and has right flank pain with gross hematuria. She is hemodynamically stable. CT urogram shows a markedly dilated right renal pelvis with thin parenchyma, medial perirenal contrast extravasation, and no contrast in the right ureter on 15-minute delayed images; the left kidney and ureter are normal. The next step is:

options.A: retrograde pyelogram with possible stent placement.
options.C: bed rest, antibiotics, and repeat CT in 48 hours.

rationale: The pre-existing hydronephrosis made this kidney vulnerable to rupture, and the absence of ureteral opacification on delayed imaging suggests the collecting system may have disrupted at the UPJ rather than at a fornix. UPJ avulsion is easily missed and renal loss increases with delayed diagnosis, so retrograde pyelography should be performed promptly to define the injury; if the ureter is intact a stent can be placed, and if it is disrupted the study directs surgical repair. Observation alone risks urinoma and loss of the kidney, nephrostomy does not define the ureter, and a renal scan evaluates function rather than anatomy. Exploration without knowing the ureteral status is premature.
learning_point: Blunt renal trauma in a child with a pre-existing hydronephrotic kidney and contrast extravasation but no distal ureteral filling on CT urogram raises concern for UPJ disruption; a retrograde pyelogram is needed to define ureteral continuity before planning repair, and a stent can be placed at the same time.
key_facts: Pre-existing UPJ obstruction predisposes the dilated kidney to rupture with relatively minor trauma.
Nonvisualization of the ipsilateral ureter on delayed imaging is the key sign of UPJ avulsion.
Retrograde pyelography confirms the diagnosis and allows stenting; delayed diagnosis compromises renal salvage.
Observation is appropriate for simple forniceal rupture with an intact ureter.

question: A 68-year-old woman taking prednisone and methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis undergoes complete resection of a solitary 1.8 cm high-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma of the lateral bladder wall. Pathology shows focal lamina propria invasion with muscularis propria present and uninvolved, and no CIS. The next step is:
rationale: A single, small, minimally invasive T1 tumor without CIS is appropriately treated with intravesical therapy and close surveillance rather than immediate extirpative surgery. Because this patient is systemically immunosuppressed, BCG, alone or with interferon, is both less likely to work and more hazardous given the risk of disseminated mycobacterial infection. Mitomycin C acts directly on tumor cells and does not rely on an immune response, making it the best option, with cystectomy held in reserve if the disease recurs or progresses. Partial cystectomy is not standard for high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma.
learning_point: A solitary, focally invasive (T1a) high-grade bladder tumor can usually be managed with intravesical therapy; in a patient on chronic immunosuppression, BCG and interferon are less effective and carry infection risk, so intravesical mitomycin C is the appropriate first choice, with cystectomy reserved for refractory disease.
key_facts: Roughly 70% of unifocal minimally invasive T1 tumors are controlled with intravesical therapy and surveillance.
BCG efficacy depends on a functioning immune system and is relatively contraindicated with immunosuppression.
Mitomycin C is a cytotoxic agent whose effect does not depend on host immunity.
Early cystectomy is considered for extensive T1, variant histology, LVI, CIS, or BCG failure.

question: A four-month-old girl with a single functioning left kidney has had antenatally detected hydronephrosis that has persisted postnatally. Voiding cystourethrogram shows no reflux. A MAG-3 diuretic renogram demonstrates a washout half-time of 28 minutes. Her serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL and the urine is sterile. The best management is:

options.A: continuous antibiotic prophylaxis and ultrasound in six months.
options.B: repeat diuretic renogram in four months.

rationale: This infant has a solitary kidney, a diuretic renogram with prolonged washout indicating obstruction, and a serum creatinine that is elevated for age, so renal function is already being compromised. Pyeloplasty is the standard definitive repair with success rates above 95% in infants and should not be delayed. Repeating the renogram or watching with ultrasound and prophylaxis simply allows further obstruction of the only kidney. A Whitaker test is invasive, carries complications in a solitary kidney, and would not change management when the renogram is already clearly obstructive. Endopyelotomy has inferior success and a less favorable safety profile compared with pyeloplasty in infants.
learning_point: Antenatally detected UPJ obstruction in a solitary kidney with a clearly obstructive diuretic renogram and a rising creatinine should be repaired promptly with pyeloplasty; continued observation, repeat imaging, or a Whitaker test only prolongs obstruction of the only functioning kidney.
key_facts: Diuretic renogram washout half-time > 20 minutes is considered obstructive; a solitary kidney leaves no reserve.
Indications for pyeloplasty in infants include solitary kidney with obstruction, declining function, symptoms, or worsening dilation.
Endopyelotomy has lower success and more risk than pyeloplasty in infants; a Whitaker test is invasive and adds little when the renogram is already diagnostic.
Serum creatinine in a healthy infant should fall to about 0.3-0.4 mg/dL; a value of 0.7 at several months of age indicates reduced function.

question: A 72-year-old woman has had several months of left lower quadrant discomfort and irregular bowel habits. She now reports recurrent dysuria and urgency, and two consecutive cultures each grow more than 100,000 CFU/mL of Escherichia coli, Enterococcus faecalis, and Klebsiella pneumoniae. The most likely underlying cause is:
rationale: Repeated polymicrobial urine cultures with mixed enteric flora in a patient with a chronic bowel complaint strongly suggest a fistula between the colon and bladder. In patients older than 50, diverticular disease of the sigmoid colon is by far the most frequent etiology of colovesical fistula. Crohn's disease is an important cause but typically presents in younger patients and involves the ileum more than the colon. Colon cancer causes a smaller fraction of fistulas, although it must be excluded. Simple infections, stones, and urachal remnants rarely produce truly mixed enteric flora on culture.
learning_point: A urine culture growing multiple enteric organisms in an older adult with bowel symptoms points to a colovesical fistula, and in patients over 50 the most common cause is diverticular disease.
key_facts: Polymicrobial bacteriuria with E. coli, enterococci, and other gut flora suggests an enterovesical communication.
Diverticulitis is the leading cause of colovesical fistula in older adults; Crohn's disease is the usual cause in younger patients.
Pneumaturia and fecaluria are classic but may be absent; CT with oral/rectal contrast is the best initial imaging.
Colon cancer accounts for a minority of fistulas and must still be excluded by colonoscopy before repair.

question: A 70-year-old man who underwent a radical prostatectomy three years ago has a bladder neck contracture treated with transurethral incision. Over the following two months he develops pneumaturia, passage of urine per rectum, and two episodes of urosepsis. Cystoscopy shows a wide posterior defect at the bladder neck, and a cystogram demonstrates contrast filling the rectum. After starting antibiotics, the next step is:

options.A: perineal repair with gracilis muscle interposition.
options.E: prolonged urethral catheter drainage with rectal tube.

rationale: This is a large iatrogenic rectovesical fistula created by deep posterior incision of the bladder neck, complicated by recurrent sepsis. A defect of this size will not seal with catheter or rectal tube drainage, and attempting primary repair in an infected, inflamed field carries a high failure rate. Fecal diversion with a colostomy is therefore the first step: it removes ongoing contamination, allows resolution of infection, and gives the eventual repair the best chance of success. Once the field is clean, transanal, posterior (York-Mason), perineal with gracilis, or abdominal repairs all have good results; the choice is made later.
learning_point: A large iatrogenic rectourethral/rectovesical fistula with recurrent sepsis after post-prostatectomy bladder neck incision will not close spontaneously; the first step before any definitive repair is antibiotics plus fecal diversion to clear infection and optimize healing.
key_facts: Large fistulas, especially after radiation or with sepsis, almost never heal with catheter drainage alone.
Fecal diversion (colostomy) controls contamination and is performed first; definitive repair follows weeks to months later.
Repair may be transanal, perineal (with or without gracilis interposition), or abdominal once the field is clean.
A rectal tube provides inadequate diversion for a large defect.

question: A five-year-old boy is brought in for rapid growth, deepening voice, pubic hair, and penile enlargement over six months. Bone age is 11 years. Serum testosterone is 350 ng/dL while LH and FSH are in the prepubertal range. Scrotal examination is limited by bilateral communicating hydroceles. The test most likely to establish the diagnosis is:

options.E: CT scan of the adrenal glands.
