Ultrasound to look for a subclinical varicocele does not alter management because repair of subclinical varicoceles has not been shown to improve fertility. Antisperm antibody testing is not indicated, and empiric clomiphene is not supported with normal gonadotropins. Intrauterine insemination is the appropriate next step toward conception.
learning_point: Isolated oligospermia with a normal examination, normal hormones, and no correctable cause, confirmed on two concordant semen analyses, is treated with assisted reproduction beginning with intrauterine insemination; further testing adds nothing.
key_facts: Two concordant semen analyses establish the diagnosis; a third is unnecessary.
Scrotal ultrasound for subclinical varicocele does not change management.
Antisperm antibody testing has no indication here.
IUI is appropriate for mild to moderate isolated oligospermia with a normal female partner.

question: A 47-year-old man with recurrent calcium oxalate stones has urinary uric acid of 920 mg/day on 24-hour collection. He asks which protein sources he may eat liberally. In addition to legumes and other vegetables, the recommended protein source is:
rationale: Hyperuricosuria promotes calcium oxalate crystallization, and the main dietary driver is purine intake from animal flesh. Chicken, fish, and beef are all purine-rich and should be limited. Dairy products supply protein without a purine load, and their calcium content also binds intestinal oxalate, which further reduces stone risk. Nuts are an alternative protein but carry a meaningful oxalate load that can raise urinary oxalate when eaten in excess.
learning_point: Calcium oxalate stone formers with hyperuricosuria should limit purine-rich animal flesh (red meat, poultry, fish) and obtain protein from vegetables and dairy; nuts should be used cautiously because they increase urinary oxalate.
key_facts: Meat, poultry, and fish are rich in purines that raise urinary uric acid.
A lacto-ovo-vegetarian diet produces the greatest reduction in uric acid stone risk.
Dairy is a low-purine protein source and dietary calcium binds intestinal oxalate.
Nuts contain substantial oxalate.

question: A term newborn undergoes Plastibell circumcision. On the day of discharge, a 4 mm area of skin dehiscence is noted on the ventral penile shaft with intact underlying dartos and no bleeding. The next step is:

options.A: urgent pediatric urology consultation for degloving injury.
options.B: full-thickness skin graft from the foreskin remnant.
options.C: primary closure with absorbable sutures at the bedside.
options.E: local wound care with wet-to-dry dressings and antibiotic ointment.

rationale: Minor skin separation or loss after neonatal circumcision is common and heals by secondary intention with excellent cosmetic results when managed with simple moist dressings and topical antibiotic. Suturing an awake neonate is unnecessary and distressing, and general anesthesia carries avoidable risk in the newborn. Grafting is reserved for extensive degloving injuries, which this small defect does not represent.
learning_point: Small areas of excess skin removal or skin separation after neonatal clamp circumcision heal well with conservative wound care (wet-to-dry dressings and antibiotic ointment); suturing, anesthesia, and grafting are unnecessary unless degloving is extensive.
key_facts: Clamp circumcision is the most common cause of pediatric penile trauma.
Exposed subcutaneous tissue re-epithelializes with excellent cosmesis.
General anesthesia in the newborn carries real risk and is avoided for minor wounds.
Skin grafting is reserved for extensive penile skin loss.

question: A 70-year-old man with minimally symptomatic metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer is scheduled for his first infusion of autologous cellular immunotherapy (sipuleucel-T). Thirty minutes before infusion he should receive acetaminophen and:
rationale: Sipuleucel-T infusions commonly cause chills, rigors, fever, and fatigue related to cytokine release from activated antigen-presenting cells. Labeling recommends premedication with acetaminophen and an oral antihistamine such as diphenhydramine. Corticosteroids are not recommended because immunosuppression could interfere with the vaccine's mechanism. Benzodiazepines and antiemetics are not part of the standard premedication regimen.
learning_point: Sipuleucel-T, an autologous dendritic-cell vaccine for asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic mCRPC, causes infusion-related chills and fever; recommended premedication is acetaminophen plus an oral antihistamine, not steroids or opioids.
key_facts: Sipuleucel-T uses autologous APCs activated with PAP-GM-CSF fusion protein.
Median overall survival benefit was about 4 months versus placebo.
Common adverse effects are chills, fatigue, fever, and back pain from cytokine release.
Glucocorticoids are avoided because they could blunt the immune response.

question: A 26-year-old man develops cola-colored urine two days after the onset of fever and pharyngitis. Blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg, creatinine is 2.2 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows 3+ blood, 2+ protein, and dysmorphic red cells without bacteria. Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis. He recalls a similar episode in college. The next step is:

options.A: start lisinopril and recheck in two weeks.

rationale: Synpharyngitic gross hematuria with proteinuria, hypertension, and renal insufficiency in a young man with a prior episode is classic for IgA nephropathy, a chronic progressive glomerulonephritis. The timing distinguishes it from post-streptococcal GN, which follows infection by weeks. Because renal function is impaired and the process appears recurrent, histologic confirmation by renal biopsy is required before committing to steroids or ACE inhibition. CT is unnecessary when ultrasound excludes obstruction and the urinalysis points to a glomerular source, and antibiotics alone do not address the nephropathy.
learning_point: Gross hematuria with proteinuria and renal insufficiency occurring concurrently with pharyngitis, especially with a prior similar episode, suggests IgA nephropathy; diagnosis requires renal biopsy before immunosuppressive or antiproteinuric therapy.
key_facts: IgA nephropathy flares within days of an upper respiratory infection; post-infectious GN appears 2-3 weeks later.
Most common primary glomerulonephritis; typically young males.
Normal renal ultrasound with proteinuria makes obstruction unlikely.
Steroids or ACE inhibitors are used only after histologic diagnosis.

question: A 26-year-old nulliparous distance runner reports urine leakage only during long training runs and races. She is otherwise continent. After four months of supervised pelvic floor physiotherapy, leakage persists. She hopes to start a family within two years. The next step is:
rationale: Activity-limited stress incontinence in a young woman planning pregnancy is best managed with a removable intravaginal support device that she wears only during the provoking activity. Mid-urethral and pubovaginal slings are effective but are generally deferred until childbearing is complete and are excessive for leakage confined to strenuous exercise. Bulking agents have modest durability and are not ideal first choice here. Duloxetine and imipramine are off-label for SUI in the United States and carry side effects without guideline endorsement.
learning_point: For situational exercise-related stress incontinence in a young nulliparous woman who has failed pelvic floor training, an incontinence pessary or intravaginal device is the next step; slings are deferred until childbearing is complete and imipramine is not guideline-supported.
key_facts: Pelvic floor muscle training is first-line for mild SUI.
Incontinence pessaries can be used only during provoking activities.
AUA/SUFU SUI guideline does not include imipramine as a treatment.
Sling surgery is generally deferred in women planning pregnancy.

question: A 29-year-old man with migraine prophylaxis on topiramate has formed three calcium phosphate stones in two years. His neurologist considers the drug essential. A 24-hour urine shows pH 7.0, citrate 180 mg/day, calcium 170 mg/day, and oxalate 30 mg/day. The best pharmacologic intervention is:
rationale: Topiramate inhibits carbonic anhydrase, producing an acquired distal renal tubular acidosis with alkaline urine, hypocitraturia, and calcium phosphate stone formation. When the medication cannot be stopped, potassium citrate is given, as in primary distal RTA, to replete citrate and correct systemic acidosis. Sodium bicarbonate also provides alkali but the sodium load increases calcium excretion and is less desirable. Thiazide addresses hypercalciuria, which is normal here; allopurinol lowers uric acid; and tiopronin is for cystinuria.
learning_point: Topiramate, a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, causes a distal renal tubular acidosis picture (high urine pH, hypocitraturia) and calcium phosphate stones; if the drug must be continued, potassium citrate is the treatment.
key_facts: Topiramate and zonisamide inhibit carbonic anhydrase, raising urine pH and lowering citrate.
Resulting stones are calcium phosphate.
Potassium citrate corrects hypocitraturia and metabolic acidosis; sodium bicarbonate adds a sodium load.
Thiazide treats hypercalciuria, which is not the main lithogenic defect.

question: A 66-year-old man with metastatic urothelial carcinoma achieves stable disease after six cycles of gemcitabine and cisplatin. Eight months later CT shows new liver and nodal metastases. His ECOG performance status is 1 and creatinine clearance is 42 mL/min. The next step is:
rationale: Progression within a year of platinum chemotherapy defines platinum-refractory disease, and PD-1/PD-L1 blockade with agents such as nivolumab is the standard second-line treatment, with durable responses in roughly one in five patients and no renal toxicity. Re-challenging with cisplatin is both ineffective after failure and unsafe with his reduced clearance; carboplatin spares the kidney but is less active and still unlikely to work after platinum failure. With a good performance status, supportive care alone is premature, and VEGF-targeted agents such as sunitinib have no established role in urothelial cancer.
learning_point: Metastatic urothelial carcinoma progressing within 12 months after platinum-based chemotherapy, particularly with impaired renal function, should be treated with a PD-1/PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor (e.g., nivolumab) rather than re-challenge with platinum.
key_facts: Checkpoint inhibitors (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, atezolizumab, etc.) are approved for platinum-refractory urothelial cancer.
They avoid cisplatin nephrotoxicity; objective response rates are about 20%.
Carboplatin is inferior to cisplatin and unlikely to help after platinum failure.
Cabozantinib is not established therapy in this setting.

question: A 61-year-old man taking daily oxycodone for two years for lumbar radiculopathy is scheduled for robotic radical cystectomy for a cT2 posterior-wall urothelial carcinoma with normal renal function and an uninvolved prostatic urethra. In planning his enhanced recovery pathway, which element is contraindicated?
rationale: Alvimopan accelerates gastrointestinal recovery after cystectomy, but its label contraindicates use in patients who have received therapeutic doses of opioids for more than seven consecutive days immediately before starting the drug, because chronic opioid exposure heightens sensitivity to antagonist effects such as abdominal pain and vomiting. A thoracic epidural is reasonable despite lumbar disc disease at a distant level. Normal renal function and a clear urethral margin permit an orthotopic neobladder. Early feeding and omitting bowel preparation are standard components of enhanced recovery.
learning_point: Alvimopan, a peripheral mu-opioid antagonist that shortens ileus after cystectomy, is contraindicated in patients who have taken therapeutic opioids for more than seven consecutive days before surgery because of heightened sensitivity to antagonist effects.
key_facts: Alvimopan reduces time to bowel recovery and length of stay after radical cystectomy.
Chronic preoperative opioid use (> 7 days) is a contraindication.
Epidural analgesia is not precluded by remote cervical disc disease.
Creatinine 1.2 and a dome tumor do not preclude continent diversion or neobladder.

question: An 8-year-old boy has six weeks of frequency, dysuria, and episodic gross hematuria with repeatedly sterile urine cultures. Bladder ultrasound shows irregular, diffuse bladder wall thickening to 12 mm. Cystoscopic biopsy demonstrates a dense inflammatory infiltrate with abundant eosinophils extending through the muscularis. The next step is:

options.D: corticosteroids, antihistamines, and an oral antibiotic course.

rationale: A transmural eosinophilic infiltrate in a child with sterile hematuria and dysuria is eosinophilic cystitis, a benign inflammatory condition. Symptomatic children are treated medically with corticosteroids and antihistamines plus antibiotics, with transurethral resection reserved for an isolated lesion. Antibiotics alone do not treat the eosinophilic inflammation. Partial or radical cystectomy and intravesical BCG are inappropriate for a nonmalignant process.
learning_point: Eosinophilic cystitis in a symptomatic child, diagnosed by transmural eosinophilic infiltrate on biopsy, is treated with antibiotics, corticosteroids, and antihistamines (with TUR of an isolated lesion); isolated antibiotics or partial cystectomy are inappropriate.
key_facts: Presents in young boys with dysuria, frequency, and hematuria with sterile urine.
Ultrasound shows diffuse or focal bladder wall thickening mimicking a mass.
Self-limited in infants; symptomatic children get steroids, antihistamines, and antibiotics.
No role for radical resection.

question: A 59-year-old woman on hemodialysis for diabetic nephropathy requires contrast-enhanced MRI to characterize a complex renal cyst, and no alternative study is acceptable. The single most effective measure to lower her risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis is:

options.A: an extra peritoneal dialysis exchange that evening.
options.B: substituting gadodiamide for a macrocyclic agent.
options.E: oral N-acetylcysteine before and after the scan.

rationale: Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis results from retained gadolinium in patients with severe renal impairment. If the agent cannot be avoided, prompt hemodialysis after administration clears the majority of circulating gadolinium and is the most effective risk-reduction strategy. Peritoneal dialysis removes gadolinium inefficiently and does not substitute. Gadodiamide, a linear agent, carries higher NSF risk than macrocyclic agents, so switching to it would be harmful. Steroids and N-acetylcysteine have no proven role in preventing NSF.
learning_point: When gadolinium is unavoidable in an ESRD patient, the most effective way to reduce nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk is prompt hemodialysis immediately after the study; peritoneal dialysis clears gadolinium poorly and all agents carry some risk.
key_facts: NSF is linked to gadolinium exposure in patients with GFR < 30 or on dialysis.
Linear agents such as gadodiamide carry higher risk than macrocyclic agents (gadobutrol, gadoteridol).
Hemodialysis removes most gadolinium in a single session; peritoneal dialysis does not.
Avoiding gadolinium altogether is best when possible.

question: A 59-year-old man with progressive multiple sclerosis has had a urethral Foley for seven years and undergoes conversion to a 22 Fr suprapubic tube. Two months later he leaks continuously per urethra despite solifenacin. Cystoscopy shows a patulous, fixed-open membranous urethra, a 50 mL capacity trabeculated bladder, and a well-positioned suprapubic catheter. The best management is:

options.E: exchange to a 28 Fr suprapubic catheter.

rationale: This bladder has essentially lost all storage function and the outlet has been destroyed by years of urethral catheterization, so both components must be addressed. A bulking agent or an artificial sphincter cannot compensate for a fixed-open, eroded urethra, and an AUS in a neurogenic patient with a 50 mL bladder would risk erosion and upper tract damage. Augmentation alone enlarges the reservoir but leaves the incompetent outlet leaking. A larger suprapubic tube does not alter urethral loss. Ileal conduit diversion abandons the unsalvageable bladder and resolves the incontinence.
learning_point: A neurogenic patient with a tiny, poorly compliant bladder and a destroyed urethral outlet after years of indwelling catheterization is best managed with ileal conduit diversion; bulking, slings, or augmentation alone fail to address both the bladder and the incompetent outlet.
key_facts: Long-term urethral catheters cause urethral erosion and intrinsic sphincter deficiency.
Bladder capacity of about 60 mL indicates an end-stage, non-salvageable bladder.
Augmentation requires a competent or reconstructable outlet.
Upsizing the suprapubic tube does not stop urethral leakage.

question: After an uncomplicated office injection of a urethral bulking agent in a 72-year-old woman, the medical assistant notices the syringe lot expired two months earlier. The patient has already left the procedure room. The most appropriate next step is:

options.A: file a report with the FDA MedWatch program only.
options.B: inform the patient of the error and enter it into the institutional safety event reporting system.
options.C: prescribe a two-week course of oral antibiotics without discussing the error.
options.D: contact hospital risk management before deciding whether to inform the patient.
options.E: attempt endoscopic aspiration of the injected material.

rationale: Patients have a right to know when a deviation from standard care has occurred, and transparent disclosure combined with institutional safety reporting allows monitoring of the patient and a root cause analysis to prevent recurrence. Withholding disclosure while awaiting legal advice or quietly prescribing antibiotics violates this duty. Removing a bulking agent is not feasible. External reporting to regulators may be appropriate later but does not substitute for patient disclosure and internal safety reporting.
learning_point: When a medical error such as use of an expired implant material is discovered, the correct response is honest disclosure to the patient, monitoring, and reporting through the institutional safety event system to enable root cause analysis; regulatory notification, removal, or IV antibiotics are not the first step.
key_facts: Disclosure of adverse events to patients is an ethical obligation.
Institutional safety reporting drives root cause analysis and prevention.
Joint Commission sentinel event reporting is voluntary and does not help the individual patient.
Legal consultation does not replace disclosure.

question: A 55-year-old, 70 kg woman complains of daytime frequency. Urinalysis and glucose are normal. A three-day frequency-volume chart shows a mean 24-hour urine output of 3200 mL across 11 voids, of which 700 mL is produced during sleep over two voids. The next step is:

options.E: water deprivation test with urine osmolality.

rationale: Her output of about 46 mL/kg/day exceeds the 40 mL/kg threshold for global polyuria, so the frequency reflects excess urine production rather than bladder dysfunction. The nocturnal fraction (roughly 22%) does not meet criteria for nocturnal polyuria, making sleep apnea evaluation and desmopressin unhelpful and the latter potentially dangerous. Glucose is already normal. A water deprivation test with urine osmolality separates primary polydipsia (concentrated urine) from diabetes insipidus (dilute urine) and directs further workup. Antimuscarinics do not address polyuria.
learning_point: Total 24-hour urine output exceeding 40 mL/kg defines global polyuria; the next step is an overnight water deprivation test with urine osmolality to distinguish primary polydipsia from diabetes insipidus, not LUTS medication or nocturnal polyuria workup.
key_facts: Global polyuria: > 40 mL/kg/24 h (or > 2.8-3 L/day).
Nocturnal polyuria index > 33% in older adults defines nocturnal polyuria; this patient does not meet it.
Urine osmolality > 800 mOsm/kg after deprivation suggests primary polydipsia.
Alpha-blockers and antimuscarinics do not treat polyuria.

question: A 58-year-old woman with mixed urinary incontinence undergoes videourodynamics. Within seconds of starting filling, with only 15 mL instilled and no rise in detrusor pressure, contrast is seen dripping from the introitus. The next step is:

options.A: confirm catheter location with fluoroscopy and reposition.
options.B: switch from contrast to saline as the filling medium.
options.C: reduce the fill rate to 10 mL/min.
options.D: record this as low Valsalva leak point pressure.
options.E: exchange the water-filled catheter for an air-charged catheter.

rationale: Leakage at a trivially small volume without any pressure change means the infused fluid is not reaching the bladder, most commonly because the catheter has coiled back into the urethra or was inadvertently placed in the vagina. In videourodynamics a brief fluoroscopic image confirms this immediately and the catheter can be repositioned; without fluoroscopy, manual repositioning is performed. Changing the fluid, catheter type, or fill rate does not correct a malpositioned catheter, and interpreting this as a true leak point pressure would be an error.
learning_point: Immediate leakage at minimal filling volume during urodynamics almost always indicates the filling catheter is malpositioned (curled in the urethra or in the vagina); confirm position fluoroscopically or by manual repositioning before changing other parameters.
key_facts: Artifacts should be excluded before interpreting urodynamic findings.
Fluoroscopy during videourodynamics shows catheter location instantly.
Catheter size, transducer type, and fluid medium do not explain leakage at 10 mL.
Fill rate is decreased, not increased, for suspected artifactual detrusor overactivity.

question: A 39-year-old man with a history of hypospadias repair in childhood presents with a weak stream. Retrograde urethrogram demonstrates a 2.5 cm stricture of the mid-pendulous urethra. He has never had prior stricture treatment. The most appropriate initial management is:

options.E: serial dilation with filiforms and followers.

rationale: Strictures of the penile urethra have a poor response to dilation or internal urethrotomy, with recurrence being the rule, so urethroplasty is recommended as the initial definitive treatment. Unlike the bulbar urethra, where excision and anastomosis works well for short strictures, the penile urethra lacks the redundancy to allow excision without tethering and chordee, so tissue transfer with a buccal graft or skin flap is preferred. Perineal urethrostomy is a salvage option for patients who decline or are unfit for reconstruction.
learning_point: Penile (pendulous) urethral strictures recur at high rates after dilation or urethrotomy, so primary urethroplasty is recommended; in the penile urethra, substitution/augmentation (buccal graft or flap) is preferred over excision and anastomosis to avoid chordee.
key_facts: Endoscopic management is reasonable initially for short bulbar strictures but not penile strictures.
Excision with primary anastomosis in the penile urethra causes shortening and ventral curvature.
Buccal mucosa graft onlay is the workhorse for penile strictures.
Meatal/fossa navicularis strictures may be managed initially with dilation.

question: A 64-year-old woman with a vaginal bulge and demonstrable stress incontinence has POP-Q measurements of Aa +1, Ba +2, C +1, D -6, Ap -2, Bp -2, TVL 9 cm. PVR is 60 mL. She desires definitive surgical treatment. In addition to a mid-urethral sling, the operation should include:
rationale: The anterior wall and cervix are both beyond the hymen, so two compartments need repair, while posterior support (Bp -2) is normal and does not require a rectocele repair. The 7 cm distance between point C and point D indicates a markedly elongated cervix; uterine-preserving procedures such as sacrospinous hysteropexy or sacrohysteropexy suspend the uterus but leave the elongated cervix protruding. Anterior repair alone ignores the apical defect and would fail. Vaginal hysterectomy with anterior repair addresses both prolapsed compartments.
learning_point: Stage 2 apical (uterine) prolapse with anterior wall descent and an elongated cervix (large C-to-D discrepancy) is best treated with vaginal hysterectomy plus anterior repair at the time of sling; uterine-sparing hysteropexy leaves the elongated cervix, and posterior repair is not indicated without posterior descent.
key_facts: POP-Q point C is the cervix, D the posterior fornix; a large C-D gap indicates cervical elongation.
Ba > -1 indicates anterior compartment prolapse; Bp at -2 or less is normal posterior support.
Hysteropexy/sacrouteropexy do not shorten an elongated cervix.
Concomitant SUI is treated with a sling.

question: A 55-year-old man with refractory urgency incontinence undergoes percutaneous nerve evaluation for sacral neuromodulation. Test stimulation produces a bellows contraction of the perineum and a pulling sensation around the anus, but there is no toe or foot movement at any amplitude. The next step is:

options.A: move the needle to the next foramen caudally.
options.B: reposition the needle one foramen cephalad.
options.C: withdraw the needle 1 cm and retest at the same level.
options.D: cross to the contralateral foramen at the same level.
options.E: accept this response and secure the lead.

rationale: An isolated bellows response without any lower-extremity motor response is characteristic of S4 stimulation. The target is S3, which produces a bellows contraction together with flexion of the great toe and sensation in the perineum or genitals. Because S4 lies caudal to S3, the needle should be moved one level cephalad. Moving caudally to S5 or adjusting depth will not generate an S3 response, and switching sides is reserved for an inadequate response once the correct level has been identified.
learning_point: During sacral neuromodulation lead testing, anal bellows with perianal tapping but no great-toe dorsiflexion indicates S4 placement; the needle should be moved one level cephalad to S3, which gives bellows plus plantar flexion/dorsiflexion of the great toe.
key_facts: S3 response: bellows contraction of the perineum and great toe flexion; sensation in perineum/rectum/vagina.
S2 response: clamp-like anal sphincter contraction, leg/heel rotation, plantar flexion of whole foot.
S4 response: bellows only, no lower extremity movement.
Contralateral side is tried if ipsilateral S3 response is inadequate.

question: A 41-year-old man had a vasectomy five months ago. His first post-vasectomy semen analysis at 12 weeks showed 400,000 non-motile sperm/mL and a second at 16 weeks showed 150,000 non-motile sperm/mL. A fresh, uncentrifuged specimen today shows 60,000 non-motile sperm/mL. The appropriate advice is:

options.A: obtain a centrifuged specimen to confirm azoospermia.
options.B: obtain scrotal ultrasound to evaluate for a sperm granuloma.
options.C: continue alternative contraception and repeat testing in six weeks.
options.D: the vasectomy is successful and other contraception may be discontinued.
options.E: schedule repeat vasectomy for persistent sperm.

rationale: The AUA vasectomy guideline defines occlusive success as a single fresh uncentrifuged PVSA showing either azoospermia or only rare non-motile sperm below 100,000/mL. This man's current result of 60,000 non-motile sperm/mL meets that threshold, so he may rely on the vasectomy for contraception. The declining counts simply reflect clearance of residual distal sperm. Repeat vasectomy would be indicated for persistent motile sperm or recanalization, not here, and centrifugation or ultrasound adds nothing to the decision.
learning_point: Per AUA guidelines, a man may stop other contraception when a single fresh, uncentrifuged post-vasectomy semen analysis shows azoospermia or rare non-motile sperm (< 100,000/mL); no repeat testing or further intervention is needed.
key_facts: Threshold for vasectomy success: azoospermia or < 100,000 non-motile sperm/mL.
Any motile sperm or >= 100,000 non-motile sperm/mL warrants repeat testing.
PVSA is typically performed 8-16 weeks after vasectomy.
Post-ejaculate urinalysis is for retrograde ejaculation, not PVSA.

question: During open left radical nephrectomy for a 14 cm upper-pole tumor displacing the renal hilum medially, a large anteriorly directed arterial trunk arising from the aorta just above the left renal vein is encountered. If misidentified as the renal artery and divided, this vessel is most likely the:
rationale: The superior mesenteric artery arises from the anterior aorta just cephalad to the left renal vein and, when a large left-sided mass distorts hilar anatomy, it can be mistaken for the left renal artery. Division is catastrophic because it supplies the entire small bowel and the right and transverse colon, and a vascular surgeon must repair it immediately. The inferior mesenteric artery arises more caudally and is small; the celiac trunk is more cephalad behind the pancreas; the gonadal and inferior phrenic arteries are small branches unlikely to be confused with the renal artery.
learning_point: During left radical nephrectomy for a large tumor, the superior mesenteric artery can be mistaken for the left renal artery and ligated, a catastrophic error requiring immediate vascular repair; the SMA arises anteriorly from the aorta near the level of the left renal vein.
key_facts: The SMA originates from the anterior aorta behind the neck of the pancreas and crosses the duodenum.
The left renal vein passes between the aorta and the SMA.
The IMA arises lower and is smaller; it can usually be ligated safely.
SMA injury threatens the entire small bowel and right colon.

question: A 48-year-old man with erectile dysfunction asks about avanafil after seeing an advertisement. Compared with sildenafil, vardenafil, and tadalafil, the characteristic unique to avanafil is:

options.B: absorption unaffected by a high-fat meal.
options.C: highest response rate in diabetic men.
options.D: approved for dosing about 15 minutes before intercourse.
options.E: lowest incidence of headache and flushing.

rationale: Avanafil has the shortest time to peak concentration of the PDE-5 inhibitors and is the only one FDA-labeled for administration as early as approximately 15 minutes before sexual activity. Its half-life of 3-5 hours is comparable to sildenafil and vardenafil, while tadalafil has by far the longest duration. Like sildenafil and vardenafil, avanafil's absorption is slowed by a high-fat meal; only tadalafil is unaffected by food. There is no evidence that avanafil is more effective or better tolerated than the other agents.
learning_point: Avanafil is distinguished from other PDE-5 inhibitors by its rapid onset, with FDA labeling allowing dosing approximately 15 minutes before intercourse; it does not have superior efficacy, fewer side effects, the longest half-life, or food independence.
key_facts: Avanafil Tmax is 0.3-0.5 hours; labeled for use as early as 15 minutes before sex.
Half-life 3-5 hours, similar to sildenafil and vardenafil; tadalafil is about 17.5 hours.
High-fat meals delay absorption of avanafil, sildenafil, and vardenafil.
No head-to-head evidence of better efficacy or tolerability.

question: A 58-year-old man with back pain and malaise has creatinine of 4.6 mg/dL and potassium of 5.2 mEq/L. Non-contrast CT shows a soft-tissue mantle surrounding the infrarenal aorta and both common iliac arteries with medial deviation of both ureters but no pelvicaliceal dilation. CT-guided core biopsy shows fibrosis and chronic inflammation without malignancy. The next step is:
rationale: Dense retroperitoneal fibrosis can encase the ureters and renal pelves so rigidly that obstruction occurs without hydronephrosis, as suggested here by the medial ureteral deviation and acute kidney injury. Relieving the obstruction with bilateral ureteral stents is the first priority to recover renal function and correct hyperkalemia; percutaneous nephrostomy is an alternative but difficult without dilated calyces. Steroids, tamoxifen, or ureterolysis treat the underlying fibrosis but should follow decompression. Nuclear renography is uninformative at this level of renal dysfunction.
learning_point: Retroperitoneal fibrosis can obstruct the ureters and renal pelves without visible hydronephrosis; in a patient with acute kidney injury and a periaortic mass with benign biopsy, bilateral ureteral stents (or nephrostomies) should be placed first to relieve obstruction before steroids or ureterolysis.
key_facts: Encasement of the collecting system can prevent dilation despite obstruction.
Diuretic renography is unreliable with severely reduced GFR.
Corticosteroids and ureterolysis are definitive treatments after decompression.
Biopsy excludes lymphoma or metastatic disease mimicking RPF.

question: A 70-year-old man has had four separate low-grade Ta bladder tumors resected over four years and completed a six-week BCG induction course after the most recent recurrence. Surveillance cystoscopy 10 months later reveals a single 3 mm papillary lesion with normal upper tract imaging. After cystoscopic fulguration, the next step is:
rationale: This patient has recurrent low-grade non-invasive disease, which has a high recurrence rate but a very low risk of progression to higher stage or grade. After fulguration of a tiny papillary recurrence, continued surveillance is appropriate; intravesical chemotherapy or less frequent cystoscopy are reasonable alternative strategies. Repeat or maintenance BCG is unlikely to change the recurrence pattern of low-grade disease and exposes him to local and systemic toxicity. Valrubicin is approved for BCG-refractory CIS, and cystectomy is not indicated for low-volume low-grade disease.
learning_point: A small recurrent low-grade Ta tumor after induction BCG in a patient with a history of only low-grade Ta disease remains low/intermediate risk; management is fulguration (or office ablation) with surveillance, not further BCG, valrubicin, or cystectomy.
key_facts: Recurrent low-grade Ta disease has a 5-year recurrence risk of 60-70% but progression risk under 5%.
BCG does little to alter the recurrence pattern of low-grade disease and carries morbidity.
Valrubicin is indicated for BCG-refractory CIS.
Office fulguration and surveillance reduce treatment burden; intravesical chemotherapy is an alternative.

question: A 51-year-old man with Peyronie's disease received his first intralesional collagenase injection three days ago. He wakes at night with a popping sensation during a nocturnal erection followed by severe pain, rapid detumescence, and marked ecchymosis extending to the scrotum. The next step is:

options.B: penile duplex ultrasound to decide on surgery.
options.C: postpone the second injection by two weeks.

rationale: Collagenase weakens the tunica albuginea, and a small percentage of men sustain a corporal rupture during erection in the days after injection. Acute pain with a pop, detumescence, and spreading ecchymosis is clinically diagnostic of penile fracture and should prompt surgical exploration and repair to preserve erectile function and prevent deformity. Ultrasound may be falsely negative when swelling is extensive and should not delay surgery. Conservative measures or simply rescheduling the next injection would leave a tunical defect untreated, and a urethrogram is only needed when urethral injury is suspected.
learning_point: Sudden severe penile pain and swelling within days of intralesional collagenase (Xiaflex) injection for Peyronie's disease should be presumed to be a corporal rupture (penile fracture), which occurs in about 0.5% of treated men, and warrants surgical exploration rather than observation or NSAIDs.
key_facts: Mild bruising, pain, and swelling are expected for days to weeks after injection.
Corporal rupture occurs in roughly 0.5% of patients, often with modeling or erection.
Ultrasound can be falsely negative with marked swelling and should not exclude surgery.
Cystoscopy is reserved for suspected ventral fractures with urethral injury.

question: A 27-year-old motorcyclist sustains a degloving scrotal injury. In the emergency department both testes are intact and exposed; roughly half of the remaining scrotal skin is contused, dusky, and of uncertain viability. Tetanus prophylaxis and antibiotics are given. The next step is:

options.A: negative pressure wound therapy over the exposed testes.
options.B: meshed split-thickness skin graft to the testes.
options.C: placement of the testes in medial thigh pouches.
options.D: immediate debridement of all dusky skin with primary closure.
options.E: saline-moistened dressings and reassessment at 24 hours.

rationale: Scrotal skin that appears dusky immediately after trauma frequently survives, and a short period of observation with moist dressings allows the line between viable and nonviable tissue to become clear. Immediate aggressive debridement risks removing salvageable skin, and definitive reconstructive choices such as thigh pouches, grafting, or negative pressure therapy should be made only after demarcation. Because scrotal skin is so elastic, many patients can undergo primary closure once the truly nonviable tissue is removed.
learning_point: In scrotal avulsion injuries with large areas of questionable skin viability, the initial step is a 24-hour period of observation with moist saline dressings to allow demarcation before deciding on debridement, closure, thigh pouches, or grafting.
key_facts: Dusky or bruised scrotal skin may be viable; premature debridement sacrifices tissue.
Scrotal skin is highly elastic; even 50% loss can often be closed primarily after demarcation.
Thigh pouches and split-thickness grafts are reserved for extensive, nonviable skin loss.
Keep exposed testes moist while awaiting demarcation.

question: A 61-year-old woman with an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 underwent laparoscopic cryoablation of a 2.8 cm biopsy-proven clear cell RCC of the left kidney. Follow-up MRI at 12 months showed a non-enhancing ablation zone, but MRI at 24 months shows a new 1.6 cm enhancing nodule within the ablation bed. She is asymptomatic. The next step is:

options.D: systemic therapy with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

rationale: A new enhancing nodule within a previously non-enhancing ablation zone represents local recurrence, which occurs in roughly 7-10% of cryoablated tumors. Continued surveillance is inappropriate for an enhancing, growing lesion in a patient with a long life expectancy. Repeat ablation is the usual salvage and is less morbid and more effective when performed percutaneously. Salvage partial nephrectomy after ablation is associated with high complication rates because of perinephric fibrosis, and radical nephrectomy would unnecessarily sacrifice nephrons in a patient with chronic kidney disease. Systemic therapy is not indicated for localized recurrence.
learning_point: Local recurrence after renal cryoablation (7-10% risk), seen as a new enhancing mass in the ablation bed, is best treated with repeat ablation, preferably percutaneous; surveillance is inadequate for a growing enhancing lesion, salvage partial nephrectomy carries high complication rates, and radical nephrectomy is undesirable with CKD.
key_facts: Any new or increasing enhancement in a treated bed on follow-up imaging signals recurrence.
Repeat cryoablation is the most common salvage; percutaneous approach reduces morbidity.
Salvage partial nephrectomy after ablation is technically difficult; open approach if attempted.
Preserve nephrons in patients with reduced GFR.

question: A 44-year-old man has had four calcium phosphate (apatite) stones over five years. A 24-hour urine on his usual diet shows volume 2.2 L, calcium 210 mg (upper normal 250), oxalate 28 mg, citrate 620 mg, sodium 120 mEq, uric acid 580 mg, and pH 6.9. The most appropriate intervention to lower his stone risk is:
rationale: Although his parameters fall within the laboratory reference range, he is a recurrent stone former with high-normal urinary calcium, and guidelines support thiazide therapy to reduce calcium excretion in this setting. Potassium citrate would raise an already alkaline urine pH and increase calcium phosphate supersaturation. Sodium excretion is normal, so further sodium restriction would not help, and allopurinol or pyridoxine target uric acid and oxalate abnormalities that he does not have.
learning_point: In a recurrent calcium phosphate stone former with high-normal urinary calcium and alkaline urine, thiazide is the recommended therapy; potassium citrate should be avoided because further alkalinization promotes calcium phosphate precipitation.
key_facts: AUA guideline: thiazide for recurrent calcium stones with high or high-normal urinary calcium.
Calcium phosphate stones form in alkaline urine; alkali therapy can worsen them.
Sodium restriction helps only if urinary sodium is elevated.
Magnesium/pyridoxine target hyperoxaluria; protein restriction does not address phosphate stones.

question: A 27-year-old man has multiple 3-5 mm reddish-brown papules on the penile shaft. Biopsy shows full-thickness epithelial atypia indistinguishable from carcinoma in situ, and the diagnosis of Bowenoid papulosis is made. The feature that this condition shares with penile carcinoma in situ is:

options.A: need for ablative or topical chemotherapeutic treatment.
options.B: likelihood of progression to invasive carcinoma.
options.C: presentation as a solitary velvety plaque.

rationale: Bowenoid papulosis and penile CIS look identical under the microscope and both are strongly linked to HPV-16, which is believed to be causative. The clinical behavior differs sharply: Bowenoid papulosis affects younger men, appears as multiple pigmented papules rather than a solitary plaque, and has an essentially benign course without malignant progression, so treatment is usually unnecessary. Penile CIS, by contrast, can progress and is treated with topical 5-FU, imiquimod, or laser ablation.
learning_point: Bowenoid papulosis and penile carcinoma in situ are histologically indistinguishable and both are associated with HPV-16, but Bowenoid papulosis occurs in younger men, presents as multiple pigmented papules, follows a benign course, and typically requires no treatment.
key_facts: Bowenoid papulosis: multiple 2-30 mm pigmented papules in men in their 20s-30s.
HPV-16 DNA is found in both Bowenoid papulosis and penile CIS.
Despite CIS-like histology, Bowenoid papulosis essentially never progresses to invasive cancer.
Penile CIS is treated with topical 5-FU, imiquimod, or laser.

question: A 52-year-old man with a history of calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis takes 2 g of ascorbic acid daily as a supplement. The expected effect on his 24-hour urine is:
rationale: Ascorbic acid is metabolized in part to oxalate, and gram-level daily doses measurably increase urinary oxalate excretion in both healthy people and stone formers, raising calcium oxalate supersaturation. Studies show no significant change in urine pH, and vitamin C does not directly affect calcium, citrate, or uric acid excretion. Patients with calcium oxalate stones should therefore avoid high-dose vitamin C supplements.
learning_point: High-dose vitamin C (1-2 g/day) is metabolized to oxalate and increases urinary oxalate excretion without changing urine pH, so it should be avoided by calcium oxalate stone formers.
key_facts: Ascorbic acid is metabolized to oxalate.
1-2 g/day raises urinary oxalate in both normal subjects and stone formers.
Urine pH is not meaningfully altered.
Supplemental vitamin C is discouraged in calcium oxalate stone formers.

question: A 30-year-old man undergoing infertility evaluation has an ejaculate volume of 0.8 mL with pH 6.5 and no sperm on two centrifuged specimens. Testes are 20 mL bilaterally, FSH is 4 IU/L, and neither vas deferens is palpable. Before proceeding with sperm retrieval and IVF, the genetic test that must be obtained for him and his partner is:
rationale: Low-volume acidic azoospermia with normal testicular size and gonadotropins and nonpalpable vasa indicates obstructive azoospermia from congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, which is a genital form of cystic fibrosis in most men. CFTR testing is mandatory for the patient and essential for the partner so the couple can be counseled about the risk of cystic fibrosis in offspring conceived with retrieved sperm. Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing (including AZF analysis) are reserved for non-obstructive azoospermia with testicular failure, and KAL-1 mutations cause hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which is excluded by normal FSH.
learning_point: Low-volume azoospermia with bilaterally absent vasa and partial epididymal absence is congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, which requires CFTR mutation testing of the patient and partner before sperm retrieval and IVF; karyotype and Y-microdeletion testing are for non-obstructive azoospermia.
key_facts: CBAVD is associated with CFTR mutations in the majority of cases; seminal vesicles are often absent/hypoplastic giving low volume, acidic ejaculate.
Partner must be tested for CFTR carrier status before ICSI.
Karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion are indicated in NOA (small testes, high FSH).
Unilateral vasal absence warrants renal ultrasound; bilateral absence suggests CFTR.

question: A 63-year-old woman with a history of radical hysterectomy and pelvic radiation for cervical cancer has had bilateral ureteral stents exchanged every three months for four years. She presents with two episodes of brisk gross hematuria requiring transfusion. Cystoscopy shows blood emanating from the right ureteral orifice around the stent, and CT urography is unremarkable. The next step is:

options.C: exchange of the right ureteral stent.

rationale: Massive intermittent hematuria in a patient with chronic ureteral stents after pelvic surgery and radiation is the classic presentation of a ureteroiliac arterial fistula. Routine hematuria evaluation with cystoscopy and CT is usually normal because the fistula is intermittently tamponaded by the stent. Selective or provocative iliac angiography has the highest yield and permits immediate endovascular treatment with embolization or a covered stent. Ureteroscopy or stent exchange can precipitate life-threatening hemorrhage, observation risks exsanguination, and nephroureterectomy does not address the arterial defect.
learning_point: Persistent or intermittent gross hematuria in a patient with chronic indwelling ureteral stents and prior pelvic radiation or vascular surgery should raise suspicion for a ureteroarterial (usually ureteroiliac) fistula; standard cystoscopy and CT are often normal, and selective iliac angiography is diagnostic and allows endovascular treatment.
key_facts: Risk factors: chronic ureteral stents, pelvic radiation, pelvic surgery, vascular disease or grafts.
Hematuria may be intermittent and massive, often provoked by stent manipulation.
CT and cystoscopy frequently miss the fistula.
Angiography with embolization or covered stent graft is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

question: A 63-year-old woman is three weeks out from radical cystectomy with an Indiana pouch. Her nurse notes stool-like material in the pouch catheter drainage. She is afebrile with a soft abdomen and normal white count. CT with oral contrast shows a communication between the reservoir and the ileocolic anastomosis without downstream obstruction or abscess. The pouch is drained with an indwelling catheter. The next step is:

options.A: loop ileostomy proximal to the anastomosis.
options.C: bowel rest with total parenteral nutrition.

rationale: A stable patient with a low-output pouch-enteric fistula and no distal obstruction should first be given a trial of pouch drainage with an elemental, low-residue diet; most such fistulas close spontaneously. TPN with NPO status is the escalation if the diet trial fails, not the first move. Nephrostomy tubes do not address the pressure gradient from bowel into the reservoir. Fecal diversion or reoperation is reserved for septic or high-output fistulas, or for fistulas that persist after conservative management.
learning_point: An enteric-pouch fistula after continent cutaneous diversion in a stable, non-obstructed patient is managed conservatively first: pouch catheter drainage plus an elemental/low-residue diet, escalating to NPO/TPN if it fails; most close without surgery.
key_facts: Pouch-to-bowel fistula occurs in under 5% of continent cutaneous diversions; roughly two-thirds close with conservative measures.
Stepwise approach: pouch catheter and elemental diet, then NPO with TPN, then delayed surgical revision for persistent fistulas.
Proximal nephrostomy drainage does not stop enteric content from flowing into a low-pressure reservoir.
Early fecal diversion or re-do anastomosis is reserved for sepsis or very high-output fistulas.

question: A 29-year-old man being evaluated for primary infertility has decreased libido. Serum testosterone is 170 ng/dL (normal 300-1000) with an LH of 1.2 IU/L and normal prolactin. His only regular medications are listed below. The agent most likely to explain these findings is:
rationale: Low testosterone with a low LH indicates central (hypogonadotropic) hypogonadism, which is a well-recognized effect of chronic opioid therapy through suppression of GnRH release. Exogenous testosterone would suppress LH but would raise, not lower, the measured serum testosterone. SSRIs cause ejaculatory and orgasmic dysfunction rather than this hormonal pattern. Antipsychotics can lower libido via dopamine blockade and hyperprolactinemia, but prolactin here is normal, and 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors slightly increase testosterone.
learning_point: Chronic opioid use causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low testosterone with low or inappropriately normal LH). Exogenous testosterone also suppresses LH, but it raises serum testosterone rather than lowering it.
key_facts: Opioids suppress hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, producing low T with low LH.
Exogenous androgens suppress LH but produce high, not low, serum testosterone.
SSRIs mainly cause anorgasmia/delayed ejaculation; antipsychotics raise prolactin and reduce libido via dopamine blockade.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitors mildly raise testosterone and do not produce this picture.

question: A 67-year-old woman with biopsy-proven carcinoma in situ of the bladder completes a six-week induction course of intravesical BCG. Cystoscopy and bladder biopsies at three months show persistent CIS without papillary tumor or muscle invasion. Upper tract imaging and cytology of the prostatic urethra are not applicable; she is otherwise healthy. The next step is:

options.E: second induction course of intravesical BCG.

rationale: A patient whose CIS persists after only one induction course of BCG has not yet received adequate BCG; guidelines recommend a second induction course rather than switching agents. Gemcitabine, mitomycin, or systemic pembrolizumab are considered only after BCG-unresponsive disease is established, and in the case of pembrolizumab, for patients who are ineligible for or decline cystectomy. Cystectomy is reasonable for BCG-unresponsive CIS but neoadjuvant chemotherapy has no role in the absence of muscle invasion.
learning_point: Persistent CIS after a single induction course of BCG should be treated with a second induction course of BCG, not a switch to another intravesical agent; cystectomy without neoadjuvant chemotherapy is the alternative for those who fail two courses.
key_facts: AUA NMIBC guideline: offer a second BCG course for persistent or recurrent CIS/Ta after one induction course.
BCG-unresponsive disease is defined only after adequate BCG (induction plus a second induction or maintenance).
Alternative intravesical agents are for BCG-unresponsive patients unfit for or refusing cystectomy.
Neoadjuvant cisplatin chemotherapy is for muscle-invasive disease, not for CIS alone.

question: A 34-year-old healthy woman with her first episode of acute cystitis asks whether ciprofloxacin is appropriate. The FDA safety communication on fluoroquinolones advises against their use in this situation because:

options.A: fluoroquinolones are contraindicated in women of childbearing age.
options.B: serious musculoskeletal and neurologic adverse effects outweigh the benefit in uncomplicated cystitis when alternatives exist.
options.C: courses shorter than seven days promote resistance.
options.D: fluoroquinolones should be reserved only for prophylaxis before urologic procedures.
options.E: fluoroquinolones have poor urinary concentrations in women.

rationale: The FDA warning states that for uncomplicated urinary tract infections, acute sinusitis, and acute bronchitis the serious risks of fluoroquinolones (tendon rupture, neuropathy, CNS effects) generally outweigh their benefit, so they should be reserved for patients without other treatment options. Fluoroquinolones achieve excellent urinary concentrations, so efficacy is not the issue. The warning does not address treatment duration or periprocedural prophylaxis, and it is not framed around sex or age; men with UTI are simply considered complicated infections.
learning_point: The FDA boxed warning advises that fluoroquinolones be reserved for uncomplicated cystitis (and sinusitis/bronchitis) only when no alternative exists, because the risk of serious, potentially permanent adverse effects outweighs the benefit in these self-limited infections.
key_facts: Fluoroquinolone adverse effects: tendinopathy/tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, aortic aneurysm, worsening of myasthenia gravis.
Uncomplicated UTI is defined in otherwise healthy women without anatomic or functional abnormality; all male UTIs are considered complicated.
The warning does not restrict duration of therapy or preprocedural prophylaxis specifically.
First-line agents for uncomplicated cystitis include nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, and fosfomycin.

question: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing type 2 diabetes complicated by grade 2 sensory neuropathy in both feet has newly diagnosed muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma (cT2N0M0) with diffuse CIS throughout the bladder. Creatinine clearance is 85 mL/min and hearing is normal. The best management is:

options.D: neoadjuvant dose-dense MVAC followed by cystectomy.
options.E: radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection.

rationale: Significant peripheral neuropathy is one of the accepted contraindications to cisplatin, so both MVAC and gemcitabine-cisplatin are inappropriate despite good renal function. Carboplatin-based neoadjuvant therapy has not shown a survival benefit and is not recommended as a cisplatin substitute before cystectomy. Multifocal CIS predicts poor outcomes with bladder-preserving chemoradiation. The correct approach is to proceed to upfront radical cystectomy with lymphadenectomy.
learning_point: Patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer who are cisplatin-ineligible (e.g., significant peripheral neuropathy, CrCl <60, hearing loss, poor performance status, NYHA class III+) should proceed directly to radical cystectomy; carboplatin-based neoadjuvant regimens are not supported, and multifocal CIS is a poor candidate feature for bladder preservation.
key_facts: Cisplatin-ineligibility criteria (Galsky): ECOG >=2, CrCl <60 mL/min, grade >=2 hearing loss, grade >=2 neuropathy, NYHA class >=III.
Carboplatin substitution has no proven survival benefit in the neoadjuvant setting.
Trimodal therapy is best for unifocal T2 tumors without hydronephrosis or extensive CIS.
Cisplatin-ineligible patients go straight to cystectomy; adjuvant immunotherapy may be considered based on pathology.

question: A 27-year-old woman with known cystinuria takes potassium citrate and tiopronin. Her most recent 24-hour urine shows cystine well below the solubility threshold and a urine pH of 7.3. Over the past four months she has nevertheless passed two more stones. The next step is:

options.A: send a passed stone for compositional analysis.

rationale: When a cystinuric patient on apparently effective therapy continues to form stones, the stones may not be cystine at all; alkalinization and associated metabolic abnormalities frequently produce calcium phosphate or other stones. Stone analysis directs the next therapeutic change. Raising potassium citrate further risks pushing urine pH above 7.5 and promoting calcium phosphate crystallization. Adding captopril or changing thiol drugs only makes sense if the stones are confirmed to be cystine, and a nitroprusside screen is unnecessary when the diagnosis is already established.
learning_point: A cystinuric patient who keeps forming stones despite appropriate therapy (reduced cystine excretion, urine pH 7-7.5) needs stone analysis, because cystinurics commonly form non-cystine stones (calcium phosphate, calcium oxalate, uric acid) that require different treatment.
key_facts: Cystinuria often coexists with hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, and hyperuricosuria.
Over-alkalinization above pH 7.5 promotes calcium phosphate stone formation.
Methionine is a cystine precursor and should be restricted, not increased.
Nitroprusside testing is a screening test for cystinuria and adds nothing once the diagnosis is known.

question: A resident preparing to counsel a patient about a treatment choice finds a recently published single-center randomized trial with p < 0.01, a basic-science review of the drug's mechanism, and a Cochrane systematic review on the same question. According to the principles of evidence-based medicine, the resident should give priority to:

options.A: the mechanistic review because it explains biologic plausibility.
options.B: the single randomized trial because it is the most recent.
options.C: expert opinion from a senior colleague.
options.D: the trial because a p value below 0.05 establishes clinical importance.
options.E: the systematic review because it is a critically appraised secondary source.

rationale: Evidence-based practice emphasizes pre-appraised secondary resources such as systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which synthesize multiple studies and formally assess validity and clinical importance. A single trial, however recent, is a primary source that may not be generalizable, and statistical significance alone does not establish clinical importance. Mechanistic literature offers background rather than evidence for management decisions, and unstructured expert opinion sits at the bottom of the evidence hierarchy.
learning_point: Evidence-based medicine prioritizes pre-appraised secondary sources (systematic reviews, meta-analyses, evidence-based guidelines) over individual primary studies or mechanistic literature when applying evidence to patient care.
key_facts: Secondary sources incorporate formal critical appraisal of validity and clinical importance.
Single primary studies, even with significant p-values, may lack validity or clinical relevance.
Mechanistic/etiologic literature provides background but does not directly guide management decisions.
The hierarchy of evidence places systematic reviews of RCTs at the top.

question: A 58-year-old woman underwent left PCNL for a complete staghorn calculus three months ago. She has had continuous urine drainage from the flank tract ever since despite a well-positioned ureteral stent and Foley catheter for the past two months. Serum creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL and a MAG-3 scan shows 12% function on the left. The next step is:

options.A: fibrin glue injection of the fistula tract.
options.C: exchange for a larger-caliber ureteral stent.
options.E: continued observation with the stent in place.

rationale: A fistula that persists for months despite adequate internal drainage is unlikely to close with any further drainage maneuver, and a kidney contributing only about 10% of function with chronic infection is not worth salvaging when the contralateral kidney is normal. Nephrectomy both cures the fistula and removes the infected, nonfunctioning unit. Upsizing the stent or adding a nephrostomy tube merely repeats a strategy that has already failed, and tract glue does not address the underlying poorly functioning, infected kidney.
learning_point: A nephrocutaneous fistula persisting for months after PCNL despite adequate internal and bladder drainage, in a kidney with minimal (about 10%) function and a normal contralateral kidney, is best treated with nephrectomy.
key_facts: Most post-PCNL fistulas result from distal obstruction and close with stent drainage.
Persistent fistula suggests chronic infection such as xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis or tuberculosis.
Changing drainage strategy in a kidney with 10% function is unlikely to achieve closure after prolonged failure.
Nephrectomy is appropriate when the affected kidney is poorly functioning and overall GFR is preserved.

question: Four weeks after a left sacrospinous ligament suspension for apical prolapse, a 71-year-old woman still has shooting pain from the left buttock down the back of her thigh to the calf that has not responded to analgesics and physical therapy. The structure most likely entrapped by the fixation suture is the:
rationale: Pain radiating down the posterior leg that persists weeks after sacrospinous fixation is characteristic of sciatic nerve entrapment by a suture placed too deeply or too laterally toward the ischial spine. Inferior gluteal nerve irritation is the most common cause of postoperative buttock pain but is transient and does not radiate below the gluteal region. Pudendal nerve injury produces perineal and gluteal pain rather than leg pain. The femoral and obturator nerves are not in the operative field.
learning_point: Persistent pain radiating down the leg after sacrospinous ligament fixation indicates sciatic nerve entrapment from a deeply placed suture; gluteal pain alone is more typical of transient inferior gluteal or pudendal nerve irritation.
key_facts: Sacrospinous sutures should be placed 1.5-2 cm medial to the ischial spine to avoid the pudendal neurovascular bundle and sciatic nerve.
Sciatic injury produces radicular pain down the posterior leg; persistent symptoms may require suture removal.
Inferior gluteal nerve irritation causes buttock pain that is usually transient.
The obturator and femoral nerves are anatomically remote from the sacrospinous ligament.

question: A 41-year-old woman with a T6 spinal cord injury received 200 U of intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA ten weeks ago with only partial improvement in incontinence between catheterizations. Six weeks ago she also received 150 U of onabotulinumtoxinA for lower-limb spasticity. Urine culture is negative. The appropriate plan is:
rationale: The total onabotulinumtoxinA dose from every indication should not exceed 400 U in a three-month period. This patient has had 350 U in the past ten weeks, so a 200 U dose cannot be given until the earlier bladder dose falls outside the three-month window, which is in about six weeks. A 100 U dose is unlikely to help when 200 U was insufficient, and 300 U is not an approved dose for neurogenic detrusor overactivity. Augmentation is premature when repeat injections have not yet been tried.
learning_point: Cumulative onabotulinumtoxinA from all indications should not exceed 400 U within any three-month window; a repeat 200 U bladder injection must be timed so that the total stays within this limit.
key_facts: Approved dose for neurogenic detrusor overactivity is 200 U; 100 U is for idiopathic OAB.
Doses for spasticity, cosmetic, or other uses count toward the 400 U/3-month ceiling.
300 U is not an approved bladder dose.
Repeat injections are safe and effective; augmentation is considered only after repeated failures.

question: A 29-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 158/98 mm Hg despite adherence to amlodipine 10 mg daily. Serum creatinine is 0.7 mg/dL. CT angiography shows alternating stenoses and aneurysmal dilations in the distal two-thirds of the right main renal artery, consistent with medial fibroplasia. The next step is:
rationale: The beaded appearance of the distal renal artery in a young woman is medial fibroplasia, a form of fibromuscular dysplasia that seldom progresses to occlusion or renal functional loss. When blood pressure remains elevated on a single agent, the correct step is to intensify medical therapy, for which an ACE inhibitor or ARB is an appropriate addition. Functional renography is not needed because the lesion does not threaten the kidney. Angioplasty is considered only if medications fail or are not tolerated, and stenting and surgical revascularization are not first-line treatments for this lesion.
learning_point: Medial fibroplasia (classic 'string of beads' fibromuscular dysplasia) in a young woman rarely progresses to occlusion or renal loss; uncontrolled hypertension should first be managed by intensifying medical therapy rather than by angioplasty or surgery.
key_facts: Medial fibroplasia affects women aged 25-50 and involves the distal main renal artery.
Progression to total occlusion or loss of renal function is uncommon, so functional imaging is unnecessary.
ACE inhibitors or ARBs are effective add-on therapy for renovascular hypertension with a normal contralateral kidney.
Angioplasty is reserved for medication-refractory or intolerant patients; stenting is generally avoided in FMD.

question: A 36-year-old man and his partner have been unable to conceive. He reports normal orgasmic sensation but no fluid emerges from the urethra, a change that began about 18 months ago. Genital examination, serum testosterone, and FSH are normal. The next step is:

options.D: transrectal ultrasound of the seminal vesicles.
options.E: centrifuged post-orgasm urine specimen for sperm.

rationale: Orgasm without any antegrade semen (aspermia) is caused either by retrograde flow of semen into the bladder or by failure of emission. A post-ejaculatory urinalysis separates these: sperm in the urine confirms retrograde ejaculation, whereas their absence indicates anejaculation. Ejaculatory duct obstruction typically produces a low-volume rather than absent ejaculate, so TRUS is not the first test. Imaging the spine or checking for diabetes may clarify etiology later, and sympathomimetic therapy should not be started before the mechanism is defined.
learning_point: In a man with orgasm but no antegrade ejaculate and normal exam and hormones, the first diagnostic step is a post-ejaculatory urinalysis to distinguish retrograde ejaculation (sperm in urine) from failure of emission (no sperm).
key_facts: Aspermia differential: retrograde ejaculation versus anejaculation/failure of emission.
Complete absence of ejaculate makes ejaculatory duct obstruction unlikely, so TRUS is not the first test.
Spine MRI and HbA1c may identify a cause but do not establish the mechanism.
Sympathomimetics such as pseudoephedrine treat retrograde ejaculation only after it is confirmed.

question: Eight days after completing nitrofurantoin for cystitis, a 62-year-old woman develops profuse watery diarrhea and abdominal cramping. Temperature is 38.6 C, WBC is 22,000/mm3, creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, and stool PCR is positive for C. difficile toxin. There is no ileus or hypotension. The appropriate treatment is:

options.D: intravenous metronidazole plus vancomycin retention enemas.

rationale: Fever and a white count above 15,000 define severe C. difficile infection, for which oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) is the recommended therapy; oral metronidazole is reserved for mild disease and is inferior in severe cases. Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen and has no role. The combination of IV metronidazole with rectal vancomycin is reserved for fulminant disease complicated by ileus or shock, which is absent here. Fecal transplantation is used for recurrent, not initial, infection.
learning_point: C. difficile colitis with systemic features (fever, marked leukocytosis) is classified as severe and should be treated with oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) rather than metronidazole; IV metronidazole and rectal vancomycin are adjuncts for ileus or fulminant disease, not monotherapy.
key_facts: Severe CDI markers: WBC >= 15,000 or creatinine > 1.5 mg/dL.
Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin is now first-line for initial episodes; metronidazole is reserved for mild disease when alternatives are unavailable.
Combination oral vancomycin plus metronidazole has no added benefit in non-fulminant disease.
IV metronidazole is added only in fulminant disease with ileus or shock; vancomycin enemas are adjunctive when oral delivery to the colon is impaired.

question: A newborn with ambiguous genitalia has a small phallus with proximal hypospadias and a single palpable gonad in the right labioscrotal fold. Pelvic ultrasound shows a small uterus. Karyotype is 45,X/46,XY. At laparoscopy a left streak gonad with an adjacent fallopian tube is identified; the right gonad has the appearance of a testis. The most likely diagnosis is:
rationale: The combination of a testis on one side, a streak gonad on the other, a mosaic 45,X/46,XY karyotype, and persistent Mullerian derivatives with undervirilized genitalia is diagnostic of mixed gonadal dysgenesis. Ovotesticular DSD requires histologic ovarian tissue, not a streak. Persistent Mullerian duct syndrome features two normal testes and a normal male phenotype. Complete (pure) gonadal dysgenesis has bilateral streaks, and CAH patients are 46,XX with ovaries and no testicular tissue.
learning_point: A testis on one side and a streak gonad on the other, with persistent Mullerian structures and incomplete virilization, defines mixed gonadal dysgenesis, usually with a 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype.
key_facts: Mixed gonadal dysgenesis: unilateral testis + contralateral streak gonad; Mullerian remnants persist on the streak side due to absent local MIS.
Pure gonadal dysgenesis has bilateral streak gonads (46,XX or 46,XY).
Persistent Mullerian duct syndrome has two normal testes with a uterus and tubes.
Ovotesticular DSD requires both ovarian and testicular tissue; CAH (46,XX) has ovaries only.

question: During a robotic sacrocolpopexy, brisk dark bleeding begins from the anterior sacrum as the second mesh-fixation suture is placed near S3. Pressure with a sponge stick slows but does not stop the bleeding. After converting to an open approach and resuscitating with fluids, the most effective next maneuver is:

options.A: request emergent angiographic embolization of the internal iliac arteries.
options.B: figure-of-eight suture ligation of the bleeding vessel.
options.D: drive a sterile titanium thumbtack into the bleeding site on the sacrum.
options.E: pack the pelvis, close, and reoperate in 48 hours.

rationale: Presacral hemorrhage arises from the presacral and basivertebral venous plexus, which retracts into the bone; a sterile tack pressed into the sacrum over the bleeding point (or bone wax or a hemostatic matrix) compresses these channels and is the recognized definitive maneuver. Suture ligation typically tears the thin-walled veins and worsens bleeding. The bleeding is venous and low pressure, so arterial embolization and iliac vessel clamping are ineffective. Packing and abandoning the case is a last resort only when the tack and adjuncts fail.
learning_point: Presacral venous hemorrhage during sacrocolpopexy is controlled by direct pressure followed by a sterile thumbtack (or bone wax/hemostatic agent) driven into the sacrum; suture ligation, iliac clamping, and embolization are ineffective for this venous plexus bleeding.
key_facts: Presacral veins communicate with basivertebral veins and retract into bone, so suture ligation usually fails.
Sutures placed low on the sacrum (S2-S4) increase bleeding risk; S1 promontory placement is safer.
Initial step is firm packing/pressure; definitive control is a sterile sacral tack, bone wax, or hemostatic matrix.
Arterial embolization and iliac clamping do not control low-pressure venous plexus bleeding.

question: A patient undergoing radical cystectomy asks whether her orthotopic neobladder should include an antireflux valve to protect her kidneys. Based on the randomized trial comparing antirefluxing and refluxing ileal neobladders, you tell her that the antireflux design:

options.A: leads to more reoperations related to the diversion without reducing late complications.
options.B: lowers the long-term incidence of pyelonephritis.
options.C: decreases the risk of ureteroenteric stricture.
options.D: preserves renal function better than a refluxing anastomosis.

rationale: The phase 3 trial randomizing patients to a T-pouch (antireflux) or Studer (refluxing) neobladder found equivalent rates of overall late complications and moderate renal failure, but patients with the antireflux mechanism needed significantly more secondary surgeries for diversion-related problems. There was no demonstrated protection against infection or renal deterioration. The antireflux design does not affect continence, and complex antireflux anastomoses tend to increase rather than decrease stricture-related interventions.
learning_point: The randomized trial comparing an antirefluxing (T-pouch) versus freely refluxing (Studer) orthotopic neobladder found no benefit in late complications or renal function but a higher need for secondary diversion-related surgery with the antireflux mechanism.
key_facts: Antireflux valves in neobladders do not reduce infection, renal deterioration, or overall late complications.
They increase the rate of reoperation for valve or anastomotic problems.
Freely refluxing ureteroileal anastomoses are now the standard for orthotopic diversion.
Low-pressure reservoirs make reflux clinically unimportant.

question: A 54-year-old man with Peyronie's disease of eight months' duration asks about extracorporeal shock wave therapy, which he read about online. According to the AUA guideline, the only aspect of his condition for which ESWT may reasonably be offered is:

options.D: prevention of progression during the active phase.

rationale: The AUA guideline permits ESWT as an option for men whose chief complaint is penile pain, while acknowledging its low overall utility and that pain usually resolves on its own. The guideline explicitly recommends against ESWT for reducing curvature or plaque size, so it is not appropriate for a 60-degree bend or a calcified plaque. It has no established role in treating hourglass deformity or in halting disease progression.
learning_point: Per the AUA Peyronie's guideline, low-intensity extracorporeal shock wave therapy may be offered only to improve penile pain; it should not be used to reduce curvature or plaque size and has no role for calcified plaques or hourglass deformity.
key_facts: ESWT for pain: conditional recommendation, grade B evidence; overall utility judged low.
ESWT should not be used for curvature or plaque reduction (moderate recommendation).
Pain in the active phase usually resolves spontaneously.
Curvature >30 degrees with stable disease is treated with intralesional collagenase or surgery.

question: Eighteen months after cystectomy and ileal conduit diversion, a 66-year-old woman has mild bilateral flank fullness and a rising creatinine. A loopogram shows a long, capacious conduit with contrast refluxing freely into both renal pelves, which are markedly dilated. The explanation most consistent with these findings is:
rationale: A dilated, elongated conduit that refluxes freely into dilated upper tracts means the obstruction lies distal to the entire loop, at the stoma or fascial level, and stomal stenosis is the most frequent culprit. Anastomotic strictures or recurrent tumor would obstruct the ureters without distending the conduit and would not allow reflux. An ischemic conduit is narrow and rigid rather than capacious. Parastomal hernia rarely produces functional obstruction of the loop.
learning_point: Bilateral upper-tract dilation with free reflux into an elongated, dilated ileal conduit indicates obstruction at the stoma; stomal stenosis is the most common cause, whereas anastomotic strictures or recurrence would not dilate the conduit itself.
key_facts: Stomal stenosis produces a distended, elongated conduit with bilateral refluxing hydronephrosis.
Ureteroileal strictures cause unilateral or bilateral hydronephrosis with a normal-caliber conduit.
Ischemic 'pipe-stem' conduits are thin, non-compliant, and strictured along their length.
Parastomal hernias seldom obstruct the conduit; antiperistaltic conduits function normally.

question: A seven-year-old boy wets his pants several times a day at school. His teacher reports that he frequently crosses his legs and presses his heel against his perineum before an accident. He has daily soft bowel movements and a normal post-void residual on ultrasound. Timed voiding has not helped. The next step is:
rationale: Daytime urgency incontinence with holding maneuvers in a child who empties completely reflects detrusor overactivity, and an antimuscarinic is the accepted next step once behavioral measures have failed. Biofeedback targets dysfunctional voiding with incomplete emptying, which this child does not have. Holding exercises and fluid restriction can worsen dysfunctional elimination, and laxatives are not indicated when bowel habits are normal. Tibial nerve stimulation is not approved for children and is reserved for refractory adult cases.
learning_point: A school-age child with urgency incontinence and classic holding maneuvers (squatting, Vincent's curtsy) has detrusor overactivity, for which antimuscarinic therapy is the standard treatment after basic urotherapy.
key_facts: Holding maneuvers (curtsy, squatting on heel) are hallmarks of pediatric overactive bladder.
Antimuscarinics (oxybutynin, solifenacin) are first-line pharmacotherapy and can be weaned as bladder function matures.
Biofeedback is most useful for dysfunctional voiding with elevated post-void residual.
Holding exercises and fluid restriction are not effective and may promote dysfunctional elimination; tibial nerve stimulation is not approved in children.

question: A 17-year-old boy with myelomeningocele underwent ileocystoplasty and creation of a Monti channel at age 10. He catheterizes the channel every four hours, is dry, and has now had three cystolitholapaxies for struvite bladder stones over two years. In addition to starting daily bladder irrigation, the most effective way to lower his stone risk is to:

options.C: begin catheterizing once daily through the urethra as well.
options.D: instill intravesical gentamicin after each catheterization.

rationale: Stones after augmentation form on retained mucus in incompletely emptied, chronically colonized reservoirs, and abdominal stomas tend to leave a dependent residual. Adding daily per-urethral catheterization ensures complete drainage and, combined with irrigation to clear mucus, is the most effective preventive strategy.
