rationale: Sports drinks contain citrate and malate salts that are metabolized to bicarbonate, producing a modest alkaline load that increases urinary citrate and pH, both of which inhibit calcium stone formation. Studies have not shown a meaningful rise in urinary sodium excretion despite the sodium in the beverage, and no effect on urinary calcium, oxalate, or uric acid has been demonstrated. The caveat is that the fructose and total carbohydrate content of these drinks carries its own metabolic and lithogenic concerns, so they should supplement rather than replace water as a stone former's primary fluid.
learning_point: Commercial sports drinks raise urinary citrate and pH, a mildly protective effect against stone formation, but their high fructose and carbohydrate load make them inappropriate as the primary fluid for stone formers; they do not increase urinary sodium, calcium, oxalate, or uric acid.
key_facts: Citrate and malate in sports drinks are metabolized to bicarbonate, raising urinary citrate and pH.
Despite their sodium content, sports drinks have not been shown to raise urinary sodium excretion meaningfully.
High fructose intake is independently associated with kidney stone risk.
Water and citrus juices (e.g., lemonade) remain preferred hydration for stone prevention.

question: A 70-year-old woman with prior pelvic radiation for cervical cancer requires cystectomy, and the surgeon chooses a transverse colon conduit rather than an ileal conduit. Compared with ileum, an advantage of the colonic segment is:

options.A: a lower risk of long-term vitamin B12 deficiency and bile salt malabsorption.
options.B: elimination of the need for a stoma appliance.
options.C: a lower rate of ureteral anastomotic stricture with refluxing anastomoses.
options.D: a shorter mesentery that reaches the pelvis more easily.
options.E: a lower incidence of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

rationale: Using colon spares the terminal ileum, so the patient avoids the vitamin B12 deficiency and bile acid malabsorption that can follow resection of a long ileal segment, provided the ileocecal valve is preserved. Electrolyte abnormalities, chiefly hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, occur with either colon or ileum because both absorb ammonium and chloride. Colon reaches the urethra and pelvis reliably, so reach is not a differentiating advantage. Ureteral stricture rates are not inherently lower with refluxing colonic anastomoses, although colon does allow easier tunneled antireflux anastomoses. Any conduit requires an external appliance.
learning_point: Compared with ileum, colonic segments used for urinary diversion cause fewer nutritional problems (no B12 or bile salt malabsorption if the ileocecal valve is spared), fewer bowel anastomotic obstructions, and allow easier submucosal tunneled antireflux anastomoses; electrolyte derangements are similar and reach to the urethra is not a problem.
key_facts: Transverse colon is favored after pelvic radiation because it lies outside the treated field.
Loss of >60 cm of terminal ileum causes vitamin B12 deficiency and bile acid diarrhea; colon avoids this.
Both ileum and colon produce hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
Colon's larger diameter yields a lower bowel-anastomotic obstruction rate.

question: A 61-year-old man undergoes partial penectomy for a 3 cm glans squamous cell carcinoma. Pathology shows invasion limited to the lamina propria with perineural invasion and high-grade histology, no spongiosal or cavernosal involvement. On examination he has a 3 cm matted, immobile left inguinal mass; CT shows no pelvic or retroperitoneal adenopathy. Using AJCC 8th edition criteria, his stage is:
rationale: Invasion confined to the subepithelial connective tissue is T1, and the presence of perineural invasion or high-grade histology upstages it to T1b; without spongiosal or cavernosal invasion it cannot be T2 or T3. Clinically, a fixed or matted inguinal mass is cN3 irrespective of its size or laterality, whereas cN1 and cN2 describe mobile nodes. The combination is therefore pT1b cN3, a stage for which guidelines recommend neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy prior to inguinal and pelvic lymph node dissection rather than upfront surgery.
learning_point: Under AJCC 8th edition penile cancer staging, invasion of subepithelial connective tissue with lymphovascular or perineural invasion or high grade is pT1b, invasion of corpus spongiosum is pT2 and corpus cavernosum pT3; a fixed inguinal mass or any palpable fixed node is clinical N3, which calls for neoadjuvant chemotherapy before lymphadenectomy.
key_facts: pT1a: lamina propria invasion without LVI, PNI, or high grade; pT1b: with any of those features.
cN1: single palpable mobile unilateral node; cN2: two or more unilateral or bilateral mobile nodes; cN3: fixed nodal mass or pelvic adenopathy.
pN1: up to two unilateral nodes; pN2: three or more or bilateral; pN3: extranodal extension or pelvic nodes.
cN3 disease is treated with neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by consolidative lymphadenectomy.

question: A 52-year-old woman develops continuous urinary leakage three weeks after an abdominal hysterectomy. Cystoscopy shows a 6 mm fistula in the posterior bladder wall well above the ureteral orifices, and vaginal examination confirms the tract at the vaginal cuff. Her surgeon plans a transvaginal repair with a well-vascularized interposition layer. The most appropriate tissue is:
rationale: A post-hysterectomy fistula at the vaginal cuff lies immediately below the peritoneal reflection of the cul-de-sac, so during a vaginal approach the surgeon can easily raise a vascularized peritoneal flap and advance it between the bladder and vaginal closures. A Martius graft from the labia has a limited arc of rotation and reaches the apex only with tension and compromised blood supply. Omentum is used during abdominal repairs and is not available vaginally unless previously brought into the pelvis. Gracilis and labial myocutaneous flaps are more extensive reconstructions reserved for large, irradiated, or recurrent defects or when vaginal length is lost.
learning_point: For transvaginal repair of a high, post-hysterectomy vesicovaginal fistula at the vaginal apex, a peritoneal flap is the preferred interposition because it is readily mobilized at that location; Martius flaps are hard to reach the apex, and gracilis or labial flaps are reserved for complex or recurrent repairs.
key_facts: Peritoneum from the vesicouterine/cul-de-sac region lies directly adjacent to apical fistulas and is easily advanced.
Martius (labial fibrofatty) flaps suit distal and mid-vaginal fistulas, especially after radiation.
Omental interposition is the standard flap for abdominal (transvesical) repairs.
Gracilis and labial myocutaneous flaps are for large defects, radiation damage, or vaginal foreshortening.

question: A 58-year-old woman returns for a routine visit three years after a retropubic midurethral polypropylene sling. She has no incontinence, pain, discharge, or bleeding, and both she and her husband deny any discomfort with intercourse. On examination there is a 0.8 cm area of visible mesh through the anterior vaginal wall without surrounding granulation. She uses vaginal estrogen cream twice weekly. The next step is:

options.B: pelvic rest with abstinence for three months.
options.C: excise the exposed mesh and close the vaginal epithelium.

rationale: A small mesh exposure that is causing no symptoms for either the patient or her partner does not require surgical intervention; observation with continued topical estrogen is appropriate, and estrogen should be maintained rather than stopped because it promotes vaginal epithelial health. Excising the exposed segment and reapproximating the vaginal wall is the correct treatment when exposure causes dyspareunia, partner irritation, bleeding, or discharge. Removing the entire sling is more extensive than needed and would likely cause recurrent stress incontinence. Abstinence does not promote epithelial regrowth over exposed mesh.
learning_point: A small, asymptomatic vaginal exposure of a polypropylene midurethral sling in a patient and partner without complaints can be observed, continuing vaginal estrogen; excision of the exposed portion is reserved for symptomatic exposure, and total sling removal is unnecessary and risks recurrent incontinence.
key_facts: Mesh exposure (extrusion into the vagina) occurs in roughly 1-3% of synthetic midurethral slings.
Symptoms that prompt intervention: dyspareunia, partner discomfort, vaginal discharge or bleeding, pain.
Symptomatic exposure: excise exposed mesh and reapproximate healthy vaginal epithelium.
Local estrogen supports epithelial health and should be continued, not stopped.

question: A 34-year-old man started pantoprazole six weeks ago for reflux; he also takes a daily multivitamin and loratadine. He now has a faint maculopapular rash on his trunk, low-grade fever, and aching knees. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein, 15 RBC/hpf, 20 WBC/hpf with white cell casts, and eosinophiluria. Serum creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 2.2 mg/dL and renal ultrasound shows mildly enlarged, echogenic kidneys without obstruction. The next step is:

options.C: percutaneous renal biopsy before any change in therapy.
options.D: start an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor for proteinuria.

rationale: Subacute kidney injury with sterile pyuria, white cell casts, eosinophiluria, rash, fever, and arthralgia following a new proton pump inhibitor is the classic picture of drug-induced acute interstitial nephritis. The essential first step is withdrawal of the causative medication, which often leads to recovery on its own. Corticosteroids may be added if renal function does not improve within days to a couple of weeks after drug cessation, but they are not the initial move. ACE inhibitors have no role in treating AIN and may worsen acute kidney injury. Biopsy is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, and loratadine is not a recognized cause.
learning_point: Acute interstitial nephritis presents with rising creatinine, hematuria, mild proteinuria, urinary eosinophils or sterile pyuria, and often rash, fever, or arthralgia after a culprit drug such as a proton pump inhibitor, NSAID, or antibiotic; the first step is to stop the offending agent, with steroids considered if recovery lags.
key_facts: Common AIN culprits: PPIs, NSAIDs, beta-lactams, sulfonamides, fluoroquinolones, allopurinol.
Classic triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia is present in a minority; urine eosinophils and WBC casts support the diagnosis.
Renal ultrasound is normal or shows enlarged echogenic kidneys; biopsy confirms when uncertain.
Oral contraceptives and ACE inhibitors are not recognized causes; ACE inhibitors are not a treatment for AIN.

question: A 25-year-old man sustains a grade 4 left renal laceration in a motorcycle crash. He is hemodynamically stable after initial resuscitation. The trauma team asks which CT findings, together with the depth of the laceration and an arterial contrast blush, would predict ongoing hemorrhage and a likely need for angioembolization. The additional predictor is:

options.A: a perirenal hematoma greater than 3.5 cm in thickness.
options.C: contrast extravasation from the collecting system on delayed images.
options.E: an anterior rather than posterior laceration.

rationale: Studies of high-grade blunt renal trauma identified three imaging predictors of persistent bleeding and intervention: a large perirenal hematoma (greater than about 3.5 cm from the renal capsule), a medially located hematoma suggesting hilar vascular injury, and active arterial contrast blush. Urinary extravasation and devitalized segments increase the risk of urinoma and infection but not of hemorrhage, and are usually managed with drainage or observation. The anterior-posterior location of a laceration and the energy of the mechanism do not independently predict bleeding once injury grade is accounted for.
learning_point: In grade 3-4 blunt renal injuries, the CT features predicting ongoing bleeding and need for intervention are perirenal hematoma thickness greater than about 3.5 cm, medial hematoma location, and active arterial contrast blush; urinary extravasation and devitalized fragments predict urinoma rather than hemorrhage.
key_facts: Hematoma rim distance >3.5 cm, medial hematoma, and intravascular contrast extravasation each independently predict bleeding.
Presence of two or more of these findings should prompt consideration of angiography and embolization.
Urinary extravasation is managed with observation or stenting; most leaks resolve.
Mechanism and exact laceration location do not predict complications independent of grade.

question: A 13-year-old girl presents with worsening cyclic lower abdominal pain six months after menarche despite regular menses. Examination under anesthesia reveals a longitudinal vaginal septum with a bulging left hemivagina; incision of the septum releases old blood, and at follow-up she is pain-free with normal cycles. The next step is:
rationale: An obstructed hemivagina with a longitudinal septum and regular menstruation from the contralateral side is the classic OHVIRA complex, which results from a Müllerian anomaly closely linked to Wolffian duct maldevelopment; roughly 40% of such patients have ipsilateral renal agenesis or another renal anomaly. A renal ultrasound is therefore mandatory to evaluate the kidneys even though the vaginal problem has been relieved. Pelvic MRI can later detail uterine anatomy for reproductive counseling but does not assess the kidneys adequately on its own. VCUG and cystoscopy evaluate the lower urinary tract and do not identify absent or dysplastic kidneys, and no further evaluation would miss a clinically important anomaly.
learning_point: Müllerian duct anomalies such as a duplicated or septate vagina with obstructed hemivagina are strongly associated with ipsilateral renal agenesis (OHVIRA/Herlyn-Werner-Wunderlich), so after relief of the obstruction a renal ultrasound is required to evaluate the upper tracts.
key_facts: About 40% of women with Müllerian duplication anomalies have unilateral renal agenesis; conversely a third of women with URA have genital anomalies.
Wolffian and Müllerian duct development are linked, so vaginal/uterine anomalies signal possible renal anomalies on the same side.
Pelvic MRI defines uterine anatomy but does not substitute for renal evaluation.
VCUG does not assess renal presence or upper tract obstruction.

question: A 2-day-old infant is evaluated for atypical genitalia: there is marked clitoromegaly with a single perineal opening, partially fused and rugated labioscrotal folds, and a firm gonad palpable in the right labioscrotal fold. The anus is normally placed. Karyotype returns 46,XX and a genitogram shows a short urogenital sinus with a vagina joining the urethra distally. The most likely diagnosis is:
rationale: A 46,XX infant with virilized external genitalia, a vagina, and a palpable gonad has ovotesticular DSD; a palpable gonad must contain testicular tissue because ovaries do not descend. Congenital adrenal hyperplasia also virilizes a 46,XX fetus but the gonads are normal ovaries and are never palpable. Partial androgen insensitivity requires a 46,XY karyotype and functioning testes whose MIS suppresses Mullerian structures, so a vagina would not form. Mixed gonadal dysgenesis typically has a 45,X/46,XY mosaic karyotype, and complete gonadal dysgenesis produces phenotypically normal female genitalia without virilization.
learning_point: A 46,XX newborn with ambiguous genitalia, a palpable gonad, and a urogenital sinus with a vagina most likely has ovotesticular DSD; a palpable gonad excludes simple androgen exposure of an XX fetus (ovaries do not descend), and vaginal development excludes 46,XY partial androgen insensitivity.
key_facts: Ovotesticular DSD = both ovarian and testicular tissue (testis, ovary, or ovotestis); most common karyotype is 46,XX, sometimes with a Y-bearing mosaic line.
Only a testis or ovotestis descends enough to be palpable; CAH or maternal androgen exposure in an XX infant gives non-palpable gonads.
Partial androgen insensitivity is 46,XY with functioning testes that make MIS, so no vagina/uterus develops.
Mixed gonadal dysgenesis is classically 45,X/46,XY mosaic with a testis on one side and a streak gonad on the other; pure gonadal dysgenesis has normal-appearing genitalia.

question: A 59-year-old man undergoes a 5-hour robot-assisted radical cystectomy in steep Trendelenburg. To keep him from sliding, the team places padded shoulder braces against the acromion bilaterally and tucks the arms at his sides. On postoperative day 1 the most likely position-related neurologic complaint attributable to the braces is:

options.A: foot drop with numbness of the lateral calf.
options.D: weakness of hip flexion when climbing stairs.
options.E: weakness of elbow flexion and wrist extension with finger tingling.

rationale: Shoulder braces in steep head-down position transmit the patient's weight onto the shoulder girdle and stretch or compress the brachial plexus, producing upper-extremity weakness (biceps, wrist extensors) and finger paresthesias; this is preventable by avoiding braces and using non-slip padding. Thigh adduction weakness reflects obturator nerve injury during pelvic node dissection, not positioning braces. Anterior thigh numbness follows genitofemoral nerve injury on the psoas, and hip flexion weakness follows femoral nerve compression from hip hyperextension. Foot drop from peroneal nerve compression is a lithotomy/stirrup complication unrelated to the braces.
learning_point: Shoulder braces used to keep a patient from sliding in steep Trendelenburg can compress and stretch the brachial plexus, producing upper-extremity weakness and paresthesias (e.g., biceps and wrist extensor weakness); avoid braces, use non-slip padding, and keep arms abducted less than 90 degrees.
key_facts: Brachial plexus injury in Trendelenburg: shoulder braces and arm abduction beyond 90 degrees are the main preventable causes.
Obturator nerve injury during pelvic lymph node dissection causes weak thigh adduction.
Genitofemoral nerve injury over the psoas causes anterior thigh numbness; femoral nerve compression under the inguinal ligament from hip hyperextension causes weak hip flexion.
Robotic arms lowered onto the foot during docking can cause dorsal foot pain.

question: A 72-year-old woman with metastatic urothelial carcinoma of the renal pelvis and a creatinine clearance of 48 mL/min is offered gemcitabine with carboplatin instead of gemcitabine with cisplatin. Compared with the cisplatin-based combination, the carboplatin regimen is expected to:

options.B: shorten the planned duration of treatment.
options.C: produce a lower complete and overall response rate.
options.D: produce equivalent response rates with superior survival.
options.E: produce a higher complete response rate with more neurotoxicity.

rationale: Randomized comparisons pooled in meta-analysis show that carboplatin substitution reduces the probability of complete response roughly threefold and lowers the overall response rate, although a survival difference has not been demonstrated. Carboplatin is chosen precisely because it is less nephrotoxic, so increased renal toxicity is wrong. It does not improve survival or raise response rates, and the planned number of cycles is unchanged.
learning_point: In advanced urothelial carcinoma, replacing cisplatin with carboplatin in combination chemotherapy significantly lowers complete and overall response rates without a demonstrated difference in survival; carboplatin is less nephrotoxic and does not change treatment duration.
key_facts: Meta-analysis of randomized trials (Galsky et al.): carboplatin-based regimens had about a threefold lower complete response probability and lower overall response rate.
No statistically significant survival difference was shown, but cisplatin remains the standard for eligible patients.
Carboplatin has a better renal safety profile, which is why it is used in cisplatin-ineligible patients.
Course length/number of cycles is not altered by the substitution.

question: A 28-year-old man with recurrent calcium oxalate stones develops right flank pain 6 months after a complicated ureteroscopy. Creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. CT urogram shows right hydronephrosis with a 5 cm stricture extending from the ureteropelvic junction to the mid-ureter, and a MAG-3 scan shows 42% right function with an obstructive drainage curve. The best management is:
rationale: A 5 cm proximal-to-mid ureteral defect is too long for end-to-end anastomosis, and a psoas hitch or Boari flap alone will not bridge a defect reaching the UPJ without extensive renal mobilization; with normal creatinine, an ileal ureter is the standard reconstruction. Endoureterotomy has poor results for strictures over 2 cm. Transureteroureterostomy is contraindicated in a stone former because stones could obstruct the single shared distal ureter and jeopardize the healthy kidney. Nephrectomy is a last resort when the kidney contributes 42% of function.
learning_point: A long (greater than about 3 cm) proximal/mid-ureteral stricture in a young patient with preserved renal function and a history of stone disease is best reconstructed with an ileal ureter (or renal mobilization with long Boari flap/autotransplantation); endoscopic incision fails for strictures over 2 cm, and transureteroureterostomy is contraindicated in stone formers.
key_facts: Endoureterotomy/endopyelotomy: poor results for strictures longer than 2 cm.
Ureteroureterostomy suits short upper/mid strictures only; ureterocalicostomy suits short proximal strictures with thin lower-pole parenchyma.
Transureteroureterostomy is avoided in patients with nephrolithiasis or urothelial cancer because it places the healthy ureter at risk.
Ileal ureter requires serum creatinine below about 2.0 mg/dL and adequate bowel; alternatives are long Boari flap or autotransplantation.

question: A 12-year-old girl with spina bifida underwent sigmoid cystoplasty and a Mitrofanoff channel 3 years ago and empties by catheterization through the stoma. She has recurrent cloudy urine, and ultrasound shows four bladder calculi measuring 8 to 15 mm. The best approach is:

options.C: ureteroscope-assisted lithotripsy through the Mitrofanoff channel.
options.D: SWL followed by daily bladder irrigation.

rationale: Percutaneous cystolithotripsy through a suprapubic tract allows a large working sheath, efficient fragmentation and extraction, and protects the continent channel; it matches open cystolithotomy for clearance with less morbidity. Passing instruments repeatedly through the narrow Mitrofanoff channel risks damaging its continence mechanism, and a small child's urethra (often with a prior bladder neck procedure) is likewise unsuitable for a sizable stone burden. SWL fragments will not clear from an augmented bladder that depends on catheterization. Laparoscopy after prior bowel surgery carries a higher risk of visceral injury and offers no advantage.
learning_point: Multiple bladder stones in a child with an augmented bladder and a catheterizable channel are best treated by percutaneous cystolithotripsy, which spares the small-caliber channel and urethra, avoids re-entering a hostile abdomen, and has shorter recovery than open cystolithotomy.
key_facts: Up to half of children with reconstructed bladders form bladder stones (mucus, stasis, infection, incomplete emptying).
Transurethral or trans-stomal lithotripsy risks injuring the bladder neck reconstruction or continent channel and requires many passes through narrow channels.
SWL fragments will not clear from a poorly emptying augmented bladder.
Prior laparotomy increases risk of bowel injury with a laparoscopic approach; percutaneous access via suprapubic puncture is safe and efficient.

question: A 58-year-old man reports hesitancy, weak stream, and nocturia twice nightly with an IPSS of 16. Prostate is smooth and about 30 g; PSA is 1.1 ng/mL, urinalysis is normal, and PVR is 120 mL. He is scheduled for cataract extraction in 3 weeks. The most appropriate plan is:

options.C: begin alfuzosin after the cataract operation.

rationale: He has bothersome LUTS suggestive of outlet obstruction and should receive empiric alpha-blocker therapy, but because any alpha-blocker can produce intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, treatment is best deferred until after his imminent cataract surgery. Starting tamsulosin now unnecessarily exposes him to this complication. A 5-ARI is not indicated with a 30 g prostate and low PSA. Urodynamics are reserved for when invasive therapy is contemplated, and an antimuscarinic alone is inappropriate for obstructive symptoms with an elevated PVR.
learning_point: In a man with moderate LUTS and a non-enlarged prostate who is scheduled for cataract surgery, empiric alpha-blocker therapy is appropriate but should be started only after the eye surgery to avoid intraoperative floppy iris syndrome; urodynamics are not needed before medical therapy and 5-ARIs are not indicated without prostate enlargement.
key_facts: Alpha-blockers (especially tamsulosin) cause intraoperative floppy iris syndrome; ophthalmologists should know about use, and new starts should be deferred until after planned cataract surgery.
Pressure-flow urodynamics are reserved for when invasive or irreversible therapy is being considered.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitors benefit men with prostate enlargement (roughly over 30 to 40 g or elevated PSA), not small glands.
Antimuscarinic monotherapy is inappropriate with predominantly obstructive symptoms and an elevated PVR.

question: A 71-year-old woman with coronary disease and insulin-dependent diabetes has an incidentally found 5.5 cm mostly endophytic, hilar, enhancing left renal mass with a R.E.N.A.L. nephrometry score of 11. Her eGFR is 85 mL/min/1.73 m2, urinalysis shows no protein, and the right kidney is normal. According to AUA guidelines, the preferred treatment is:

options.A: active surveillance with imaging in 6 months.
options.E: renal mass biopsy followed by ablation if malignant.

rationale: This mass is large and highly complex, so partial nephrectomy would be technically demanding; with normal renal function, no proteinuria, a normal contralateral kidney, and significant comorbidity, the guideline-preferred operation is radical nephrectomy. Partial nephrectomy is prioritized when there is CKD, a solitary kidney, or bilateral/hereditary disease, none of which apply. Thermal ablation is unreliable for tumors over 3 cm, and a 5.5 cm enhancing mass exceeds the size appropriate for active surveillance in a reasonable surgical candidate.
learning_point: Per AUA guidelines, radical nephrectomy is preferred for a solid renal mass with increased oncologic potential (larger size, high complexity) when partial nephrectomy would be challenging, there is no CKD or proteinuria, and the contralateral kidney is normal; ablation is suboptimal above 3 cm.
key_facts: AUA renal mass guideline: consider RN when tumor complexity is high, PN would be difficult even for experts, no preexisting CKD/proteinuria, and the contralateral kidney is normal.
Thermal ablation has markedly lower success for tumors over 3 cm.
Active surveillance is for small (generally under 2 to 3 cm) or low-risk masses or patients with limited life expectancy.
Comorbidity favors minimizing operative risk, which supports RN over a complex PN.

question: A 26-year-old woman with an incomplete C7 spinal cord injury reports straining and incomplete emptying. Videourodynamics show a detrusor pressure of 70 cm H2O during voiding, Qmax of 4 mL/s, PVR of 250 mL, a non-funneling bladder neck on fluoroscopy, and appropriate silencing of the perineal EMG during voiding. The best pharmacologic treatment is:
rationale: A closed bladder neck during a high-pressure void with normal external sphincter relaxation defines smooth-sphincter (internal) dyssynergia, which can occur with cervical and upper thoracic lesions above the sympathetic outflow; a selective alpha-1 antagonist such as tamsulosin relaxes the smooth-muscle bladder neck. Baclofen and diazepam act on striated muscle and would address external sphincter dyssynergia, which is absent here. Phenoxybenzamine is nonselective and poorly tolerated. Oxybutynin would further impair emptying.
learning_point: In a suprasacral (above T10-L2 sympathetic outflow) spinal cord injury, high-pressure voiding with a closed bladder neck and a relaxing external sphincter indicates detrusor-internal (smooth) sphincter dyssynergia, which is treated with a selective alpha-1 blocker such as tamsulosin.
key_facts: Smooth-sphincter dyssynergia occurs only with lesions above the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow.
Skeletal muscle relaxants (baclofen, dantrolene, diazepam) target the striated external sphincter and do not help smooth muscle.
Phenoxybenzamine (nonselective alpha-blocker) works in theory but has high rates of orthostasis, tachycardia, and mutagenicity concerns.
Videourodynamics clue: closed bladder neck during voiding with quiet EMG.

question: A 13-year-old boy with a known horseshoe kidney has a 2.2 cm calculus in the left renal pelvis with moderate hydronephrosis of that moiety. Urine culture is sterile. The best treatment is:

options.B: observation with repeat imaging in 6 months.
options.D: PCNL via an upper-pole posterior calyx.

rationale: Stone burdens over 1.5 cm in a horseshoe kidney are most effectively cleared by PCNL; the malrotated, low-lying kidney is accessed through a superior posterior calyx. SWL has poor fragment clearance in horseshoe kidneys because of the high ureteral insertion and dependent pelvis, and ureteroscopy for a 2.2 cm stone would require multiple procedures with lower stone-free rates. Pyelolithotomy is technically hazardous because of aberrant anterior vessels and is not preferred. An obstructing 2.2 cm stone should not simply be observed.
learning_point: In a horseshoe kidney, a renal pelvic stone burden greater than 1.5 cm is best treated with PCNL (usually via an upper-pole posterior calyx); SWL and ureteroscopy have lower single-session clearance because of dependent drainage and anatomy, and open or laparoscopic pyelolithotomy is hampered by aberrant vessels.
key_facts: Horseshoe kidney: high insertion of the ureter and malrotation impair fragment clearance after SWL.
Stones under 1.5 cm may be treated with SWL or URS; over 1.5 cm, PCNL gives the best single-procedure stone-free rate.
PCNL access is typically through a superior, posterior calyx because the kidney lies low and medial.
Pyelolithotomy (open or laparoscopic) is not first line because of aberrant anterior vasculature.

question: A 69-year-old man with an asymptomatic 2.5 cm lower-pole renal mass had a drug-eluting stent placed in his left anterior descending artery 2 months ago and takes aspirin and clopidogrel. He asks when he could safely undergo elective partial nephrectomy requiring clopidogrel interruption. The minimum recommended interval from stent placement is:
rationale: Current perioperative guidance calls for deferring elective surgery that requires stopping a P2Y12 inhibitor until at least 6 months after drug-eluting stent placement, with 12 months being the preferred interval if the condition allows; a small, slow-growing renal mass can safely wait. Six weeks and 3 months carry a high risk of in-stent thrombosis, which is frequently fatal. Twelve months is ideal rather than the minimum, and 24 months is not a recommended threshold. Aspirin should be continued through surgery when bleeding risk permits.
learning_point: After drug-eluting coronary stent placement, elective surgery requiring interruption of a P2Y12 inhibitor should be delayed at least 6 months (ideally 12), balancing stent thrombosis risk against surgical bleeding; aspirin is continued whenever possible.
key_facts: Minimum delay for elective surgery after DES: 6 months; 12 months is ideal and lowers perioperative stent thrombosis and cardiac event risk.
Decisions are multidisciplinary (cardiology, surgery, anesthesia).
If surgery cannot wait, minimize time off dual antiplatelet therapy and continue aspirin.
Bare-metal stents require a shorter delay (about 4 to 6 weeks) than DES.

question: A 52-year-old woman with stress urinary incontinence and no neurologic history undergoes multichannel urodynamics with patch perineal EMG. Gentle traction on the urethral catheter produces no change in EMG activity, but a strong cough produces brisk EMG recruitment, and anal tone is normal. This finding most likely represents:

options.A: a sacral root lesion requiring lumbosacral MRI.

rationale: The bulbocavernosus reflex is absent in up to about 30% of neurologically normal women, so its absence alone is not pathologic, particularly when the EMG recruits normally with coughing and anal tone is intact. Good recruitment with cough excludes electrode malfunction. There is nothing in the history to suggest a sacral root lesion, demyelinating disease, or pudendal neuropathy, and imaging is not warranted on this finding alone.
learning_point: Absence of a bulbocavernosus reflex on EMG during urodynamics is a normal finding in a substantial minority (about 30%) of neurologically intact women, especially when EMG recruits appropriately with cough; it does not by itself indicate a sacral lesion.
key_facts: Bulbocavernosus reflex tests the S2-S4 sacral reflex arc; elicited by clitoral/glans squeeze or tugging a Foley.
Present in roughly 70% of neurologically normal women (nearly all normal men).
Intact EMG recruitment with cough confirms the electrodes are functioning and the pelvic floor is innervated.
Absent BCR should be interpreted in the context of history and the rest of the neurologic examination.

question: During prone PCNL for a 3 cm stone, 20 mL of room air is injected through the ureteral catheter to outline the posterior calyces. Within a minute the end-tidal CO2 falls abruptly, oxygen saturation drops to 82%, blood pressure falls to 70/40 mm Hg, and the anesthesiologist hears a churning cardiac murmur. The most appropriate immediate maneuver is to:

options.A: turn the patient supine and begin vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam.
options.B: place the patient left side down with the head lowered.
options.C: place the patient right side down with the head elevated.
options.D: withdraw the ureteral catheter and complete the procedure quickly.
options.E: give intravenous epinephrine for anaphylaxis to contrast.

rationale: Abrupt hypoxemia, a drop in end-tidal CO2, hypotension, and a mill-wheel murmur immediately after air injection define venous gas embolism; the air should be trapped in the right atrium by positioning the patient left lateral decubitus with the head down (right side up), along with 100% oxygen and resuscitation. Right side down with head up would drive air into the pulmonary outflow tract. Supine repositioning aids CPR but is not the specific maneuver, and antibiotics treat sepsis, not embolism. Epinephrine for anaphylaxis addresses the wrong diagnosis, and continuing the operation is unsafe.
learning_point: Sudden hypoxia and hemodynamic collapse after air injection into the collecting system during PCNL indicates venous gas embolism; immediate management is to place the patient left lateral decubitus with head down (Durant position) so air stays in the right atrium rather than the pulmonary outflow tract.
key_facts: Gas embolism presents with abrupt hypoxemia, hypotension, arrhythmia, decreased end-tidal CO2, and a mill-wheel murmur.
Treatment: stop gas source, 100% oxygen, left lateral decubitus head-down positioning, supportive resuscitation, consider central venous aspiration.
Using air for calyceal delineation is avoided by many; CO2 is safer because it is highly soluble.
Hydrocortisone treats anaphylaxis; antibiotics treat sepsis; neither addresses embolism.

question: A 44-year-old woman with a staghorn calculus has a urine pH of 7.8 and stone analysis showing magnesium ammonium phosphate. Her preoperative urine culture grows a gram-positive coccus in clusters. The organism most likely to have contributed to this stone by producing urease is:
rationale: Struvite stones require urease-producing bacteria, and among gram-positive organisms Staphylococcus aureus is a reliable urease producer (over 90% of isolates), making it the organism most associated with infection stones after Proteus species. Streptococci and enterococci do not produce clinically significant urease. E. coli, although the most common uropathogen, is not a gram-positive coccus and only rarely produces urease.
learning_point: Struvite (infection) stones form only in the presence of urease-producing organisms; besides Proteus, more than 90% of Staphylococcus aureus isolates produce urease, whereas E. coli, Serratia, and streptococci essentially do not.
key_facts: Urease splits urea to ammonia, alkalinizing urine (pH above 7.2) and precipitating magnesium ammonium phosphate and carbonate apatite.
Common urease producers: Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Providencia, Morganella, Staphylococcus aureus, Ureaplasma urealyticum, Corynebacterium urealyticum.
E. coli is the most common uropathogen but is rarely a urease producer, so it is not a typical struvite organism.
Treatment requires complete stone removal; acetohydroxamic acid is a urease inhibitor adjunct.

question: A 29-year-old man sustains a handgun wound to the scrotum and perineum. Retrograde urethrography shows a focal contrast leak from the mid-bulbar urethra, and exploration reveals a clean 1.5 cm ventral urethral laceration with viable surrounding spongiosum; the testes and rectum are uninjured. The best management is:

options.A: marsupialization of the urethra with second-stage closure at 6 months.
options.B: suprapubic cystostomy and delayed urethroplasty in 3 months.
options.C: placement of an 18 Fr urethral catheter across the defect without repair.
options.D: debridement and primary spatulated closure over a catheter.

rationale: A short, clean anterior urethral defect from a low-velocity projectile is best managed at exploration by conservative debridement and immediate primary repair over a catheter, which yields the lowest stricture rate. Simple catheter realignment leaves the defect to heal by scar and strictures more often. Suprapubic diversion with delayed repair is appropriate for blunt or high-velocity injuries with extensive tissue loss, and staged marsupialization is reserved for large defects. Grafts or flaps placed into freshly traumatized tissue have poorer take and higher stricture rates.
learning_point: A small, isolated anterior urethral defect from a low-velocity gunshot wound should be explored, debrided, and repaired primarily; realignment alone gives more strictures, suprapubic diversion is reserved for blunt or high-velocity injuries, and grafts/flaps or staged repair are for larger defects.
key_facts: All penetrating genital/urethral injuries warrant surgical exploration, debridement, and staging.
Low-velocity anterior urethral injury with a short defect: immediate primary anastomotic repair over a catheter.
Large defects or high-velocity/blast wounds: debride, marsupialize, and perform staged urethroplasty later; avoid grafts/flaps in acutely injured tissue.
Catheter realignment alone yields higher stricture rates than primary repair for penetrating anterior injuries.

question: A urologist wants to lower the radiation dose received by patients during ureteroscopy. Which of the following changes accomplishes this?

options.A: moving the x-ray tube beneath the table.
options.B: having the circulating nurse operate the fluoroscopy pedal.
options.C: relying on the last-image-hold display rather than re-imaging.
options.D: switching from pulsed to continuous fluoroscopy.
options.E: activating the boost (high-dose) mode for clearer images.

rationale: Last-image hold freezes the most recent frame on the monitor so the surgeon can review anatomy without re-exposing the patient, directly cutting the number of exposures. Continuous (rather than pulsed) imaging and boost mode both increase dose. Positioning the tube under the table reduces scatter to the surgical team but does not change the patient's dose. The surgeon, not a remote nurse or technician, should control the pedal so that imaging is limited to moments when it is needed.
learning_point: Patient fluoroscopy dose is reduced by techniques that limit beam-on time and repetition, such as last-image hold, pulsed/spot imaging, surgeon control of the pedal, and collimation; magnification/boost and continuous imaging raise dose, and under-table tube placement protects staff rather than the patient.
key_facts: Last-image hold displays the final frame without additional exposure, avoiding repeat shots.
Pulsed fluoroscopy and spot images lower dose compared with continuous imaging; boost/magnification increases dose rate.
Under-table tube position reduces scatter to the operator but does not change patient entrance dose.
Surgeon control of the foot pedal minimizes unnecessary beam-on time.

question: A 61-year-old man with refractory urgency incontinence is undergoing first-stage sacral neuromodulation lead placement. Test stimulation produces a clamp-like contraction of the anal sphincter, plantar flexion of the entire foot with outward rotation, and a sensation in the buttock. The appropriate response is to:

options.A: move the lead one level caudad and retest.
options.B: secure the lead in this position since motor responses are present.
options.C: increase the amplitude until great toe flexion appears.
options.D: advance the lead deeper and retest.
options.E: move the lead one level cephalad and retest.

rationale: Whole-foot plantar flexion with rotation, a clamp-like anal contraction, and buttock sensation are S2 responses; the lead is one level too high and should be repositioned caudally into S3 and retested for a bellows response with great-toe flexion and perineal sensation. Fixing the lead at S2 risks ineffective therapy and uncomfortable leg stimulation. Changing depth or amplitude within the S2 foramen will not produce an S3 pattern, and moving cephalad to S1 is wrong.
learning_point: During sacral neuromodulation lead testing, plantar flexion with foot rotation and buttock sensation indicates S2 stimulation; the lead should be moved one foramen caudally to S3, where the correct response is a bellows contraction of the perineum and plantar flexion of the great toe with sensation in the vagina/rectum/perineum.
key_facts: S2: clamp-like anal contraction, plantar flexion of the whole foot with lateral rotation/calf cramp, sensation in leg or buttock.
S3: bellows (anal wink/perineal lifting), great toe plantar flexion, sensation in rectum/vagina/scrotum.
S4: bellows only, no leg movement, sensation in rectum.
Depth adjustment in the wrong foramen does not convert an S2 response to an S3 response.

question: A 46-year-old woman with a BMI of 38 was found to have a 4 mm right distal ureteral stone on non-contrast CT; the scout radiograph and a subsequent KUB did not show it. After 5 weeks of observation with tamsulosin she is pain-free but has not seen a stone pass. The best imaging study is:
rationale: The stone must be confirmed before any intervention, and in a patient with a BMI well above 30 the most sensitive study is a standard-dose non-contrast CT; low-dose protocols lose sensitivity in obese patients. Plain films will not help because the stone was radiographically invisible at diagnosis. Ultrasound detects distal ureteral stones poorly and is further limited by body habitus. Proceeding directly to ureteroscopy risks an unnecessary procedure for a stone that may have passed.
learning_point: To confirm persistence of a small distal ureteral stone that was never visible on plain film in an obese patient, standard-dose non-contrast CT is the appropriate follow-up study; low-dose CT loses sensitivity above BMI 30, KUB is useless for a radiographically invisible stone, and ureteroscopy should not proceed without confirming the stone.
key_facts: Low-dose CT is not recommended for BMI over 30 because sensitivity falls.
KUB follow-up is appropriate only if the stone was seen on the initial KUB or scout film.
Ultrasound has poor sensitivity for distal ureteral stones, especially in obese patients.
AUA guidance: observation of distal stones up to 4 to 6 weeks, then reimaging before intervention.

question: A 6-year-old boy who had endoscopic valve ablation in infancy wets during the day and most nights. Renal ultrasound shows normal kidneys and no hydroureteronephrosis, VCUG shows a mildly thick-walled bladder without reflux or residual valve leaflets, PVR is 5 mL, and urinalysis is normal. The most appropriate next step is:
rationale: Incontinence is extremely common in boys with a history of valves, and when upper tracts are normal, emptying is complete, and there is no residual obstruction, a trial of behavioral therapy with timed voiding is the appropriate first step before invasive testing. Urodynamics are reasonable if conservative measures fail. Antimuscarinics must be used carefully because an evolving myogenic bladder can decompensate into retention. Overnight drainage is for polyuria with hydroureteronephrosis, and desmopressin does not treat bladder dysfunction.
learning_point: Daytime and nighttime incontinence in a boy after posterior urethral valve ablation with normal upper tracts, complete emptying, and no residual obstruction should first be managed with conservative measures such as timed voiding before urodynamics, antimuscarinics, or nighttime drainage.
key_facts: Over 80% of boys with PUV have incontinence at age 5 owing to valve bladder dysfunction (overactivity, poor compliance, or myogenic failure).
Overnight catheter drainage is reserved for polyuria from a concentrating defect with hydroureteronephrosis.
Antimuscarinics may precipitate retention if there is underlying myogenic failure; use cautiously after evaluation.
Desmopressin treats nocturnal polyuria, not the bladder dysfunction that drives PUV-related incontinence.

question: A 70-year-old man on continuous androgen deprivation has a rising PSA to 12 ng/mL with a castrate testosterone and three new bone lesions on bone scan. He has no pain, has not received chemotherapy, and has an ECOG performance status of 0. Sipuleucel-T is appropriate for him because he has:

options.A: asymptomatic metastatic castration-resistant disease with good performance status.
options.E: a PSA rising faster than 2 ng/mL per month.

rationale: Sipuleucel-T improved overall survival in the IMPACT trial among men with asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic metastatic CRPC, and the AUA guideline recommends it in that population with good performance status and no prior docetaxel. It is not offered for non-metastatic CRPC, symptomatic bone pain, post-chemotherapy disease, or poor performance status. PSA kinetics are not an indication, and patients should understand that PSA often does not fall with this therapy.
learning_point: Sipuleucel-T is indicated for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with good performance status; it should not be offered for non-metastatic disease, symptomatic metastases, after docetaxel, or in poor-performance patients, and PSA/radiographic responses are uncommon despite a survival benefit.
key_facts: IMPACT trial: median overall survival 25.8 vs 21.7 months (about 4 months), 22% relative reduction in risk of death.
Autologous cellular immunotherapy given as three infusions 2 weeks apart.
Patients should be counseled that PSA decline and imaging improvement are rare.
AUA CRPC guideline restricts it to asymptomatic/minimally symptomatic mCRPC without visceral metastases and good performance status.

question: A 60-year-old woman has straining, incomplete emptying, and leakage 2 years after abdominoperineal resection for rectal cancer; she voided normally before the operation. Urodynamics are most likely to demonstrate:

options.A: detrusor overactivity, reduced compliance, and a relaxing external sphincter.
options.B: normal compliance, acontractile detrusor, and a relaxing external sphincter.
options.C: detrusor overactivity with external sphincter dyssynergia.
options.D: detrusor overactivity, normal compliance, and a relaxing external sphincter.
options.E: acontractile detrusor, reduced compliance, and fixed external sphincter tone.

rationale: Radical pelvic surgery injures the pelvic plexus, producing a lower motor neuron pattern: an underactive or acontractile detrusor, poor compliance, and a striated sphincter that neither relaxes nor contracts normally (fixed tone), often with an open smooth sphincter. Detrusor overactivity is a feature of suprasacral neurologic lesions, not a peripheral denervation injury. True detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia requires an intact but uncoordinated reflex arc, which is not the mechanism here. A normally relaxing sphincter with an acontractile bladder omits the characteristic fixed sphincter tone and compliance loss.
learning_point: Radical pelvic surgery (radical hysterectomy, abdominoperineal resection) can cause a peripheral parasympathetic/pelvic plexus injury producing detrusor underactivity or acontractility, reduced compliance, and fixed (non-relaxing) striated sphincter tone with an often open, incompetent smooth sphincter.
key_facts: Incidence of voiding dysfunction: radical hysterectomy 16 to 80%, APR 20 to 68%, anterior resection 20 to 25%.
Urodynamic triad: impaired detrusor contractility, decreased compliance, fixed external sphincter tone causing functional obstruction.
Smooth sphincter is often open; stress incontinence and overflow may coexist.
Many recover within 6 to 12 months; persistent cases are managed with CIC.

question: A 66-year-old man undergoes robotic salvage prostatectomy for biopsy-proven recurrence 4 years after external beam radiation. During posterior dissection a 1.5 cm full-thickness rectal injury is identified and repaired in two layers after irrigation. In addition to broad-spectrum antibiotics and anal dilation, the next step is:

options.C: prolonged urethral catheter drainage for 3 weeks without diversion.

rationale: Irradiated rectal tissue has impaired blood supply and healing, so a primary repair alone carries an unacceptable risk of breakdown and rectourethral fistula; temporary fecal diversion with a colostomy is advised whenever a rectal injury occurs in a previously irradiated pelvis. Omental or peritoneal interposition without diversion is appropriate for injuries during primary (non-irradiated) prostatectomy. TPN and prolonged catheterization are adjuncts that do not substitute for diverting the fecal stream.
learning_point: A rectal injury recognized during salvage prostatectomy in a previously irradiated pelvis should be closed primarily and protected with a diverting colostomy because irradiated tissue heals poorly and carries a high risk of rectourethral fistula; interposition alone suffices only in non-irradiated patients.
key_facts: Rectal injury incidence: 1 to 3% in primary prostatectomy, 6 to 15% in salvage prostatectomy after radiation.
Non-irradiated, small, clean injuries: two-layer closure with omental or peritoneal interposition, antibiotics, anal dilation, prolonged catheter drainage.
Prior radiation: add fecal diversion at the time of repair.
Unrecognized injury presents with fever, pneumaturia, fecaluria, or fistula.

question: A 24-year-old man undergoes a 6-hour perineal urethroplasty in exaggerated lithotomy. In the recovery room he has severe left calf pain unrelieved by opioids, a tense calf that is exquisitely painful with passive dorsiflexion of the foot, and numbness of the first web space. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and capillary refill is brisk. The next step is:

options.A: CT angiography of the lower extremity.
options.B: venous duplex ultrasound to exclude deep vein thrombosis.
options.D: elevation of the leg and reassessment in 4 hours.
options.E: nerve conduction studies and EMG of the leg.

rationale: Pain disproportionate to examination, pain with passive stretch, a tense compartment, and sensory change after prolonged lithotomy are early signs of compartment syndrome; normal pulses do not exclude it because arterial compromise is a late finding. Compartment pressure measurement confirms the diagnosis and leads to emergent fasciotomy. Duplex ultrasound and EMG evaluate DVT and neuropraxia, which are less likely and less time-critical. Waiting with elevation (which actually lowers perfusion pressure) or obtaining angiography delays limb-saving treatment.
learning_point: Severe calf pain out of proportion to findings, pain on passive stretch, and paresthesias after prolonged lithotomy positioning indicate lower-extremity compartment syndrome; the next step is compartment pressure measurement followed by emergent fasciotomy, even with intact pulses, because pulselessness is a late sign.
key_facts: Risk factors: lithotomy longer than 4 to 5 hours, elevated legs, hypotension, obesity, intermittent compression devices misuse.
Early signs: pain, pain on passive dorsiflexion, tense compartment, paresthesia; late signs: pulselessness, paralysis.
Diagnosis by intracompartmental pressure (over 30 mm Hg or within 30 mm Hg of diastolic); treatment is immediate fasciotomy.
Delay leads to rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, permanent neuromuscular loss, and limb loss.

question: A 48-year-old woman with urgency and urgency incontinence has completed 12 weeks of bladder training, caffeine reduction, and pelvic floor exercises with minimal improvement. Urinalysis is negative and pelvic examination is unremarkable. According to the AUA/SUFU overactive bladder guideline, the next step is:

options.D: a beta-3 agonist such as vibegron or mirabegron.

rationale: When behavioral therapy fails, the guideline moves to second-line oral pharmacotherapy with an antimuscarinic or a beta-3 agonist; a beta-3 agonist avoids anticholinergic side effects. Botulinum toxin and tibial nerve stimulation are third-line options reserved for failure of medications. Urodynamics and cystoscopy are unnecessary in uncomplicated OAB with a negative urinalysis and would not change initial management.
learning_point: Per the AUA/SUFU overactive bladder guideline, after failure of first-line behavioral therapy the next step is second-line pharmacotherapy (antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist); urodynamics, cystoscopy, and third-line therapies such as neuromodulation or botulinum toxin are not indicated at this stage in an uncomplicated patient.
key_facts: First line: behavioral therapy (bladder training, fluid management, pelvic floor training); may be combined with medications.
Second line: antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists (mirabegron, vibegron); choose beta-3 or ER formulations to limit dry mouth/constipation.
Third line: onabotulinumtoxinA, peripheral tibial nerve stimulation, sacral neuromodulation, after failure of second line.
Urodynamics, cystoscopy, and upper tract imaging are not needed for the initial workup of uncomplicated OAB.

question: A trial of a new drug for monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis enrolls 900 children and measures the mean number of wet nights per week. Investigators want to compare outcomes among three dose groups while accounting for whether the child also has daytime wetting and whether the child has had a UTI. The most appropriate statistical test is:
rationale: A continuous outcome (wet nights per week) compared across several groups and influenced by more than one categorical factor is analyzed with a factorial ANOVA. A t-test can compare only two groups. Fisher's exact test applies to binary outcomes in small contingency tables, and the Pearson coefficient describes the linear relationship between two continuous variables rather than group differences. Kaplan-Meier analysis is for time-to-event data, not mean outcomes.
learning_point: When a continuous outcome is compared across multiple groups or depends on several categorical independent variables (e.g., treatment plus comorbid subgroups), analysis of variance (ANOVA) is the appropriate test; a t-test handles only two groups, Fisher's exact test is for small binary contingency tables, and Pearson correlation measures the association between two continuous variables.
key_facts: ANOVA compares means across three or more groups or evaluates multiple categorical factors (factorial ANOVA) on one continuous outcome.
t-test: two groups, continuous outcome; paired or unpaired.
Chi-square/Fisher's exact: categorical outcomes; Fisher's when expected cell counts are under 5.
Multiple linear regression is the general model of which ANOVA is a special case; Pearson r assesses linear correlation between two continuous variables.

question: A 58-year-old man with an Indiana pouch created 8 years ago for bladder cancer has newly diagnosed alcoholic cirrhosis. He presents confused with asterixis, an ammonia level of 160 micromol/L, and mildly elevated transaminases; the pouch is palpably full and he has been catheterizing only twice daily. Along with lactulose, the most important immediate urologic step is:

options.C: placement of an indwelling catheter in the pouch for continuous drainage.

rationale: Ammonia in urine is readily reabsorbed across intestinal mucosa, and in a cirrhotic patient this adds to the systemic ammonia load and worsens encephalopathy; minimizing urine contact time by continuous pouch drainage is the key immediate step. Bicarbonate treats acidosis and hydrocortisone treats adrenal crisis or allergy, neither of which is the issue. A pouchogram is unnecessary without signs of rupture. Conversion to a conduit may ultimately be considered but is not an acute intervention.
learning_point: Urine stored in a bowel reservoir allows reabsorption of urinary ammonia; in a patient with hepatic insufficiency and encephalopathy, the first step is continuous catheter drainage of the pouch to prevent ammonia reabsorption, in addition to treating the liver disease.
key_facts: Bowel mucosa reabsorbs ammonium, hydrogen, and chloride from stored urine (hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis).
Hepatic dysfunction impairs ammonia clearance, so reservoir dwell time can precipitate or worsen encephalopathy.
Continent diversions are relatively contraindicated in significant hepatic disease.
Other reservoir complications: hypokalemia, B12 deficiency, stones, hyperammonemia with urease-producing infection.

question: A 34-year-old man with a T4 complete spinal cord injury is undergoing PCNL for a left staghorn calculus. Preoperative urine culture was sterile and he received ceftriaxone and gentamicin. Forty minutes into lithotripsy his heart rate rises to 130 and blood pressure falls to 78/40 mm Hg with a temperature of 38.9 C; estimated blood loss is minimal. After starting fluid boluses, the next step is:

options.A: continue lithotripsy at a reduced irrigation rate.
options.B: exchange the access sheath for a larger one to improve outflow.
options.C: transfuse two units of packed red blood cells.
options.D: terminate the procedure and leave a nephrostomy tube.
options.E: drain the bladder to treat autonomic dysreflexia.

rationale: Fever, tachycardia, and hypotension during fragmentation of an infection stone indicate urosepsis from organisms and endotoxin released from within the stone, which occurs even with sterile preoperative urine and antibiotic prophylaxis; the only safe response is to stop operating, secure drainage with a nephrostomy tube, and resuscitate. Continuing at lower irrigation pressure still liberates bacteria. Autonomic dysreflexia causes hypertension with bradycardia, not hypotension. Transfusion is not indicated with minimal blood loss, and a larger sheath does not address the sepsis.
learning_point: Intraoperative hypotension and tachycardia during PCNL for an infection (struvite) stone signal urosepsis from bacteria and endotoxin released from the stone despite a negative preoperative culture and prophylaxis; the procedure should be stopped immediately with drainage established and resuscitation begun.
key_facts: Struvite stones harbor bacteria within their matrix; stone cultures are positive even when voided urine culture is sterile.
Continued fragmentation and irrigation liberate more endotoxin; abort, leave a nephrostomy tube, and resuscitate.
Autonomic dysreflexia in high spinal cord injury presents with hypertension and bradycardia, the opposite pattern.
Prolonged, high-pressure irrigation increases pyelovenous backflow and sepsis risk; limit operative time in infected stones.

question: A 10-year-old girl with myelomeningocele underwent ileocystoplasty 3 years ago and reports catheterizing 'four or five times a day.' Surveillance ultrasound shows new moderate bilateral hydroureteronephrosis. Videourodynamics show a capacity of 500 mL with detrusor pressure of 12 cm H2O at 350 mL and 35 cm H2O at 500 mL, no detrusor overactivity, and no reflux. The next step is:

options.A: ask her to catheterize more often and repeat ultrasound in 6 months.
options.E: place an indwelling catheter and repeat ultrasound in 1 to 2 weeks.

rationale: The urodynamic study shows a compliant, adequately sized augmented bladder, so the hydronephrosis is most likely from infrequent or incomplete emptying rather than intrinsic bladder dysfunction; continuous drainage with an indwelling catheter should resolve the upper tract dilation quickly and confirms the diagnosis while allowing measurement of urine output. Simply instructing more frequent catheterization does not address poor adherence or technique and delays reassessment. Antimuscarinics are unnecessary without overactivity or poor compliance. Renal scan and nephrostomy tubes are considered only if hydronephrosis persists after bladder decompression.
learning_point: New bilateral hydroureteronephrosis after augmentation cystoplasty with normal capacity and compliance on urodynamics most often reflects poor adherence to or technique of catheterization; an indwelling catheter with repeat ultrasound in 1 to 2 weeks confirms the cause and resolves the hydronephrosis.
key_facts: Good compliance: pressures below 40 cm H2O at expected capacity, no overactivity, so antimuscarinics add nothing.
Chronic overdistension from infrequent or incomplete catheterization raises storage pressure and causes bilateral upper tract dilation.
Indwelling catheter trial also allows measurement of 24-hour urine output to detect polyuria.
Nephrostomy tubes and renal scan are reserved for persistent hydronephrosis after bladder decompression.

question: A 45-year-old woman develops a continuous left upper quadrant bruit 10 days after a percutaneous biopsy of her native left kidney for proteinuria. She has no hematuria, blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg, and creatinine is unchanged. Angiography shows early opacification of the left renal vein from a segmental artery. The most appropriate management is:

options.A: covered stent placement in the segmental artery.

rationale: Post-biopsy renal arteriovenous fistulas are usually small and roughly 70% close on their own within 18 months, so an asymptomatic normotensive patient without hematuria is observed. Embolization or stenting is appropriate if the fistula persists or causes hematuria, hypertension, or cardiac overload. Anticoagulation is for thrombosis, which is not present, and surgery is reserved for fistulas due to renal tumors or those refractory to endovascular treatment.
learning_point: An acquired renal arteriovenous fistula after percutaneous renal biopsy in a hemodynamically stable, normotensive patient is managed expectantly because about 70% close spontaneously within 18 months; embolization is reserved for persistent fistulas, hematuria, hypertension, or heart failure.
key_facts: About 75% of renal AV fistulas produce an abdominal bruit; arteriography shows early renal vein opacification.
Causes: iatrogenic (biopsy, nephrostomy, surgery), trauma, congenital (cirsoid), and renal cell carcinoma (requires nephrectomy).
Indications for intervention: hematuria, hypertension, high-output cardiac failure, enlarging fistula, or persistence.
Anticoagulation has no role; there is no thrombus.

question: A 41-year-old man has a 3.5 cm left adrenal nodule found on abdominal ultrasound performed for gallstones. Plasma metanephrines, overnight dexamethasone suppression, and aldosterone-renin ratio are normal. The best next step is:
rationale: Ultrasound cannot characterize adrenal tissue; the recommended first imaging step is an unenhanced CT because an attenuation of 10 HU or less identifies a lipid-rich adenoma with high specificity, and higher values direct further washout or MRI evaluation. A single-phase contrast CT is of limited diagnostic value because adenomas and non-adenomas overlap after contrast. Biopsy cannot reliably separate adenoma from carcinoma and is reserved for suspected metastasis. Surveillance by ultrasound is inadequate for a lesion of this size, and surgery is premature before imaging characterization.
learning_point: An incidental adrenal mass found on ultrasound with a normal hormonal workup should be characterized with unenhanced CT; attenuation of 10 HU or less is diagnostic of a lipid-rich adenoma, while higher values prompt a washout study or chemical-shift MRI. Biopsy has little role, and repeat ultrasound is inadequate for a 3 cm lesion.
key_facts: Unenhanced CT attenuation 10 HU or less: adenoma with about 98% specificity (lipid-rich).
Lipid-poor adenomas (under 30%) have more than 10 HU; next step is CT washout (absolute washout over 60% at 15 min favors adenoma) or chemical-shift MRI.
Single-phase contrast CT has limited value because post-contrast attenuation overlaps between adenomas and non-adenomas.
Biopsy cannot distinguish adenoma from adrenocortical carcinoma; it is used mainly to confirm metastasis in patients with another known cancer, and only after excluding pheochromocytoma.

question: A 74-year-old woman with CKD (creatinine 1.9 mg/dL) underwent percutaneous radiofrequency ablation of a 2.8 cm biopsy-proven grade 3 clear cell carcinoma of the posterior right kidney. At 9 months, contrast CT shows a 1.2 cm nodular area of enhancement within the ablation zone. The most appropriate management is:

options.C: systemic therapy with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor.

rationale: Nodular enhancement in the ablation zone represents residual viable tumor, and the standard salvage for local failure after ablation is repeat ablation, which preserves nephrons in a patient with CKD and a posterior, accessible lesion. Radical nephrectomy would likely precipitate dialysis, and partial nephrectomy in a scarred ablation bed carries more renal loss and morbidity. Biopsy adds nothing since the lesion is already proven malignant and enhancing. Observation is inappropriate for a high-grade tumor, and systemic therapy is for metastatic disease.
learning_point: Persistent or new enhancement in the tumor bed after thermal ablation indicates residual or recurrent tumor; for a biopsy-proven high-grade RCC in a patient with renal insufficiency, repeat ablation is the treatment of choice because it is effective, nephron-sparing, and avoids the difficulty of surgery in an ablated bed.
key_facts: Local recurrence after cryoablation 3 to 10%, after radiofrequency ablation 5 to 20%; most are salvageable with repeat ablation.
Persistent central enhancement on follow-up imaging is the usual sign of treatment failure.
Re-biopsy is unnecessary when the prior biopsy was positive and the lesion enhances.
Partial nephrectomy after ablation is technically harder, and radical nephrectomy in CKD risks dialysis.

question: A 55-year-old woman is undergoing staged sacral neuromodulation under general anesthesia for refractory urgency incontinence. Fluoroscopy confirms the foramen needle in S3 bilaterally, but stimulation up to 6 mA produces no bellows response or toe movement on either side. The next step is:

options.A: convert to bilateral lead placement at S4.
options.B: abandon the procedure and schedule onabotulinumtoxinA.
options.E: ask anesthesia whether a neuromuscular blocking agent is on board.

rationale: Bilateral absence of any motor response despite fluoroscopically correct needle position is almost always due to residual neuromuscular blockade, so the first step is to verify with anesthesia and allow reversal or wear-off before retesting. Changing stimulation parameters or polarity would not overcome paralysis, and moving to another sacral level targets the wrong roots. Abandoning the case is premature when a correctable anesthetic cause is likely.
learning_point: When no motor response is obtained at either S3 foramen during sacral neuromodulation under general anesthesia, first confirm that the patient is not under neuromuscular blockade, since paralytics abolish the bellows and great-toe responses regardless of lead position or stimulation settings.
key_facts: Communicate with anesthesia preoperatively: no long-acting paralytics for sacral neuromodulation lead placement.
Fluoroscopic confirmation of S3 position plus motor response is the standard for lead placement; sensory responses are unavailable under general anesthesia.
Pulse width or bipolar settings are not the cause of an absent response bilaterally.
Placing the lead without a motor response risks a non-functioning or poorly tolerated lead.

question: A 19-year-old man is evaluated for bilateral breast enlargement. He is 190 cm tall with long limbs, little facial or chest hair, and reduced muscle bulk; both testes are 3 mL and firm. Which statement about his most likely condition is correct?

options.A: Serum LH is expected to be normal.
options.B: Verbal and executive cognitive function are typically unaffected.
options.C: Serum estradiol is expected to be low.
options.D: Testicular biopsy would show absent Leydig cells.
options.E: He is at increased risk of Leydig and Sertoli cell tumors of the testis.

rationale: Tall habitus, gynecomastia, sparse androgenic hair, and small firm testes indicate Klinefelter syndrome, which carries increased risks of extragonadal germ cell tumors, non-germ cell (Leydig and Sertoli cell) testicular tumors, and breast cancer. The testes fail primarily, so LH and FSH are elevated rather than normal, and estradiol is relatively increased, which drives the gynecomastia. Leydig cells are present (often clustered or hyperplastic) despite low testosterone output. Deficits in verbal skills and frontal executive function are well documented.
learning_point: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) presents with tall stature, gynecomastia, sparse body hair, and small firm testes; it features elevated LH/FSH with low testosterone and relatively high estradiol, cognitive/verbal deficits, and an increased risk of breast cancer, extragonadal germ cell tumors, and Leydig/Sertoli cell testicular tumors.
key_facts: Most common karyotype 47,XXY; seminiferous tubule hyalinization causes small firm testes and azoospermia (sperm sometimes retrievable by microTESE).
Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: high LH and FSH, low testosterone, elevated estradiol-to-testosterone ratio.
Leydig cells are present (often hyperplastic) but dysfunctional.
Increased risk of breast cancer, mediastinal germ cell tumors, non-germ cell (Leydig/Sertoli) testicular tumors; reduced verbal and executive function.

question: Ten weeks after robotic radical prostatectomy with extended pelvic lymph node dissection, a 62-year-old man reports steadily worsening urinary frequency, urgency, and a feeling of suprapubic fullness. He empties well with a PVR of 30 mL; urinalysis shows a few leukocytes without hematuria, and a 4-week trial of solifenacin failed. A urine culture is sent. The next step is:

options.C: refer for pelvic floor physical therapy.

rationale: Progressive irritative symptoms and pelvic fullness after a lymph node dissection suggest a pelvic lymphocele compressing the bladder, which is confirmed by pelvic imaging and treated by drainage. Additional antimuscarinic or beta-3 therapy and pelvic floor therapy treat the symptoms without addressing the mass effect. Empiric antibiotics should wait for culture results, and cystoscopy offers little without hematuria or suspected anastomotic stricture.
learning_point: New or worsening frequency and urgency after robotic prostatectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy should prompt pelvic imaging to exclude a symptomatic lymphocele compressing the bladder before attributing symptoms to postoperative overactivity or infection.
key_facts: Lymphoceles complicate pelvic lymph node dissection in roughly 5 to 10% of cases; most are asymptomatic.
Symptomatic lymphoceles cause pelvic pressure, frequency/urgency from bladder compression, leg swelling, DVT, or infection.
Diagnosis is by pelvic ultrasound or CT; treatment is percutaneous drainage with or without sclerotherapy or laparoscopic marsupialization.
Antibiotics are reserved for culture-proven infection; cystoscopy is not indicated without hematuria or suspected anastomotic problem.

question: A 14-year-old boy with spina bifida, prior bladder neck sling, augmentation cystoplasty, and an appendicovesicostomy presents 10 hours after his last catheterization unable to pass a catheter through the stoma. Attempts per urethra also fail. He is uncomfortable, and bedside ultrasound shows a markedly distended bladder. The most appropriate next step is:

options.A: ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle decompression of the bladder.
options.B: immediate surgical revision of the appendicovesicostomy.
options.D: cystoscopy through the stoma under general anesthesia.

rationale: The distended bladder compresses the flap valve of the continent channel; percutaneous aspiration relieves the pressure, after which catheterization through the channel is usually possible, and it can be done without general anesthesia. Endoscopy of the channel against a tense bladder risks appendiceal injury and generally needs anesthesia, while urethral access is impractical after a sling and bladder neck procedure. An open suprapubic tube is more invasive than needed, revision is premature, and a diuretic would worsen the distension.
learning_point: When a patient with an augmented bladder and continent catheterizable channel cannot catheterize and the bladder is distended, the flap-valve channel is occluded by overdistension; percutaneous suprapubic aspiration decompresses the bladder, usually allowing catheter passage, and is less invasive than endoscopy or open suprapubic tube placement.
key_facts: Overdistension stretches the flap valve, kinking or compressing the channel so a catheter cannot pass.
Needle aspiration under ultrasound guidance can be done at the bedside with local anesthesia or sedation.
Cystoscopy via a reconstructed bladder neck is difficult, and scoping the channel when the bladder is full risks perforating the appendix.
Channel revision is considered only for recurrent difficulty after acute decompression.

question: A 62-year-old woman with cT2N0 urothelial carcinoma of the bladder elects trimodality therapy. After maximal TURBT and induction with cisplatin plus 40 Gy, restaging resection shows residual high-grade urothelial carcinoma invading the lamina propria with negative muscle. The next step is:

options.A: repeat TURBT in 6 weeks before deciding.
options.D: induction intravesical BCG followed by consolidation radiation.
options.E: switch to gemcitabine-cisplatin and repeat restaging in 3 months.

rationale: Persistent invasive carcinoma at the mid-treatment restaging indicates failure of induction and is the defined trigger for salvage cystectomy in bladder-preservation protocols; continuing radiation would delay definitive treatment of radioresistant disease. BCG is used only for delayed non-muscle-invasive recurrences after completed trimodality therapy, not for persistent disease during induction. Switching systemic chemotherapy or performing another resection does not address the demonstrated inadequate local response.
learning_point: In trimodality bladder preservation, the mid-course (post-induction) cystoscopic evaluation determines continuation: persistent invasive urothelial carcinoma (e.g., T1) indicates inadequate response and mandates prompt salvage radical cystectomy rather than completing chemoradiation.
key_facts: Protocol: maximal TURBT, induction chemoradiation (about 40 Gy with cisplatin), restaging TURBT/biopsy; complete responders finish consolidation chemoradiation.
Incomplete response at mid-treatment: salvage cystectomy (about 20 to 30% of patients).
Delayed non-muscle-invasive recurrence after completed TMT can be treated with TURBT and intravesical BCG.
Changing chemotherapy or escalating radiation at mid-course is not a substitute for cystectomy.

question: A 47-year-old woman with a spinal cord injury had an ileocystoplasty 12 years ago and empties by CIC. Over the past year she has developed urinary leakage that persists despite solifenacin and catheterizing every 3 hours. Urinalysis is sterile and renal/bladder ultrasound shows no stones or hydronephrosis. The next step is:

options.E: repeat augmentation with a second bowel segment.

rationale: Incontinence after augmentation may stem from high-pressure storage (overactivity or poor compliance of the native bladder or bowel patch) or from an incompetent outlet, and only videourodynamics can distinguish these and guide treatment. Botulinum toxin, an outlet sling, or re-augmentation are each appropriate for a specific urodynamic diagnosis but should not be chosen empirically. Cystoscopy is reasonable if urodynamics are normal, since infection and stones have already been excluded.
learning_point: New incontinence many years after augmentation cystoplasty that fails antimuscarinics and more frequent catheterization requires videourodynamics to distinguish storage failure (overactivity of the native bladder or augment, poor compliance) from outlet incompetence before selecting therapy.
key_facts: Videourodynamics evaluates compliance, phasic contractions of the native detrusor or bowel segment, capacity, and bladder neck competence/leak point pressure.
Treatment is directed by findings: onabotulinumtoxinA into the native bladder, augment revision, or an outlet procedure (sling, AUS, bladder neck reconstruction).
Rule out infection and stones first (normal UA and ultrasound here); cystoscopy follows if urodynamics are unrevealing.
Empiric outlet surgery without urodynamics risks worsening upper tracts if storage pressures are high.

question: During a left laparoscopic donor nephrectomy, the renal artery and vein are stapled close to the aorta and vena cava. Immediately after division, brisk dark venous bleeding appears from behind the stump of the renal vein. The most likely source is the:

options.B: a lumbar vein entering the posterior renal vein.

rationale: A lumbar vein commonly drains into the posterior surface of the left renal vein near its junction with the cava and is easily avulsed or left unsecured when the vein is divided medially, producing dark bleeding from behind the stump. The gonadal and adrenal veins enter the inferior and superior surfaces and are usually seen and controlled during dissection.
