The left gastric and short gastric arteries supply the stomach itself and do not reach the omentum.
learning_point: An omental pedicle flap is most reliably based on the right gastroepiploic artery (branch of the gastroduodenal), which is larger in caliber than the left gastroepiploic artery (branch of the splenic).
key_facts: The right and left gastroepiploic arteries run along the greater curvature and supply the omentum; either can carry a pedicled flap.
The right gastroepiploic artery is usually the dominant vessel and is preferred for long omental flaps reaching the pelvis.
Short gastric arteries supply the fundus, and the left gastric supplies the lesser curvature; neither supplies the omentum.

question: A 41-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate stones is found to have primary hyperparathyroidism. The elevated parathyroid hormone increases renal tubular calcium reabsorption predominantly at the:
rationale: Parathyroid hormone and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D act on the distal tubule to increase active, transcellular calcium reabsorption; this is the only nephron segment in which calcium handling is under direct hormonal control. The proximal tubule reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered calcium but does so passively along with sodium and water, independent of PTH. The thin descending limb has essentially no active transport, and the collecting ducts regulate sodium, potassium, acid and water, not calcium. Hyperparathyroidism nonetheless produces hypercalciuria because the filtered load from hypercalcemia overwhelms distal reabsorption.
learning_point: Hormonally regulated calcium reabsorption under parathyroid hormone and active vitamin D occurs in the distal tubule; proximal and loop reabsorption of calcium is largely passive and not PTH-dependent.
key_facts: About 60-70% of filtered calcium is reabsorbed passively in the proximal tubule, roughly 15-20% in the thick ascending limb.
The distal convoluted tubule and connecting segment reabsorb a smaller fraction, but this is the site regulated by PTH and calcitriol.
Thiazides increase distal calcium reabsorption, explaining their hypocalciuric effect; aldosterone acts on the cortical collecting tubule.

question: A 24-year-old sexually active woman has two days of dysuria, frequency and suprapubic discomfort. Urinalysis shows 25 WBC/hpf, and a clean-catch culture grows 1,000 CFU/mL of Staphylococcus saprophyticus. The next step is:

options.A: a short course of an appropriate antimicrobial.

rationale: A symptomatic woman with pyuria and growth of a known uropathogen has a urinary tract infection even when the colony count is well below 10^5 CFU/mL; the classic threshold was derived for asymptomatic bacteriuria in epidemiologic studies. Coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. saprophyticus are slow growing and commonly produce low counts despite true infection. Repeating the culture or catheterizing the patient adds cost and delay without changing management, and mycobacterial cultures are reserved for sterile pyuria. Phenazopyridine alone treats symptoms but not the infection.
learning_point: In a symptomatic woman with pyuria, a low colony count (10^2-10^3 CFU/mL) of a recognized uropathogen such as coagulase-negative staphylococci represents true infection and should be treated; the 10^5 threshold applies to asymptomatic screening.
key_facts: Staphylococcus saprophyticus and other coagulase-negative staphylococci grow slowly and may be present at low counts in true cystitis.
Acute dysuria-pyuria syndrome with as few as 10^2 CFU/mL of a uropathogen warrants antimicrobial therapy.
Mycobacterial culture is for sterile pyuria; repeat or catheterized cultures only delay treatment.

question: A 61-year-old woman is four months out from radical cystectomy with an orthotopic ileal neobladder. She voids every 1.5 hours during the day and leaks at night. Videourodynamics show a smooth-walled reservoir of 280 mL with no reflux, a pressure of 12 cm H2O at capacity, leakage with Valsalva at 120 cm H2O, and a residual of 60 mL. The next step is:

options.C: augmentation of the neobladder with additional ileum.
options.D: clean intermittent catheterization every two hours.

rationale: At four months the neobladder is still maturing; a 280 mL low-pressure reservoir that empties well is expected to enlarge and continence typically improves through the first year and beyond. Observation with scheduled voiding and pelvic floor training is appropriate. Frequent catheterization would prevent the reservoir from expanding, an alpha-blocker reduces urethral resistance and may worsen leakage, and augmentation or an outlet procedure cannot be justified before the reservoir has reached its mature capacity.
learning_point: Early (first 3-6 months) frequency and incontinence after an orthotopic neobladder with a modest capacity, low pressure and acceptable emptying should be observed, because reservoir capacity and continence improve for 6-12 months or longer; frequent CIC, sphincter surgery or augmentation are premature.
key_facts: Neobladder capacity increases over the first year as the bowel segment stretches; daytime continence approaches 85-90% and nighttime continence lags.
Too-frequent catheterization keeps the reservoir empty and prevents capacity gain.
Alpha-blockers reduce outlet resistance and can worsen leakage; AUS is reserved for persistent sphincteric incontinence after a year.

question: A 15-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and absence of menses. She has a low posterior hairline, widely spaced nipples and a bicuspid aortic valve; karyotype is 45,X. The renal anomaly most likely to be found on screening ultrasound is:
rationale: The phenotype and 45,X karyotype are diagnostic of Turner syndrome, in which structural renal anomalies are common and horseshoe kidney is the most characteristic. Guidelines recommend a baseline renal ultrasound at diagnosis. Renal agenesis, multicystic dysplastic kidney and ureterocele are not increased in Turner syndrome, and polycystic kidney disease is an unrelated inherited condition.
learning_point: Turner syndrome (45,X) is associated with an increased prevalence of horseshoe kidney and other renal anomalies, so renal ultrasound is part of the initial evaluation; reflux, renal agenesis and vaginal agenesis are not characteristic.
key_facts: Turner stigmata: short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, streak gonads, primary amenorrhea, coarctation/bicuspid aortic valve.
Renal anomalies occur in 30-40%, with horseshoe kidney and collecting system duplications most common.
Mosaic 45,X/46,XY patients carry Y material and need gonadectomy because of gonadoblastoma risk.

question: A 66-year-old man has persistent leakage with coughing and lifting 14 months after robotic prostatectomy. During multichannel urodynamics the bladder is stable to 400 mL with normal compliance; at 300 mL repeated Valsalva maneuvers raise vesical pressure to 140 cm H2O but no leakage is seen fluoroscopically. The next step is:

options.A: repeat the study with a suprapubic catheter.
options.B: proceed with artificial urinary sphincter placement based on history.
options.E: withdraw the urethral catheter and repeat the Valsalva maneuver.

rationale: The history strongly suggests sphincteric incontinence, and the failure to demonstrate leakage despite high abdominal pressures is most likely artifactual: the urodynamic catheter can plug the anastomotic area and prevent leakage. Simply removing the catheter and repeating the stress maneuver usually reveals the incontinence. A suprapubic catheter study is unnecessarily invasive once bladder behavior has been characterized. Cystoscopy and urethrography evaluate stricture and the anastomosis but cannot confirm stress incontinence, and surgery should not proceed without objective demonstration of leakage.
learning_point: When post-prostatectomy stress incontinence is suspected but no leakage occurs with Valsalva during urodynamics, the urethral catheter may be occluding the anastomosis; remove the catheter and repeat the stress maneuver before pursuing other tests.
key_facts: A urethral catheter can mask stress incontinence, particularly across a narrow vesicourethral anastomosis.
Repeat Valsalva or cough after catheter removal is a standard step in urodynamic protocol.
Cystoscopy to assess the anastomosis is appropriate later, before surgical treatment, but does not demonstrate leakage.

question: A 31-year-old man with congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and anosmia has been treated with hCG and recombinant FSH for 20 months. Testosterone is now 520 ng/dL. Semen analysis shows a volume of 1.2 mL, concentration of 8 million/mL and 70% motility. His 29-year-old partner has a normal fertility evaluation and 12 months of timed intercourse have failed. The next step is:
rationale: His total motile sperm count is roughly 6.7 million (1.2 mL x 8 million/mL x 0.70), which exceeds the threshold at which intrauterine insemination offers a reasonable chance of pregnancy; IUI bypasses the cervical mucus and compensates for the low ejaculate volume characteristic of Kallmann syndrome. IVF/ICSI is more invasive and costly and is reserved for lower counts or IUI failure. The low volume is explained by small accessory glands, not ejaculatory duct obstruction, so TRUS is unnecessary. Testis biopsy has no role in a man with sperm in the ejaculate, and scrotal ultrasound is not indicated without an abnormal examination.
learning_point: After gonadotropin therapy in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, a man with a total motile sperm count above about 5 million can be offered intrauterine insemination; IVF/ICSI, imaging and biopsy are not indicated.
key_facts: Total motile sperm count = volume x concentration x % motility; >5 million is generally adequate for IUI.
Kallmann syndrome produces low semen volume and modest counts because accessory glands and testes are small, but sperm quality is usually normal.
TRUS is for suspected ejaculatory duct obstruction (low volume azoospermia); scrotal ultrasound is reserved for abnormal exam.

question: A 70-year-old man who underwent cystectomy with ileal conduit eight years ago is being evaluated for progressive hydronephrosis. His physician wants a urine-based measure of intrinsic renal function that is least distorted by the intestinal segment. The most reliable parameter is:

options.A: maximal urinary osmolality after water deprivation.
options.C: urinary pH response to ammonium chloride loading.

rationale: Urine stored in or passing through an ileal segment is modified: creatinine and urea are reabsorbed, chloride and ammonium are exchanged, bicarbonate is secreted and osmolality is altered, so clearance, concentrating tests, acid-loading tests and protein measurements no longer reflect the kidney alone. Sodium is handled relatively faithfully because ammonium rather than sodium is the main cation exchanged across ileal mucosa, so fractional sodium excretion remains a usable index of tubular function. Creatinine clearance in particular underestimates GFR after ileal diversion.
learning_point: In a patient with an ileal conduit, creatinine clearance, concentrating ability, acid-loading tests and proteinuria are all confounded by intestinal absorption and secretion; fractional excretion of sodium is the parameter least altered and thus most accurately reflects renal function.
key_facts: Ileum reabsorbs urea, creatinine, ammonium and chloride from urine and secretes bicarbonate, distorting clearance and acid-base measurements.
Sodium handling in ileal segments is relatively preserved because ammonium substitutes for sodium in the Na/H exchanger.
Nuclear renography or serum-based estimates are often used clinically to follow function after diversion.

question: A 2-year-old boy with proximal hypospadias and bilateral undescended testes repaired in infancy develops nephrotic syndrome; renal biopsy shows diffuse mesangial sclerosis and he progresses toward end-stage renal disease. Genetic testing confirms a WT1 mutation. He is at highest risk for developing:

options.C: yolk sac tumor of the testis.

rationale: The triad of ambiguous or undervirilized male genitalia, early progressive glomerulopathy and a WT1 mutation is Denys-Drash syndrome, in which the lifetime risk of Wilms tumor is extremely high. Such children require frequent renal imaging, and bilateral nephrectomy is usually performed once renal failure develops or at the time of transplantation. Gonadoblastoma is the gonadal tumor associated with dysgenetic gonads and WAGR/mixed gonadal dysgenesis, but the dominant risk in Denys-Drash is nephroblastoma. RCC, yolk sac tumor and Leydig cell tumor are not features of this syndrome.
learning_point: Denys-Drash syndrome (male pseudohermaphroditism with proximal hypospadias and cryptorchidism, mesangial sclerosis/membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis with renal failure, WT1 mutation) carries a very high risk of Wilms tumor, warranting close renal surveillance and nephrectomy when renal failure develops.
key_facts: Denys-Drash: WT1 mutation; Wilms risk approaches 90%; prophylactic nephrectomy at renal failure/transplant.
WAGR: Wilms, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, intellectual disability (11p13 deletion).
Beckwith-Wiedemann: macroglossia, hemihypertrophy, organomegaly; Wilms and hepatoblastoma risk.

question: A 7-year-old boy has had two days of gradually worsening right scrotal pain without fever or voiding symptoms. On examination there is a tender nodule at the upper pole of the right testis with a faint bluish discoloration; the testis itself is non-tender. Urinalysis is normal. Doppler ultrasound shows symmetric testicular flow, an enlarged hyperemic right epididymis and a small reactive hydrocele. The best management is:

options.D: renal and bladder ultrasound with VCUG.

rationale: A tender upper-pole nodule with a blue dot, preserved testicular perfusion and epididymal hyperemia in a prepubertal boy indicates torsion of an appendix testis with secondary reactive epididymitis. This is self-limited and is treated symptomatically with anti-inflammatory medication, rest and scrotal elevation. Bacterial epididymitis is uncommon at this age and the normal urinalysis argues against infection, so antibiotics and a VCUG are unnecessary. Exploration is reserved for suspected testicular torsion or diagnostic uncertainty, and a nuclear scan adds nothing after a diagnostic Doppler study.
learning_point: In a prepubertal boy with scrotal pain, a normal urinalysis, a viable testis with normal flow and an enlarged hyperemic epididymis most likely has torsion of an appendix testis/epididymis with reactive epididymitis; management is NSAIDs, rest and scrotal support, not antibiotics or exploration.
key_facts: Bacterial epididymitis is rare in prepubertal boys with normal urinalysis; antibiotics are not indicated.
A 'blue dot' sign or focal tenderness at the upper pole suggests torsed appendix testis.
Exploration is reserved for suspected testicular torsion; VCUG is for infection with abnormal upper tracts.

question: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department three hours after a dog bite that removed roughly 40% of his scrotal skin. Both testes, the penis and urethra are intact and uninjured. Following tetanus prophylaxis, broad-spectrum antibiotics and irrigation with debridement, the best management of the scrotal defect is:

options.A: meshed split-thickness skin graft at this operation.
options.B: burial of the testes in medial thigh pouches.
options.C: full-thickness skin graft from the groin.
options.D: primary scrotal closure over a drain.
options.E: wet-to-dry dressings with closure in one week.

rationale: When at least half of the scrotal skin remains and the wound has been adequately cleaned and debrided within hours of injury, the redundant, well-vascularized scrotal skin can be closed primarily; a drain is placed because bite wounds carry contamination risk. Skin grafts and thigh pouches are reserved for near-total skin loss or when primary closure fails. Delayed secondary closure is appropriate for grossly contaminated or devitalized wounds but is unnecessary for a fresh, debrided injury with ample remaining skin.
learning_point: Acute partial scrotal skin loss (about half the scrotum) from an animal bite is managed with tetanus prophylaxis, antibiotics, debridement and primary closure with a drain, taking advantage of the scrotum's elasticity and vascularity; grafts and thigh pouches are rarely needed.
key_facts: Primary closure of the scrotum is feasible with loss of up to about 50-60% of skin.
If grafting is eventually needed, a meshed split-thickness graft is preferred for drainage and cosmesis.
Thigh pouches are reserved for extensive loss where coverage cannot be achieved; exposed testes can be managed with moist dressings in the interim.

question: A 36-year-old woman has a longstanding partially obstructing right UPJ obstruction with a 30% differential function on renogram. Compared with the normal left kidney, the renal function that is expected to remain intact in the obstructed kidney is:

options.D: distal hydrogen ion and ammonium excretion.

rationale: Chronic obstruction injures the distal tubule and medullary interstitium, producing a vasopressin-resistant concentrating defect, impaired acid and ammonium excretion, and defective sodium and potassium handling. The diluting mechanism, which depends on solute reabsorption in relatively spared proximal and loop segments, remains functional. This pattern explains why obstructed kidneys produce a large volume of dilute urine after relief of obstruction.
learning_point: Chronic unilateral partial ureteral obstruction impairs concentrating ability, sodium and potassium reabsorption and ammonia/acid excretion, but the ability to dilute urine is preserved.
key_facts: Obstruction damages the medulla and distal nephron, producing a concentrating defect (nephrogenic DI-like) and distal RTA pattern.
Diluting capacity relies on proximal and loop function that is relatively spared.
Post-obstructive diuresis after relief of bilateral obstruction reflects these tubular defects plus volume and solute load.

question: A 26-year-old man undergoes an orchiectomy through a scrotal incision at an outside hospital for a presumed hydrocele; pathology shows a 3 cm embryonal carcinoma-predominant NSGCT with lymphovascular invasion. Post-orchiectomy tumor markers normalize and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no adenopathy. He elects primary RPLND with excision of the remaining cord and the scrotal scar. Additional treatment of the inguinal and scrotal region should consist of:

options.A: sentinel node mapping of the inguinal nodes.
options.C: adjuvant radiation to the hemiscrotum and groin.

rationale: Scrotal violation raises the risk of local recurrence only slightly and has no effect on metastatic relapse or survival, so excising the scrotal scar and residual cord at the time of RPLND is sufficient. Prophylactic inguinal lymph node dissection, sentinel node biopsy or radiation would treat a region with a very low probability of involvement in a patient with a negative metastatic evaluation. Chemotherapy decisions are based on stage and pathology after RPLND, and the scrotal approach itself is not an indication for systemic therapy.
learning_point: Scrotal violation during orchiectomy for germ cell tumor modestly increases local recurrence but does not affect systemic relapse or survival; management is excision of the scrotal scar and spermatic cord remnant with otherwise stage-appropriate treatment, without prophylactic inguinal node dissection, radiation or chemotherapy.
key_facts: Local recurrence rises from about 0.4% to about 3% after scrotal violation; survival is unchanged.
Inguinal nodes become a potential landing site only if there is clinical or radiographic inguinal disease.
Treatment of the retroperitoneum is dictated by stage and histology, not by the scrotal approach.

question: A 52-year-old man has had four UTIs with the same E. coli strain over 18 months, each resolving with a short course of antibiotics. He now has three days of dysuria, perineal pressure and frequency; urinalysis shows pyuria with bacteriuria and his prostate is mildly tender. Before any antibiotic is given, the appropriate specimen to send is a:

options.A: pre- and post-prostatic massage voided urine.

rationale: Recurrent infection with a single organism suggests a prostatic reservoir, but segmented localization studies are only valid when the bladder urine is sterile; with active bacteriuria every specimen will grow the organism and nothing can be localized. The correct step is a midstream culture to document the pathogen and sensitivities, followed by an agent such as nitrofurantoin that clears the bladder without sterilizing the prostate. Localization cultures are then performed once the urine is clear, and if prostatic infection is confirmed a prolonged fluoroquinolone course is given. A suprapubic aspirate is unnecessarily invasive, and a first-voided specimen reflects only the urethra.
learning_point: When a man with suspected chronic bacterial prostatitis is actively symptomatic with bacteriuria, localization cultures (Meares-Stamey) are uninterpretable; obtain a midstream culture, sterilize the urine with an agent such as nitrofurantoin, then perform localization once the urine is clear.
key_facts: Bacteriuria contaminates all four specimens of a localization study, making it useless until the urine is sterile.
Nitrofurantoin clears bladder bacteriuria without penetrating prostate tissue, preserving the ability to localize prostatic infection afterward.
Confirmed chronic bacterial prostatitis is treated with 4-6 weeks of a fluoroquinolone (or 3 months of TMP-SMX).

question: A 27-year-old woman notices a fullness in her left abdomen. She is otherwise well with a creatinine of 0.8 mg/dL. CT demonstrates an 18 cm mass with predominantly fat attenuation (-80 HU) and prominent vessels, arising from and splaying the left renal parenchyma with a claw sign, without displacement of the kidney; the right kidney is normal. The next step is:
rationale: A mass containing macroscopic fat that clearly originates within the renal parenchyma is an angiomyolipoma and the imaging is diagnostic, so biopsy is not required. The alternative concern, retroperitoneal liposarcoma, displaces rather than arises from the kidney and would be the only reason to consider preoperative radiation. An 18 cm AML in a young woman carries a substantial risk of spontaneous hemorrhage, making observation inappropriate, and lesions this large are poorly controlled by embolization alone because of multiple feeding vessels and persistent risk. Surgical removal, which at this size usually requires nephrectomy, is the best definitive management.
learning_point: A very large fat-containing renal mass arising from within the kidney is an angiomyolipoma; because of its size and hemorrhage risk in a young woman, surgical resection (nephrectomy if partial is not feasible) is preferred, since biopsy is unnecessary, observation is unsafe and massive AMLs are poorly controlled by embolization.
key_facts: Macroscopic fat on CT (negative Hounsfield units) in a mass arising from renal parenchyma is diagnostic of AML; no biopsy needed.
Retroperitoneal liposarcoma displaces the kidney rather than arising from it and rarely contains defects in the renal parenchyma.
AML >4 cm, symptoms, or women of childbearing age raise bleeding risk; embolization is ideal for acute hemorrhage or moderate-size lesions but is less effective for giant tumors.

question: A 50-year-old man with a 1.2 cm lower pole renal stone has undergone two failed SWL sessions with minimal fragmentation. Stone analysis from a previous episode is reviewed. The composition most likely to account for this failure is:
rationale: Brushite is the hardest and most SWL-resistant of the common stone compositions, more so than cystine and calcium oxalate monohydrate; it is also prone to rapid recurrence. Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) is the most fragile stone, and uric acid, calcium oxalate dihydrate and apatite all fragment reasonably well with shock waves. Recognizing a brushite stone should prompt endoscopic management rather than repeated SWL.
learning_point: Brushite (calcium hydrogen phosphate) is the stone composition most resistant to shock wave lithotripsy, followed by cystine and calcium oxalate monohydrate; struvite, uric acid, calcium oxalate dihydrate and apatite fragment more readily.
key_facts: SWL-resistant stones: brushite > cystine > calcium oxalate monohydrate; these typically have high CT attenuation (>1000 HU).
Struvite is the most fragile; uric acid and calcium oxalate dihydrate fragment well.
Resistant compositions favor ureteroscopy or PCNL over SWL.

question: A 68-year-old woman has had five culture-proven E. coli cystitis episodes in the past ten months, each promptly recurring after antibiotics. She has vaginal dryness and atrophic mucosa on examination. Post-void residual is 20 mL and renal ultrasound is normal. The best initial preventive strategy is:
rationale: Postmenopausal vaginal atrophy raises vaginal pH and depletes lactobacilli, allowing colonization by uropathogens; topical vaginal estrogen reverses these changes and has been shown in controlled trials to reduce recurrent UTIs markedly with negligible systemic absorption. Oral estrogen has not reliably reduced UTIs and carries cardiovascular and thromboembolic risk. Antimicrobial prophylaxis is effective but exposes the patient to drug toxicity and resistance and is held in reserve. Probiotics have not demonstrated consistent benefit in rigorous trials.
learning_point: For recurrent UTIs in a postmenopausal woman with normal anatomy, topical vaginal estrogen is the preferred first preventive measure because it restores lactobacilli and lowers vaginal pH; oral estrogen has systemic risks and antibiotic prophylaxis is a second-line option.
key_facts: Vaginal estrogen reduces UTI frequency substantially in randomized trials (e.g., from about 6 to 0.5 episodes per year).
Oral estrogen has not consistently reduced UTIs and carries thrombotic and stroke risk.
Fluoroquinolone and nitrofurantoin prophylaxis carry toxicity concerns; probiotics lack robust trial support.

question: A 64-year-old man with hypertension and well-controlled diabetes is noted during an evaluation for hematuria to have an empty left hemiscrotum. Ultrasound identifies a 1.8 cm homogeneous, atrophic testis in the left inguinal canal with no mass or microlithiasis. The best management is:
rationale: A post-pubertal undescended testis carries an increased risk of germ cell tumor, but that risk declines with age and after about 50 the small mortality risk of anesthesia and surgery exceeds the risk of dying from a future testis cancer; observation is therefore recommended in this age group. Orchiectomy is appropriate for healthy men between puberty and roughly 50. Orchiopexy in an adult does not reduce cancer risk and the atrophic gland adds no reproductive value. A negative biopsy cannot exclude malignancy elsewhere in the testis, and hormonal therapy is ineffective in adults.
learning_point: A cryptorchid testis discovered in a man over about 50 years of age should be observed, because the risk of operative mortality exceeds the risk of death from germ cell cancer; orchiectomy is reasonable in healthy post-pubertal men up to about 50, and biopsy or hormonal therapy has no role.
key_facts: Orchiectomy for a post-pubertal undescended testis is considered between puberty and roughly age 50 in ASA I-II patients.
Beyond age 50 or with significant anesthetic risk, the malignancy risk no longer justifies surgery; observation is recommended.
Negative biopsy cannot exclude cancer elsewhere in the testis; hCG does not reliably induce descent and is not recommended.

question: A 35-year-old woman with T10 paraplegia performs CIC five times daily and is seen for routine follow-up. Her urine is cloudy and culture grows >100,000 CFU/mL of Klebsiella pneumoniae with 20 WBC/hpf. She feels well. Among the following, the finding that would most justify antimicrobial treatment is:
rationale: In a patient catheterizing intermittently, bacteriuria with pyuria is expected and asymptomatic colonization should be left untreated regardless of colony count, odor or the resistance pattern of the organism. Treatment is reserved for symptomatic infection, which in spinal cord injury often presents atypically as new leakage between catheterizations, increased spasticity, fever, flank or abdominal discomfort, autonomic dysreflexia or malaise. Among the options only new incontinence represents a symptom; the others are laboratory or sensory findings that do not distinguish infection from colonization.
learning_point: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in patients on CIC is common and should not be treated; treatment is indicated for symptoms such as fever, new leakage between catheterizations, increased spasticity, autonomic dysreflexia or malaise, not for pyuria, high colony counts, odor, or resistant organisms.
key_facts: Bacteriuria occurs in a large proportion of CIC users and does not by itself warrant antibiotics.
Neurogenic patients lack typical dysuria; surrogate symptoms include incontinence between catheterizations, spasticity, fever, flank pain and lethargy.
Treating asymptomatic colonization promotes resistance without benefit.

question: A 52-year-old man with a BMI of 41 and loud snoring with witnessed apneas has developed bedwetting twice weekly over six months. He has no daytime urgency or incontinence, a normal urinalysis, PVR of 20 mL, and a frequency-volume chart showing nocturnal urine volume exceeding 40% of his 24-hour output. The most likely mechanism is:

options.A: deep sleep from carbon dioxide retention.
options.B: hypoxia-induced release of atrial natriuretic peptide.
options.D: redistribution of dependent edema when supine.
options.E: excess nocturnal release of antidiuretic hormone.

rationale: The frequency-volume chart documents nocturnal polyuria, and in a patient with obvious obstructive sleep apnea the mechanism is release of atrial natriuretic peptide triggered by repetitive hypoxia and increased atrial transmural pressure during obstructed breathing; ANP promotes natriuresis and suppresses ADH, so nocturnal urine production rises. Increased ADH would reduce, not increase, nighttime urine. Nocturnal detrusor overactivity in isolation is unlikely without daytime symptoms, hypercarbia does not increase urine output, and he has no edema to mobilize. CPAP treatment typically reverses the enuresis.
learning_point: Obstructive sleep apnea causes nocturia and secondary nocturnal enuresis through hypoxia-induced increases in atrial natriuretic peptide (with suppression of ADH), producing nocturnal polyuria; CPAP therapy improves the enuresis.
key_facts: Negative intrathoracic pressure against a closed airway raises right atrial transmural pressure and stretches the atrium, releasing ANP.
ANP increases sodium and water excretion and suppresses renin-aldosterone and ADH.
Isolated nocturnal detrusor overactivity without daytime symptoms is unlikely; edema mobilization causes mild nocturia at most.

question: A 56-year-old woman treated with external beam and brachytherapy for stage IIB cervical cancer five years ago develops continuous vaginal urine leakage. Cystoscopy shows a 2.5 cm fistula with indurated, pale edges on the posterior bladder wall above the trigone. CT urogram shows normal upper tracts and no mass. Before planning definitive management, the next step is:
rationale: Any fistula developing after definitive radiation for cervical cancer may be caused by locally recurrent tumor, and the indurated edges here are concerning; tissue diagnosis must precede reconstruction because repair is futile in the presence of cancer and the finding would redirect care toward oncologic treatment. Imaging without a visible mass does not exclude recurrence at the fistula site. Stents or nephrostomies do not establish the diagnosis, fibrin glue is only suited to tiny non-radiated tracts, and both flap repair and diversion are definitive choices made only after malignancy is excluded.
learning_point: A vesicovaginal fistula appearing years after pelvic radiation for cervical cancer must first be biopsied to exclude recurrent malignancy before any repair is planned; radiation fistulas result from endarteritis obliterans, but recurrent tumor is common and changes management entirely.
key_facts: Fistula during or soon after radiation reflects tumor necrosis; late fistula reflects radiation-induced ischemia, yet recurrence must still be excluded.
Repair of a radiated fistula requires healthy tissue interposition (omentum or Martius/gracilis flap) and often urinary diversion; it is contraindicated with active cancer.
Fibrin glue is only for tiny, non-radiated tracts; nephrostomies do not establish a diagnosis.

question: A 28-year-old woman received a living-donor kidney transplant three years ago. Her creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, urine protein is negative, blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg, and she has had no rejection episodes. She asks about becoming pregnant. She should be counseled that:

options.A: pregnancy is reasonable and she may proceed.
options.B: her child has a substantially increased risk of congenital malformations.
options.C: delivery must be by Cesarean section to protect the graft.
options.D: she should expect a post-term delivery.
options.E: her immunosuppressants should be tapered once pregnant.

rationale: She meets all the criteria associated with good maternal, fetal and graft outcomes: stable function more than a year after transplant, no proteinuria, normal blood pressure and no rejection, so proceeding with pregnancy is appropriate with coordinated obstetric and transplant care. Immunosuppression must be continued (and often increased because of the larger volume of distribution), not tapered, although mycophenolate should be exchanged for a non-teratogenic agent before conception. The pelvic allograft rarely obstructs labor and vaginal delivery is standard. Pregnancies in transplant recipients tend toward preterm rather than post-term delivery, and malformation rates with standard agents are similar to the general population.
learning_point: A renal transplant recipient with stable graft function, no proteinuria and controlled blood pressure at least 1-2 years after transplantation can be advised to proceed with pregnancy; vaginal delivery is usually possible, birth defect risk is not increased with standard agents, and immunosuppression is maintained (and may need increased dosing).
key_facts: Favorable predictors: >1 year post-transplant, creatinine <1.5 mg/dL, no proteinuria, no recent rejection, controlled BP.
Preterm (not late) delivery and preeclampsia are more common; Cesarean is performed only for obstetric indications since the graft sits in the iliac fossa.
Mycophenolate is teratogenic and must be switched (e.g., to azathioprine) before conception; calcineurin inhibitor doses often need to increase in pregnancy.

question: A 44-year-old man with a six-hour ischemic priapism after intracavernosal alprostadil is treated with corporal aspiration and repeated intracavernosal injections of dilute phenylephrine. The hemodynamic response most likely to occur as a systemic side effect is:
rationale: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist; systemic absorption produces arterial vasoconstriction and a rise in blood pressure, and the baroreceptor reflex then slows the heart. It has no beta-1 activity, so direct tachycardia or arrhythmia is unlikely, which is why it is preferred over epinephrine or ephedrine for detumescence. Hypotension would not be expected from a vasoconstrictor. Blood pressure and pulse should be monitored throughout treatment, particularly in men with cardiovascular disease.
learning_point: Intracavernosal phenylephrine, a pure alpha-1 agonist used to reverse priapism, can cause systemic hypertension with reflex bradycardia; blood pressure and heart rate should be monitored during injections.
key_facts: Phenylephrine lacks beta activity, so its systemic effect is vasoconstriction-driven hypertension with baroreceptor-mediated bradycardia.
Mixed agonists (epinephrine, ephedrine) are more likely to cause tachycardia and arrhythmia.
Dilute phenylephrine (100-500 mcg/mL) is injected every 3-5 minutes with cardiovascular monitoring, especially in patients with cardiac disease.

question: A 69-year-old man with diffuse aortic atherosclerosis and bilateral renal artery calcifications on preoperative CT undergoes left radical nephrectomy for a 7 cm tumor. On postoperative day two he develops a blood pressure of 185/105 mmHg and mild pulmonary congestion; pulmonary embolus has been excluded. The antihypertensive most likely to be effective is a(n):
rationale: With one kidney removed and the remaining renal artery likely stenotic, this patient has the physiology of the one-kidney, one-clip model: there is no normal kidney to excrete sodium and water, so volume expansion sustains the blood pressure and renin is suppressed. In this setting angiotensin blockade produces little reduction in pressure and may precipitate acute kidney injury in the solitary stenotic kidney. Calcium channel and alpha blockers are also relatively ineffective until the volume excess is corrected. A diuretic addresses the underlying mechanism and is the best choice.
learning_point: After removal of one kidney in a patient whose remaining kidney has renal artery stenosis (one-kidney, one-clip model), hypertension is volume- and sodium-dependent rather than renin-dependent, so a diuretic is the most effective agent and ACE inhibitors/ARBs are relatively ineffective.
key_facts: Two-kidney, one-clip: contralateral normal kidney excretes the volume load; hypertension is renin/angiotensin II dependent and responds to ACE inhibitors.
One-kidney, one-clip: no normal kidney to excrete sodium; volume expansion suppresses renin, so hypertension is volume mediated.
ACE inhibitors in a solitary stenotic kidney also risk acute renal failure.

question: A 17-year-old girl with a solitary right kidney found incidentally on ultrasound has cyclic pelvic pain since menarche. Given her renal anomaly, the associated finding most likely to be present is a(n):

options.E: obstructed hemivagina or other Mullerian duct anomaly.

rationale: The ureteric bud and the Mullerian and Wolffian ducts develop in close proximity, so failure of the ipsilateral kidney to form is frequently accompanied by genital duct anomalies; in women this includes uterine didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina (OHVIRA), unicornuate uterus and vaginal septa, which commonly present with cyclic pain after menarche. The adrenal develops separately from mesoderm and is almost always present even when the kidney is absent. Urethral anomalies, hernias and bladder diverticula are not features of unilateral renal agenesis.
learning_point: Unilateral renal agenesis is strongly associated with ipsilateral genital duct anomalies: Mullerian abnormalities (unicornuate uterus, vaginal septum, etc.) in women and absent vas/seminal vesicle in men; adrenal agenesis, anorchia, urethral anomalies and two-vessel cord are not characteristically increased.
key_facts: URA occurs in about 1 in 1,100; it is more common on the left and may be familial.
Up to one-third of women with URA have Mullerian anomalies; nearly half of men lack ipsilateral Wolffian structures beyond the epididymal head.
The ipsilateral adrenal is usually present; the ipsilateral ureter is absent in about half.

question: A 58-year-old man who smokes has fatigue and a 7 kg unintentional weight loss. CT shows an 8 cm heterogeneous right adrenal mass with central necrosis and irregular margins; the kidney is uninvolved. Plasma metanephrines, cortisol suppression testing and aldosterone/renin ratio are normal. The next step is:

options.C: percutaneous needle biopsy of the mass.
options.D: adrenal protocol CT with delayed washout.

rationale: An 8 cm necrotic, heterogeneous adrenal mass in a smoker with weight loss is almost certainly malignant; the main possibilities are adrenocortical carcinoma and metastatic disease, most often from a lung primary. Chest imaging is required before either biopsy or surgery because it both stages a presumed adrenal carcinoma and may reveal a lung primary that would make biopsy and systemic treatment, rather than adrenalectomy, the appropriate path. Washout CT distinguishes lipid-poor adenomas from other lesions and is unhelpful when the mass is this large and heterogeneous. Biopsy and adrenalectomy are premature without staging, and mitotane requires a tissue diagnosis.
learning_point: A large (>6 cm), heterogeneous, non-functional adrenal mass is likely malignant (adrenocortical carcinoma or metastasis, especially lung); chest CT for staging and to identify a primary should be obtained before biopsy or adrenalectomy, and washout CT is not helpful for such a lesion.
key_facts: Size >4-6 cm, heterogeneity, irregular margins and high unenhanced attenuation predict malignancy.
Lung cancer is the most common source of adrenal metastasis; a lung primary would change management toward biopsy and systemic therapy.
Adrenal biopsy is reserved for suspected metastasis with a known or suspected primary, after excluding pheochromocytoma.

question: A 41-year-old man with a C6 complete spinal cord injury develops a pounding headache, facial flushing and heart rate of 48/min during cystometry. The bladder is drained and the catheters are removed, but ten minutes later his blood pressure is 182/104 mmHg and he remains symptomatic. The next step is:

options.D: topical nitroglycerin paste applied above the level of injury.

rationale: This is autonomic dysreflexia from bladder distension in a high cervical injury; after removing the trigger, a systolic pressure that stays above 150 mmHg with symptoms requires a rapid-onset, short-acting antihypertensive while other causes (such as fecal impaction) are sought. Nitroglycerin paste is applied to skin above the lesion where perfusion is intact and can be wiped off immediately if the pressure falls too far. Nifedipine has caused severe rebound hypotension, stroke and infarction and is no longer recommended. Hydralazine or other intravenous agents are later options that produce labile pressures and require admission, and atropine addresses the reflex bradycardia rather than the underlying hypertension.
learning_point: Autonomic dysreflexia during urodynamics is treated by stopping the stimulus (drain the bladder, remove catheters, sit the patient up); if systolic pressure remains above about 150 mmHg, apply topical nitroglycerin paste above the lesion level as a rapid, reversible antihypertensive. Nifedipine is discouraged because of rebound hypotension.
key_facts: AD occurs with lesions at or above T6; baseline SBP in these patients is often 90-110 mmHg, so a 20-40 mmHg rise is significant.
Second most common trigger after bladder distension is fecal impaction.
IV hydralazine is a later option requiring monitoring; atropine is not used because bradycardia is reflexive to hypertension.

question: A 29-year-old man and his partner have 18 months of infertility. His testes measure 3.6 cm bilaterally and are soft; vasa are palpable. Two semen analyses show azoospermia with ejaculate volumes of 2.8 and 3.4 mL. Serum testosterone is 260 ng/dL, LH is 6.8 IU/L, FSH is 9.2 IU/L and prolactin is normal. The next step is:
rationale: Normal ejaculate volume with palpable vasa excludes ejaculatory duct obstruction and congenital vasal absence, and small soft testes with an FSH above the 7.6 IU/L threshold indicate impaired spermatogenesis (non-obstructive azoospermia) with a probability near 90%, so a diagnostic biopsy adds nothing. His testosterone is low, and raising intratesticular testosterone with clomiphene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator that stimulates endogenous gonadotropins, may improve spermatogenesis before any sperm retrieval attempt. Exogenous testosterone would suppress gonadotropins and worsen spermatogenesis. Recombinant FSH is for men with low FSH, and epididymovasostomy treats obstruction, which he does not have.
learning_point: A man with normal-volume azoospermia, small soft testes, low testosterone and FSH in the upper-normal range has non-obstructive azoospermia with a suboptimal hormonal milieu; clomiphene citrate to raise intratesticular testosterone is the appropriate next step before considering sperm retrieval, and biopsy or reconstruction are not indicated.
key_facts: Testis long axis <4.6 cm plus FSH >7.6 IU/L predicts non-obstructive azoospermia in about 89%; diagnostic biopsy is unnecessary.
Clomiphene (a SERM) raises LH/FSH and testosterone; titrate to mid-normal testosterone. Exogenous testosterone would suppress spermatogenesis.
Recombinant FSH is reserved for hypogonadotropic men with low FSH; epididymovasostomy treats obstruction only.

question: During a left retroperitoneal lymph node dissection, the inferior mesenteric artery is divided at its origin to improve exposure. Viability of the descending and sigmoid colon afterward depends chiefly on collateral flow from the:

options.C: middle colic artery and middle hemorrhoidal arteries.
options.D: left colic artery and superior hemorrhoidal artery.
options.E: superior hemorrhoidal artery and marginal artery.

rationale: The left colic, sigmoid and superior hemorrhoidal arteries all arise from the inferior mesenteric artery and lose their inflow when it is ligated, so options naming them cannot be the source of collateral supply. Perfusion is maintained from above by the middle colic artery of the superior mesenteric system through the marginal artery of Drummond, and from below by the middle (and inferior) hemorrhoidal arteries of the internal iliac system through the rectal anastomoses. The ileocolic and right colic arteries supply the right colon and are too distant to perfuse the sigmoid directly. Preserving the marginal artery during dissection is essential for this collateral pathway.
learning_point: After ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery, the left colon is perfused by collaterals from the middle colic artery (superior mesenteric system) via the marginal artery of Drummond proximally and from the middle and inferior hemorrhoidal (rectal) arteries via the internal iliac distally.
key_facts: The IMA gives rise to the left colic, sigmoid and superior hemorrhoidal arteries.
The marginal artery of Drummond runs along the mesenteric border of the colon connecting SMA and IMA territories; it must be preserved during left colon mobilization.
Middle and inferior rectal arteries arise from the internal iliac and internal pudendal systems and perfuse the rectum retrograde after IMA loss.

question: A 38-year-old farm worker has his scrotal skin completely torn off when clothing is caught in a power take-off shaft. Both testes are exposed but intact, and the penile skin is spared. The avulsed skin arrives with him on ice. After debridement and antibiotics, the best initial management is:

options.A: moist saline dressings with delayed reconstruction.
options.B: defatting and reapplication of the avulsed skin as a graft.
options.C: immediate meshed split-thickness grafting of the testes.
options.E: immediate burial of the testes in thigh pouches.

rationale: Machinery avulsions are contaminated wounds in which the torn skin has had its vascular plexus sheared, so reapplying it as a graft will almost certainly fail. The exposed testes tolerate moist wet-to-dry dressings well, which clean the bed and promote granulation; definitive coverage by delayed primary closure or meshed split-thickness grafting is performed days later once the wound is clean. Immediate grafting, thigh pouches or flap reconstruction all risk infection and loss in the acute setting and are reserved for later or for cases where delayed closure proves impossible.
learning_point: Complete scrotal skin avulsion from a machinery injury is managed with debridement, saline wet-to-dry dressings and delayed reconstruction (primary closure or skin grafting); the avulsed skin is usually too damaged to reuse, and immediate grafting, thigh pouches or flaps risk failure in a contaminated wound.
key_facts: Avulsion in machinery accidents damages the skin's intrinsic vasculature, so the avulsed segment is unsuitable as a graft.
Moist dressings allow granulation and wound cleansing before delayed meshed split-thickness grafting.
The scrotum's elasticity allows primary closure even after loss of 50-60% of skin; thigh pouches and flaps are elective options later.

question: A 62-year-old woman with a 7 cm enhancing renal mass has a positive preoperative stress test; catheterization shows a critical left anterior descending lesion treated with a bare-metal stent. Her cardiologist asks how soon the nephrectomy may safely proceed. The minimum recommended interval after stent placement is:
rationale: Guidelines advise waiting at least four weeks after bare-metal stent implantation before elective non-cardiac surgery so that the stent struts are covered by endothelium and the highest-risk window for thrombosis has passed; this is why a bare-metal stent is selected when surgery cannot be deferred for long. Drug-eluting stents delay endothelialization and traditionally require about a 12-month delay. One week is unsafe, while six weeks or six months are longer than necessary for a patient with a malignancy awaiting resection. Antiplatelet therapy should be continued perioperatively in coordination with cardiology.
learning_point: Elective non-cardiac surgery should be delayed at least 4 weeks after bare-metal coronary stent placement (and about 12 months after a drug-eluting stent) to allow endothelialization and reduce perioperative stent thrombosis; antiplatelet therapy should be continued when possible.
key_facts: Stent thrombosis risk is highest in the first weeks when the stent is not yet endothelialized and antiplatelet drugs are interrupted.
Bare-metal stents are chosen when surgery is anticipated within a year because they endothelialize faster.
Dual antiplatelet therapy is typically continued through the perioperative period or aspirin alone is maintained.

question: A 66-year-old woman with a 10 cm left renal mass has progressive right thigh pain with weight bearing. Imaging shows multiple bone metastases, including a 4.5 cm lytic lesion destroying more than half the cortex of the right femoral shaft. Biopsy confirms clear cell RCC. The next step is:

options.A: palliative external beam radiation to the femur.
options.B: prophylactic intramedullary fixation of the femur.

rationale: A large lytic lesion involving the cortex of a weight-bearing bone with mechanical pain meets criteria for impending pathologic fracture, and a femoral fracture in a patient with metastatic RCC would severely compromise the remainder of her life. Orthopedic stabilization should therefore precede systemic treatment, which is then started once she has recovered. Radiation and bone-seeking radiopharmaceuticals can relieve pain but do not restore structural integrity and may even weaken bone transiently. Both tyrosine kinase inhibitors and checkpoint inhibitor combinations are appropriate systemic choices after the femur is fixed.
learning_point: A large (>3 cm) lytic cortical metastasis in a weight-bearing bone from RCC is at high risk of pathologic fracture and should be surgically stabilized before systemic therapy; radiation or radiopharmaceuticals palliate pain but do not prevent fracture.
key_facts: Impending fracture criteria (e.g., Mirels): lytic lesion, >2/3 cortical involvement, weight-bearing bone, functional pain.
RCC bone metastases are highly vascular and lytic; prophylactic fixation preserves function and quality of life.
TKIs or checkpoint inhibitor combinations are started after stabilization; strontium-89 is for diffuse painful blastic disease.

question: A 62-year-old man received six months of a GnRH antagonist before robotic radical prostatectomy with extended lymph node dissection. The pathology report should be expected to omit a reliable assessment of:
rationale: Androgen deprivation produces treatment effect in prostate tissue: shrunken glands, clear cytoplasm, and pyknotic nuclei that can resemble Gleason pattern 4 or 5. Because this would artificially inflate the score, pathology guidelines recommend that a Gleason grade not be assigned in hormonally treated specimens. Extraprostatic extension, seminal vesicle invasion, nodal status, and surgical margins can all still be assessed, and in fact tend to look more favorable after neoadjuvant therapy even though biochemical recurrence rates are unchanged.
learning_point: After neoadjuvant androgen deprivation, treatment effect distorts gland architecture so that a Gleason score/grade group should not be assigned; stage, volume, nodal status, and margins remain evaluable.
key_facts: Hormonal therapy causes cytoplasmic clearing, nuclear pyknosis, and gland atrophy that mimics higher-grade patterns.
Pathologists are advised to report 'treatment effect' rather than a Gleason score after ADT.
Neoadjuvant ADT lowers positive margin and apparent stage rates but has not improved biochemical recurrence-free survival.

question: Four weeks after ureteroscopic lithotripsy, a 44-year-old woman has persistent left flank pain. CT shows mild hydroureteronephrosis above a 3 mm calcific density that appears to sit within the wall of the proximal ureter, and retrograde ureteroscopy confirms a fragment covered by intact urothelium with no stone in the lumen. The best treatment is:

options.C: laser unroofing and extraction of the fragment with stent placement.
options.D: percutaneous nephrostomy and delayed antegrade ureteroscopy.

rationale: A fragment displaced into the ureteral wall is a submucosal stone. It will not pass, SWL cannot fragment it effectively, and a stent only temporizes the obstruction. The recommended initial treatment is to unroof the overlying urothelium with the laser, remove the fragment, and leave a stent to allow healing and reduce stricture risk. Segmental resection with repair is reserved for failure of endoscopic excision or an established stricture; nephrostomy adds nothing in a stable patient.
learning_point: A symptomatic stone fragment embedded in the ureteral wall (submucosal stone) is managed by laser unroofing/excision of the fragment followed by ureteral stent placement; SWL and stenting alone are ineffective.
key_facts: Submucosal stones result from iatrogenic displacement of fragments into the ureteral wall during ureteroscopy.
They cause persistent obstruction and inflammation and predispose to stricture.
If laser excision fails, the next step is segmental ureteral resection and repair; buccal graft is reserved for complex strictures.

question: A six-year-old girl is dry overnight and empties well on observation, but her mother reports that her underwear is damp a few minutes after every trip to the bathroom. She is overweight and has mild vulvar irritation. Urinalysis is normal. The next step is:

options.A: instruction in sitting backward or straddling the toilet and leaning forward before standing.
options.B: renal and bladder ultrasound with PVR.

rationale: Leakage occurring shortly after voiding in an otherwise normally voiding girl is classic for vaginal voiding, in which urine pools in the vagina (often with knees held together or in overweight girls) and drains once she stands. The remedy is positional: straddling or sitting backward on the toilet, leaning forward, and drying thoroughly before standing. Anticholinergics treat urgency, not pooling; timed voiding does not empty the vagina; and imaging is unnecessary when the history is this characteristic.
learning_point: Post-void dribbling in a toilet-trained girl is usually vaginal voiding (urine pooling in the vagina and leaking on standing); first-line management is toileting posture changes that promote vaginal drainage, not medication or imaging.
key_facts: Maneuvers include sitting backward or straddling the toilet, leaning forward, suprapubic pressure, and careful drying before standing.
Perineal irritation or vulvitis is a common accompanying finding.
VCUG often shows vaginal reflux in young girls but is not needed for diagnosis.

question: A seven-year-old boy who underwent valve ablation as a newborn is asymptomatic but has new bilateral hydronephrosis on surveillance ultrasound, and his creatinine has risen from 0.7 to 1.2 mg/dL over one year. Cystoscopy shows no residual valve tissue; videourodynamics show no VUR, complete emptying, and detrusor pressure rising from 12 cm H2O at 200 mL to 35 cm H2O at 260 mL. The next step is:

options.E: a 48-hour frequency-volume and fluid intake diary.

rationale: This boy has no residual obstruction or reflux, but his bladder loses compliance above about 200 mL. Children with valve bladders frequently have a renal concentrating defect with very high urine output, so the bladder may exceed its safe capacity within an hour of voiding, producing hydronephrosis and rising creatinine. Rational therapy, whether timed voiding, anticholinergics, CIC, or overnight catheter drainage, depends on knowing how much urine he makes and how often he voids, which a diary provides. An alpha-blocker is pointless without outlet obstruction.
learning_point: In a child with treated posterior urethral valves and worsening hydronephrosis without obstruction or reflux, concentrating defect-driven polyuria may overwhelm bladder capacity; a voiding/intake diary quantifying urine output is required before choosing CIC, anticholinergics, or overnight drainage.
key_facts: Valve patients often have nephrogenic concentrating defects with very high obligate urine output that increases with growth.
Reduced compliance means the 'safe' volume (pressure under about 30-40 cm H2O) may be reached quickly between voids.
Alpha-blockers have no role once obstruction has been excluded.

question: During resection of a posterior wall bladder tumor in a 69-year-old man, the resectoscope loop enters perivesical fat and irrigant return becomes poor. The abdomen is tense. A cystogram on the table shows contrast outlining loops of small bowel and pooling under the right hemidiaphragm. The next step is:

options.A: place an image-guided pelvic drain and a urethral catheter.
options.B: stop the resection and proceed to surgical repair of the bladder.
options.C: finish the resection, then place a large-bore urethral catheter for 10 days.
options.D: place bilateral ureteral stents and a urethral catheter.
options.E: stop the resection and place a urethral catheter with repeat cystogram in one week.

rationale: Contrast surrounding bowel loops and collecting under the diaphragm indicates a free intraperitoneal perforation, not a contained extraperitoneal leak. Intraperitoneal perforations, particularly large ones with abdominal distension, should be formally repaired because catheter drainage alone risks urinary ascites, ileus, peritonitis, and ongoing absorption of irrigant. The remainder of the resection must be abandoned once perforation is recognized. A percutaneous drain or ureteral stents do not address the bladder defect, and catheter drainage alone is appropriate only for extraperitoneal injuries.
learning_point: A recognized large intraperitoneal bladder perforation during TURBT requires aborting the resection and performing open (or laparoscopic) surgical repair; catheter drainage alone is appropriate only for extraperitoneal perforations.
key_facts: Clues to intraperitoneal perforation: visible fat or bowel, abdominal distension, poor irrigant return, contrast outlining bowel loops or tracking into upper quadrants on cystogram.
Extraperitoneal perforation (flame-shaped perivesical contrast) is usually managed with 7-10 days of catheter drainage.
Stop resection immediately when perforation is recognized to limit irrigant absorption and tumor seeding.

question: A five-year-old girl toilet trained at age three and voids a normal stream several times daily, yet her mother reports she is never completely dry and her underwear is constantly damp day and night. Examination of the introitus is unremarkable, urinalysis is normal, and renal ultrasound shows two normal-appearing kidneys without duplication. The study most likely to establish the diagnosis is:

options.A: MRI of the abdomen and pelvis.

rationale: A girl who voids normally but is constantly wet almost certainly has an ectopic ureter emptying beyond the sphincter. The upper-pole moiety that it drains is often so small and dysplastic that ultrasound, DMSA, and MAG-3 fail to show it. MRI, particularly T2-weighted and MR urographic sequences, is excellent at detecting fluid-filled dilated ectopic ureters and defining their insertion. VCUG shows reflux only if the orifice is in the bladder or urethra, and endoscopic identification of the ectopic orifice is frequently unsuccessful.
learning_point: Continuous dribbling despite a normal voiding pattern in a girl suggests an ectopic ureter draining a small dysplastic upper-pole moiety; when ultrasound is normal, MRI/MR urography is the most sensitive study to localize it.
key_facts: Ectopic ureters in girls insert distal to the sphincter (urethra, vestibule, vagina), producing constant wetness.
The upper pole is often tiny and poorly functioning, so ultrasound and MAG-3 may appear normal.
T2-weighted MRI highlights fluid-filled dilated ectopic ureters even when the moiety is dysplastic; cystoscopy/vaginoscopy is less sensitive.

question: A 66-year-old man with Grade Group 4 prostate cancer and PSA 18 ng/mL is scheduled for radical prostatectomy with extended pelvic lymphadenectomy. The nodal packet with the highest independent likelihood of containing metastasis is the:
rationale: Mapping studies of extended lymphadenectomy show that the internal iliac (hypogastric) nodes have the highest independent rate of involvement in prostate cancer. The obturator and external iliac regions are commonly positive as well but less often as an isolated station, which is why a limited obturator-only dissection misses a significant proportion of node-positive men. Common iliac and presacral nodes are secondary echelons and are less frequently the first or only site of spread.
learning_point: The internal iliac (hypogastric) nodal region carries the highest independent probability of harboring metastases from prostate cancer; it must be included in an extended pelvic lymph node dissection.
key_facts: Extended PLND covers external iliac, obturator, and internal iliac nodes; omitting the internal iliac packet misses a large fraction of positive nodes.
Common iliac and presacral nodes are involved less frequently and usually along with more distal stations.
Limited (obturator-only) dissection understages a substantial proportion of men.

question: A 72-year-old man had a left middle cerebral artery infarct four months ago and now reports urgency with frequent large-volume leaks. Videourodynamics are expected to show involuntary detrusor contractions accompanied by:

options.A: delayed relaxation of the striated sphincter with a smooth sphincter that opens normally.
options.B: contraction of both the smooth and striated sphincters.
options.C: an open smooth sphincter with involuntary striated sphincter contraction.
options.D: a closed smooth sphincter with striated sphincter relaxation.
options.E: relaxation of both the smooth and striated sphincters.

rationale: A stroke is a suprapontine lesion; the pontine micturition center and its sacral connections are intact, so the detrusor and the outlet remain coordinated. The characteristic finding is neurogenic detrusor overactivity with synergic relaxation of both the smooth (bladder neck) and striated sphincters, producing incontinence. True detrusor-striated sphincter dyssynergia requires a lesion between the pons and the sacral cord, and smooth sphincter dyssynergia is seen with thoracolumbar autonomic lesions. Delayed striated sphincter relaxation (bradykinesia) is a Parkinson finding.
learning_point: Suprapontine lesions such as stroke cause neurogenic detrusor overactivity with a coordinated (synergic) outlet, i.e., both the smooth and striated sphincters relax appropriately during involuntary contractions.
key_facts: Detrusor-external sphincter dyssynergia is a feature of suprasacral spinal cord lesions and some MS patients, not stroke.
Pseudodyssynergia: voluntary guarding contraction of the external sphincter during an involuntary contraction can mimic DESD in stroke patients.
Sphincter bradykinesia (delayed relaxation) is associated with Parkinson disease.

question: A 15-year-old boy with myelomeningocele underwent ileocystoplasty at age nine and has been dry on CIC every four hours. Over the past three months he has had two febrile UTIs and has started leaking between catheterizations. Urinalysis today shows pyuria. The next step is:

options.A: review his catheterization log and directly observe his technique.
options.B: renal and bladder ultrasound to look for stones.

rationale: The most common reason an augmented adolescent develops new leakage and infections is that catheterizations have become infrequent, incomplete, or technically poor, which teenagers often do not volunteer. Verifying adherence by diary and watching the patient catheterize is inexpensive and frequently reveals the problem. Imaging for stones, urodynamics for altered compliance, and cystoscopy are appropriate only after adherence has been confirmed, and changing prophylaxis does not address the cause.
learning_point: New incontinence and UTIs in an adolescent with an augmented neurogenic bladder should first prompt verification of CIC adherence and technique (observed catheterization and a catheterization diary) before escalating to imaging or urodynamics.
key_facts: Adolescents frequently become non-adherent with CIC and may not disclose it.
Infrequent or incomplete catheterization causes overdistension, mucus retention, infection, and overflow leakage.
If adherence is confirmed, evaluate for stones, changes in storage dynamics, and reservoir perforation.

question: A 64-year-old man with three UTIs in the past year, each growing mixed enteric flora, describes bubbles in his urine stream. CT shows gas in the bladder lumen, a thickened posterior bladder wall tethered to an inflamed diverticular sigmoid loop, and no prior catheterization. Cystoscopy shows a boggy erythematous patch on the posterior wall without a visible opening. The next step is:

options.A: six months of suppressive antibiotics and repeat cystoscopy.
options.C: referral for sigmoid resection and fistula repair.

rationale: Recurrent polymicrobial UTIs, pneumaturia, and the CT triad of intravesical air, focal bladder wall thickening, and adjacent thickened diverticular colon establish the diagnosis of colovesical fistula. Cystoscopy is commonly nonspecific because the fistula tract is small and edematous, so failure to see an opening does not cast doubt on the diagnosis. Additional imaging such as cystogram, MRI, or small bowel study would not change management. Definitive treatment in a healthy patient is resection of the diseased bowel segment with closure of the bladder; antibiotics alone are reserved for those unfit for surgery.
learning_point: Pneumaturia-type findings on CT (air in the bladder without instrumentation, bladder wall thickening abutting thickened sigmoid colon) are diagnostic of colovesical fistula; no further imaging is needed and management is surgical (colon resection and fistula repair), with antibiotic suppression reserved for poor surgical candidates.
key_facts: Diverticulitis is the most common cause of colovesical fistula; cystoscopy shows nonspecific localized erythema or bullous edema in most cases, and the tract itself in under half.
CT is the imaging modality of choice; cystogram and small bowel follow-through add little.
Colonoscopy may be performed preoperatively to exclude malignancy in the affected segment.

question: A 29-year-old man with lifelong premature ejaculation takes phenelzine for treatment-resistant depression managed by his psychiatrist. He asks for a medication to prolong intravaginal latency. The best recommendation is:
rationale: Phenelzine is an MAOI. Every oral drug commonly used for premature ejaculation, including SSRIs such as paroxetine and dapoxetine, the tricyclic clomipramine, and tramadol, raises serotonergic tone and is contraindicated with an MAOI because of the risk of serotonin syndrome. Topical anesthetics reduce penile sensitivity, delay ejaculation, and have no systemic interaction, making them the appropriate pharmacologic choice alongside behavioral therapy.
learning_point: In a man taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, serotonergic agents for premature ejaculation (SSRIs, clomipramine, tramadol) are contraindicated because of serotonin syndrome risk; topical anesthetic (lidocaine/prilocaine) is the appropriate pharmacologic option.
key_facts: Daily paroxetine, sertraline, fluoxetine, clomipramine and on-demand tramadol all increase synaptic serotonin.
MAOI plus serotonergic drug can precipitate life-threatening serotonin syndrome.
Behavioral techniques (stop-start, squeeze) and topical anesthetics have no drug interaction.

question: A 58-year-old man arrives for a consultation requested by his primary care physician because of microscopic hematuria found on two urinalyses. The urinalysis reports and basic labs were not sent with the referral. He is anxious to proceed today. The most appropriate action is:

options.A: have your staff call the primary care office and request the results be sent now.
options.B: have the patient sign a HIPAA authorization and mail it to the primary care office before any records can be shared.
options.C: proceed directly to CT urography and cystoscopy without the prior results.
options.D: reschedule the consultation once the patient brings his records.
options.E: repeat the urinalysis and labs in your office and bill the patient's insurer.

rationale: The HIPAA Privacy Rule explicitly allows one treating provider to disclose protected health information to another for the patient's treatment, so a signed authorization is not required and asking for one only delays care. Calling the referring office to obtain the results is efficient, cost-effective, and respectful of the patient's time. Rescheduling is unprofessional, repeating tests duplicates cost, and committing the patient to a full hematuria workup without confirming the finding is premature.
learning_point: HIPAA permits a referring provider to share protected health information with another treating provider for treatment purposes without the patient's written authorization; the professional step when referral labs are missing is simply to contact the referring office for the results.
key_facts: Treatment, payment, and health care operations are permitted disclosures under the Privacy Rule.
The privacy notice a patient signs at registration acknowledges your policies; it is not a release.
Rescheduling or repeating tests inconveniences the patient and wastes resources.

question: A 39-year-old woman has an incidental 2.5 cm markedly echogenic lesion in the right kidney on ultrasound. An MRI is ordered to confirm the suspected diagnosis of angiomyolipoma. The finding that confirms the diagnosis is:

options.A: avid arterial-phase enhancement on T1 post-gadolinium imaging.
options.B: absence of enhancement on T1 post-gadolinium imaging.
options.C: loss of signal within the lesion on fat-suppressed T2-weighted images.
options.D: homogeneous high signal on standard T2-weighted images.

rationale: The diagnostic hallmark of a classic angiomyolipoma is macroscopic fat. On MRI, fat is bright on non-suppressed T1 and T2 images and loses signal when a fat-suppression pulse is applied, so comparing the lesion on fat-suppressed T2 (or T1) sequences with non-suppressed images confirms the diagnosis. Enhancement patterns cannot separate AML from RCC because both enhance; absence of enhancement would suggest a cyst, not AML; and non-suppressed T2 brightness and diffusion characteristics are nonspecific.
learning_point: Angiomyolipoma is confirmed on MRI by demonstrating macroscopic fat, which appears as signal loss on fat-suppressed sequences (classically T2 with fat suppression) compared with non-suppressed images.
key_facts: Hyperechoic renal mass on ultrasound suggests AML but small RCCs can also be echogenic.
Gadolinium enhancement does not distinguish AML from RCC because AMLs enhance.
Non-contrast CT with attenuation below about -10 HU is an alternative way to prove macroscopic fat.

question: A 68-year-old woman reports leaking with sudden urges several times a day without leakage during coughing or exercise. Examination shows pale, thin vaginal epithelium and no significant prolapse; cough stress test is negative and PVR is 30 mL. She has already begun a bladder diary with fluid and caffeine reduction. The next step is:
rationale: This woman has pure urgency urinary incontinence. Guidelines place behavioral therapy, which includes pelvic floor muscle training along with bladder training and dietary modification, as first-line treatment, and PFMT is effective for both stress and urgency incontinence. Estrogen in any form may relieve atrophy symptoms but has not been shown to reduce incontinence episodes, and systemic estrogen can worsen them. Duloxetine and urethral bulking are aimed at stress incontinence, which she does not have.
learning_point: Pelvic floor muscle training is first-line therapy for urgency urinary incontinence in women (alongside behavioral measures); vaginal or oral estrogen treats atrophy symptoms but has not been shown to improve incontinence, and duloxetine/bulking agents target stress incontinence.
key_facts: AUA/SUFU OAB guideline: behavioral therapies including PFMT, bladder training, fluid management are first line for all patients.
Systemic estrogen may worsen incontinence; local estrogen helps genitourinary syndrome of menopause but not UUI.
Duloxetine is not FDA-approved for SUI in the US and has no benefit for UUI.

question: A 41-year-old woman with a T4 complete spinal cord injury manages her bladder with a long-term suprapubic catheter. Over two months the catheter has occluded with gritty debris every 7-10 days despite changes every two weeks. Urine pH is 8.5. The next step is:

options.A: non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
options.C: obtain a urine culture to look for a urease-producing organism.
options.D: convert to intermittent catheterization by a caregiver.
options.E: begin daily acetic acid bladder irrigation.

rationale: Rapid, recurrent encrustation with an alkaline urine pH points to a urease-producing biofilm organism such as Proteus, Providencia, or Morganella. Identifying the organism by culture is the first step because targeted antibiotic treatment is needed to break the cycle, and a positive result should also trigger evaluation for infection stones in the bladder or kidneys that perpetuate colonization. Larger catheters and acid irrigations only delay blockage, and CT is reasonable later but is not the initial step before the organism is identified.
learning_point: Recurrent catheter encrustation and blockage is caused by biofilm from urease-producing bacteria (e.g., Proteus mirabilis); the next step is a urine culture to identify such an organism, followed by treatment and evaluation for stones that may act as a nidus.
key_facts: Urease splits urea to ammonia, raising urine pH and precipitating struvite and carbonate apatite on the catheter.
Irrigation, catheter size changes, or converting to a suprapubic tube only temporize.
Once a urease producer is confirmed, image the bladder and upper tracts (non-contrast CT) and consider cystoscopy for stones.

question: A 51-year-old man is found to have a 2 cm filling defect in the left renal pelvis with mild hydronephrosis on CT urography performed for microscopic hematuria; ureteroscopic biopsy shows high-grade urothelial carcinoma. He had colon cancer at age 44, his sister had endometrial cancer at 47, and his father died of colon cancer at 55. Germline testing is most likely to identify a pathogenic variant in:
rationale: Early-onset colorectal cancer, endometrial cancer in a first-degree relative, and now upper tract urothelial carcinoma in a man around 50 fulfill the pattern of Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer). Lynch is caused by defects in DNA mismatch repair genes, and MSH2 mutations in particular carry the highest risk of urothelial tumors of the upper tract. VHL predisposes to clear cell RCC and pheochromocytoma, FH to hereditary leiomyomatosis and RCC, TP53 to sarcomas and breast cancer, and BRCA2 to breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancer.
learning_point: Upper tract urothelial carcinoma in a patient with a personal or family history of colorectal, endometrial, or ovarian cancer suggests Lynch syndrome, caused by germline mutations in mismatch repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, or EPCAM deletion).
key_facts: UTUC is the third most common Lynch-associated malignancy; MSH2 carriers have the highest urothelial risk.
Suspect Lynch in UTUC patients under 60 or with Amsterdam criteria family histories; tumors show microsatellite instability.
BRCA1 relates to breast/ovarian cancer, VHL to clear cell RCC, TP53 to Li-Fraumeni, PTEN to Cowden syndrome.

question: A 70-year-old man was hospitalized for right pyelonephritis with bacteremia from a susceptible Klebsiella species. Six weeks after completing antibiotics he feels well, urine culture is sterile, and PVR is 35 mL. He has never had a urologic evaluation. The next step is:

options.D: no further evaluation unless infection recurs.

rationale: A febrile upper tract infection in an older man is by definition complicated and carries a meaningful chance of an underlying structural cause such as an obstructing stone, ureteral or urethral stricture, or urothelial tumor. Upper tract imaging with CT urography plus cystoscopy evaluates both the kidneys/ureters and the lower tract. Simple observation misses treatable causes, prophylaxis without a diagnosis is not justified, urodynamics is indicated only if emptying dysfunction is suspected, and localization cultures address chronic prostatitis rather than pyelonephritis.
learning_point: A febrile, complicated UTI (pyelonephritis) in an older man warrants anatomic evaluation of the urinary tract after treatment, typically upper tract imaging (CT urogram) and cystoscopy, because of the higher prevalence of underlying obstruction, stones, strictures, or tumor.
key_facts: UTI in men is considered complicated; a single febrile episode in an older man justifies imaging and endoscopy.
A normal PVR does not exclude ureteral stricture, stone, or urothelial lesion.
Prophylaxis, urodynamics, or localization cultures alone are not sufficient evaluations.

question: A 79-year-old widow returns three years after a retropubic mid-urethral sling. She is dry, has no discharge, bleeding, or pain, and is not sexually active. Speculum examination reveals a 4 mm area of exposed mesh at the suburethral incision with healthy surrounding epithelium; urinalysis is normal. The next step is:
