options.B: excision of the exposed segment with placement of a new sling.

rationale: A tiny exposure that causes no symptoms in a woman who is continent and not sexually active does not require intervention; watchful waiting with examination is appropriate, and topical vaginal estrogen can be added to encourage healing. Excision is indicated for symptomatic, enlarging, or infected exposures, and complete sling removal is reserved for pain syndromes or urinary tract erosion because it risks recurrent incontinence. Oral estrogen does not aid local healing, and sling replacement is unnecessary even after partial excision since continence is usually maintained.
learning_point: A small, asymptomatic vaginal mesh exposure after a mid-urethral sling in a continent, non-sexually-active woman can be observed; excision is reserved for symptomatic or larger exposures, and mesh involving the urinary tract must be removed.
key_facts: Symptoms prompting excision include vaginal discharge, bleeding, pain, or partner dyspareunia.
Vaginal (not oral) estrogen may promote epithelial healing over small exposures.
Partial sling excision usually preserves continence, so simultaneous replacement is unnecessary.

question: A 56-year-old man living at high altitude is found to have a hemoglobin of 18.5 g/dL. The physiologic trigger for his increased red cell production is:

options.A: decreased tissue oxygen tension sensed by renal interstitial cells.
options.B: release of erythropoietin by cardiac myocytes.
options.D: release of erythropoietin by medullary collecting duct cells.
options.E: reduced perfusion pressure at the afferent arteriole.

rationale: Red cell mass is regulated by erythropoietin, which is synthesized mainly by peritubular interstitial fibroblast-like cells in the renal cortex. These cells respond to decreased oxygen tension through hypoxia-inducible factor, so chronic hypobaric hypoxia at altitude raises EPO and hemoglobin. Carbon dioxide levels and afferent arteriolar pressure are not the stimulus, collecting duct cells do not make EPO, and the heart is not a source of the hormone.
learning_point: Erythropoietin is produced by peritubular interstitial fibroblasts in the renal cortex in response to tissue hypoxia (via HIF stabilization); hypoxia, not CO2 or arteriolar pressure, is the physiologic stimulus.
key_facts: HIF-2alpha accumulates when oxygen tension falls, driving EPO transcription.
The kidney makes about 90% of adult EPO; the liver makes the remainder and is the fetal source.
Collecting duct cells and the heart do not produce EPO; EPO acts on erythroid burst-forming units.

question: A 46-year-old woman with hypertension requiring three medications is being screened for an endocrine cause. If she has primary aldosteronism, the laboratory finding most consistently present is:

options.C: weight gain exceeding 2 kg from fluid retention.

rationale: In primary aldosteronism the adrenal secretes aldosterone independently of the renin-angiotensin system, so the resulting sodium retention and volume expansion feed back to suppress renin; a low renin with a high aldosterone-to-renin ratio is the basis of screening. Hypokalemia, although classic, is absent in the majority of patients diagnosed today. Sodium remains normal because water is retained with it, angiotensin II falls along with renin, and mineralocorticoid escape limits volume expansion to roughly 1-1.5 kg.
learning_point: Primary hyperaldosteronism is characterized by autonomous aldosterone secretion with suppressed plasma renin; most contemporary patients are normokalemic, sodium stays normal, and volume expansion is limited by mineralocorticoid escape.
key_facts: Screening uses the aldosterone-to-renin ratio; a high ratio with suppressed renin suggests primary disease.
Hypokalemia is present in only a minority (roughly 10-40%) at diagnosis.
Secondary hyperaldosteronism (renal artery stenosis, heart failure) has elevated renin.

question: A 50-year-old man with an InterStim II implanted for refractory urgency incontinence develops new-onset seizures, and his neurologist requests a brain MRI on a 1.5-Tesla scanner. The appropriate advice is:

options.A: the MRI is contraindicated; recommend head CT instead.
options.B: remove the tined lead only, then perform the MRI.
options.C: remove the lead and generator, then perform the MRI.
options.D: proceed with the MRI with the stimulator left on at the usual amplitude.
options.E: turn the stimulator off and proceed with the MRI.

rationale: InterStim II is labeled as conditionally safe for head MRI at 1.5 Tesla provided the neurostimulator output is turned off for the scan, after which it can be reactivated. There is no need to explant the lead or generator for a routine diagnostic head scan, and refusing the study would deny the patient needed neurologic evaluation. Leaving the device active risks heating or unintended stimulation. Body MRI on older systems is more restricted, whereas newer sacral neuromodulation systems carry full-body MRI conditional labeling.
learning_point: A patient with an InterStim II sacral neuromodulator may undergo a 1.5-Tesla MRI of the head with the stimulator turned off; the device does not need to be removed and the scan should not be refused.
key_facts: Older InterStim models require checking serial numbers and disabling the magnet switch; head-only 1.5 T scans are labeled as acceptable with the device off.
Newer systems (InterStim Micro, InterStim X, Axonics) are labeled for full-body 1.5 T and 3 T MRI under specified conditions.
Removing the lead or generator for a routine scan is unnecessary.

question: A 48-year-old man with four prior calcium oxalate stone episodes undergoes left PCNL. Postoperative ultrasound shows a 3 mm echogenic focus in a lower-pole calyx and no hydronephrosis; he is asymptomatic. The next step is:

options.E: stone-protocol non-contrast CT to confirm fragment size.

rationale: A 3 mm lower-pole fragment is clinically insignificant in the short term and is unlikely to require treatment, so ureteroscopy or SWL is not indicated. Confirmatory CT is unnecessary because ultrasound already overestimates small stones and the result would not change management. What does alter outcomes for a recurrent stone former is metabolic evaluation with a 24-hour urine collection to tailor dietary and pharmacologic prevention, which has been shown to increase remission of residual fragments compared with observation alone.
learning_point: A small (under 4 mm) asymptomatic residual lower-pole fragment after PCNL in a recurrent stone former needs no immediate intervention or repeat imaging; the next step is a 24-hour urine metabolic evaluation to direct preventive therapy, which improves fragment remission.
key_facts: Ultrasound tends to overestimate the size of small renal stones, so confirmatory CT adds little for a tiny fragment.
Medical prevention after PCNL residual fragments significantly reduces stone events versus observation alone.
Lower-pole fragments rarely pass but often remain asymptomatic; fragments over 2 mm in the pelvis or ureter predict events.

question: A 30-year-old man with sickle cell trait and poorly controlled hypertension has had erections lasting two to four hours several nights a week for two months. Daily low-dose tadalafil and baclofen have not helped. He wants to continue having intercourse. The next step is:
rationale: Recurrent prolonged erections in a man with a sickle hemoglobinopathy represent stuttering priapism, which requires prevention before a full-blown ischemic event occurs. An oral antiandrogen such as bicalutamide reduces episode frequency while usually allowing continued sexual activity, making it the preferred hormonal strategy here. Sympathomimetics like pseudoephedrine are hazardous in uncontrolled hypertension, GnRH agonists abolish libido and erections, estrogens carry unacceptable thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk, and intracavernosal phenylephrine is reserved for aborting individual episodes rather than nightly use.
learning_point: For stuttering (recurrent ischemic) priapism in a hypertensive man with sickle cell trait who wants to preserve sexual function, an oral antiandrogen such as bicalutamide is appropriate prevention; alpha-agonists are risky with hypertension, estrogens carry cardiovascular risk, and intracavernosal phenylephrine is for acute episodes only.
key_facts: Stuttering priapism tends to escalate into major ischemic episodes that threaten erectile tissue.
Preventive options include PDE5 inhibitors (daily low dose), antiandrogens, GnRH agonists/antagonists, ketoconazole, and oral alpha-agonists.
Antiandrogens generally preserve libido and erectile function better than GnRH agonists or estrogens.

question: During a transperitoneal laparoscopic right radical nephrectomy, after the ascending colon has been reflected medially, the structure that must be mobilized to expose the renal vein and artery at the hilum is the:
rationale: On the right, once the colon is reflected, the descending (second) portion of the duodenum drapes across the inferior vena cava and the right renal hilum. Sweeping it medially with a Kocher maneuver uncovers the renal vein, the artery behind it, and the IVC. The hepatocolic attachments are divided for upper-pole access rather than the hilum, the pancreatic head is rarely mobilized in nephrectomy, and the superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric vein are landmarks for left-sided and midline retroperitoneal dissection.
learning_point: The second (descending) portion of the duodenum lies directly anterior to the right renal hilum and pelvis; transperitoneal exposure of the right renal hilum requires medial mobilization of the duodenum (Kocher maneuver).
key_facts: Reflecting the right colon exposes the duodenum; kocherization then reveals the IVC, right renal vein, and hilum.
The hepatocolic ligament must be divided to reach the upper pole, not the hilum.
The superior mesenteric vessels and inferior mesenteric vein are relevant to left-sided exposure, not the right hilum.

question: A 64-year-old man was treated with external beam radiation for Grade Group 2, cT1c prostate cancer with a pretreatment PSA of 7.8 ng/mL. His nadir of 0.8 ng/mL occurred at 24 months; PSA then rose to 1.9, 3.6, and 6.2 ng/mL at six-month intervals. The variable that best predicts his risk of dying from prostate cancer is:

options.C: time from treatment to biochemical failure.

rationale: This patient meets the Phoenix definition of failure (nadir plus 2 ng/mL) and his PSA is doubling in roughly six months. Multiple cohorts after both prostatectomy and radiation show that PSA doubling time is the single most powerful predictor of metastasis and prostate cancer-specific death among men with recurrence. A higher nadir and a shorter interval to recurrence are unfavorable but less discriminating, pretreatment PSA under 10 is favorable, and Gleason pattern matters chiefly when the score is 8-10.
learning_point: Among men with biochemical recurrence after definitive local therapy, a short PSA doubling time is the strongest predictor of prostate cancer-specific mortality, outweighing nadir, pretreatment PSA, Gleason pattern, and interval to failure.
key_facts: Phoenix definition of radiation failure: PSA rise of 2 ng/mL above nadir.
PSADT under about 3-6 months identifies men at high risk of metastasis and death.
Gleason 8-10 and time to recurrence under 3 years are adverse but less predictive than PSADT.

question: A 52-year-old woman had excellent control of urgency incontinence after sacral neuromodulation implanted three years ago, but her leakage has returned over the past month. Device interrogation shows impedance above 4000 ohms on electrode 2 with normal values on electrodes 0, 1, and 3 and an estimated battery life of over a year. The next step is:

options.D: reprogram stimulation using the electrodes with normal impedance.

rationale: A single electrode with very high impedance indicates an open circuit affecting that contact, most often from a lead fracture or connection problem, while the remaining three contacts are intact. Reprogramming the active configuration to exclude the faulty electrode frequently restores symptom control and avoids surgery. Lead or full-system revision is indicated only when reprogramming fails or when all contacts are abnormal. Adding medications or injecting botulinum toxin would be considered only if the device cannot be salvaged.
learning_point: When symptoms recur after sacral neuromodulation and interrogation shows an abnormal impedance on only one of four lead electrodes, the next step is reprogramming to use the functioning electrodes; surgical revision is reserved for failure of reprogramming.
key_facts: Normal impedance is roughly 400-1500 ohms; very high impedance (over 4000) indicates an open circuit from lead fracture or loose connection, very low suggests a short.
Reprogramming alternative electrode configurations often restores efficacy without surgery.
Adding medication or botulinum toxin is premature if the device can be made to work.

question: A nine-month-old boy with repaired lumbar myelomeningocele managed by observation is found on routine ultrasound to have new bilateral hydroureteronephrosis. VCUG shows grade 4 reflux bilaterally. Cystometry shows a smooth filling curve with no detrusor overactivity, an estimated capacity of 90 mL, and leakage around the catheter at a detrusor pressure of 48 cm H2O. In addition to antibiotic prophylaxis, the next step is:

options.E: continued observation with repeat ultrasound in three months.

rationale: A detrusor leak point pressure near 50 cm H2O exceeds the threshold of roughly 40 cm H2O above which the upper tracts are at risk, and this infant already shows the consequences: hydronephrosis and high-grade reflux. Starting CIC empties the bladder before it reaches hostile pressures and, with prophylaxis, protects the kidneys. Capacity is reasonable and there is no overactivity, so anticholinergics are not needed up front; a catheterization diary will determine whether pressures at typical volumes require adding them or botulinum toxin. Observation risks renal damage, and reimplantation is not undertaken before storage pressures are controlled.
learning_point: An infant with myelomeningocele who develops hydronephrosis and high-grade reflux with an elevated detrusor leak point pressure (above about 40 cm H2O) requires CIC with antibiotic prophylaxis; anticholinergics are added based on pressures at typical catheterized volumes, and reimplantation is not initial management.
key_facts: DLPP over 40 cm H2O predicts upper tract deterioration.
CIC lowers storage pressures by emptying before the bladder reaches hostile volumes; a catheterization diary then guides need for antimuscarinics or onabotulinumtoxinA.
Reflux in neurogenic bladders often resolves once storage pressures are controlled.

question: A 61-year-old man with a normal DRE and PSA of 8.4 ng/mL has a prostate volume of 36 mL on MRI. Systematic biopsy shows Grade Group 1 cancer in 2 of 12 cores, each involving 20% of the core. Under NCCN criteria he is classified as low-risk rather than very-low-risk because of his:
rationale: He meets the very-low-risk criteria for clinical stage (T1c), Grade Group 1, PSA under 10, two or fewer positive cores, and under 50% core involvement. His PSA density, however, is 8.4/36 or about 0.23 ng/mL/mL, well above the 0.15 threshold, which is what relegates him to the low-risk category. Age does not enter NCCN risk grouping. PSA density is clinically important because it is a strong predictor of harboring higher-grade disease and of progression on active surveillance.
learning_point: NCCN very-low-risk prostate cancer requires cT1c, Grade Group 1, PSA under 10 ng/mL, fewer than 3 positive cores with no core over 50% involved, and PSA density under 0.15 ng/mL/mL; a PSA density at or above 0.15 moves an otherwise qualifying patient to the low-risk group.
key_facts: PSA density is one of the strongest predictors of upgrading or progression on active surveillance.
Low risk: cT1-T2a, Grade Group 1, PSA under 10 without meeting all very-low-risk criteria.
Age is not part of the risk stratification.

question: A 58-year-old man with multiple system atrophy undergoes needle EMG of the external anal sphincter, which shows chronic denervation. The spinal cell group whose degeneration accounts for this finding normally controls:

options.A: detrusor contraction via pelvic nerve parasympathetics.
options.B: bladder neck closure via the hypogastric nerve.
options.C: contraction of the external striated urethral sphincter.

rationale: Onuf's nucleus, located in the anterior horn of the sacral cord (S2-S4), houses the somatic motor neurons whose axons travel in the pudendal nerve to the external striated urethral and anal sphincters; its loss in multiple system atrophy produces the characteristic sphincter denervation on EMG. Detrusor contraction is mediated by sacral parasympathetic neurons in the intermediolateral region, bladder neck closure and detrusor relaxation during filling are sympathetic functions arising from the thoracolumbar cord, and bladder sensation is carried by afferent neurons in the dorsal root ganglia.
learning_point: Onuf's nucleus in the ventral horn of S2-S4 contains the somatic (pudendal) motor neurons that innervate the external striated urethral and anal sphincters.
key_facts: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons for detrusor contraction lie in the sacral intermediolateral cell column, not Onuf's nucleus.
Sympathetic input to the bladder neck (internal sphincter) comes from T10-L2 via the hypogastric nerve.
Onuf's nucleus is relatively spared in ALS but degenerates in multiple system atrophy, producing sphincter denervation.

question: A 59-year-old woman undergoes right radical nephrectomy for an 8 cm clear cell RCC confined to the kidney (pT2a) with negative margins; no nodes were sampled and preoperative chest CT was clear. According to the 2013 AUA follow-up guideline, appropriate surveillance after baseline postoperative imaging is:

options.A: chest and abdominal imaging every six months for at least three years, then yearly to five years.
options.B: chest x-ray alone each year for five years.
options.C: yearly abdominal CT and chest x-ray for five years.
options.D: abdominal ultrasound every six months for two years.
options.E: abdominal CT and chest x-ray at one year, then discharge if negative.

rationale: A pT2 tumor places this patient in the moderate-to-high recurrence risk group under the 2013 AUA guideline, which recommends baseline chest and abdominal cross-sectional imaging within 3-6 months of surgery, repeat chest and abdominal imaging every 6 months for at least 3 years, and then annually through year 5. Annual-only imaging or chest x-ray alone is the lower-intensity schedule reserved for low-risk pT1 disease, and stopping after one year would miss the period of greatest recurrence risk.
learning_point: Per the 2013 AUA guideline, moderate- to high-risk localized RCC (pT2-pT4 or N+) after nephrectomy should have baseline chest and abdominal imaging at 3-6 months, then imaging every 6 months for at least 3 years, then annually to 5 years.
key_facts: Low-risk (pT1N0) patients need less intensive follow-up: baseline abdominal imaging within 3-12 months and periodic chest x-ray.
The 2021 AUA renal mass guideline update stratifies follow-up by low/intermediate/high risk with different intervals; the source item reflects the 2013 schedule.
Routine bone scan or brain imaging is only for symptoms or laboratory abnormalities.

question: A 49-year-old woman is bothered by voiding ten times daily and leaking when she cannot reach the toilet in time. She denies leakage with exercise or sneezing, although a small spurt is seen with cough at examination. There is stage 1 anterior wall descent, urinalysis is normal, and PVR is 20 mL. The next step is:

options.B: bladder training with fluid management and an antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist.

rationale: Her bother comes from urgency frequency and urgency incontinence, so management should follow the overactive bladder algorithm: behavioral strategies such as bladder training, fluid and caffeine modification, and pelvic floor exercises, with or without an antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist. The demonstrable stress leakage is not symptomatic, so a sling or bulking agent would treat a problem she does not complain of. Stage 1 anterior descent is a normal finding and does not warrant colporrhaphy.
learning_point: When a woman's bothersome complaint is urgency and frequency, initial treatment follows the OAB pathway (behavioral therapy with or without antimuscarinic/beta-3 agonist) even if a cough stress test is positive; SUI procedures are not first-line for an asymptomatic stress component, and stage 1 prolapse needs no repair.
key_facts: AUA/SUFU OAB guideline: behavioral therapy first-line, oral pharmacotherapy second-line.
Treat the predominant, bothersome symptom in mixed incontinence; an incidental positive stress test does not mandate a sling.
Stage 1 anterior prolapse is within normal limits and is not an indication for surgery.

question: A 24-year-old man undergoes emergency laparotomy after a stab wound with an expanding left perirenal hematoma. The hematoma extends across the midline and the aortic pulsation cannot be palpated or seen. The landmark that guides dissection to the anterior surface of the aorta for early renal vascular control is the:
rationale: The classic approach to renal vascular control is to open the retroperitoneum over the aorta between the inferior mesenteric artery and the ligament of Treitz and then dissect cephalad to the left renal vein, behind which both renal arteries originate. When the hematoma hides the aorta, the inferior mesenteric vein remains visible running along the left side of the mesentery; dissecting immediately medial to it reliably leads down to the anterior aorta. The left renal vein is the target rather than the landmark, the gonadal vein lies too lateral, and the superior mesenteric artery is cephalad and deep.
learning_point: When a large retroperitoneal hematoma obscures the aorta during exploration for renal trauma, the inferior mesenteric vein is the landmark: dissection just medial to it leads to the anterior aorta, allowing early control of the renal vessels before Gerota's fascia is opened.
key_facts: Standard approach: incise the posterior peritoneum over the aorta medial to the IMV from the IMA to the ligament of Treitz.
The left renal vein crosses anterior to the aorta and is the first vessel encountered cephalad to the IMA; both renal arteries lie posterior to it.
Vascular control before opening the hematoma reduces nephrectomy rates.

question: A 66-year-old woman with recurrent intermediate-risk Ta low-grade bladder cancer is to begin a six-week induction course of intravesical mitomycin C. Besides emptying the bladder completely before instillation, which measure increases the drug's effectiveness?

options.B: aggressive oral hydration before each instillation.
options.C: diluting the dose to 40 mg in 60 mL to coat the bladder.
options.D: oral sodium bicarbonate the night before and morning of treatment.
options.E: an antimuscarinic to reduce dwell-time urgency.

rationale: The optimized mitomycin C regimen rests on maximizing intravesical drug concentration and stability: a 40 mg dose in a small volume (20 mL), complete bladder emptying, overnight fasting or fluid restriction to limit urinary dilution, and oral sodium bicarbonate to raise urine pH because mitomycin degrades in acidic urine. Hydration and larger instillation volumes dilute the drug, and prophylactic antibiotics or antimuscarinics have no demonstrated effect on efficacy.
learning_point: Intravesical mitomycin C efficacy is optimized by increasing drug concentration (40 mg in 20 mL), eliminating residual urine, overnight fluid restriction, and oral sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine and prevent drug degradation.
key_facts: Mitomycin C is unstable at acidic pH; alkalinization preserves activity.
Dehydration and complete emptying reduce dilution of the agent in the bladder.
Antibiotics, NSAIDs, and anticholinergics do not improve response.

question: A 47-year-old woman develops continuous vaginal urine leakage three weeks after an abdominal hysterectomy. Cystoscopy and vaginoscopy demonstrate a 6 mm fistula at the vaginal cuff communicating with the posterior bladder wall above the trigone, and transvaginal repair is planned. The most suitable tissue to interpose between the bladder and vaginal closures is:

options.A: omentum pedicled on the right gastroepiploic artery.
options.B: a peritoneal flap from the anterior cul-de-sac.

rationale: A fistula at the vaginal cuff after hysterectomy lies high in the vault, immediately beneath the peritoneum of the anterior cul-de-sac. During a transvaginal repair this peritoneum can be mobilized easily and placed over the bladder closure as a well-vascularized interposing layer. A Martius flap is ideal for distal fistulas near the urethra and bladder neck but reaching a well-supported apex requires extensive tunneling that compromises its blood supply. Omental and rectus flaps require an abdominal approach, and gracilis flaps are reserved for complex radiated or recurrent fistulas.
learning_point: For transvaginal repair of a high apical post-hysterectomy vesicovaginal fistula, a peritoneal flap mobilized from the anterior cul-de-sac is the preferred interposition; a Martius flap suits distal fistulas (bladder neck/urethra) and omentum is only available via an abdominal approach.
key_facts: Martius labial fat pad is supplied by posterior labial, external pudendal, and obturator branches; tunneling to the vault is difficult and jeopardizes its blood supply.
The peritoneal flap is dissected beyond the bladder, left unopened, and laid over the closed fistula as an extra layer.
Omental flaps based on the gastroepiploic vessels are used in transabdominal repairs.

question: A 12-year-old boy had a first episode of C. difficile colitis after perioperative antibiotics for a dismembered pyeloplasty and improved on a ten-day course of oral metronidazole. Three weeks after finishing, he returns with watery diarrhea, fever, and cramping; WBC is 22,000/cu mm and creatinine has risen from 0.5 to 1.3 mg/dL. Blood pressure is normal and the abdomen is soft without distension. The best treatment is:
rationale: This is a first recurrence of C. difficile infection, and the marked leukocytosis with a creatinine more than 1.5 times baseline classifies it as severe. Severe disease, whether initial or recurrent, is treated with oral vancomycin (fidaxomicin is an acceptable alternative). Intravenous metronidazole is added only when the infection is fulminant with hypotension, shock, ileus, or megacolon, none of which is present. Intravenous vancomycin does not reach the bowel lumen, repeating metronidazole is inadequate for severe disease, and fecal transplantation is reserved for multiple recurrences.
learning_point: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection that is severe (WBC above 15,000 or creatinine above 1.5 times baseline) is treated with oral vancomycin; IV metronidazole is added only for fulminant disease (hypotension, ileus, megacolon), rectal vancomycin for ileus, and fecal transplant for multiple recurrences.
key_facts: Oral metronidazole is no longer preferred even for an initial non-severe episode in current guidelines; fidaxomicin or oral vancomycin are favored.
IV vancomycin does not reach the colon lumen and is ineffective for C. difficile.
Severity is judged by leukocytosis and renal function, not by fever alone.

question: While performing a retropubic mid-urethral sling in a 54-year-old woman, you notice steady dark bleeding from the vaginal incision after the second trocar is passed; vital signs are stable and cystoscopy shows no bladder injury. The next step is:

options.A: perform a Pfannenstiel incision to explore the retropubic space.
options.C: complete the sling, close the incision, and place a vaginal pack.
options.D: extend the vaginal dissection to identify and ligate the bleeding vessel.
options.E: abandon the sling and pack the vagina.

rationale: Venous oozing from the retropubic space after trocar passage is common and usually self-limited. The appropriate response in a stable patient is to finish the procedure, close the vagina, and tamponade with a vaginal pack (often with the catheter on gentle traction), which controls the bleeding in most cases. Chasing the vessel with more vaginal dissection enlarges the raw area and rarely finds a discrete bleeder. Abdominal exploration or embolization is reserved for ongoing bleeding or hemodynamic instability after a period of compression, which would indicate a major vascular injury.
learning_point: Brisk venous bleeding after retropubic trocar passage during a mid-urethral sling is managed by completing the procedure, closing the vaginal incision, and packing the vagina for tamponade; further dissection to find the bleeder is counterproductive, and embolization or exploration is reserved for continued bleeding suggesting major vessel injury.
key_facts: Bleeding usually arises from perforation of the endopelvic fascia and retropubic venous plexus and stops with compression.
Hemodynamic instability or a persistent expanding hematoma despite packing suggests external iliac or obturator vessel injury requiring angiography or exploration.
Postoperative retropubic hematomas are generally managed conservatively.

question: A 59-year-old man with stable Peyronie disease for 18 months has an 80-degree ventral curvature that prevents intercourse. His erections are soft even with maximum-dose tadalafil, with an IIEF-5 score of 12. He wants to resume penetrative sex. The best treatment is:

options.B: inflatable penile prosthesis without correction of the curvature.
options.C: inflatable penile prosthesis with intraoperative modeling.

rationale: This patient has two problems: a severe stable curvature and moderate erectile dysfunction that has failed oral therapy. Procedures that only straighten the penis, such as plication, incision with grafting, or collagenase injections, leave him unable to achieve rigidity, and grafting can further impair erections. A penile prosthesis addresses the ED, but with deformity of this magnitude the cylinders alone will not straighten the penis adequately, so intraoperative modeling (with adjunct plication, incision, or grafting if residual curvature persists) is performed at the same time.
learning_point: A man with Peyronie disease who has severe curvature plus erectile dysfunction inadequately responsive to PDE5 inhibitors is best treated with an inflatable penile prosthesis combined with intraoperative straightening maneuvers (modeling, with plication, incision, or grafting if needed).
key_facts: Plication or grafting alone corrects curvature but leaves the ED untreated and grafting may worsen rigidity.
Prosthesis alone often leaves residual curvature when deformity exceeds about 30 degrees.
Modeling corrects most curvature; residual deformity is managed with adjunct incisions or grafts over the cylinders.

question: A 68-year-old man undergoes TURBT of a 4 cm solid mass on the right lateral bladder wall seen on CT. Pathology shows urothelial carcinoma invading the muscularis propria with a 40% small cell neuroendocrine component. Staging CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is negative, and his creatinine clearance is 85 mL/min. The next step is:

options.B: neoadjuvant carboplatin and paclitaxel followed by cystectomy.
options.C: immediate radical cystectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy.
options.D: cisplatin and etoposide chemotherapy followed by definitive local therapy.
options.E: neoadjuvant gemcitabine and cisplatin followed by cystectomy.

rationale: The presence of a small cell neuroendocrine component dictates management, because these tumors behave like small cell carcinoma of the lung with a high rate of occult systemic disease. Treatment therefore begins with platinum-etoposide chemotherapy and is combined with local therapy, either radiation or consolidative cystectomy, rather than surgery first. Standard urothelial regimens such as gemcitabine-cisplatin or 5-FU/mitomycin chemoradiation are not appropriate for the neuroendocrine component, and carboplatin-paclitaxel is not a standard regimen in this setting.
learning_point: Muscle-invasive bladder cancer containing a small cell (neuroendocrine) component is treated like small cell lung cancer: platinum plus etoposide chemotherapy combined with local therapy (radiation or subsequent cystectomy), rather than up-front cystectomy, gemcitabine-based regimens, or 5-FU/mitomycin chemoradiation.
key_facts: Small cell bladder cancer is aggressive with early micrometastasis; multimodal therapy improves survival over surgery alone.
Neoadjuvant cisplatin/etoposide followed by cystectomy is an alternative to chemoradiation.
Immunotherapy has no established neoadjuvant role in small cell bladder cancer.

question: A 12-year-old girl with cloacal exstrophy underwent sigmoid cystoplasty, bladder neck closure, and a continent catheterizable umbilical channel four years ago. She now has suprapubic pain, foul-smelling urine, and recurrent UTIs. Ultrasound shows three bladder stones, the largest 2.2 cm. The best treatment is:
rationale: Stones this size and number will not clear with irrigation and are too large and numerous for SWL in an augmented bladder. Endoscopic fragmentation through the catheterizable channel risks stricture or incontinence of the channel, and with a closed bladder neck there is no urethral access. Percutaneous cystolithotomy through a suprapubic tract is an efficient way to remove all fragments while protecting the continence mechanism; very large burdens can be handled by open cystolithotomy. Stone formation is an expected complication of enterocystoplasty and does not warrant dismantling the reconstruction.
learning_point: Multiple 1-2 cm bladder stones in a child with enterocystoplasty and prior bladder neck reconstruction are best cleared by percutaneous (or open) cystolithotomy; transurethral or channel-based endoscopic lithotripsy risks damaging the reconstructed outlet or catheterizable channel, and SWL or irrigation is ineffective.
key_facts: Bladder stones occur in 30-50% of augmented bladders, related to mucus, infection, and incomplete emptying.
Preserve the continence mechanism and the Mitrofanoff channel: avoid passing large instruments through them.
Stone formation does not justify converting to an incontinent diversion; prevention is daily irrigation and complete emptying.

question: A 74-year-old woman is diagnosed with pure carcinoma in situ of the bladder on biopsies taken for positive cytology. Her hospital has no BCG supply and none is expected for several months. The next step is:

options.B: repeat cystoscopy and cytology in three months.
options.C: induction intravesical mitomycin C followed by maintenance.
options.D: defer treatment until BCG becomes available.
options.E: radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection.

rationale: Carcinoma in situ carries a high risk of progression to muscle-invasive disease, so waiting months for BCG or merely surveilling is unsafe. When BCG cannot be obtained, the AUA's shortage guidance designates intravesical mitomycin C (six-week induction with monthly maintenance) as the preferred alternative, with gemcitabine, epirubicin, docetaxel, or sequential combinations as other choices. Valrubicin is indicated only for BCG-refractory CIS in patients who cannot undergo cystectomy, and up-front cystectomy is not the initial treatment for CIS without additional adverse features.
learning_point: For newly diagnosed carcinoma in situ of the bladder when BCG is unavailable, the AUA recommends intravesical mitomycin C induction (with maintenance) as the preferred alternative, with gemcitabine, epirubicin, docetaxel, or sequential therapy as other options; delaying treatment or proceeding to cystectomy is not appropriate.
key_facts: CIS is high-risk disease with a substantial progression risk if untreated.
Valrubicin is approved only for BCG-refractory CIS in patients unfit for cystectomy.
During shortages, reduced-dose (one-third) BCG may be used for induction if any supply exists.

question: A 66-year-old woman who underwent radical cystectomy with ileal conduit three years ago now has a bulge adjacent to her stoma that enlarges with Valsalva, and CT confirms a parastomal hernia. She received neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy, smoked for 30 years, and has a BMI of 24. The factor most likely responsible for this complication is:

options.D: inadequate mesenteric blood supply to the conduit.
options.E: stoma brought through the fascia lateral to the rectus muscle.

rationale: Parastomal hernias develop when the fascial defect around the bowel segment gradually widens, and the dominant technical risk factor is siting the stoma outside the rectus sheath; hernia rates are several-fold higher when the stoma exits lateral to the rectus compared with through the muscle belly. Smoking, COPD, age, sex, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy have not been shown to be significant predisposing factors. Compromised mesenteric blood supply leads to conduit necrosis or stomal stenosis, not herniation. Obesity, wound infection, steroid use, and malnutrition are the other recognized associations, none of which this patient has.
learning_point: Parastomal hernia after ileal conduit is most strongly predisposed by bringing the stoma through the fascia lateral to the rectus muscle rather than through the rectus body. Age, smoking, radiation, and chemotherapy are not established risk factors.
key_facts: Stoma placed lateral to rectus: hernia rate roughly 20% vs under 5% when brought through the rectus muscle.
Obesity, wound infection, steroids, malnutrition, and abdominal distention are also associated with parastomal hernia.
Prior radiation and poor mesenteric blood supply predispose to conduit ischemia and stomal stenosis, not hernia.
Prevention: keep the entire fascial opening within the body of the rectus muscle.

question: Two months after a laparoscopic sacrocolpopexy for apical prolapse, a 58-year-old woman reports progressive low back pain, intermittent temperatures to 38.2 C, and unsteadiness when walking. Her incisions are well healed and vaginal examination is unremarkable. The next step is:

options.C: observation with repeat examination in six weeks.

rationale: The combination of back pain, low-grade fever, and difficulty ambulating after sacral fixation is the classic presentation of L5-S1 discitis, a recognized complication when fixation sutures are placed into the disc space rather than the S1 anterior longitudinal ligament. MRI is the study of choice to confirm discitis or vertebral osteomyelitis. Empiric antibiotics without a diagnosis are not appropriate, and pelvic ultrasound cannot evaluate the disc space. Mesh removal may ultimately be required but should not precede a definitive diagnosis and specialist consultation, and simple reassurance is inappropriate once symptoms have persisted this long.
learning_point: New low back pain, fevers, or gait difficulty weeks after sacrocolpopexy suggests L5-S1 discitis or osteomyelitis from sutures placed too high on the sacral promontory into the disc space; the next step is MRI of the lumbosacral spine to establish the diagnosis before any treatment.
key_facts: Sacral sutures should be placed in the anterior longitudinal ligament at S1, below the L5-S1 disc.
Minimally invasive approaches have been associated with dissection too proximal on the promontory.
Multifilament permanent sutures have been linked to discitis and are now used less often.
Mesh or suture removal is not undertaken until imaging confirms the diagnosis; multidisciplinary input is appropriate.

question: During a laparoscopic nephrectomy, pulsatile bleeding is seen dripping from the lateral 12 mm port site into the abdomen after trocar insertion. Angling the trocar against the abdominal wall stops the bleeding, but it restarts each time the instrument is moved over the next 20 minutes. The next step is:

options.A: pass a full-thickness suture around the bleeding site using a port-closure device.
options.B: convert to an open incision to explore the abdominal wall.
options.D: remove the trocar and apply pressure externally for 10 minutes.
options.E: fulgurate the peritoneal edges of the port site.

rationale: Pulsatile bleeding that recurs whenever tamponade is released indicates injury to an inferior epigastric artery branch, which will not reliably stop without ligation. A port-closure device allows a full-thickness suture to be passed alongside the tract and tied over the fascia, compressing and securing the vessel; a figure-of-eight may be needed. Upsizing the trocar only tamponades temporarily and does not treat the arterial injury, and cautery is unreliable because the transected vessel retracts into the muscle. External pressure alone is also temporary. Open exploration is a last resort if suture ligation fails.
learning_point: Persistent arterial bleeding from a trocar site (inferior epigastric vessel injury) that recurs after tamponade requires formal control; the next step is a suture passed through the abdominal wall with a port-closure device (e.g., Carter-Thomason) to ligate the vessel.
key_facts: Arterial bleeding from an epigastric branch rarely stops with trocar tamponade alone.
Cauterizing the tract is usually ineffective because vessel ends retract into the abdominal wall.
A full-thickness figure-of-eight suture beside the trocar via a closure device secures the vessel; re-inspect the site at case end.
Open exploration is reserved for failure of these measures.

question: A 63-year-old woman is undergoing radical cystectomy with planned ileal orthotopic neobladder for cT2 high-grade urothelial carcinoma after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. During the pelvic lymphadenectomy, a solitary 2 cm obturator node is excised and frozen section shows metastatic urothelial carcinoma; the remaining nodal tissue appears normal and resectable. The next step is:

options.A: stop the operation and give second-line systemic therapy before reattempting cystectomy.
options.B: complete the lymphadenectomy, cystectomy, and orthotopic neobladder as planned.
options.C: complete the lymphadenectomy only and close for postoperative chemoradiation.
options.D: complete the cystectomy but convert to an ileal conduit.
options.E: stop the operation and refer for definitive chemoradiation.

rationale: A single resectable positive node found intraoperatively should prompt completion of a thorough lymphadenectomy and cystectomy, since local control provides benefit and a subset of patients with limited nodal disease are cured by surgery. Aborting for systemic therapy or chemoradiation has not been shown to improve outcomes and leaves the primary tumor in place. Nodal metastasis is not a contraindication to orthotopic diversion, so there is no reason to switch to a conduit against the patient's wishes. Systemic therapy decisions are made postoperatively based on final pathology.
learning_point: Discovery of limited, resectable grossly positive pelvic lymph nodes during radical cystectomy is not a reason to abort; the surgeon should complete the lymphadenectomy and cystectomy, and node positivity does not preclude orthotopic neobladder.
key_facts: About one quarter of cystectomy patients have nodal metastases.
Local control from cystectomy plus lymphadenectomy benefits patients with limited nodal disease.
No evidence shows aborting surgery for chemotherapy or chemoradiation is superior to completing resection.
Positive nodes are not a contraindication to orthotopic diversion; adjuvant chemotherapy is considered postoperatively.

question: An 84-year-old man with advanced Parkinson's disease, tremor, and limited hand dexterity develops complete urinary retention after years of slowly worsening voiding symptoms. Urodynamics show a detrusor pressure at maximum flow of 10 cm H2O with a flow of 3 mL/sec, and the prostate is estimated at 35 g. The most appropriate long-term management is:

options.C: holmium laser enucleation of the prostate.
options.E: clean intermittent catheterization performed by the patient.

rationale: The pressure-flow pattern of low detrusor pressure with low flow indicates detrusor underactivity rather than outlet obstruction, so prostate outlet reduction is unlikely to restore emptying. Bethanechol lacks reproducible evidence of benefit and carries cholinergic side effects. Sacral neuromodulation is approved for nonobstructive retention but has limited data in Parkinson's disease and requires the patient to manage a controller. Self-catheterization is effective in principle but impractical with tremor and poor dexterity. A suprapubic tube provides reliable drainage and is better tolerated than long-term urethral catheterization.
learning_point: Urinary retention with low detrusor pressure and low flow in a patient with advanced Parkinson's disease reflects detrusor underactivity, not obstruction; outlet surgery is unlikely to help and CIC may be impractical, so a suprapubic tube is the most viable management.
key_facts: Low-pressure, low-flow pressure-flow study indicates underactive detrusor rather than bladder outlet obstruction.
Bethanechol has no reproducible urodynamic evidence of benefit and has significant cholinergic side effects.
Sacral neuromodulation has limited evidence in Parkinson's disease and requires patient operation of the device.
TURP is not contraindicated in obstructed Parkinson's patients but fails when detrusor contractility is poor.

question: A 29-year-old man has formed three calcium phosphate stones in two years. Serum studies show potassium 3.2 mEq/L, chloride 110 mEq/L, and bicarbonate 19 mEq/L with a normal anion gap. A 24-hour urine shows volume 2.1 L, citrate 120 mg, and pH 6.9. The best initial treatment is:
rationale: Non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia, an inappropriately alkaline urine, severe hypocitraturia, and calcium phosphate stones defines distal renal tubular acidosis. Potassium citrate corrects the systemic acidosis, raises urinary citrate, and replaces potassium in one agent. Sodium bicarbonate also corrects the acidosis but the sodium load increases urinary calcium and is not first-line. Potassium chloride treats only the hypokalemia. A thiazide is used for hypercalciuria and would aggravate the potassium deficit, and acetohydroxamic acid is a urease inhibitor for struvite stones.
learning_point: Calcium phosphate stones with hypocitraturia, persistently high urine pH, hypokalemia, and low serum bicarbonate indicate incomplete distal renal tubular acidosis; potassium citrate is the first-line treatment because it corrects acidosis, hypokalemia, and hypocitraturia without a sodium load.
key_facts: Distal RTA: non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, urine pH above about 6, low urinary citrate, calcium phosphate stones.
Alkali therapy raises urinary citrate; potassium salts are preferred over sodium salts, which increase calciuria.
Thiazides treat hypercalciuria and would worsen hypokalemia.
Potassium chloride repletes potassium but does not correct the acidosis or citrate.

question: A 29-year-old man sustains an unstable pelvic ring fracture in a motorcycle collision. A urethral catheter is passed without difficulty and drains gross hematuria; CT cystography shows extravasation confined to the perivesical space. Which of the following associated findings would still allow conservative catheter management of the bladder injury?

options.A: persistent clot obstruction of the catheter.
options.B: a partial membranous urethral disruption traversed by the catheter.
options.C: contrast extravasation through the bladder neck.
options.D: a 2 cm rectal laceration adjacent to the bladder.
options.E: contrast outlining loops of small bowel.

rationale: An isolated extraperitoneal rupture heals with catheter drainage alone, and a membranous urethral injury successfully bridged by the catheter does not change that plan because drainage is already established. Bladder neck injury, rectal injury, and clot retention that prevents adequate drainage are indications to repair an extraperitoneal rupture. Contrast around bowel loops indicates an intraperitoneal component, which always requires operative closure. Had the catheter failed to cross the urethral injury, a suprapubic tube would be placed and bladder repair at the same time would be reasonable.
learning_point: Extraperitoneal bladder rupture is managed with catheter drainage alone unless there is a bladder neck injury, concomitant rectal or vaginal injury, clot retention or inadequate drainage, or an associated intraperitoneal component; a membranous urethral injury across which a catheter has been passed does not by itself mandate repair.
key_facts: All intraperitoneal bladder ruptures require operative repair.
Extraperitoneal rupture: catheter drainage for 10 to 14 days with cystogram before removal.
Indications for repairing extraperitoneal injuries: bladder neck involvement, rectal or vaginal injury, bone fragments in the bladder, clot retention, or concurrent open pelvic fixation.
If a catheter cannot traverse a urethral injury, place a suprapubic tube and consider concurrent bladder repair.

question: A 71-year-old man is admitted with acute kidney injury. Laboratory values show urine sodium 70 mEq/L, plasma sodium 140 mEq/L, urine creatinine 50 mg/dL, and plasma creatinine 4.0 mg/dL. Based on the fractional excretion of sodium, the most likely etiology is:
rationale: FENa is calculated as (70 x 4.0) / (140 x 50) x 100 = 280 / 7000 x 100 = 4%, which falls at the threshold for a postrenal cause. Prerenal states such as hypovolemia and sepsis cause avid sodium reabsorption with FENa under 1%. Intrinsic tubular injury from aminoglycosides or NSAIDs produces intermediate values in the 1 to 4% range. Of the choices, only urinary retention produces bilateral postrenal obstruction and therefore a high FENa.
learning_point: The fractional excretion of sodium (FENa = [urine Na x plasma Cr] / [plasma Na x urine Cr] x 100) distinguishes causes of acute kidney injury: under 1% prerenal, 1 to 4% intrinsic, and above 4% postrenal; among urologic causes only bilateral obstruction (such as retention) produces a high FENa.
key_facts: FENa below 1% indicates avid sodium retention from prerenal states such as hypovolemia or sepsis.
Intrinsic tubular injury (aminoglycosides, NSAIDs, contrast) gives intermediate values; the source uses 1 to 4%.
Postrenal obstruction impairs tubular sodium handling, raising FENa above 4%.
Many nephrology texts cite FENa above 2% for ATN; the SASP rule uses the 4% cutoff for postrenal causes.

question: A 35-week male fetus has bilateral renal pelvic dilation that has progressed over serial ultrasounds, newly dilated ureters bilaterally, and a distended bladder with a 6 mm wall. Amniotic fluid index is normal and the mother is otherwise healthy. The best plan is:

options.A: term delivery followed by MAG3 renal scan in the first week.
options.C: renal ultrasound at four to six weeks of life.
options.D: term delivery followed by renal ultrasound and VCUG before hospital discharge.
options.E: fetal MRI to characterize the bladder outlet.

rationale: Progressive bilateral hydroureteronephrosis with a thickened bladder wall in a male fetus raises strong concern for posterior urethral valves, so the infant should undergo renal ultrasound and VCUG before leaving the hospital to diagnose and relieve any outlet obstruction and reduce infection risk. Normal amniotic fluid indicates preserved renal function, so there is no benefit to early delivery, and fetal MRI would not alter management. Deferring imaging to one month is appropriate only for low-grade isolated hydronephrosis. A renal scan has a role later for assessing differential function and drainage, not as the initial study.
learning_point: A male fetus with bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and a thick-walled bladder but normal amniotic fluid should be delivered at term and evaluated before discharge with renal ultrasound and VCUG to exclude posterior urethral valves; early delivery and fetal MRI are not indicated.
key_facts: Normal amniotic fluid means renal function is adequate; no indication for early delivery or fetal intervention.
Bilateral dilation with thick bladder wall in a male suggests bladder outlet obstruction (posterior urethral valves).
Postnatal evaluation is prompt (before discharge), not deferred to one month, because of UTI and obstruction risk.
Renal scan is reserved for later assessment of function and drainage.

question: A 58-year-old woman on hemodialysis missed her last two sessions and presents with generalized weakness. Serum potassium is 7.6 mEq/L and the ECG shows peaked T waves. While dialysis is being arranged, the intervention that will most rapidly reduce her serum potassium concentration is:
rationale: Insulin promotes cellular potassium uptake via the Na-K ATPase and lowers serum potassium within minutes; dextrose is given concurrently to avoid hypoglycemia. Calcium chloride is indicated for ECG changes because it stabilizes the myocardium, but it does not lower the potassium level. Bicarbonate is of little benefit in ESRD patients, and oral or NG binding resins act only in the colon over many hours. Furosemide requires functioning kidneys and is ineffective in an anuric dialysis patient; dialysis remains the definitive therapy.
learning_point: Intravenous insulin with glucose is the fastest way to lower serum potassium in severe hyperkalemia by driving potassium into cells; calcium stabilizes the myocardium but does not lower potassium, and oral binding resins and bicarbonate act slowly or poorly in ESRD.
key_facts: Insulin activates Na-K ATPase, shifting potassium intracellularly within 15 to 30 minutes; glucose is co-administered to prevent hypoglycemia.
IV calcium gluconate antagonizes cardiac membrane effects but does not change serum potassium.
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate works in the colon over hours and is ineffective acutely when given orally or by NG tube.
Bicarbonate is minimally effective in dialysis patients; definitive removal requires dialysis.

question: A five-year-old girl has had three febrile UTIs in the past year along with daytime urgency, frequency, and bedwetting. Renal ultrasound is normal; VCUG demonstrates grade 2 left vesicoureteral reflux, a bladder capacity well below expected for age, and a dilated proximal urethra with a narrowed distal segment during voiding. In addition to continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, the next step is:

options.C: oxybutynin with a timed voiding and bowel program.

rationale: This child has overactive bladder with external sphincter overactivity (spinning-top urethra), small functional capacity, and low-grade reflux, a pattern of bladder-bowel dysfunction that drives her infections. Antimuscarinic therapy together with timed voiding and bowel management treats the storage dysfunction and improves the likelihood of spontaneous reflux resolution. Surgical reflux correction, whether endoscopic or open, has higher failure rates when voiding dysfunction is untreated. Urethral dilation has no proven benefit, desmopressin does not address the secondary enuresis from low capacity, and biofeedback is better suited to older children with documented dyssynergia.
learning_point: Recurrent UTIs with urgency, small capacity bladder, spinning-top urethra, and low-grade VUR in a young child reflect bladder-bowel dysfunction with overactive bladder; treat the bladder dysfunction (antimuscarinics plus prophylaxis) before considering surgical correction of reflux.
key_facts: Lower urinary tract dysfunction lowers spontaneous resolution and surgical success rates for VUR; treat it first.
Spinning-top urethra reflects external sphincter overactivity; urethral dilation or cystoscopy is not beneficial.
DDAVP is not indicated when enuresis is secondary to small functional capacity, and not in children this young.
Biofeedback is an option in older children after uroflow-EMG confirms dyssynergia.

question: A 31-year-old man sustains a complete conus medullaris injury in a fall. Six months later, spinal shock has resolved and he asks about his erectile function. He should be counseled that he most likely has:

options.A: preserved reflexogenic erections that will not respond to sildenafil.
options.B: preserved psychogenic erections with loss of reflexogenic erections.
options.D: preserved reflexogenic erections with loss of psychogenic erections.
options.E: complete loss of both reflexogenic and psychogenic erections.

rationale: Reflexogenic erections depend on the sacral parasympathetic reflex arc, which is destroyed in a conus medullaris or sacral lesion. Psychogenic erections are generated centrally and transmitted through sympathetic fibers exiting at T11-L2, above the level of injury, so they remain possible. The reverse pattern (reflexogenic preserved, psychogenic lost) is characteristic of complete suprasacral lesions above T9. There is no reason for a diminished response to PDE5 inhibitors in these men.
learning_point: A complete sacral (lower motor neuron) spinal cord lesion abolishes reflexogenic erections, which depend on the S2-S4 parasympathetic arc, but psychogenic erections mediated by thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow (T11-L2) are preserved; PDE5 inhibitor response is not reduced.
key_facts: Reflexogenic erections require an intact sacral reflex arc (S2-S4); preserved in suprasacral lesions.
Psychogenic erections are mediated through T11-L2 sympathetic outflow and persist in lesions below that level.
Lesions above T9 generally eliminate psychogenic erections.
Erectile quality may be reduced but PDE5 inhibitors remain effective.

question: A 41-year-old man has an IPSS of 24 with predominant voiding symptoms that have not improved after four months of silodosin. His prostate is 22 g and smooth on examination, urinalysis and PSA are normal, and uroflowmetry shows a maximum flow of 7 mL/sec on a 180 mL void with a postvoid residual of 110 mL. The next step is:
rationale: In a young man with a small prostate, a poor flow rate is just as consistent with detrusor underactivity, dysfunctional voiding, or primary bladder neck obstruction as it is with prostatic obstruction. Videourodynamics combines pressure-flow analysis with fluoroscopy to localize obstruction or document a weak detrusor, guiding appropriate therapy. Proceeding directly to TUIP or a prostatic urethral lift without confirming obstruction risks an ineffective operation and ejaculatory side effects. A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor offers little in a 22 g gland, and mirabegron treats storage rather than emptying.
learning_point: A young man with severe LUTS, a small prostate, low flow, and failure of alpha-blocker therapy should undergo videourodynamics before any outlet surgery to distinguish obstruction (including primary bladder neck obstruction or dysfunctional voiding) from detrusor underactivity.
key_facts: Low uroflow alone cannot differentiate bladder outlet obstruction from detrusor underactivity.
Primary bladder neck obstruction and dysfunctional voiding are common in young men and are identified on fluoroscopy with pressure-flow data.
Outlet surgery without confirmation of obstruction risks failure and retrograde ejaculation in a young man.
Antimuscarinics address storage symptoms but not impaired emptying.

question: A 61-year-old man undergoing bipolar TURP under spinal anesthesia develops a rigid erection that prevents advancement of the resectoscope. The instrument is withdrawn and after 20 minutes of waiting the erection has not subsided. The next step is:

options.A: inject intracavernosal phenylephrine after alerting the anesthesiologist.
options.B: perform a perineal urethrostomy to complete the resection.
options.C: convert to general anesthesia and continue.
options.E: apply ice packs to the penis and resume resection in 10 minutes.

rationale: When an intraoperative erection persists despite a period of observation, intracavernosal injection of a sympathomimetic such as phenylephrine is the appropriate step to induce detumescence and allow the operation to proceed. Because the drug can raise blood pressure and heart rate, the anesthesia team should be informed before injection. Deepening anesthesia does not reliably resolve the erection, and attempting to resect around a rigid penis risks corporal injury and incomplete resection. Perineal urethrostomy is appropriate only in a dire situation after pharmacologic failure; in a nonemergent case aborting would be preferable to urethrostomy.
learning_point: A persistent intraoperative erection during endoscopic prostate surgery that does not resolve spontaneously after removal of instruments should be treated with intracavernosal phenylephrine, with the anesthesiologist monitoring for hemodynamic effects.
key_facts: Allow time for spontaneous detumescence first after withdrawing the resectoscope.
Intracavernosal alpha-agonist (phenylephrine) is the pharmacologic treatment of choice; alert anesthesia before injection.
Converting to general anesthesia has not been shown to resolve the erection.
Perineal urethrostomy is reserved for emergencies when drugs fail; aborting is otherwise preferable to urethrostomy.

question: A 47-year-old man undergoes partial penectomy for a 3.5 cm exophytic lesion of the glans; pathology shows verrucous carcinoma with negative margins and no conventional squamous component. On examination he has a 1.5 cm mobile, mildly tender left inguinal lymph node. The next step is:

options.A: neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by inguinal dissection.
options.D: PET/CT followed by pelvic lymph node dissection.
options.E: observation with repeat examination in several weeks.

rationale: Verrucous carcinoma has a very low metastatic potential, so a palpable, tender, mobile inguinal node after resection is far more likely to be reactive than metastatic, and observation is appropriate. If the node persists or enlarges over follow-up, fine-needle or excisional biopsy is indicated, and lymphadenectomy is performed only for biopsy-proven metastasis. Up-front unilateral or bilateral inguinal dissection carries significant morbidity without expected benefit in this histology, and pelvic dissection or chemotherapy has no role in the absence of documented nodal disease.
learning_point: Verrucous carcinoma of the penis (Buschke-Lowenstein tumor) is locally destructive but almost never metastasizes; palpable inguinal nodes after resection are presumed reactive and should be observed, with biopsy reserved for nodes that persist or enlarge.
key_facts: Verrucous carcinoma is distinguished from condyloma by local tissue compression and destruction.
Unlike conventional penile squamous cell carcinoma, nodal metastasis is exceedingly rare.
Palpable adenopathy is usually inflammatory; observe and biopsy only if persistent or growing.
Lymphadenectomy is reserved for biopsy-proven nodal metastasis.

question: A 46-year-old woman presents with new facial hair, deepening voice, central obesity, and hypertension. Morning cortisol remains high after 1 mg overnight dexamethasone, plasma ACTH is suppressed, and serum DHEA-S and urinary 17-ketosteroids are markedly elevated. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.C: small cell lung carcinoma with ectopic ACTH.

rationale: Hypercortisolism that fails to suppress with dexamethasone and is accompanied by a low ACTH localizes the problem to the adrenal gland. The additional finding of marked androgen excess, reflected in elevated DHEA-S and 17-ketosteroids with clinical virilization, is characteristic of adrenocortical carcinoma, which frequently co-secretes multiple steroid classes. Benign adenomas usually secrete cortisol alone and produce little virilization. A pituitary source is ACTH-dependent, ectopic ACTH would not suppress ACTH levels, and exogenous anabolic steroids cause virilization without raising endogenous ketosteroid excretion.
learning_point: ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome (no suppression with low-dose dexamethasone) accompanied by virilization and markedly elevated DHEA and 17-ketosteroids points to adrenocortical carcinoma, which characteristically co-secretes cortisol and androgen precursors.
key_facts: Failure of low-dose dexamethasone suppression plus suppressed ACTH indicates an adrenal source.
Pituitary Cushing disease is ACTH-dependent and typically suppresses with high-dose dexamethasone.
Benign cortisol-producing adenomas rarely cause significant virilization; mixed cortisol plus androgen excess suggests carcinoma.
Ectopic ACTH and exogenous anabolic steroids do not raise 17-ketosteroids or DHEA in this pattern.

question: During cystectomy in a 61-year-old man with a narrow, deep pelvis, a right colon and terminal ileum reservoir has been constructed for orthotopic diversion, but the pouch outlet lies 3 cm short of the urethral stump despite full mobilization of the right colon. The next step is:

options.A: convert to a continent cutaneous reservoir using the same pouch.
options.C: ligate the right colic artery to release the mesentery.
options.D: ligate the middle colic artery to release the mesentery.
options.E: ligate the ileocolic artery to release the mesentery.

rationale: The right colic artery can be divided safely because the marginal artery of Drummond maintains perfusion of the right colon from the ileocolic and middle colic arteries, and its division releases tethering mesentery so the pouch can descend to the urethra. The ileocolic artery supplies the cecum and terminal ileum that form the reservoir, and dividing it would cause pouch ischemia. The middle colic artery supplies the transverse colon and the anastomosis; dividing it adds no useful length and risks ischemia. Changing to a conduit or cutaneous reservoir should be considered only after all lengthening maneuvers fail.
learning_point: When a right colon-based orthotopic reservoir will not reach the urethra because of mesenteric tension, dividing the right colic artery provides additional mesenteric length while collateral flow through the marginal artery preserves the pouch; the ileocolic and middle colic arteries must not be divided.
key_facts: Right colic artery usually arises from the SMA (or from the ileocolic or middle colic) and can be sacrificed because of the arc of Drummond.
Division of the ileocolic artery devascularizes the cecum and terminal ileum used in the pouch.
Dividing the middle colic artery does not add length and jeopardizes the bowel anastomosis.
Alternate diversions are a last resort after mobilization maneuvers are exhausted.

question: A 50-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate stones has eliminated dairy from her diet on the advice of a friend. If no other dietary changes are made, the expected effect on her 24-hour urine is:
rationale: Dietary calcium complexes with oxalate in the intestine to form insoluble calcium oxalate that is excreted in stool. When calcium intake falls, more oxalate remains free for absorption, and urinary oxalate rises; because oxalate is a more potent driver of supersaturation than calcium, stone risk increases. This is why low-calcium diets are associated with more, not fewer, stones. Calcium restriction has no meaningful direct effect on urinary citrate, pH, or sodium.
learning_point: Restricting dietary calcium increases calcium oxalate stone risk because less intestinal calcium is available to bind oxalate, increasing oxalate absorption and urinary oxalate excretion; stone formers should maintain normal calcium intake of about 1000 to 1200 mg daily.
key_facts: Low-calcium diets are associated with higher stone recurrence rates in epidemiologic and randomized data.
Dietary calcium binds oxalate in the gut lumen; less calcium means more free oxalate absorbed.
Calcium restriction does not meaningfully change urinary citrate or pH.
AUA guidance: normal calcium intake with reduced sodium and animal protein for calcium stone formers.

question: A 69-year-old woman with multifocal bladder carcinoma in situ completes a six-week induction course of intravesical BCG. At her six-month surveillance cystoscopy, the technique most likely to identify persistent or recurrent carcinoma in situ is:
rationale: Photoactive porphyrins accumulate preferentially in neoplastic urothelium after intravesical hexaminolevulinate, so blue-light cystoscopy highlights flat CIS that is invisible or equivocal under white light, raising detection from about two thirds to over 90% of lesions and reducing recurrence rates. Narrow band imaging improves visualization of tumor vasculature but has not been shown to reduce recurrence. Cytology and FISH can indicate that high-grade disease is present but cannot localize it for biopsy or resection. Random biopsies sample only a tiny fraction of the urothelium and have a low yield.
learning_point: Blue-light (hexaminolevulinate) fluorescence cystoscopy is the best method to detect residual or recurrent carcinoma in situ at surveillance cystoscopy after BCG, improving CIS detection from roughly 68% to 95% versus white light and reducing recurrence.
key_facts: White light cystoscopy misses up to about one third of CIS lesions.
Blue-light cystoscopy improves detection of both CIS and papillary tumors and lowers short- and long-term recurrence, though not progression.
Narrow band imaging enhances vascular contrast but lacks recurrence outcome data.
Cytology and FISH are sensitive for CIS but do not localize lesions or reduce recurrence.

question: A 44-year-old man has had four calcium oxalate stone episodes. His 24-hour urine shows volume 2.4 L, calcium 170 mg, oxalate 32 mg, citrate 680 mg, sodium 120 mEq, and uric acid 980 mg; serum uric acid is normal. The intervention most likely to reduce his stone recurrence is:
rationale: The only abnormality in this profile is hyperuricosuria; urinary calcium, oxalate, citrate, and sodium are all within normal limits. A randomized controlled trial demonstrated that allopurinol reduces recurrent calcium oxalate stones specifically in patients with hyperuricosuria and normal urinary calcium, and the AUA guideline recommends it in this setting regardless of serum uric acid. Thiazides and sodium restriction target hypercalciuria, potassium citrate targets hypocitraturia, and oxalate restriction targets hyperoxaluria, none of which is present here.
learning_point: Recurrent calcium oxalate stone formers with hyperuricosuria (urine uric acid above 800 mg/day) and normal urinary calcium should be offered allopurinol, which has randomized trial evidence for reducing recurrence; elevated serum uric acid is not required.
key_facts: AUA guideline: allopurinol for recurrent calcium oxalate stones with hyperuricosuria and normocalciuria.
Thiazides are for hypercalciuria; potassium citrate for hypocitraturia; low-oxalate diet for hyperoxaluria.
Low sodium diet mainly helps in the setting of hypercalciuria.
Limiting non-dairy animal protein complements allopurinol by lowering urate load.

question: A 28-year-old man has multiple warty lesions extending from the fossa navicularis through the pendulous urethra on cystoscopy, with involvement too extensive for simple fulguration. The best initial treatment is:

options.B: topical imiquimod applied into the urethra.

rationale: Extensive intraurethral condylomata are treated with intraurethral 5-fluorouracil cream as first-line therapy, with holmium laser ablation an alternative for focal or refractory lesions. Imiquimod and podophyllotoxin cause significant toxicity to normal mucosa and are approved only for external or meatal use. Cryotherapy can be applied to the meatus but cannot be delivered along the proximal urethra. The CO2 laser is absorbed by water and therefore cannot be used through a cystoscope in an irrigated field.
learning_point: Extensive condyloma within the urethra is treated with intraurethral 5-fluorouracil cream (or holmium laser ablation); podophyllin, imiquimod, cryotherapy, and CO2 laser are limited to the meatus or external skin and are not suitable for the proximal urethra.
key_facts: Podophyllin and imiquimod are not approved for internal use because of toxicity to normal urethral tissue.
Liquid nitrogen cryotherapy reaches only the meatus.
CO2 laser energy is absorbed by water and cannot be delivered through a cystoscope; holmium laser can.
5-FU cream is the initial choice for extensive intraurethral disease.

question: A 67-year-old man is scheduled for open radical cystectomy with ileal conduit. According to the AUA Best Practice Statement on antimicrobial prophylaxis, the recommended intravenous regimen is:

options.A: ampicillin, gentamicin, and metronidazole continued for 48 hours.
options.B: a first-generation cephalosporin at induction continued until drains are removed.
options.C: a fluoroquinolone within one hour before incision, continued for 5 days.
options.D: vancomycin at induction continued for 72 hours.
options.E: a second- or third-generation cephalosporin within one hour before incision, stopped within 24 hours.

rationale: Procedures that open bowel require coverage of both skin flora and enteric organisms, and the AUA statement recommends a second- or third-generation cephalosporin given within one hour of incision and discontinued within 24 hours. Aminoglycoside plus metronidazole is the listed alternative, but a three-drug regimen or any regimen prolonged to 48 or 72 hours or beyond adds resistance and C. difficile risk without reducing surgical site infection. A first-generation cephalosporin lacks adequate anaerobic and gram-negative coverage for bowel surgery, and continuing until drain removal is not supported.
learning_point: For radical cystectomy with intestinal diversion, the AUA Best Practice Statement recommends a single preoperative dose of a second- or third-generation cephalosporin within one hour of incision, discontinued within 24 hours; aminoglycoside plus metronidazole is an acceptable alternative.
key_facts: Prolonged perioperative antibiotic courses increase resistance and C. difficile or fungal infection without reducing SSI.
Prophylaxis should be stopped within 24 hours of surgery.
The role of mechanical and oral antibiotic bowel preparation is controversial.
Alternative regimen: aminoglycoside plus metronidazole (or clindamycin) within one hour of incision.

question: A 44-year-old man undergoes partial penectomy for a 4 cm mass arising in the pendulous urethra. Pathology shows poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma invading the corpus spongiosum and both corpora cavernosa with negative margins. Inguinal examination and CT of the abdomen and pelvis show no adenopathy or metastases. The next step is:

options.B: adjuvant external beam radiation to the groins.
options.E: concurrent chemoradiation to the perineum and groins.

rationale: For urethral squamous cell carcinoma that has been completely resected with negative margins and no palpable or radiographic nodal disease, there is no evidence that prophylactic inguinal node dissection improves survival, in contrast to higher-risk penile cancer. Inguinal lymphadenectomy is reserved for patients with palpable nodes in the absence of distant disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy, radiation, or chemoradiation is used mainly for proximal or locally advanced tumors or for genital preservation, and none has demonstrated a survival benefit in this margin-negative distal urethral setting. Surveillance is therefore appropriate.
learning_point: After complete resection of a distal (pendulous) urethral squamous cell carcinoma with negative margins and no clinical or radiographic nodal disease, observation is appropriate; prophylactic inguinal lymphadenectomy and adjuvant chemotherapy or radiation have not shown survival benefit in urethral cancer.
key_facts: Unlike penile cancer, prophylactic inguinal dissection for cN0 urethral cancer has no demonstrated survival advantage.
Inguinal lymphadenectomy is indicated for palpable nodes without distant metastases.
Chemoradiation is used for organ preservation in anterior urethral tumors and for advanced proximal tumors.
Adjuvant therapy after margin-negative resection of distal urethral SCC lacks supporting evidence.

question: A 37-year-old man reports lifelong rapid ejaculation and, over the past year, difficulty maintaining erections. Penile duplex Doppler after intracavernosal injection shows a peak systolic velocity of 42 cm/s and end-diastolic velocity of 1 cm/s bilaterally. The best initial treatment is:
rationale: When premature ejaculation and erectile dysfunction coexist, guidelines recommend treating the ED first because ejaculatory control often improves once reliable erections are restored. The duplex findings of a high peak systolic velocity and a very low end-diastolic velocity indicate normal arterial inflow and normal veno-occlusion, so the ED is most likely psychogenic, and a PDE5 inhibitor is the least invasive effective treatment. SSRIs and topical anesthetics target ejaculation and are deferred. Injection therapy and prosthesis are reserved for PDE5 inhibitor failure or severe vasculogenic disease.
learning_point: In a man with both erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation, treat the ED first; a penile duplex showing normal peak systolic velocity (above 35 cm/s) and low end-diastolic velocity indicates normal hemodynamics (likely psychogenic ED), for which a PDE5 inhibitor is the appropriate first-line therapy.
key_facts: PSV below 25 cm/s suggests arterial insufficiency; PSV above 35 cm/s is normal inflow.
EDV above 5 cm/s with adequate PSV suggests veno-occlusive dysfunction.
Premature ejaculation often improves when coexisting ED is treated.
SSRIs and topical anesthetics are second-line until ED is addressed.

question: A radiologist interpreting a PSMA PET scan notes intense physiologic tracer uptake in the salivary glands and small bowel in addition to the prostate. The target molecule responsible for this distribution is:
rationale: PSMA is a type II transmembrane glutamate carboxypeptidase that functions in folate and nutrient absorption and is therefore normally expressed in the small intestine and salivary and lacrimal glands, as well as proximal renal tubules; this accounts for the characteristic physiologic uptake pattern on PSMA PET. Prostatic acid phosphatase is concentrated more than 200-fold in prostate relative to other tissues. PCA3 is a urinary non-coding RNA biomarker, PSCA is a surface antigen shared with bladder urothelium, and PSA is a serine protease secreted into seminal fluid without salivary or intestinal expression.
learning_point: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a transmembrane enzyme expressed by prostate epithelium that is also found in the small intestine (as folate hydrolase) and salivary glands, which explains physiologic uptake on PSMA PET imaging.
key_facts: PSMA is a glutamate carboxypeptidase involved in nutrient (folate) uptake; expressed in small bowel, salivary and lacrimal glands, kidney, and prostate.
PSMA PET has higher sensitivity than bone scan or conventional CT for staging and is used for targeted radioligand therapy.
