rationale: The anterior wall points (Aa and Ba at -3) show the anterior compartment is fully supported, so anterior repair is not indicated. Ap and Bp at +1 indicate posterior wall prolapse protruding beyond the hymen, and C at +1 indicates apical (vault or cervical) descent. Both prolapsed compartments must be addressed at the time of the sling, so a posterior repair combined with an apical suspension is appropriate. A sling alone treats only the stress incontinence, and a posterior repair alone leaves the apical defect, which is a common cause of recurrence.
learning_point: POP-Q points identify which compartments are prolapsed: Ap/Bp beyond the hymen indicate posterior wall prolapse and point C at or beyond the hymen indicates apical descent. When a midurethral sling is placed for stress incontinence, symptomatic prolapse in each affected compartment should be repaired concurrently; a well-supported compartment should not be repaired.
key_facts: Aa/Ba describe the anterior wall, Ap/Bp the posterior wall, C the cervix or vaginal cuff; values of -3 are fully supported, 0 is at the hymen, positive values are beyond it.
Apical descent (C near or beyond 0) requires an apical suspension; a posterior repair alone will not correct it.
A sling corrects stress incontinence only and does nothing for coexisting prolapse.

question: A 62-year-old man with resected stage II colon cancer has a 2.8 cm homogeneous left adrenal mass on surveillance imaging. Unenhanced attenuation is 22 HU; after contrast the lesion measures 95 HU and on 15-minute delayed images 44 HU, giving an absolute washout of 70%. The most likely diagnosis is:
rationale: An unenhanced attenuation of 22 HU excludes a lipid-rich adenoma, which is defined by values below 10 HU, so the lesion is indeterminate on the non-contrast study alone. The absolute washout of 70% exceeds the 60% threshold, which is characteristic of adenoma and effectively separates lipid-poor adenomas from malignant tissue. Metastases and adrenocortical carcinoma retain contrast and typically wash out less than 60%. Pheochromocytoma also tends to show slow washout and is usually more avidly enhancing and heterogeneous.
learning_point: An adrenal mass with unenhanced attenuation above 10 HU is indeterminate (not lipid-rich), but an absolute contrast washout of more than 60% on delayed CT identifies a lipid-poor adenoma rather than a malignant lesion. Metastases and adrenocortical carcinoma typically wash out slowly (<60%).
key_facts: About 70% of adenomas are lipid-rich: unenhanced CT <10 HU is diagnostic.
About 30% are lipid-poor (>10 HU) and require washout imaging; absolute washout >60% (relative >40%) favors adenoma.
Myelolipoma contains macroscopic fat and shows negative Hounsfield units.
Malignant lesions and pheochromocytoma generally show washout <60%.

question: A 58-year-old man undergoes partial penectomy for a pT2, high-grade squamous cell carcinoma with no palpable inguinal adenopathy and is taken for bilateral staging superficial inguinal lymph node dissection. Proceeding to a deep (femoral triangle) dissection on a given side is indicated by:

options.A: high grade of the primary tumor.
options.C: perineural invasion in the primary tumor.
options.D: metastasis in the superficial nodes on frozen section.

rationale: The superficial inguinal dissection serves as a staging procedure, and the nodes are sent for frozen section. Because metastasis to the deep nodes beneath the fascia lata has not been described without superficial nodal involvement, a deep dissection is added only when the superficial nodes contain cancer. Grade, stage, perineural or lymphovascular invasion are predictors of nodal metastasis that justify performing a staging dissection in the first place but do not dictate how extensive it should be. Palpable nodes are frequently inflammatory, so palpability alone should not drive a deep dissection without histologic confirmation.
learning_point: During staging inguinal lymphadenectomy for penile cancer, the decision to extend from a superficial (above fascia lata) to a deep (femoral triangle) dissection is based on frozen-section confirmation of metastasis in the superficial nodes. Primary tumor features determine who needs staging dissection, not its extent.
key_facts: Superficial dissection removes nodes superficial to the fascia lata; deep dissection adds nodes within the femoral triangle beneath it.
Deep nodal metastases essentially do not occur without positive superficial nodes.
Grade, stage, and lymphovascular invasion predict nodal risk and select patients for staging dissection.
Palpable nodes are malignant only about 40% of the time, so histologic confirmation guides extent.

question: A 31-year-old woman sustains a burst fracture at L1-L2 with a complete conus medullaris injury. Three months later, after spinal shock has resolved, videourodynamics are most likely to show:

options.B: voluntary control of the external sphincter.
options.D: an open bladder neck at rest.

rationale: A conus injury at the L1-L2 vertebral level destroys the sacral parasympathetic and somatic (pudendal) nuclei, so the detrusor is acontractile and voluntary control of the striated sphincter is lost. Because the thoracolumbar sympathetic outflow to the bladder neck is above the lesion and intact, the smooth sphincter remains closed and competent on fluoroscopy. Detrusor overactivity and striated sphincter dyssynergia characterize suprasacral injuries where the sacral reflex arc is preserved but disconnected from pontine control. An open bladder neck at rest is seen with sympathetic (thoracolumbar) injury or prior surgery, not an isolated conus lesion.
learning_point: A complete lesion of the sacral cord or conus (vertebral level L1-L2 or below) produces an areflexic, poorly contractile detrusor with loss of voluntary external sphincter control, but the sympathetically innervated bladder neck remains closed and competent. Detrusor overactivity and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia are features of suprasacral lesions.
key_facts: Sacral/conus injury: detrusor acontractility or hypocontractility, non-relaxing or weak striated sphincter, possible stress or overflow incontinence.
Bladder neck (smooth sphincter) competence is preserved because sympathetic outflow (T10-L2) is intact.
Suprasacral complete lesions cause detrusor overactivity, smooth sphincter synergy, and striated sphincter dyssynergia.

question: A 5-month-old girl had a febrile E. coli urinary tract infection at six weeks of age; renal and bladder ultrasound and fluoroscopic VCUG at that time were normal. She now presents with a second febrile UTI, and a repeat renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis or scarring. After treatment of the infection, the next step is:
rationale: Recurrent febrile UTI in infancy after a negative work-up should prompt a search for reflux that was missed on the first cystogram, since a single VCUG fails to demonstrate reflux in a substantial minority of children. A nuclear cystogram is sensitive, including for low-grade reflux, and exposes the child to less radiation than repeat fluoroscopy; the urethra has already been evaluated. Observation alone risks pyelonephritis and scarring in an infant. Prophylaxis without an identified anatomic abnormality is of debated value, a MAG-3 study adds little when two ultrasounds show no dilation, and a DMSA scan documents scarring but does not identify the cause of recurrent infection.
learning_point: A normal initial VCUG does not exclude vesicoureteral reflux, which may be missed on up to 30% of studies. An infant who has a second febrile UTI after a negative evaluation should have the VCUG repeated, preferably as a radionuclide cystogram, which is sensitive for reflux with less radiation.
key_facts: Initial febrile UTI in an infant boy: renal/bladder ultrasound and fluoroscopic VCUG (also assesses urethra).
A normal ultrasound does not rule out reflux; recurrence warrants repeat cystography.
Nuclear cystography has lower radiation and high sensitivity for low-grade reflux but does not show urethral anatomy.
Observation risks renal scarring; prophylaxis without a defined anomaly is of uncertain benefit.

question: A 15-year-old boy with 21-hydroxylase deficiency and inconsistent adherence to hydrocortisone has two months of bilateral testicular aching. Examination reveals firm, bilateral paratesticular-appearing masses, and ultrasound shows bilateral hypoechoic lesions adjacent to the mediastinum testis. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone and ACTH are markedly elevated. The next step is:
rationale: Bilateral hilar testicular masses in a boy with poorly controlled CAH and elevated ACTH are testicular adrenal rest tumors, which are hyperplastic adrenal tissue rather than germ cell neoplasms. Suppressing ACTH by increasing the glucocorticoid dose typically shrinks the lesions and relieves pain. Biopsy, testis-sparing excision, or orchiectomy are not indicated unless the masses fail to regress with optimized medical therapy. Scrotal MRI would not change management because the diagnosis is clinical in this setting.
learning_point: Bilateral testicular masses in a boy with congenital adrenal hyperplasia are testicular adrenal rest tumors (TART), caused by ACTH stimulation of ectopic adrenal tissue. Treatment is intensification of glucocorticoid therapy to suppress ACTH; biopsy or excision is reserved for failure of medical therapy.
key_facts: TART arise from aberrant adrenal rests that descend with the testes and enlarge under high ACTH, typically with poor disease control.
Lesions are usually bilateral, hilar, hypoechoic on ultrasound, and may cause pain or later infertility.
First-line management: increase glucocorticoid dose; surgery only if unresponsive.

question: A 29-year-old man finished salvage VeIP chemotherapy for a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor three weeks ago and reports fatigue and muscle cramps. He is normotensive and euvolemic. Serum sodium is 139 mEq/L, chloride 112 mEq/L, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L, potassium 2.9 mEq/L, and creatinine 1.0 mg/dL; arterial pH is 7.28. Urine pH is 7.0. The best treatment is:
rationale: The patient has a non-anion-gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia, and his urine remains alkaline despite systemic acidemia, demonstrating an inability to secrete hydrogen ions distally. This is a drug-induced distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis attributable to the ifosfamide in his regimen. Oral potassium citrate replaces the alkali and potassium deficits together and is the standard therapy. He is euvolemic with a normal creatinine, so intravenous saline or dextrose infusions are unnecessary and would not correct the underlying defect. Hydrocortisone and potassium-sparing diuretics have no role and could worsen the metabolic picture.
learning_point: Hypokalemic, hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis with an inappropriately alkaline urine after ifosfamide indicates acquired distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis. Treatment is oral alkali with potassium, such as potassium citrate; intravenous fluids, steroids, and diuretics are not indicated.
key_facts: Type 1 (distal) RTA: failure of distal H+ secretion, urine pH >5.5 despite systemic acidosis, hypokalemia, nephrocalcinosis risk.
Type 2 (proximal) RTA: bicarbonate wasting; urine can acidify below 5.5 once serum bicarbonate falls.
Ifosfamide causes tubular toxicity (distal RTA, Fanconi syndrome); cisplatin causes magnesium wasting.
Oral potassium citrate corrects both the acidosis and the hypokalemia.

question: An 8-year-old girl develops left flank pain and new hydronephrosis four months after a prolonged ureteroscopy for an impacted distal ureteral stone. Retrograde pyelography shows a 1.5 cm stricture of the distal ureter just above the ureterovesical junction. Renal function is preserved. The next step is:
rationale: A child with a benign distal ureteral stricture needs a reconstruction that will remain patent for decades, and ureteral reimplantation, with a psoas hitch if extra length is needed, achieves near-universal long-term success for distal strictures. Balloon dilation, endoureterotomy, and passive stenting have unpredictable and often temporary results and would commit a young patient to repeat procedures or lifelong stent exchanges. Ureteroureterostomy is not appropriate for a stricture at the ureterovesical junction, where the bladder is readily available for reimplantation.
learning_point: A distal ureteral stricture in a child requires durable, definitive repair because the patient must have lifelong success; ureteral reimplantation (with or without a psoas hitch) is the operation of choice. Endoscopic management (stenting, balloon dilation, endoureterotomy) has variable, non-durable results, and ureteroureterostomy is inappropriate so close to the bladder.
key_facts: Iatrogenic distal ureteral strictures after ureteroscopy are best managed by reimplantation in children.
Endoscopic incision or dilation has roughly 50-80% success in adults and is poorly durable over a lifetime.
Ureteroureterostomy is reserved for mid or proximal strictures where the bladder cannot be reached.

question: A 38-year-old woman has intermittent right flank pain 18 months after a right ureteral reimplantation with a Boari flap for a distal ureteral injury. CT demonstrates moderate right hydroureteronephrosis to the level of the bladder. A diuretic MAG-3 renogram, performed with a urethral catheter draining the bladder, shows a right T1/2 of 17 minutes and 42% differential function. The next step is:
rationale: A Boari flap reimplant is typically not tunneled, so vesicoureteral reflux is a common and expected cause of dilation and flank pain after this operation, and it can produce an indeterminate half-time on renography. A VCUG is a simple study that directly answers whether reflux is present and should be performed before invasive maneuvers. A Whitaker test is more invasive and is reserved for cases that remain unresolved after renography and cystography. Ureteroscopy, a retrograde pyelogram, a stent, or a nephrostomy tube may show anatomy or relieve dilation but do not distinguish reflux from functional obstruction.
learning_point: After a non-tunneled ureteral reimplant such as a Boari flap, hydronephrosis with an equivocal diuretic renogram half-time may be caused by vesicoureteral reflux rather than obstruction. A VCUG should be obtained before invasive testing or drainage, and future renograms should be done with a bladder catheter.
key_facts: Boari flap and many adult reimplants are refluxing; reflux causes upper tract dilation and prolongs T1/2 on MAG-3.
Equivocal T1/2 is roughly 10-20 minutes; a draining urethral catheter is required in refluxing patients to avoid false results.
Whitaker test is reserved for cases unresolved by renography; stents or nephrostomy tubes do not establish the diagnosis.

question: A 58-year-old woman with mixed incontinence underwent a retropubic midurethral sling four months ago; her stress leakage resolved but urgency and urgency incontinence have become markedly worse, with a slow, hesitant stream. Urinalysis is negative and PVR is 90 mL. Urodynamics show detrusor overactivity during filling, and during voiding a detrusor pressure at maximum flow of 42 cm H2O with a Qmax of 8 mL/s without EMG or fluoroscopy. The most likely explanation for her symptoms is:

options.B: bladder outlet obstruction from the sling.

rationale: Worsening of storage symptoms immediately after a sling, combined with a high detrusor voiding pressure and a low flow rate, is the classic picture of sling-induced bladder outlet obstruction. Female pressure-flow values in this range meet most proposed definitions of female obstruction even though they might fall in an equivocal zone on male nomograms. Progression of her underlying overactive bladder is far less likely given the abrupt temporal association and the obstructed voiding pattern. Pelvic floor dysfunction cannot be diagnosed without EMG or fluoroscopic imaging of the outlet during voiding, infection is excluded by the urinalysis, and mesh erosion is unlikely with a normal urinalysis, though cystoscopy should precede any sling incision.
learning_point: New or worsened urgency symptoms soon after a midurethral sling with a pressure-flow study showing elevated detrusor pressure and low flow indicate sling-related bladder outlet obstruction. Male-derived nomograms underestimate obstruction in women, who normally void at low pressures; a Qmax of 12 mL/s or less with Pdet above 25 cm H2O is a commonly used definition.
key_facts: Temporal relation to sling placement plus high-pressure/low-flow voiding supports obstruction.
Female obstruction thresholds: Qmax <= 12 mL/s with Pdet@Qmax > 25 cm H2O (various definitions).
Pelvic floor voiding dysfunction cannot be diagnosed without EMG or fluoroscopy during voiding.
Mesh erosion is unlikely with a normal urinalysis, but cystoscopy is mandatory before sling incision.

question: A 34-year-old woman is re-explored 48 hours after damage-control laparotomy for a high-velocity gunshot wound to the pelvis. A 1 cm area of ecchymosis is noted on the distal left ureter without visible laceration, and intravenous methylene blue shows no extravasation. The ureter appears viable. The next step is:
rationale: A small contusion of a viable ureter without urine leak is best managed by internal stenting, which maintains drainage and supports the segment while it heals, reducing the risk of delayed obstruction or stricture from blast injury. Observation risks unrecognized obstruction or late necrosis. Ureteroneocystostomy is reserved for distal injuries with significant devitalized tissue or a large contusion, and ureteroureterostomy is not appropriate for the distal ureter. Wrapping with omentum or placing a drain without stenting does not protect the lumen, and a nephrostomy alone diverts urine but leaves the contused segment unstented.
learning_point: A minor ureteral contusion found at exploration, with no devitalized tissue and no extravasation, is managed with ureteral stenting to prevent delayed stricture or necrosis; observation alone risks obstruction. Large contusions or devitalized distal ureter from high-velocity injury require reimplantation.
key_facts: High-velocity gunshot wounds cause blast injury with delayed necrosis; contused segments should be stented.
Distal ureteral injuries requiring repair are managed by ureteroneocystostomy, not ureteroureterostomy.
Nephrostomy diverts urine but does not protect the contused segment from stricture.
Ureteral injuries are often missed at the initial laparotomy and recognized at re-exploration.

question: A 26-year-old man undergoes right radical orchiectomy for a 4 cm pT2 mixed germ cell tumor. CT shows a 3 cm interaortocaval lymph node and no other disease. Pre-orchiectomy AFP was 6,500 ng/mL with normal hCG and LDH; three weeks after orchiectomy AFP is 4,200 ng/mL, hCG remains normal, and LDH is normal. The next step is:

options.C: four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin.

rationale: The patient has clinical stage II disease by anatomy but S2 markers because his post-orchiectomy AFP has not fallen appropriately and remains between 1,000 and 10,000 ng/mL, which makes this stage IIIB, intermediate-risk NSGCT by IGCCCG criteria. Intermediate-risk patients should receive four cycles of BEP. Three cycles of BEP or four cycles of EP are good-risk regimens and would undertreat him, while VIP is reserved for intermediate or poor-risk patients with a contraindication to bleomycin. Primary RPLND is contraindicated when serum markers are persistently elevated because systemic disease is present.
learning_point: In metastatic NSGCT, the IGCCCG risk group is assigned from post-orchiectomy markers (at the start of chemotherapy); an AFP between 1,000 and 10,000 ng/mL (S2) places a patient with retroperitoneal disease in the intermediate-risk group, which is treated with four cycles of BEP. Three cycles of BEP or four cycles of EP are reserved for good-risk disease, and RPLND is not performed with elevated markers.
key_facts: IGCCCG good risk: testis/retroperitoneal primary, no non-pulmonary visceral metastases, S0-S1 markers.
Intermediate risk: same anatomy but S2 markers (AFP 1,000-10,000, hCG 5,000-50,000, LDH 1.5-10x ULN).
Good risk: BEP x3 or EP x4; intermediate/poor risk: BEP x4 (or VIP x4 if bleomycin contraindicated).
AFP half-life is 5-7 days; failure to decline appropriately post-orchiectomy indicates residual disease.

question: A 52-year-old woman with recurrent calcium oxalate stones takes chlorthalidone 25 mg daily for hypercalciuria and vitamin D3 800 IU daily for a prior low 25-hydroxyvitamin D level. Routine labs show serum calcium 10.9 mg/dL, phosphorus 3.4 mg/dL, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, and a PTH within the normal range. After potassium repletion, the next step is:
rationale: Mild hypercalcemia accompanied by hypokalemia, a normal phosphorus, and a non-suppressed, normal PTH in a patient on a thiazide-type diuretic is thiazide-induced hypercalcemia, which responds to dose reduction. Her low-dose vitamin D replacement is unlikely to be responsible; vitamin D excess would suppress PTH and would not cause hypokalemia. Primary hyperparathyroidism typically shows a frankly elevated PTH with low phosphorus, so parathyroidectomy is not indicated. Dietary calcium restriction increases oxalate absorption and stone risk, and potassium citrate corrects hypocitraturia but does not address serum calcium. Exchanging one thiazide for another at an equivalent dose would not resolve the problem.
learning_point: Hypercalcemia with a normal PTH, normal phosphorus, and hypokalemia in a stone former taking a thiazide is thiazide-induced hypercalcemia; the treatment is to reduce the thiazide dose. Vitamin D excess causes a suppressed PTH, and switching between thiazide-type diuretics without reducing the dose does not help.
key_facts: Thiazides increase distal tubular calcium reabsorption; hypercalcemia with normal PTH, low urinary calcium, and hypokalemia suggests thiazide effect.
Primary hyperparathyroidism: elevated or inappropriately normal PTH with low phosphorus.
Vitamin D intoxication, sarcoidosis, TB: suppressed PTH, no hypokalemia.
Potassium citrate treats thiazide-induced hypocitraturia and hypokalemia but does not lower serum calcium.

question: A 9-month-old boy is referred for a right testis that has never been palpable, including under anesthesia-free examination in a warm room. The left testis is descended and measures 1.4 cm in length. The next step is:

options.E: MRI of the abdomen and pelvis.

rationale: A nonpalpable testis with a contralateral testis of normal size implies that the missing gonad is probably present in the abdomen, so diagnostic laparoscopy is indicated to locate it and proceed with orchiopexy or to document blind-ending vessels. Ultrasound and MRI frequently miss intra-abdominal testes and would not spare the child surgery, so they add cost without changing management. Primary scrotal exploration is reasonable only when the contralateral testis is hypertrophied, suggesting a vanished testis with vessels in the canal. Waiting until 18 months delays recommended treatment, and hormonal therapy has low efficacy.
learning_point: An infant with a nonpalpable testis and a normal-sized (non-hypertrophied) contralateral testis most likely has a viable intra-abdominal testis, and diagnostic laparoscopy is the next step. Imaging does not reliably exclude an intra-abdominal testis and does not obviate surgical exploration, and hormonal therapy is ineffective.
key_facts: Contralateral hypertrophy (>2 cm length prepubertally) suggests a vanished testis but is neither sensitive nor specific.
Ultrasound, CT, and MRI have poor sensitivity for intra-abdominal testes and do not change the need for exploration.
Laparoscopy identifies an intra-abdominal testis, blind-ending vessels (vanished testis), or vessels entering the inguinal canal.
Orchiopexy is recommended between 6 and 18 months of age.

question: A 61-year-old man with long-standing gout has taken allopurinol 300 mg daily for eight years with a serum uric acid in the normal range. He passes a 4 mm stone. If this is a pure stone, its most likely composition is:
rationale: Gout patients are commonly assumed to form uric acid stones, but even untreated they form calcium oxalate monohydrate stones nearly as often, and effective allopurinol therapy substantially reduces uric acid stone formation. In treated patients, calcium oxalate monohydrate therefore becomes the most common pure stone composition. Xanthine stones can occur with xanthine oxidase inhibition but are rare. Calcium phosphate and sodium urate stones are not characteristic of treated gout, and calcium oxalate dihydrate is more typical of hypercalciuria than of gout.
learning_point: Patients with gout form uric acid and calcium oxalate monohydrate stones in roughly equal proportions; once treated with allopurinol, uric acid stone risk falls and calcium oxalate monohydrate becomes the most common pure composition. Stone type should be confirmed rather than assumed before starting alkalinization.
key_facts: Untreated gout: approximately 52% uric acid and 45% calcium oxalate monohydrate stones.
Allopurinol lowers uric acid stone prevalence to about 30%, leaving calcium oxalate monohydrate most common.
Xanthine stones are a rare complication of xanthine oxidase inhibition.
Calcium oxalate dihydrate is more typical of hypercalciuric stone formers.

question: A 71-year-old man treated with radical prostatectomy and later salvage radiation has been on leuprolide for biochemical recurrence. His PSA has risen from 1.8 ng/mL to 4.1 ng/mL over four months while serum testosterone is 18 ng/dL. Bone scan, CT, and PSMA PET show no metastatic disease. The next step is to continue androgen deprivation and add:
rationale: A rising PSA with castrate-level testosterone and negative imaging defines non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, and his PSA doubling time is well under 10 months. Randomized trials demonstrated that enzalutamide, apalutamide, or darolutamide added to ongoing androgen deprivation significantly delays metastasis in this setting, and guidelines recommend one of these agents. Docetaxel and abiraterone are indicated for metastatic disease, radium-223 requires symptomatic bone metastases, and sipuleucel-T is for asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic metastatic castration-resistant disease.
learning_point: Non-metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (rising PSA with castrate testosterone and negative imaging), especially with a PSA doubling time under 10 months, is treated with a next-generation androgen receptor antagonist (enzalutamide, apalutamide, or darolutamide), which prolongs metastasis-free survival. Abiraterone, docetaxel, sipuleucel-T, and radium-223 are indicated for metastatic disease.
key_facts: PROSPER (enzalutamide), SPARTAN (apalutamide), and ARAMIS (darolutamide) enrolled nmCRPC with PSADT < 10 months.
AUA/NCCN recommend AR antagonists for nmCRPC with PSADT <= 10 months; observation remains an option for long PSADT.
Pembrolizumab requires MSI-high/dMMR tumors; sipuleucel-T is for asymptomatic mCRPC.
Abiraterone and docetaxel are approved in metastatic hormone-sensitive and metastatic castration-resistant settings.

question: A 22-year-old otherwise healthy man is told by a new partner that his erect penis bends noticeably to the left and downward. He has no pain, has never sustained a penile injury, and in retrospect believes it has always looked this way. Examination shows a normally positioned meatus and no palpable induration along the shaft; a photograph of the erection shows a smooth 40-degree ventrolateral arc. The most likely diagnosis is:
rationale: The combination of youth, a lifelong smooth curve without a plaque, absence of pain or trauma, and recognition only after a partner's comment is classic for congenital penile curvature, also termed chordee without hypospadias. Peyronie's disease occurs in older men and produces a palpable plaque with pain and a changing curvature during the active phase. Penile fracture or acquired curvature requires a history of injury, which is absent. The meatus is normally positioned, excluding hypospadias with chordee, and there is no history of priapism to cause corporal fibrosis.
learning_point: A young, healthy man who presents with a smooth lateral or ventral curvature first noticed when he became sexually active, without trauma, pain, or a palpable plaque, has congenital penile curvature (chordee without hypospadias). Peyronie's disease occurs in older men with a plaque and progressive, often painful curvature; intralesional therapy has no role in congenital curvature.
key_facts: Congenital curvature: present since puberty, smooth arc, no plaque, usually ventral or left-lateral; patients age 18-30 at presentation.
Caused by corporal disproportion; treated by plication when bothersome.
Peyronie's: fibrous tunical plaque, pain in acute phase, older men, change in curvature over time.
Acquired curvature after trauma or penile fracture is associated with a history of injury.

question: A 34-year-old lineman sustains a high-voltage electrical injury with a contact point on the penis. Six hours later the penile shaft skin is erythematous with blistering and patchy superficial sloughing extending onto the glans; he has not voided. The next step is:
rationale: High-voltage electrical injury to the penis is almost always deeper than it first appears, and tissue including the urethra may necrose over the following days. Placing a suprapubic tube provides reliable bladder drainage while avoiding passage of a catheter through a potentially injured urethra, and it can remain for the prolonged period often required. Urethral catheterization, cystoscopy, and retrograde urethrography risk further urethral damage and provide little useful information this early. Debridement should wait until viable and nonviable tissue have demarcated.
learning_point: Electrical or deep thermal burns of the penis evolve over days, often becoming full thickness with sloughing of skin and urethra. Initial management is conservative with suprapubic urinary diversion until the extent of injury is clear; urethral catheterization, instrumentation, contrast studies, and early debridement are avoided.
key_facts: Genital burns are frequently full thickness; the final depth is not apparent for several days.
Suprapubic tube avoids additional urethral trauma and allows prolonged drainage.
Debridement is deferred until demarcation of nonviable tissue.
Retrograde urethrogram in the first hours adds nothing and risks further injury.

question: A 61-year-old man undergoes CT for diverticulitis, which incidentally shows a 3 cm left interpolar renal cyst measuring 12 HU with a smooth, hairline-thin wall, two thin septa containing fine calcification, and no measurable enhancement of the wall or septa on the post-contrast phase. The next step is:
rationale: A cyst with a thin smooth wall and a few thin septa that may contain fine calcification, none of which enhance, is a Bosniak II lesion. These are benign, and neither surveillance imaging nor intervention is recommended. Follow-up CT or MRI at six and twelve months applies to Bosniak IIF cysts, which have more numerous or minimally thickened septa. Percutaneous biopsy of a purely cystic lesion is frequently non-diagnostic and unnecessary here, and surgery is reserved for Bosniak III and IV lesions with enhancing components.
learning_point: A renal cyst with thin smooth walls, a few thin non-enhancing septa, and fine calcification is Bosniak II, which is considered benign and requires neither follow-up imaging nor biopsy. Surveillance is reserved for Bosniak IIF lesions, and intervention for III and IV.
key_facts: Bosniak I: hairline wall, water density, no septa or calcification; II: few thin septa, fine calcification, or homogeneous hyperdense <3 cm, all non-enhancing.
IIF: minimally thickened wall/septa or many hairline septa; imaging follow-up at 6 and 12 months, then yearly.
III: thickened or irregular enhancing walls/septa; IV: enhancing soft-tissue nodule.
Biopsy of a cystic lesion without a solid component is low yield.

question: A 61-year-old woman who underwent a transobturator midurethral sling eight years ago has had eight months of recurrent leakage with coughing and lifting. Examination demonstrates stress leakage with minimal urethral mobility on cotton swab testing. Urinalysis is normal, PVR is 20 mL, and there is no mesh exposure. She wants the most durable option. The best treatment is:
rationale: For recurrent stress incontinence after a prior sling, a repeat midurethral sling placed through the retropubic route provides better cure rates than a transobturator sling, probably because it offers more support to a poorly mobile urethra; an autologous fascial sling would be an equally appropriate alternative. Bulking agents and single-incision mini-slings are less durable and less effective in the salvage setting. Retropubic bladder neck suspensions have been superseded by slings, and the artificial urinary sphincter is not an appropriate choice for this woman.
learning_point: Recurrent stress urinary incontinence years after a midurethral sling, particularly with a fixed or minimally mobile urethra, is best treated with a repeat sling via the retropubic route (or an autologous fascial sling), which outperforms the transobturator approach in this setting. Bulking agents are less durable, and bladder neck suspension and artificial sphincter are not preferred.
key_facts: Repeat retropubic MUS has higher cure rates than transobturator MUS for recurrent SUI, especially with limited urethral mobility.
Autologous pubovaginal fascial sling is an equally acceptable option.
Bulking agents give lower subjective improvement and durability.
Artificial urinary sphincter is rarely used in women and is not first-line for recurrent SUI.

question: A 34-year-old woman has gained 12 kg over the past year and has new hypertension, facial plethora, proximal muscle weakness, and wide purple striae on the abdomen. CT performed for abdominal pain shows a homogeneous 2 cm right adrenal nodule. The next step is:

options.E: MRI of the abdomen with chemical shift imaging.

rationale: Her weight gain, hypertension, plethora, myopathy, and striae strongly suggest Cushing's syndrome, and the adrenal nodule is a potential source, so the first step is to document hypercortisolism biochemically; the overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test is a guideline-endorsed screening test. Pituitary MRI is reserved for confirmed ACTH-dependent disease and would be premature. Chemical-shift MRI characterizes lipid content but cannot determine whether the mass is functional. Adrenal biopsy does not distinguish adenoma from carcinoma, carries risk, and should never precede hormonal evaluation. Plasma metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, which does not fit this presentation.
learning_point: A patient with clinical features of hypercortisolism and an adrenal mass should first undergo a biochemical screening test for Cushing's syndrome, such as the overnight 1 mg (low-dose) dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, or late-night salivary cortisol. Brain MRI, adrenal biopsy, and further anatomic imaging are not appropriate before hypercortisolism is confirmed.
key_facts: Screening tests: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, 24-h urinary free cortisol (x2), late-night salivary cortisol.
Urinary 17-ketosteroids are not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome.
Pituitary MRI is pursued only after ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism is established.
Adrenal biopsy cannot distinguish adenoma from carcinoma and should follow metabolic evaluation.

question: Six weeks after SWL of a 1.8 cm left renal pelvic stone, a 47-year-old woman remains asymptomatic but a CT shows a 2.5 cm column of fragments in the distal left ureter with mild hydronephrosis unchanged from four weeks earlier. She has taken tamsulosin throughout. The best treatment is:

options.C: repeat SWL of the leading fragment.

rationale: Expectant management has already been tried for six weeks with medical expulsive therapy and has failed, so intervention is indicated to prevent prolonged obstruction. Ureteroscopy with laser fragmentation of the column is definitive, with immediate success approaching 100%. Repeating SWL on the lead fragment can work but is far less predictable. A ureteral stent alone or a nephrostomy tube relieves obstruction without clearing the fragments, and antegrade ureteroscopy is reserved for salvage when retrograde access fails.
learning_point: An asymptomatic steinstrasse after SWL may initially be observed, but fragments that persist beyond several weeks require intervention, and ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy is the most definitive and predictable treatment. Repeat SWL of the lead fragment is less reliable, and a stent alone does not clear the column.
key_facts: Steinstrasse: column of fragments in the ureter after SWL, most often distal; many clear spontaneously.
Alpha-blockers can support expectant management and symptom control.
Indications for intervention: persistence, pain, infection, obstruction with functional loss.
Ureteroscopy achieves near 100% immediate clearance; antegrade (percutaneous) ureteroscopy is a salvage approach.

question: A 17-year-old boy develops painless cola-colored urine three days after the onset of a sore throat for which he is taking penicillin. Blood pressure is 148/88 mmHg, temperature 38.3 C, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein with dysmorphic red cells. Renal ultrasound is normal. Kidney biopsy reveals mesangial hypercellularity with cellular crescents in several glomeruli. The most likely diagnosis is:
rationale: Hematuria appearing within days of a pharyngitis in a teenage male, together with hypertension, acute renal impairment, and a biopsy showing mesangial proliferation with crescents, is characteristic of IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease); immunofluorescence would show mesangial IgA. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis typically follows the infection by one to three weeks rather than coinciding with it and shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation. Minimal change disease causes nephrotic syndrome with essentially normal light microscopy. Alport syndrome is a hereditary nephritis with hearing loss and basement membrane changes, and membranoproliferative GN is a chronic, insidious disorder usually found on screening.
learning_point: Gross hematuria with hypertension and acute kidney injury during or immediately after an upper respiratory infection in an adolescent male, with mesangial proliferation and crescents on biopsy, is IgA nephropathy. Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis presents 1-3 weeks after the infection with diffuse proliferation, and nephrotic syndromes present with edema and heavy proteinuria.
key_facts: IgA nephropathy: most common primary GN; peaks in second and third decades, male predominance; hematuria synchronous with URI.
Immunofluorescence shows mesangial IgA deposits; crescents indicate aggressive disease.
Post-infectious GN: latent period of 7-21 days after streptococcal pharyngitis, low complement.
Minimal change disease: nephrotic proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, normal glomeruli on light microscopy.

question: An 81-year-old woman has had an indwelling urethral catheter since a low anterior resection six days ago and is scheduled for catheter removal and a voiding trial. She has no urinary symptoms and no drug allergies. The most appropriate antimicrobial at the time of catheter removal is:
rationale: Her advanced age is a recognized risk factor that justifies antimicrobial prophylaxis when a postoperative urethral catheter is removed, since this reduces bacteriuria and symptomatic infection. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (or a fluoroquinolone) is the recommended agent. Withholding prophylaxis would be reasonable in a young patient without risk factors but not here. Amoxicillin has poor gram-negative coverage, nitrofurantoin is not listed as an agent of choice for this indication, and an aminoglycoside is a parenteral alternative reserved for when first-line oral agents cannot be used.
learning_point: Antimicrobial prophylaxis at removal of an indwelling urethral catheter is recommended for patients with risk factors such as advanced age, and the agents of choice are trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or a fluoroquinolone. Amoxicillin, first-generation cephalosporins, and aminoglycosides are not preferred for this indication.
key_facts: AUA Best Practice: prophylaxis at catheter removal benefits patients with risk factors (older age, anatomic anomalies, steroids, smoking, poor nutrition).
Preferred agents: TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolone; alternatives include an aminoglycoside with/without ampicillin only when needed.
Evidence suggests reduced bacteriuria with antibiotics around catheter removal in postoperative patients.

question: A 49-year-old man with three calcium oxalate stones in five years has a 24-hour urine showing volume 2.1 L, calcium 165 mg (normal <200), oxalate 44 mg (normal <40), citrate 600 mg (normal >550), sodium 160 mEq (normal <150), and uric acid 950 mg (normal <800). Serum uric acid is normal. The intervention most likely to reduce stone recurrence is:
rationale: The only substantial metabolic abnormality is hyperuricosuria with a normal urinary calcium, the exact population in which a randomized trial showed allopurinol reduces calcium oxalate stone recurrence, and the AUA guideline recommends it regardless of serum uric acid. A thiazide is appropriate for hypercalciuria, which is absent, and potassium citrate is indicated for hypocitraturia, but his citrate is normal. The oxalate excretion is only marginally elevated, so dietary oxalate restriction would have limited effect, and pyridoxine is used for primary hyperoxaluria. Sodium restriction primarily helps hypercalciuric patients.
learning_point: In recurrent calcium oxalate stone formers with hyperuricosuria (urinary uric acid >800 mg/day) and normal urinary calcium, allopurinol is the guideline-recommended therapy and has randomized-trial evidence of reducing recurrence. Thiazides, low-sodium diets, and potassium citrate target hypercalciuria or hypocitraturia, which are absent here.
key_facts: AUA guideline: offer allopurinol for recurrent CaOx stones with hyperuricosuria and normocalciuria.
Hyperuricemia is not required; urinary uric acid drives the indication.
Low non-dairy animal protein intake augments the effect.
Mild hyperoxaluria responds little to dietary oxalate restriction alone.

question: A 48-year-old man started trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for bacterial prostatitis 12 days ago. He now has fever, malaise, painful erosions of the lips and buccal mucosa, bilateral conjunctival injection, and a spreading dusky red macular rash with early epidermal detachment on the trunk. The next step is:

options.A: drug withdrawal and supportive skin care.

rationale: This presentation is Stevens-Johnson syndrome triggered by a sulfonamide antibiotic, a severe mucocutaneous drug reaction. The cornerstone of treatment is immediate discontinuation of the responsible drug with supportive care directed at the skin and mucosa, fluid and electrolyte balance, analgesia, and nutrition, with transfer to a burn unit if detachment is extensive. There is no strong evidence that corticosteroids, antihistamines, antivirals, or empiric antibiotics improve outcomes, and some may add harm or infection risk. Antivirals and vancomycin address diagnoses (herpes, bacterial infection) that are not present.
learning_point: Fever, a dusky macular rash, mucosal erosions, and conjunctival involvement one to three weeks after starting a sulfonamide indicate Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Management is withdrawal of the offending drug and supportive care (wound care, fluids, analgesia, nutrition, burn-unit care if extensive); no specific drug therapy, including corticosteroids, antihistamines, antivirals, or antibiotics, has strong evidence.
key_facts: Common triggers: sulfonamides, anticonvulsants, allopurinol, NSAIDs.
Onset typically 1-3 weeks after drug initiation.
Treatment: stop culprit drug, skin and mucosal care, fluids, pain control, nutrition; burn unit for extensive involvement.
Steroids, IVIG, and other systemic agents lack convincing evidence.

question: A 51-year-old man sustained a penile fracture that was surgically repaired 14 months ago. He now has a stable 55-degree dorsal curvature causing difficulty with intercourse, confirmed after intracavernosal injection, with a soft, non-calcified dorsal plaque in the mid shaft and good rigidity. He wishes to avoid surgery. The next step is:
rationale: He has stable Peyronie's disease with a dorsal curvature in the 30-90 degree range, preserved erections, and a soft mid-shaft plaque, fulfilling the criteria for intralesional collagenase, the only FDA-approved intralesional agent with randomized evidence of curvature improvement. Verapamil is used off-label and is not first-line. Shock wave therapy can relieve pain but has not been shown to correct curvature, and observation will not improve an established deformity. Plication is effective but is a surgical option reserved for men who fail or decline less invasive treatment.
learning_point: Stable Peyronie's disease with dorsal curvature between 30 and 90 degrees, intact erectile function, and no hourglass deformity or calcified plaque is appropriate for intralesional collagenase clostridium histolyticum. Verapamil is off-label, ESWT only helps pain, stem cells are experimental, and surgery follows failure of less invasive therapy.
key_facts: Collagenase criteria: stable disease, dorsal or lateral curvature 30-90 degrees, no ventral curve, no hourglass, no calcified plaque, no plaque at base.
Intralesional verapamil or interferon are alternatives but less well supported.
ESWT may reduce pain but does not reduce curvature.
Plication or grafting is reserved for failed conservative therapy or curvature >90 degrees.

question: A 70-year-old woman with an eGFR of 42 mL/min/1.73 m2 is scheduled for cystectomy with a sigmoid colon conduit. If a mechanical bowel preparation is to be given, the most appropriate agent is:
rationale: Polyethylene glycol electrolyte lavage solutions are isosmotic and essentially unabsorbed, so they do not alter serum electrolytes or renal function and are the preparation of choice in older patients and those with chronic kidney disease. Sodium phosphate preparations can cause acute phosphate nephropathy and should be avoided in renal insufficiency. Magnesium citrate and picosulfate/magnesium citrate carry a risk of magnesium absorption and hypermagnesemia when renal clearance is impaired. Sodium sulfate-based preparations are hyperosmotic cathartics that cause fluid shifts and are less suitable than PEG in this setting.
learning_point: When mechanical bowel preparation is used before colon conduit surgery in elderly patients or those with renal insufficiency, polyethylene glycol lavage is preferred because it is not absorbed. Sodium phosphate and magnesium-based cathartics risk phosphate or magnesium absorption and can precipitate further renal injury.
key_facts: PEG lavage is isosmotic and non-absorbable; safe in CKD and the elderly.
Sodium phosphate can cause acute phosphate nephropathy and irreversible renal failure.
Magnesium citrate and picosulfate/magnesium citrate risk hypermagnesemia in CKD.
Routine mechanical bowel prep is likely unnecessary for small bowel diversions.

question: A 24-year-old woman has had four culture-proven E. coli cystitis episodes in the past year, each occurring within two days of intercourse. In reviewing her history, the factor most strongly associated with post-coital E. coli bacteriuria is:

options.C: partner use of a non-lubricated condom.
options.D: use of a combined oral contraceptive.

rationale: Spermicidal products, including spermicide-coated condoms and diaphragm jelly, markedly alter the vaginal flora by killing lactobacilli, which allows E. coli to colonize the introitus and ascend into the bladder after intercourse; spermicide use is one of the most consistently identified risk factors for recurrent UTI in young women. The phase of the menstrual cycle has not been shown to affect post-coital bacteriuria. Oral contraceptives, condoms without spermicide, and intrauterine devices are not established risk factors.
learning_point: Spermicide use (alone or with a diaphragm or condom) is a strong risk factor for post-coital E. coli vaginal colonization and bacteriuria because nonoxynol-9 disrupts the protective lactobacillus flora. Menstrual cycle phase, oral contraceptives, and partner condom use without spermicide do not increase risk.
key_facts: Spermicides reduce vaginal lactobacilli and raise vaginal pH, promoting E. coli colonization.
Risk factors for recurrent UTI in young women: intercourse frequency, spermicide use, new partner, maternal history, first UTI at young age.
Counseling to switch contraceptive method is a first-line preventive strategy.

question: A 68-year-old woman admitted with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is found to have a 1.8 cm right renal stone on CT. Serum calcium is 12.4 mg/dL, phosphorus is low, and urine culture grows E. coli. The most likely mechanism of her stone formation is:

options.C: ectopic production of parathyroid hormone-related peptide.

rationale: Squamous cell lung cancer is a classic source of parathyroid hormone-related peptide, which mimics PTH to produce hypercalcemia and hypophosphatemia and leads to hypercalciuria and calcium stone formation. Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs in response to low calcium and does not produce hypercalcemia. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the leading cause of outpatient hypercalcemia but is less likely than malignancy in a hospitalized cancer patient. E. coli lacks urease, so an infection stone is not explained by this organism, and nothing in the presentation suggests renal tubular acidosis.
learning_point: Hypercalcemia in a hospitalized patient with squamous cell lung cancer is most often humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy from ectopic parathyroid hormone-related peptide, which drives hypercalciuria and calcium stone formation. E. coli does not produce urease and does not cause infection stones.
key_facts: PTHrP shares N-terminal homology with PTH and is produced by squamous lung, breast, and renal carcinomas.
Malignancy is the leading cause of hypercalcemia in inpatients; primary hyperparathyroidism leads in outpatients.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism occurs with low or normal calcium, not hypercalcemia.
Struvite stones require urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella, some Pseudomonas), not E. coli.

question: A 58-year-old woman has two solid left renal masses measuring 2.5 cm and 3.5 cm on CT, together with bulky retroperitoneal, mesenteric, and bilateral iliac lymphadenopathy, the largest node 6 cm. Chest CT is negative and the right kidney is normal; eGFR is 61 mL/min/1.73 m2. The next step is:

options.B: radical nephrectomy with retroperitoneal lymph node dissection.
options.E: percutaneous biopsy of a renal mass or lymph node.

rationale: Lymphadenopathy that is far larger than the renal lesions and extends to mesenteric and pelvic nodes outside the kidney's normal lymphatic drainage, in combination with multiple renal masses, is suspicious for lymphoma rather than renal cell carcinoma. Percutaneous biopsy establishes the diagnosis and, if lymphoma is confirmed, directs the patient to systemic chemotherapy rather than surgery. Nephrectomy or ablation would be inappropriate and ineffective for lymphoma, and biopsy is in any case recommended before ablation. Immunotherapy or targeted therapy for metastatic RCC should not be started without a tissue diagnosis.
learning_point: Multiple renal masses with bulky lymphadenopathy out of proportion to the masses and outside the kidney's expected landing zones should raise suspicion for lymphoma, and the next step is percutaneous biopsy. AUA guidelines recommend biopsy when a mass may be hematologic, metastatic, inflammatory, or infectious, and before ablation.
key_facts: Renal lymphoma: often multiple bilateral masses, bulky retroperitoneal adenopathy, treated with systemic chemotherapy.
Right kidney drains to hilar, paracaval, and interaortocaval nodes; left to hilar, para-aortic, and pre-aortic nodes.
Biopsy is recommended before ablation and whenever non-RCC pathology is suspected.
Systemic immunotherapy for RCC requires histologic confirmation.

question: A 77-year-old man who received external beam radiation for prostate cancer six years ago and a channel TURP for retention two years ago has frequent urge-associated leakage. Urinalysis is normal and PVR is 35 mL. Urodynamics show phasic detrusor contractions beginning at 110 mL that reach 45 cm H2O and are accompanied by leakage; there is no leakage with Valsalva to 150 cm H2O, compliance is normal, and he voids with a sustained contraction to completion. The next step is:
rationale: The tracing demonstrates detrusor overactivity with associated leakage and no stress incontinence despite high abdominal pressures, so the problem is urgency incontinence rather than sphincteric deficiency. Oral therapy with an antimuscarinic such as solifenacin (or a beta-3 agonist), alongside behavioral measures, is the appropriate next step and may give rapid relief for frequent low-volume contractions. OnabotulinumtoxinA is third-line therapy for refractory overactivity. A male sling, bulking agent, or artificial sphincter would address stress incontinence, which he does not have, and an alpha-blocker treats outlet obstruction rather than detrusor overactivity.
learning_point: Post-radiation, post-TURP incontinence with urodynamics showing detrusor overactivity and no stress incontinence is urgency incontinence, treated with an antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist (after behavioral therapy). Slings and artificial sphincters treat sphincteric incontinence and are not indicated without demonstrated stress leakage.
key_facts: Urodynamics distinguish urgency incontinence (detrusor overactivity) from stress incontinence (leak with Valsalva/cough, no detrusor contraction).
First line: behavioral therapy; second line: antimuscarinic or beta-3 agonist; third line: onabotulinumtoxinA or neuromodulation.
Male sling and AUS are reserved for sphincteric deficiency.
Alpha-blockers treat obstructive voiding symptoms, not detrusor overactivity.

question: A 4-year-old boy with a febrile urinary tract infection has a VCUG showing a solitary 2 cm outpouching adjacent to the left ureteral orifice in a smooth-walled bladder with a normal urethra. Congenital paraureteral diverticula of this type are most frequently:
rationale: A congenital paraureteral diverticulum develops from an inherent muscular weakness at the ureteral hiatus in a bladder without trabeculation or obstruction. As it enlarges it tends to incorporate the intravesical ureter, and vesicoureteral reflux is the most frequent association. These diverticula are not secondary to posterior urethral valves or other outlet obstruction, which produce multiple diverticula in a trabeculated bladder. They are more common in boys than girls, and the gold standard for diagnosis is voiding cystourethrography rather than cystoscopy.
learning_point: Congenital paraureteral (Hutch) diverticula arise from a weakness in the detrusor at the ureteral hiatus in an otherwise smooth, unobstructed bladder, occur mostly in boys, and are most commonly associated with vesicoureteral reflux as the ureter is incorporated into the diverticulum. VCUG is the diagnostic study of choice.
key_facts: Congenital diverticula are usually solitary, lateral to the ureteral orifice, without outlet obstruction or trabeculation.
Enlargement can engulf the ureteral tunnel, causing reflux or occasionally obstruction.
More common in boys; girls more often show spontaneous resolution with their reflux.
VCUG, not cystoscopy, is the gold standard for detection.

question: A 64-year-old man is undergoing robot-assisted radical prostatectomy in 25-degree Trendelenburg with CO2 insufflation at 15 mmHg. Compared with his pre-insufflation supine baseline, the expected physiologic change is:
rationale: Carbon dioxide is absorbed across the peritoneum at insufflation pressures of 10 mmHg or greater, so arterial CO2 rises unless ventilation is increased. Trendelenburg positioning augments venous return, which increases central venous pressure, cardiac output, and mean arterial pressure while lowering systemic vascular resistance and heart rate. Cardiac output falls only when intra-abdominal pressure exceeds about 20 mmHg and impedes venous return. Thus decreased MAP, increased SVR, decreased cardiac output, and decreased CVP are all opposite to the expected changes at 15 mmHg in head-down position.
learning_point: With CO2 pneumoperitoneum at 10-15 mmHg in steep Trendelenburg, arterial CO2 rises from peritoneal absorption while cardiac output and mean arterial pressure increase and systemic vascular resistance falls; heart rate decreases. Cardiac output falls only when insufflation pressure exceeds about 20 mmHg.
key_facts: Supine pneumoperitoneum <15 mmHg: CO unchanged or slightly down, MAP and SVR up.
Trendelenburg: increased venous return, higher CO and MAP, lower SVR and heart rate.
PaCO2 rises at insufflation pressures of 10 mmHg or more; minimal change at 5 mmHg.
Pressures above 20-30 mmHg reduce venous return and cardiac output.

question: A resident is asked to perform duplex ultrasonography of the penis after intracavernosal injection. Duplex ultrasonography combines:

options.A: color flow and power Doppler imaging.
options.C: two transducer frequencies for depth penetration.

rationale: Duplex refers to the simultaneous use of two modes: gray-scale B-mode imaging, which shows tissue architecture and allows vessel identification, and Doppler, which quantifies blood flow velocity and direction. Combinations of Doppler modes alone (color plus power, or power plus spectral) are not termed duplex because they lack the anatomic gray-scale component. Dual-frequency transducers and dual-energy techniques are unrelated concepts, and microbubble contrast is an adjunct to enhance flow detection rather than a defining element of duplex imaging.
learning_point: Duplex ultrasonography combines gray-scale (B-mode) anatomic imaging with Doppler flow assessment on the same display. Color Doppler encodes direction, power Doppler is more sensitive but directionless, and microbubble contrast and dual-energy are separate techniques.
key_facts: Duplex = gray-scale + Doppler (spectral and/or color).
Color convention: red toward the transducer, blue away.
Power Doppler: higher flow sensitivity, no directional information.
Dual-energy refers to CT, not ultrasound.

question: A 36-year-old man with azoospermia has an FSH of 24 mIU/mL, normal testosterone, LH, and prolactin, a 46,XY karyotype, and no AZF microdeletions. A diagnostic testicular biopsy performed elsewhere showed Sertoli cell-only pattern. He and his wife wish to attempt pregnancy with his own sperm. The next step is:

options.B: microdissection testicular sperm extraction with IVF/ICSI.

rationale: Elevated FSH with azoospermia indicates spermatogenic failure, and a Sertoli cell-only biopsy does not exclude isolated foci of spermatogenesis; microdissection TESE finds sperm in roughly a third of such men and is the recommended approach when the couple wants a genetically related child. Epididymal aspiration is only useful in obstructive azoospermia, where spermatogenesis is intact. Clomiphene or hCG are not indicated with a normal testosterone and would not overcome primary testicular failure. Donor sperm is a reasonable alternative but does not meet the couple's stated goal, and a repeat random biopsy has lower yield than micro-TESE and delays treatment.
learning_point: Men with nonobstructive azoospermia and Sertoli cell-only histology on prior biopsy still have roughly a 30% (sometimes higher) chance of sperm retrieval with microdissection TESE, which is the appropriate step when the couple wants a biological child. Epididymal aspiration is for obstructive azoospermia, and hormonal manipulation is not indicated with normal testosterone.
key_facts: Elevated FSH with azoospermia indicates nonobstructive azoospermia (spermatogenic failure).
Micro-TESE retrieves sperm in about 30-40% of Sertoli cell-only cases due to focal spermatogenesis.
Normal karyotype and absence of AZFa/AZFb deletions preserve the chance of retrieval; complete AZFa or AZFb deletion predicts failure.
PESA/MESA are for obstructive azoospermia with normal spermatogenesis.

question: A 66-year-old man with multiple prior abdominal operations is scheduled for robot-assisted radical prostatectomy and the surgeon elects an extraperitoneal approach. Compared with the transperitoneal technique, the extraperitoneal approach is associated with:

options.E: less tension on the vesicourethral anastomosis.

rationale: The extraperitoneal space is confined and highly vascular with disrupted tissue planes, and multiple studies have documented greater CO2 absorption and higher end-tidal CO2 with this approach. Because the urachus and medial umbilical ligaments are left intact, the bladder is less mobile and the anastomosis is under more rather than less tension. Keeping bowel out of the pelvis actually reduces the degree of Trendelenburg required. Blood loss, bladder injury, and rectal injury rates have not been shown to differ between approaches.
learning_point: Extraperitoneal robotic prostatectomy avoids the peritoneal cavity, needing less Trendelenburg and preventing bowel contact and urinary ascites, but the smaller working space with intact bladder attachments creates more tension on the anastomosis and is associated with greater CO2 absorption. Blood loss and bladder injury rates are not different.
key_facts: Extraperitoneal: urachus and medial umbilical ligaments preserved, smaller space, more anastomotic tension (mitigated by lowering pressure or barbed suture).
Advantages: useful after prior laparotomy, less Trendelenburg, no urinary ascites with leak, bowel kept out of field.
Several studies show higher CO2 absorption and hypercarbia with the extraperitoneal approach.
No difference in blood loss or bladder injury.

question: A 3-month-old girl with prenatally detected hydronephrosis has a postnatal ultrasound showing severe left hydroureteronephrosis with a 1.4 cm distal ureter and a normal right kidney. VCUG shows no reflux and a normal urethra. Diuretic MAG-3 shows 52% right and 48% left differential function with a right T1/2 of 7 minutes and a left T1/2 of 25 minutes. She is asymptomatic. The next steps are antibiotic prophylaxis and:

options.C: endoscopic balloon dilation of the ureterovesical junction.

rationale: A non-refluxing, dilated distal ureter with delayed drainage but well-preserved, symmetric function is a primary obstructive megaureter, which in most infants improves or resolves without surgery. Observation with prophylaxis and a repeat ultrasound in a few months is appropriate, with a repeat renal scan if the dilation worsens. Reimplantation with tapering or endoscopic dilation is reserved for infants who develop infections, symptoms, progressive dilation, or loss of function. MR urography would require anesthesia and add no actionable information, and a retrograde pyelogram is invasive and unnecessary for surveillance.
learning_point: A primary obstructive (non-refluxing) megaureter in an asymptomatic infant with preserved and symmetric renal function is managed expectantly with antibiotic prophylaxis and serial ultrasound, because most resolve spontaneously. Surgery is reserved for symptoms, recurrent UTI, progressive dilation, differential function below 40%, or a decline of 5% or more.
key_facts: Normal VCUG excludes refluxing megaureter; delayed drainage with preserved function defines primary obstructive megaureter.
Most non-refluxing megaureters improve within the first years of life.
Indications for intervention: symptoms, febrile UTI, worsening hydroureteronephrosis, function <40% or falling >=5%.
MR urography in infants requires anesthesia and is not needed for surveillance.

question: A 24-year-old man is evaluated five days after a complete T6 spinal cord injury and is in spinal shock. Videourodynamics are performed to establish a baseline. The expected findings for the smooth sphincter, striated sphincter, and guarding reflex, respectively, are:
rationale: In spinal shock, reflex activity below the level of injury is suppressed, so the detrusor is acontractile and the normal reflex increase in sphincter EMG activity during filling (the guarding reflex) is lost, as is voluntary control. The bladder neck remains closed and functions synergically because the sympathetic outflow is intact and there is no detrusor contraction to oppose it. The striated sphincter likewise retains baseline tone and is synergic; dyssynergia requires an intact sacral reflex arc producing involuntary detrusor contractions, which appears only after spinal shock resolves in suprasacral lesions. Options describing dyssynergia or a present guarding reflex are therefore incorrect for this phase.
learning_point: During spinal shock after spinal cord injury the bladder is areflexic and acontractile, the bladder neck (smooth sphincter) remains closed and synergic, and the striated sphincter retains tone and is synergic, but the guarding reflex (increasing EMG activity with filling) and voluntary sphincter control are absent.
key_facts: Spinal shock: suppression of somatic and autonomic reflex activity below the lesion; detrusor areflexia.
Bladder neck is competent unless there is a thoracolumbar sympathetic injury or prior surgery.
Some baseline EMG activity persists in the striated sphincter but the guarding reflex is lost.
Patients usually remain continent unless overdistension causes overflow.

question: A 14-year-old girl has recurrent right-sided pelvic pain. CT shows a right pelvic kidney with a dilated extrarenal pelvis containing a single 1.8 cm radiopaque calculus and no other stones. Renal function is normal. The best treatment is:
rationale: A large stone sitting in a dilated extrarenal pelvis of a pelvic kidney is ideally suited to laparoscopic pyelolithotomy, which gives the highest single-procedure clearance. SWL and ureteroscopy produce fragments that drain poorly from a non-dependent ectopic pelvis, so residual stone is common. Percutaneous access to a pelvic kidney is technically difficult and endangers the iliac vessels and anomalous renal arteries. Potassium citrate (alkalinization) only dissolves uric acid stones, and a radiopaque stone is unlikely to be uric acid.
learning_point: A large stone in the extrarenal pelvis of a pelvic (ectopic) kidney is best cleared by laparoscopic pyelolithotomy; SWL and ureteroscopy have poor clearance because of the non-dependent pelvis, and percutaneous access risks iliac and anomalous vessel injury.
key_facts: Pelvic kidneys have anomalous vasculature and lie behind bowel and near iliac vessels, making PCNL hazardous.
Non-dependent drainage of an ectopic kidney lowers fragment clearance after SWL or ureteroscopy.
Laparoscopic pyelolithotomy is favored for large-volume stones in a dilated extrarenal pelvis.
Alkalinization is reserved for radiolucent (uric acid) stones.

question: A 42-year-old nonsmoking woman underwent cystoscopy and renal ultrasound 11 months ago for microhematuria; both were normal. A follow-up microscopic urinalysis today shows 1 RBC/hpf with no proteinuria. The next step is:
rationale: This low-risk patient had a complete negative evaluation and now has a urinalysis that does not meet the definition of microhematuria (fewer than 3 RBC/hpf). The AUA/SUFU guideline permits a repeat urinalysis within 12 months and states that if it is negative, evaluation for microhematuria may be discontinued. Repeating cystoscopy, imaging, or cytology adds cost and morbidity without meaningful yield given the very low malignancy risk. Continued serial urinalyses are not required once the follow-up specimen is negative.
learning_point: After a negative microhematuria evaluation, a repeat urinalysis within 12 months that is negative (fewer than 3 RBC/hpf) allows discontinuation of further evaluation per the 2020 AUA/SUFU guideline.
key_facts: Microhematuria is defined as 3 or more RBC/hpf on microscopic urinalysis.
A repeat urinalysis may be obtained within 12 months of a negative evaluation.
If that repeat urinalysis is negative, further workup may be stopped.
Low-risk patients have a very low malignancy risk, so repeat imaging and cystoscopy are not warranted.

question: A 66-year-old woman with refractory hematuria from radiation cystitis after treatment for cervical cancer is referred for hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Which comorbidity is a relative contraindication to this treatment?
rationale: Breathing 100% oxygen at 2 to 2.5 atmospheres can trigger CNS oxygen toxicity, the hallmark of which is a generalized seizure; patients with an underlying seizure disorder are therefore at higher risk and epilepsy is considered a relative contraindication. Thrombophilias and clotting disorders are not worsened by hyperbaric oxygen. Glaucoma and cognitive impairment do not alter the safety of therapy. Stable COPD is not a contraindication, although an untreated pneumothorax would be an absolute one.
learning_point: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for radiation cystitis is relatively contraindicated in patients with a seizure disorder because high-pressure oxygen can provoke central nervous system oxygen toxicity.
key_facts: CNS oxygen toxicity from HBOT manifests as seizures; prior seizure disorder raises this risk.
Untreated pneumothorax is the classic absolute contraindication to HBOT.
Clotting disorders, dementia, glaucoma, and pulmonary hypertension are not affected by HBOT.

question: A 72-year-old man with hypertension reports waking three times nightly to void. Prostate is 35 g and benign, urinalysis is normal, and PVR is 40 mL. His frequency-volume chart shows a 24-hour output of 2,100 mL, of which 850 mL (including the first morning void) is produced overnight; he drinks nothing after dinner and takes one cup of coffee at breakfast only. He has no daytime urgency. The next step is:
rationale: His nocturnal urine volume is about 40% of 24-hour output, which defines nocturnal polyuria rather than reduced bladder capacity or outlet obstruction. He already avoids evening fluids and drinks minimal morning caffeine, so further behavioral restriction will not help. Obstructive sleep apnea is a common and treatable cause of nocturnal polyuria in an older hypertensive man, and a sleep study is the appropriate evaluation; CPAP frequently reduces nocturnal voids. Alpha-blockers address obstruction (not present, with a small PVR) and antimuscarinics or beta-3 agonists target overactive bladder symptoms he does not have.
learning_point: Nocturia with nocturnal urine volume exceeding about 33% of 24-hour output (including the first morning void) is nocturnal polyuria; when fluid and caffeine habits are already appropriate, screening for obstructive sleep apnea with a sleep study is the next step.
key_facts: Nocturnal polyuria: nocturnal volume > 20% (young) to > 33% (older adults) of total 24-hour urine output.
The first morning void counts toward nocturnal volume.
Causes include OSA, congestive heart failure, peripheral edema, diabetes, and evening fluid intake.
Desmopressin is an alternative treatment but requires serum sodium monitoring.

question: A 61-year-old woman with high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma and CIS received a full BCG induction course followed by a three-week maintenance course. Surveillance cystoscopy and biopsies three months after her last instillation show persistent CIS without papillary tumor. Upper tract imaging and chest CT are negative. The best treatment is:

options.B: gemcitabine and cisplatin followed by cystectomy.
options.C: radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection.

rationale: She has received adequate BCG and has biopsy-proven CIS within 12 months, which meets the definition of BCG-unresponsive non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer. The guideline-recommended treatment for a fit patient is radical cystectomy because the risk of progression to muscle invasion is substantial and additional BCG is unlikely to work. Salvage intravesical regimens such as gemcitabine/docetaxel are considered only when a patient is unwilling or unfit for cystectomy. Trimodal therapy is inappropriate for CIS, and neoadjuvant chemotherapy has no established benefit in non-muscle-invasive disease.
learning_point: Persistent CIS found within 12 months after adequate BCG (induction plus at least one maintenance course) is BCG-unresponsive disease; radical cystectomy is recommended rather than further intravesical therapy or trimodal therapy.
key_facts: Adequate BCG = at least 5 of 6 induction doses plus at least 2 of 3 maintenance (or second induction) doses.
BCG-unresponsive: persistent high-grade disease or CIS at 6-12 months, or recurrence within 6-12 months, after adequate BCG.
Salvage intravesical therapy is reserved for patients unfit for or refusing cystectomy.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy benefits muscle-invasive disease, not non-muscle-invasive disease.

question: A 41-year-old man with hypertension requiring three medications and a serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L has an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio and aldosterone that fails to suppress after oral sodium loading. Contrast CT shows a 7 mm nodule in each adrenal gland. He wishes to pursue a surgical cure if possible. The next step is:

options.A: adrenal MRI with chemical shift imaging.

rationale: Primary hyperaldosteronism has been confirmed biochemically, but CT shows small bilateral nodules and cannot tell whether the excess aldosterone comes from one gland or both. Adrenal venous sampling determines lateralization; if secretion lateralizes, unilateral adrenalectomy can cure the condition in a surgical candidate. Operating on one side based on imaging alone risks removing a nonfunctional nodule. MRI offers no advantage over CT for aldosterone-producing adenomas, mineralocorticoid antagonists are the choice only if sampling does not lateralize or the patient is not a surgical candidate, and bilateral adrenalectomy is never appropriate.
learning_point: In confirmed primary hyperaldosteronism without a clear unilateral adrenal adenoma over 1 cm on CT, adrenal venous sampling is required to determine lateralization before considering unilateral adrenalectomy; non-lateralizing disease is treated medically.
key_facts: Confirm hyperaldosteronism with a suppression test (saline/sodium loading) before localization.
CT is the first localization study; bilateral or small nodules need adrenal vein sampling.
Lateralization leads to unilateral adrenalectomy; bilateral disease is managed with mineralocorticoid antagonists.
Bilateral adrenalectomy is never indicated for hyperaldosteronism.

question: A 27-year-old woman sustains a single low-velocity gunshot wound to the lower abdomen. She is hemodynamically stable with gross hematuria. CT cystography demonstrates contrast extravasation confined to the perivesical space without intraperitoneal spread, and there is no pelvic fracture. The next step is:

options.B: urethral catheter drainage with repeat cystogram in 10-14 days.

rationale: Although extraperitoneal bladder ruptures from blunt trauma are managed with catheter drainage, penetrating injuries are different: the bullet track may injure bowel, rectum, vessels, or the ureter, and devitalized tissue leads to poor healing. Gunshot wounds of the bladder should therefore be explored and formally repaired, with assessment of the ureters through the cystotomy and evaluation for rectal injury. Catheter drainage alone or a suprapubic tube fails to address the associated injuries. Cystoscopic retrograde studies are difficult in a disrupted bladder and would delay definitive treatment.
learning_point: Penetrating (gunshot) bladder injuries require surgical exploration and repair even when the extravasation is extraperitoneal, unlike blunt extraperitoneal ruptures, which can usually be managed with catheter drainage.
key_facts: Blunt extraperitoneal rupture: catheter drainage with cystogram at about 2 weeks.
Penetrating bladder injury: open exploration, cystorrhaphy, and inspection for associated bowel/rectal injury.
Other indications for repair of extraperitoneal rupture: bone fragments in the bladder, bladder neck injury, concomitant rectal or vaginal injury, or planned laparotomy.
Ureteral integrity can be checked through the cystotomy with retrograde catheters.

question: A 54-year-old man with a three-month history of a dorsal penile plaque, 40 degrees of curvature, and pain with erection asks what is likely to happen if he chooses no treatment over the next year. He should be counseled that:

options.A: any coexisting palmar contracture will regress with the plaque.
options.B: curvature will straighten in most men.
options.C: obstructive voiding symptoms are likely to develop.
options.D: pain is likely to resolve on its own.
options.E: the plaque will calcify in nearly all cases.

rationale: Observational data on men with newly diagnosed Peyronie's disease who received no treatment show that nearly all had improvement in pain and most had complete pain resolution within a year as the inflammatory phase subsides. Curvature, by contrast, improved in only about one in eight men and worsened in nearly half, so straightening cannot be promised. Peyronie's disease does not cause lower urinary tract symptoms, and Dupuytren's contracture, when present, follows its own course. Plaque calcification occurs in a subset, not nearly all, of patients.
learning_point: In the natural history of Peyronie's disease, penile pain resolves spontaneously in the large majority of men within about 12 months, whereas curvature improves in only a small minority and often worsens.
key_facts: Untreated natural history: pain resolves in ~90%; curvature improves in ~12%, remains stable in ~40%, and worsens in ~48%.
Hourglass and other deformities rarely resolve on their own.
Dupuytren's contracture coexists in a minority of men and does not regress with the penile disease.
LUTS are not a feature of Peyronie's disease.

question: A 48-year-old man presents with left flank pain radiating to the groin. He is afebrile, and his pain and nausea resolve with intravenous ketorolac and ondansetron. Creatinine is normal. CT shows a 3 mm stone at the left ureterovesical junction with mild hydronephrosis and a small amount of perinephric stranding. The best management is:
rationale: A 3 mm distal ureteral stone has a very high likelihood of spontaneous passage, and the patient has no indication for urgent intervention (no fever, controlled symptoms, normal renal function). Randomized trials have shown that alpha-blockers add little to expulsion rates for stones under 5 mm, although they are reasonable for larger distal stones. Corticosteroids have not been shown to increase stone passage.
