Injection sites every 1 cm from 1 cm distal to bladder neck to proximal verumontanum, lateral lobes at 3 and 9 o'clock.
Normal saline irrigation provides visualization and urethral cooling.
Unlike prostatic urethral lift, Rezum can treat an obstructing median lobe.

question: A 66-year-old man with an ileal conduit after cystectomy for a benign contracted bladder had a negative 12-core prostate biopsy 14 months ago for PSA 6.0 ng/mL. His PSA is now 8.1 ng/mL and DRE is benign. He asks whether a biomarker can help decide on another biopsy. The most appropriate test is:
rationale: ConfirmMDx examines the archived benign biopsy cores for gene hypermethylation that reflects a field effect around an unsampled cancer, and a negative result lowers the likelihood that repeat biopsy will find disease; the test is valid within about 30 months of the prior biopsy. Urine-based assays such as SelectMDx and PCA3 require post-massage urine that has traversed the prostatic urethra, which cannot be obtained from a man whose urine exits through an ileal conduit. Oncotype Dx and Decipher are tissue-based prognostic tools used after cancer is diagnosed to inform treatment decisions and have no role in deciding whether to re-biopsy.
learning_point: For a man with a prior negative biopsy and rising PSA, ConfirmMDx (epigenetic methylation assay on the previous benign cores) predicts the yield of repeat biopsy; urine-based tests are useless when the patient has a urinary diversion, and Decipher, Prolaris, and Oncotype Dx are post-diagnosis prognostic tests.
key_facts: Pre-biopsy risk markers: serum (4Kscore, PHI), urine (PCA3, SelectMDx, ExoDx), tissue (ConfirmMDx on negative cores within 30 months).
Urine assays rely on post-DRE urine passing through the prostatic urethra; diversion bypasses this.
ConfirmMDx assesses GSTP1, APC, RASSF1 hypermethylation as a field effect.
Decipher/Prolaris/Oncotype Dx are for men already diagnosed with cancer.

question: A 22-year-old man has three days of right scrotal pain and swelling with a tender, enlarged epididymis. He has no urethral discharge or dysuria. He reports being the insertive partner in anal intercourse with a new partner two weeks ago. Along with first-void urine nucleic acid amplification testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia, the evaluation should include:

options.D: scrotal duplex ultrasound only, with no further laboratory testing.

rationale: In sexually active men under 35, epididymitis is usually caused by chlamydia or gonorrhea, detected by urine NAAT. When the man is the insertive partner in anal sex, enteric gram-negative organisms become likely pathogens, so a standard bacterial urine culture should also be sent and empiric coverage broadened accordingly. Urethral swab culture has largely been replaced by NAAT and is reserved for suspected antimicrobial failure. Serology for herpes and syphilis is irrelevant to epididymitis, and upper tract ultrasound is pursued for recurrent pediatric epididymitis suggesting an ectopic ureter.
learning_point: Acute epididymitis in a sexually active young man is evaluated with urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhea; a bacterial urine culture is added when the patient practices insertive anal intercourse (enteric organisms), is over 35, or has urinary tract abnormalities.
key_facts: Men <35: C. trachomatis and N. gonorrhoeae predominate; first-void urine NAAT is the preferred test.
Insertive anal intercourse: cover enteric organisms (e.g., ceftriaxone plus fluoroquinolone) and obtain urine culture.
Urethral swab culture is reserved for suspected treatment failure/resistance.
Renal ultrasound for recurrent childhood epididymitis (ectopic ureter), not for a sexually transmitted episode.

question: A 36-year-old man with lifelong premature ejaculation has improved from 45 seconds to about 2 minutes on daily paroxetine but remains dissatisfied. Compared with continuing medication alone, referral for structured behavioral therapy (squeeze and sensate focus techniques) is expected to:

options.A: allow discontinuation of the SSRI within two weeks.
options.B: be fully effective without any trained therapist involvement.
options.C: provide no measurable benefit beyond medication.
options.D: lengthen ejaculatory latency by roughly an additional minute.
options.E: worsen performance anxiety by increasing focus on timing.

rationale: Trials of combined pharmacologic and psychobehavioral treatment for premature ejaculation show that adding techniques such as start-stop, squeeze, or sensate focus increases intravaginal ejaculatory latency by about one minute (in some studies one to three minutes) beyond medication alone, with parallel gains in sexual satisfaction and reductions in anxiety. These interventions reduce, rather than heighten, performance anxiety by broadening the couple's repertoire of non-coital stimulation. They do not render the SSRI unnecessary in the short term, and they typically require a trained psychosexual therapist over multiple sessions.
learning_point: Adding behavioral therapy (start-stop, squeeze, sensate focus) to an SSRI for premature ejaculation further increases ejaculatory latency by roughly one minute over drug therapy alone and improves satisfaction and anxiety; it generally requires a trained psychosexual therapist.
key_facts: Combination pharmacologic plus behavioral therapy outperforms either alone on IELT and patient-reported outcomes.
Incremental latency gain of about 1 (up to 1-3) minutes over SSRI alone.
Sensate focus expands non-coital foreplay and reduces performance anxiety.
Behavioral therapy carries no adverse effects but usually requires a specialist and may not be covered by insurance.

question: A 10-year-old girl with spina bifida and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is on postoperative day two after ileocystoplasty with a suprapubic catheter in place. Over the past six hours her catheter output has fallen to 10 mL, she complains of lower abdominal fullness, her temperature is 38.3 C, and her heart rate is 125. The next step is:

options.A: start broad-spectrum antibiotics and obtain shunt series.
options.E: CT of the abdomen and pelvis.

rationale: The combination of abruptly reduced catheter drainage and abdominal fullness in a freshly augmented bladder points to mucus plugging of the suprapubic tube, which allows the bladder to distend and threatens the fresh anastomosis. Gentle irrigation restores drainage and usually resolves the tachycardia and discomfort. Giving fluids for presumed hypovolemia before confirming that the bladder is draining would be misguided. Fever this early is usually non-infectious; antibiotics and shunt evaluation are considered if infection is suspected on clinical grounds, and a cystogram or CT would simply demonstrate the obstructed catheter without treating it.
learning_point: Early after enterocystoplasty, a sudden fall in suprapubic tube output with abdominal discomfort indicates mucus occlusion of the catheter; irrigate the tube first before attributing fever to infection, giving fluid boluses, or imaging.
key_facts: Augmented bladders produce copious mucus that plugs catheters; scheduled irrigation is routine postoperatively.
An undrained augmented bladder distends, causing pain, tachycardia, and risk of suture-line leak.
Early postoperative fever is most often non-infectious; antibiotics if assessment suggests infection.
VP shunt infection is possible but should not be presumed before confirming bladder drainage.

question: A 27-year-old man and his partner have 18 months of infertility. Two semen analyses show azoospermia with a volume of 2.6 mL. Both testes measure 8 mL and are soft; vasa are palpable. FSH is 24 IU/L, LH 11 IU/L, total testosterone 240 ng/dL, and prolactin 32 ng/mL. The next step is:

options.C: a trial of pseudoephedrine before intercourse.

rationale: Small, soft testes with markedly elevated FSH and a low testosterone define primary testicular failure, so this is non-obstructive azoospermia and genetic evaluation with karyotype and Y microdeletion analysis is indicated to detect Klinefelter syndrome or AZF deletions that affect prognosis and offspring. The normal semen volume excludes ejaculatory duct obstruction and absent vasa, making TRUS and CFTR testing unnecessary. Mildly elevated prolactin in the 20-50 ng/mL range is common in hypogonadal men and does not call for pituitary imaging, which is reserved for levels above roughly 80 ng/mL with suppressed gonadotropins. Pseudoephedrine addresses retrograde ejaculation, which is excluded by the normal volume.
learning_point: Azoospermia with small testes, elevated FSH, and low testosterone indicates non-obstructive azoospermia (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism); evaluation requires karyotype and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing. Mild prolactin elevation (20-50 ng/mL) does not warrant pituitary MRI.
key_facts: Normal ejaculate volume with azoospermia rules against obstruction of the ejaculatory ducts or absent vas, so CFTR testing and TRUS are not indicated.
Karyotype (Klinefelter) and Y microdeletions are recommended in NOA with FSH >7.6 or testis <4.6 cm.
Prolactinoma typically produces prolactin >80-100 ng/mL with suppressed gonadotropins.
Pseudoephedrine is for retrograde ejaculation (low-volume or absent ejaculate).

question: A 38-year-old never-smoking man with no urologic symptoms had 7 RBC/hpf on a urinalysis obtained for a life-insurance examination and, after shared decision-making, chose a repeat test rather than immediate evaluation. Five months later the repeat urinalysis shows 6 RBC/hpf with no casts or proteinuria. The next step is:

options.A: white light cystoscopy and renal ultrasound.
options.B: white light cystoscopy and CT urogram.
options.C: urine cytology and renal ultrasound without cystoscopy.
options.D: blue light cystoscopy and renal ultrasound.
options.E: repeat urinalysis in another six months.

rationale: At presentation he met low-risk criteria (man under 40, never smoker, 3-10 RBC/hpf, asymptomatic), for which the AUA allows either immediate evaluation or a repeat urinalysis within six months. Persistent microhematuria in the 3-10 RBC/hpf range at the repeat test moves him into the intermediate-risk group, which should be evaluated with cystoscopy and renal ultrasound rather than further watchful waiting. CT urography is reserved for high-risk patients because of radiation, cost, and the low incidence of upper tract tumors in lower-risk groups. Enhanced cystoscopy has no established role in evaluating microhematuria without a known bladder cancer diagnosis, and cytology is not recommended for routine microhematuria work-up.
learning_point: A low-risk microhematuria patient who chose repeat urinalysis and has persistent 3-10 RBC/hpf is reclassified as intermediate risk and should undergo white light cystoscopy plus renal ultrasound; CT urogram is reserved for high-risk patients.
key_facts: Microhematuria = >=3 RBC/hpf on a single properly collected specimen.
Low risk: women <50 / men <40, never smoker or <10 pack-years, 3-10 RBC/hpf, no risk factors; options are repeat UA in 6 months or cystoscopy plus ultrasound.
Persistent microhematuria on repeat UA upgrades to intermediate (3-10 RBC) or high risk (>25 RBC).
Intermediate risk: cystoscopy and renal ultrasound; high risk: cystoscopy and CT urogram; enhanced cystoscopy not recommended.

question: A 31-year-old man has azoospermia on two samples with an ejaculate volume of 0.6 mL and acidic pH. Testes are 20 mL bilaterally with normal consistency. The right vas is easily palpable but the left vas cannot be felt. FSH is 4 IU/L. Renal ultrasound shows two normal kidneys. The next step is:
rationale: Low-volume, acidic azoospermia with normal testes and normal FSH indicates obstruction or absence of the seminal vesicles and distal ductal system, and a non-palpable vas confirms congenital vasal agenesis; a palpable scrotal vas on the other side may still be missing its inguinal portion and seminal vesicle. Normal kidneys make a mesonephric developmental anomaly less likely and point to a CFTR-related process, so cystic fibrosis gene testing of the patient (and partner) is the critical next step. Karyotype and testis biopsy evaluate spermatogenic failure, which is not suggested here. Scrotal ultrasound will not visualize the missing structures, and seminal fructose only confirms what the low volume and pH already imply.
learning_point: Low-volume azoospermia with a unilaterally non-palpable vas and normal-sized testes indicates congenital absence of the vas (a CBAVD variant with absent seminal vesicles); the next step is CFTR mutation testing. Normal kidneys on ultrasound favor a CFTR etiology over mesonephric maldevelopment.
key_facts: Unilateral absence of the vas with low-volume azoospermia suggests the contralateral vas is also absent proximally or the seminal vesicles are absent.
CFTR mutations are found in most men with CBAVD; test the patient and partner before ART.
Unilateral vasal agenesis with renal agenesis points to a mesonephric defect rather than CFTR.
Karyotype and testis biopsy address non-obstructive causes and are not indicated with normal testes and FSH.

question: A four-month-old boy with prenatally detected left hydronephrosis has an SFU grade 3 left kidney with no ureteral dilation and a normal right kidney on ultrasound. A MAG-3 diuretic renogram shows 46% function on the left with a drainage half-time of 25 minutes. He is thriving and has had no infections. The next step is:
rationale: A drainage half-time over 20 minutes is mildly delayed, but with 46% differential function the kidney is not being harmed and the delay may simply reflect a capacious renal pelvis. Most such infants improve or stabilize spontaneously, so observation with serial ultrasound, repeating the renal scan if dilation worsens, is appropriate. Surgery is indicated for low or falling function, increasing hydronephrosis, infection, stones, or symptoms, none of which is present. MR urography and retrograde pyelography expose the infant to anesthesia without changing management, and a stent is not indicated with preserved function.
learning_point: An infant with isolated hydronephrosis, preserved differential function (~45-50%), and only mildly prolonged drainage half-time on diuretic renography should be observed with serial ultrasound; pyeloplasty is reserved for declining function, worsening dilation, infection, stones, or symptoms.
key_facts: T1/2 >20 minutes is considered delayed but is not by itself an indication for surgery when function is preserved.
Most antenatal hydronephrosis with suspected UPJ obstruction resolves or stabilizes without surgery.
Pyeloplasty indications: differential function <40% or a fall >5-10%, progressive dilation, UTI, stones, pain, failure to thrive.
MR urography and retrograde pyelography require anesthesia in infants and add little when function is preserved.

question: A 69-year-old woman with refractory overactive bladder begins percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation. After the 34-gauge needle is inserted and the current is increased, the response that confirms correct positioning is:

options.A: numbness over the dorsum of the foot.
options.E: plantar flexion of the great toe with tingling of the sole.

rationale: The needle is placed roughly three fingerbreadths above the medial malleolus and slightly posterior to the tibia to lie near the tibial nerve, which supplies the plantar muscles and the skin of the sole. Appropriate stimulation therefore produces plantar flexion or fanning of the toes, most visibly the great toe, together with a tingling sensation across the sole. Dorsiflexion, lateral leg sensation, or dorsal foot numbness would indicate stimulation of the peroneal nerve or superficial branches rather than the tibial nerve. Gross gastrocnemius contraction is not the target response.
learning_point: Correct needle placement for percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation (about 3-4 cm cephalad to the medial malleolus) is confirmed by flexion of the great toe and a tingling sensation in the sole of the foot.
key_facts: PTNS is a third-line OAB therapy (AUA/SUFU); 12 weekly 30-minute sessions.
Tibial nerve (L4-S3) runs posterior to the medial malleolus; stimulation modulates sacral bladder reflexes.
Motor response: plantar flexion/fanning of toes, especially the great toe; sensory: tingling in the sole.
Dorsiflexion or lateral leg sensation indicates incorrect placement.

question: A 59-year-old man has three months of bilateral leg swelling. MRI shows a 9 cm left renal mass with enhancing thrombus extending into the IVC to just below the hepatic veins, and non-enhancing thrombus completely filling the infrarenal IVC to the confluence. Chest CT shows a single indeterminate 3 mm nodule. Biopsy confirms papillary RCC. He is started on anticoagulation. The best treatment is:

options.B: nephrectomy with tumor thrombectomy and ligation of the infrarenal IVC.
options.C: renal artery embolization and percutaneous IVC filter.
options.D: nephrectomy with tumor thrombectomy and intraoperative infrarenal IVC filter.

rationale: The enhancing component is tumor thrombus and the non-enhancing component filling the infrarenal cava is bland thrombus whose complete occlusion explains his leg edema. Without clear metastatic disease, the definitive treatment is radical nephrectomy with caval thrombectomy, and because the infrarenal IVC is already chronically occluded with established collaterals, ligating it is well tolerated and eliminates the risk of postoperative embolization of residual clot. An intraoperative filter is described only for a patent cava with separate iliofemoral clot, and a percutaneous filter is contraindicated because tumor thrombus can grow into the tines and complicate surgery. Embolization is palliative, and the evidence for cabozantinib or checkpoint combinations is in metastatic, predominantly clear cell disease.
learning_point: RCC with suprarenal IVC tumor thrombus and complete occlusive bland thrombus of the infrarenal IVC is managed with anticoagulation followed by radical nephrectomy with tumor thrombectomy and ligation of the infrarenal IVC; percutaneous filters are contraindicated with tumor thrombus, and systemic therapy is not first-line for non-clear cell, non-metastatic disease.
key_facts: Enhancement on contrast MRI distinguishes tumor thrombus from bland thrombus.
Chronic complete infrarenal IVC occlusion develops collaterals, so IVC ligation is well tolerated and prevents postoperative embolization.
Intraoperative IVC filter is for a patent IVC with non-contiguous iliofemoral bland clot.
Percutaneous filters can become entangled in tumor thrombus; angioembolization is palliative.

question: A 24-year-old man with hemoglobin SS disease and several prior brief priapism episodes presents with a rigid, painful erection of six hours. Corporal blood gas shows pO2 22 mmHg, pCO2 70 mmHg, and pH 7.18. The hematology service has started I.V. fluids and supplemental oxygen. The next step is:

options.C: continued hydration and oxygen with reassessment in four hours.

rationale: The blood gas confirms ischemic (low-flow) priapism, which is a compartment syndrome of the corpora and requires prompt decompression regardless of the underlying hemoglobinopathy. Aspiration followed by diluted phenylephrine injections resolves most episodes and should not be delayed for systemic sickle cell measures such as hydration, oxygen, or exchange transfusion, which are adjunctive. Waiting four more hours risks permanent cavernous fibrosis and erectile dysfunction. Daily low-dose PDE5 inhibitor therapy is a strategy to prevent recurrent stuttering episodes once the acute event is resolved, and shunt procedures are reserved for failure of aspiration and sympathomimetic injection.
learning_point: Ischemic priapism in a patient with sickle cell disease is treated the same as in other patients: corporal aspiration and intracavernosal phenylephrine first; systemic measures (hydration, oxygen, exchange transfusion) are adjuncts, and shunting is reserved for failure of aspiration/injection.
key_facts: Cavernous blood gas in ischemic priapism: pO2 <30, pCO2 >60, pH <7.25.
Phenylephrine is the preferred sympathomimetic; monitor blood pressure and heart rate.
Daily low-dose PDE5 inhibitor reduces recurrence of stuttering priapism but is not acute therapy.
Distal shunts only after failed aspiration and repeated alpha-agonist dosing.

question: A 57-year-old man undergoes TURBT of a 3 cm bladder tumor. Pathology shows high-grade urothelial carcinoma invading the lamina propria with extensive sarcomatoid differentiation and adjacent carcinoma in situ; muscularis propria is present and uninvolved. CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no adenopathy or metastasis. The best treatment is:
rationale: High-grade lamina propria invasion with carcinoma in situ is already high-risk non-muscle-invasive disease, and sarcomatoid differentiation adds a well-documented risk of occult muscle invasion and locally advanced disease at cystectomy, so the guideline recommends considering upfront radical cystectomy. BCG has little evidence of efficacy against sarcomatoid tumors and would also require a restaging TURBT first given the upstaging risk. Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy is indicated for confirmed muscle-invasive disease, not NMIBC, and its benefit in sarcomatoid histology is unproven. Chemoradiation is not recommended for NMIBC, and pembrolizumab is restricted to BCG-unresponsive CIS in patients who cannot or will not undergo cystectomy.
learning_point: High-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma with variant histology such as sarcomatoid differentiation carries a high risk of understaging and poor response to intravesical therapy; the AUA/SUO guideline supports offering upfront radical cystectomy rather than BCG.
key_facts: High-risk NMIBC features: HG T1, CIS, variant histology, LVI, prostatic urethral involvement, BCG failure.
Variant histology (micropapillary, sarcomatoid, plasmacytoid, nested) is associated with upstaging at cystectomy.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (ddMVAC) is for muscle-invasive disease; data in sarcomatoid tumors are limited.
Pembrolizumab is approved only for BCG-unresponsive CIS in patients ineligible for or declining cystectomy.

question: A 29-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation is under regional anesthesia for right ureteral stent placement for an obstructing stone with fever earlier that day now resolved on antibiotics. As her legs are placed in stirrups and she is laid flat, her blood pressure falls from 118/72 to 78/46 mmHg; heart rate stays at 84 and she is afebrile. In addition to I.V. fluids, the next step is:

options.A: give a vasopressor bolus and proceed without repositioning.
options.B: abort the procedure and place a right percutaneous nephrostomy.
options.C: Trendelenburg positioning and proceed with the stent.
options.D: tilt her to the left with a wedge under the right hip and proceed with the stent.
options.E: abort the procedure and escalate to broad-spectrum antibiotics for presumed sepsis.

rationale: Hypotension that appears exactly when a third-trimester patient is laid flat, without tachycardia or fever, is caused by the gravid uterus compressing the inferior vena cava and reducing venous return, with anesthesia blocking the normal reflex tachycardia. Displacing the uterus to the left with a wedge under the right side relieves the compression and allows the procedure to continue. Trendelenburg pushes the uterus further onto the cava and impairs ventilation. Sepsis is unlikely given the temporal relationship to positioning and the normal heart rate and temperature, and a nephrostomy would require prone or lateral positioning that would not solve, and might worsen, caval compression. Vasopressors alone treat the number without correcting the mechanical cause.
learning_point: Sudden hypotension without tachycardia or fever when a late-pregnancy patient is positioned supine/lithotomy is supine hypotensive syndrome from uterine IVC compression; place a wedge under the right hip to tilt the uterus leftward and proceed.
key_facts: Gravid uterus compresses the IVC supine, dropping cardiac output up to 30%; anesthesia blunts compensatory tachycardia and vasoconstriction.
Left lateral tilt of 15 degrees (right-side wedge) relieves compression.
Trendelenburg worsens IVC compression and reduces functional residual capacity.
Afebrile, non-tachycardic positional hypotension is not sepsis; nephrostomy would require lateral/prone positioning that may worsen compression.

question: A 27-year-old transgender woman is readmitted on postoperative day four after robotic peritoneal-flap vaginoplasty with a temperature of 38.9 C, diffuse abdominal tenderness, and a WBC of 16,000/cu mm. The labial incision is erythematous with partial dehiscence. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are started. The next step is:

options.B: examination of the neovagina under anesthesia.
options.C: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis.
options.D: bedside wound debridement and wet-to-dry dressings only.

rationale: Although the labial wound needs local care, the fever and generalized abdominal pain after a transperitoneal procedure must be evaluated promptly for bowel injury, intra-abdominal abscess, or rectovaginal fistula. Contrast-enhanced CT surveys the entire abdomen and pelvis, including small bowel, and guides whether drainage or re-exploration is required. A voiding cystourethrogram evaluates only the urethra and would not explain the abdominal findings, and a contrast enema images the rectum and colon but misses the small bowel and free intraperitoneal processes. Examination under anesthesia may follow but is not the first diagnostic step for abdominal sepsis.
learning_point: Fever and abdominal pain in the first days after robotic (peritoneal flap) vaginoplasty raise concern for bowel injury or rectovaginal fistula; contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the appropriate first test, alongside antibiotics and local wound care.
key_facts: Robotic vaginoplasty enters the peritoneal cavity, so intra-abdominal complications are possible.
CT with contrast evaluates bowel, abscess, and the neovaginal cavity in one study.
VCUG assesses only the urethra/urethrovaginal fistula; barium enema does not evaluate small bowel.
Labial wound breakdown is managed locally but should not distract from an abdominal evaluation.

question: A 44-year-old woman with left renal artery medial fibroplasia takes a single antihypertensive with excellent blood pressure control. Her annual surveillance duplex ultrasound shows the left kidney has shortened by 1.4 cm with thinning of the cortex compared with the prior study. She has no symptoms. The next step is:

options.B: repeat duplex ultrasound in six months.

rationale: A documented decrease in kidney size or function during surveillance of renal artery FMD is an indication for revascularization even when blood pressure is well controlled. Balloon angioplasty alone is the preferred intervention because it gives durable results in FMD and stenting adds no meaningful benefit except for a residual gradient or dissection. Continued observation would allow further parenchymal loss. An ACE inhibitor does not address the anatomic lesion and is not needed for pressure control here. Surgical bypass is reserved for aneurysmal disease or distal branch involvement not amenable to angioplasty.
learning_point: In renal artery fibromuscular dysplasia with controlled blood pressure, intervention is indicated when surveillance shows loss of renal size or function (or refractory hypertension); the treatment of choice is balloon angioplasty alone, without stenting.
key_facts: FMD (medial fibroplasia) is followed with duplex ultrasound every 6-12 months for kidney length and cortical thickness.
Indications for PTRA: refractory hypertension, medication intolerance, or decline in renal size or function.
Balloon angioplasty alone is highly effective in FMD; stents are reserved for a persistent gradient or dissection.
Surgical revascularization is reserved for aneurysms or distal branch-vessel disease.

question: A 66-year-old woman who underwent radical cystectomy with a Studer orthotopic neobladder four years ago has had recurrent pyelonephritis, and her creatinine has risen from 1.0 to 2.1 mg/dL. She voids to completion with a PVR of 40 mL. Pouchogram shows reflux into the afferent limb that terminates abruptly at a narrowed midpoint, and MRI shows bilateral hydroureteronephrosis with an hourglass contour of the limb. The next step is:

options.D: open excision and replacement of the afferent limb.

rationale: The findings describe afferent limb stenosis producing bilateral obstruction, infection, and renal functional loss. Drainage with bilateral nephrostomies is the appropriate first step: it relieves obstruction, allows assessment of renal recovery, and permits antegrade nephrostograms to determine whether the ureteroileal anastomoses are also strictured. Intermittent catheterization will not help because the pouch empties well and the obstruction is upstream. Antibiotic irrigation does not treat the cause of stasis. Definitive revision of the limb or conversion to conduit should wait until drainage has been established and the anatomy fully defined; the stenotic limb itself would not be reused as a conduit.
learning_point: Afferent limb stenosis of a Studer neobladder causes obstruction, hydronephrosis, renal decline, and recurrent infection; the first step is bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy drainage to recover renal function and permit antegrade study of the ureteroileal anastomoses before definitive reconstruction.
key_facts: Studer pouch has an isoperistaltic afferent ileal limb into which the ureters are implanted; mid-limb fibrosis can produce an hourglass stenosis.
Imaging clue: reflux on pouchogram that stops abruptly in the afferent limb plus bilateral hydronephrosis.
Establish drainage with PCNTs first; antegrade nephrostograms then define whether ureteroenteric strictures coexist.
Definitive repair requires replacing the stenotic limb with new bowel; CIC is useless when the PVR is low.

question: A 24-year-old man undergoes right radical orchiectomy for a 3 cm pT1 mixed nonseminomatous germ cell tumor. Serum AFP, hCG, and LDH normalize postoperatively and chest imaging is clear. Staging CT shows a single 1.3 cm interaortocaval lymph node. The next step is:

options.A: standard surveillance with the next CT scan at six months.
options.E: repeat CT scan in six to eight weeks.

rationale: Equivocal retroperitoneal nodes between roughly 0.8 and 1.5 cm are common at diagnosis and, with normal markers, should not trigger immediate treatment because a large fraction prove benign. Short-interval repeat CT clarifies the diagnosis: growth indicates metastatic disease, while stability or shrinkage supports stage I. Chemotherapy now risks overtreatment. PET is unreliable in NSGCT because teratoma is PET-negative. Biopsy of small nodes is technically difficult and often falsely negative. Waiting six months is too long for a node of uncertain significance.
learning_point: In clinical stage I NSGCT with normal post-orchiectomy markers and a borderline (0.8-1.5 cm) retroperitoneal node, repeat CT in 6-8 weeks rather than immediate treatment, because up to half of such nodes are benign.
key_facts: Borderline retroperitoneal nodes with normal markers are frequently false positives; enlargement on repeat CT suggests metastasis, stability or regression suggests benign disease.
FDG-PET is not useful in NSGCT because it cannot distinguish teratoma from viable tumor.
Percutaneous biopsy of small nodes has high false-negative rates and is not standard.
Radiotherapy has no role in NSGCT.

question: A 22-year-old woman with sickle cell trait has hematuria, weight loss, and left flank pain. CT shows a 7 cm central infiltrative left renal mass with bulky retroperitoneal adenopathy and several hepatic lesions. She is ECOG performance status 2. Percutaneous biopsy confirms renal medullary carcinoma. The next step is:

options.E: cytoreductive nephrectomy followed by systemic therapy.

rationale: Renal medullary carcinoma is a highly aggressive tumor that behaves unlike clear cell RCC and responds poorly to immunotherapy or tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Platinum-based chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel is the preferred first-line regimen for metastatic disease. Gemcitabine and doxorubicin is reserved for second-line use. Upfront nephrectomy offers no benefit in a patient with metastatic RMC and poor performance status, though consolidative surgery can be reconsidered after systemic response.
learning_point: Metastatic renal medullary carcinoma is treated first with platinum-based cytotoxic chemotherapy (carboplatin and paclitaxel); upfront cytoreductive surgery is not performed in metastatic disease, particularly with poor performance status.
key_facts: RMC arises from collecting duct epithelium in young patients with sickle cell trait; tumors are central and infiltrative.
First-line metastatic therapy: carboplatin plus paclitaxel; gemcitabine plus doxorubicin is second line.
Immune checkpoint and VEGF-targeted regimens for clear cell RCC are not effective for RMC.
Surgery may be considered in a deferred fashion only after response to systemic therapy.

question: A 41-year-old woman reports continuous urinary leakage that worsens with activity four months after excision of a urethral diverticulum. On examination she leaks with cough and urine pools in the vaginal vault. PVR is 20 mL and urinalysis is normal. Anticholinergic therapy has not helped. The next step is:

options.B: indwelling urethral catheter for three weeks.

rationale: Urine pooling in the vagina after urethral surgery should raise concern for a urethrovaginal fistula, which must be identified or excluded endoscopically before planning treatment. Proceeding to any sling without this evaluation risks missing the fistula; a synthetic sling in particular is contraindicated in the setting of urethral reconstruction. Prolonged catheter drainage is unlikely to close a tract that has already epithelialized. Urodynamics do not diagnose a fistula. Upper tract studies are not routinely needed for urethrovaginal fistula.
learning_point: Incontinence with pooling of urine in the vagina after urethral diverticulectomy suggests a urethrovaginal fistula; cystourethroscopy is the next step before any anti-incontinence surgery.
key_facts: Vaginal pooling of urine after urethral surgery points to fistula rather than simple SUI.
Upper tract imaging is needed for vesicovaginal, not urethrovaginal, fistula work-up.
Catheter drainage will not close an epithelialized tract months after surgery.
If fistula is confirmed, repair with an autologous fascial sling is reasonable; synthetic midurethral sling is avoided at urethral reconstruction.

question: Eighteen days after robotic radical prostatectomy with extended pelvic lymph node dissection, a 63-year-old man develops left leg swelling, and duplex ultrasound confirms a femoral vein thrombosis. He has no chest pain or dyspnea and vital signs are normal. Rivaroxaban is started. He has no personal or family history of thrombosis. Further management should include:
rationale: After pelvic lymphadenectomy, a unilateral DVT may be caused by a lymphocele or hematoma compressing the iliac vein, so pelvic imaging is needed to identify a treatable collection. Pulmonary imaging is not indicated in an asymptomatic, hemodynamically normal patient. The event is clearly provoked by surgery, so thrombophilia testing is not warranted. Direct oral anticoagulants are preferred over vitamin K antagonists, and a 3-6 month course is standard. A caval filter is reserved for patients who cannot be anticoagulated.
learning_point: A unilateral DVT after prostatectomy with pelvic lymphadenectomy should prompt pelvic imaging to look for a lymphocele or other collection compressing the iliac vein; a provoked DVT needs only 3-6 months of a DOAC and no thrombophilia work-up.
key_facts: Pelvic lymphocele after lymph node dissection can obstruct venous outflow and cause ipsilateral DVT.
Postoperative DVT is a provoked event: 3-6 months of anticoagulation, DOAC preferred over warfarin.
Chest imaging is unnecessary without respiratory symptoms or abnormal vitals.
Hypercoagulability testing is reserved for unprovoked, recurrent, or familial thrombosis.

question: A 24-year-old woman with known G6PD deficiency and an eGFR of 40 mL/min/1.73 m2 has two days of dysuria and frequency without fever or flank pain. Urinalysis shows pyuria and nitrites. The most appropriate antibiotic is:
rationale: Fosfomycin is a first-line oral agent for uncomplicated cystitis that is safe in both G6PD deficiency and moderate renal impairment. Nitrofurantoin and TMP-SMX are also first-line choices in general but both can trigger hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients and are avoided with reduced renal function. Fluoroquinolones are reserved as second-line therapy for simple cystitis. A parenteral cephalosporin is excessive for an afebrile lower tract infection.
learning_point: In uncomplicated cystitis, both nitrofurantoin and TMP-SMX are contraindicated in G6PD deficiency and in significant renal insufficiency; fosfomycin is the first-line agent that remains safe.
key_facts: First-line cystitis agents: nitrofurantoin, TMP-SMX, fosfomycin.
Nitrofurantoin and sulfonamides can precipitate hemolysis in G6PD deficiency and are avoided in CKD.
Fluoroquinolones are second line for uncomplicated cystitis.
Parenteral agents are unnecessary for afebrile cystitis.

question: A 56-year-old man with longstanding obstructive voiding symptoms develops gross hematuria. CT shows a 3 cm enhancing mass within a wide-mouthed left posterolateral bladder diverticulum with intact perivesical fat planes and no adenopathy. Biopsy of the mass shows pure squamous cell carcinoma; random bladder biopsies are negative and metastatic evaluation is normal. He wishes to preserve erectile function. The best treatment is:

options.A: neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed by cystectomy.
options.C: repeat transurethral resection to achieve complete endoscopic resection.
options.D: partial cystectomy with excision of the diverticulum.

rationale: A solitary squamous cell carcinoma confined to a bladder diverticulum with negative remaining urothelium is an ideal indication for partial cystectomy, which excises the tumor and the diverticulum and offers the best chance of preserving sexual function. Endoscopic resection within a diverticulum cannot be made complete or safe because the wall lacks muscle. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy regimens are validated for urothelial carcinoma, not SCC. Trimodal bladder-preserving therapy is not appropriate for a diverticular SCC in a man with obstructive symptoms. Radical cystectomy is more morbid than needed and compromises sexual function compared with partial resection.
learning_point: Organ-confined squamous cell carcinoma arising within a bladder diverticulum is best treated by partial cystectomy with diverticulectomy, which removes the tumor and preserves sexual function; neoadjuvant chemotherapy and trimodal therapy are not established for SCC.
key_facts: Bladder SCC in the U.S. is usually associated with chronic irritation or stasis (diverticulum, catheter, stones), not schistosomiasis.
Complete endoscopic resection within a diverticulum is unsafe and incomplete because there is no muscle layer.
Cisplatin-based neoadjuvant regimens for urothelial carcinoma have no proven benefit in pure SCC.
Partial cystectomy is appropriate for a solitary tumor confined to a diverticulum with negative random biopsies.

question: A 44-year-old woman describes two years of persistent, unwanted sensations of genital arousal that occur without sexual thoughts and are not relieved by orgasm. The symptoms are causing significant distress. Pelvic examination shows no clitoral engorgement or adhesions, and hormone levels are normal. The next step is:

options.A: pelvic venography with ovarian vein embolization.
options.E: neurologic evaluation including pudendal nerve assessment.

rationale: This presentation is persistent genital arousal disorder. Because peripheral and central neurologic lesions (pudendal nerve entrapment, sacral radiculopathy, small fiber neuropathy) are among the identifiable causes, a focused neurologic evaluation is a required part of the initial work-up. Empiric sympathomimetics or topical anesthetics treat symptoms without a diagnosis. Venous embolization is reserved for a documented pelvic vascular cause. Clitoral adhesions are absent on examination, so lysis has no role.
learning_point: Persistent genital arousal disorder (unwanted genital arousal without desire) requires evaluation for neurologic causes such as pudendal neuropathy or lumbosacral pathology before any empiric medical or surgical treatment.
key_facts: PGAD: persistent, distressing genital arousal or near-orgasm sensations unrelated to sexual interest, often with inconsistent physical signs of arousal.
Etiologies include pudendal nerve entrapment, small fiber neuropathy, lumbosacral disease, pelvic vascular malformations, and SSRI withdrawal.
Work-up: detailed history, vulvoscopy, focused neurologic testing, psychological assessment, labs.
Surgical procedures are not first-line without an identified cause.

question: A 47-year-old man with a C6 spinal cord injury has used a condom catheter since external sphincterotomy 12 years ago. Over four months he has had two febrile urinary tract infections. Renal ultrasound shows normal kidneys, and bladder ultrasound after reflex voiding shows 450 mL of urine. The next step is:

options.A: transrectal ultrasound to measure prostate volume.

rationale: Years after sphincterotomy, incomplete emptying can result from either recurrent outlet obstruction (sphincter regrowth, prostatic enlargement, stricture) or from a detrusor that has lost contractility. These require different treatments, so urodynamic evaluation is needed before intervening. Repeating the sphincterotomy or starting an alpha-blocker assumes obstruction without proof. Prophylactic antibiotics mask the underlying problem and foster resistance. A suprapubic tube may ultimately be chosen but is premature, and would not prevent urethral leakage if the outlet is still partly incompetent. Prostate volume alone does not determine the cause of retention.
learning_point: A spinal cord injured man managed with sphincterotomy and condom catheter who develops recurrent UTIs and a distended bladder needs urodynamics first to determine whether the problem is outlet re-obstruction or loss of detrusor contractility before changing therapy.
key_facts: Sphincterotomy aims to create a low-pressure incompetent outlet allowing reflex voiding into a condom catheter.
Late failure results from sphincter or prostatic regrowth, stricture, or detrusor decompensation.
UDS distinguishes obstruction from poor contractility and guides the next therapy.
Antibiotic prophylaxis before defining bladder function promotes resistance.

question: During retropubic surgery, the endopelvic fascia is incised lateral to the prostate. This fascial layer and the puboprostatic ligaments are condensations of connective tissue that is continuous with:
rationale: The pelvic organs are enveloped by the intermediate stratum of retroperitoneal connective tissue, which is a continuation of the transversalis fascia lining the abdominal wall. Condensations of this layer form the endopelvic fascia and the pelvic ligaments. Denonvilliers' fascia is a separate rectogenital septum. The levator ani and obturator internus are muscles with their own investing fascia and are not the source of the endopelvic fascia. The external oblique aponeurosis is an anterior abdominal wall structure unrelated to the pelvic fascia.
learning_point: The endopelvic fascia and the pelvic ligaments (puboprostatic, pubourethral, pubocervical) are condensations of the intermediate stratum of retroperitoneal connective tissue, which is derived from the transversalis fascia.
key_facts: Pelvic viscera are enclosed in the intermediate stratum of retroperitoneal connective tissue.
This stratum is continuous with the transversalis fascia of the abdominal wall.
Denonvilliers' fascia, levator ani, and obturator internus are not the origin of the endopelvic fascia.

question: The neurotransmitter primarily responsible for maintaining the flaccid state of the penis and producing detumescence is:
rationale: In the flaccid state the cavernosal arterioles and trabecular smooth muscle are tonically contracted under sympathetic control, mediated by norepinephrine acting on alpha-adrenergic receptors; the same pathway terminates an erection. Nitric oxide, released from NANC parasympathetic nerves and endothelium, is the principal pro-erectile mediator via cGMP. Acetylcholine, VIP, and prostaglandin E1 also promote smooth muscle relaxation and tumescence rather than detumescence.
learning_point: Penile flaccidity and detumescence are maintained by sympathetic adrenergic tone, with norepinephrine as the key neurotransmitter causing cavernosal smooth muscle contraction.
key_facts: Erection: parasympathetic non-adrenergic non-cholinergic release of nitric oxide, raising cGMP and relaxing smooth muscle.
Detumescence: sympathetic release of norepinephrine acting on alpha-1 receptors contracts trabecular and arteriolar smooth muscle.
Acetylcholine, VIP, prostaglandin E1, and cGMP all favor tumescence.

question: A 17-year-old phenotypic female is evaluated for primary amenorrhea and has sparse pubic and axillary hair. Karyotype is 46,XY and pelvic MRI shows bilateral intra-abdominal testes without a uterus. After counseling, she elects to keep her gonads. The malignancy for which she is at greatest risk is:
rationale: The presentation is complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. Testes left in place after puberty in CAIS have an increased, although relatively low, risk of germ cell malignancy, and seminoma is the tumor most commonly seen. Gonadoblastoma is characteristic of dysgenetic gonads containing Y-chromosome material, which is a different entity. Sertoli cell adenomas may be found in CAIS gonads but are benign. Yolk sac tumor and teratoma are not specifically associated with CAIS.
learning_point: In complete androgen insensitivity syndrome, retained testes carry an increased risk of seminoma (germ cell tumor) after puberty; gonadoblastoma risk applies to dysgenetic gonads, not CAIS.
key_facts: CAIS: 46,XY, nonfunctional androgen receptor, female external phenotype, testes often intra-abdominal or inguinal.
Malignancy risk is low before puberty and rises afterward; the characteristic tumor is seminoma.
Gonadoblastoma occurs in dysgenetic gonads with Y material (e.g., mixed gonadal dysgenesis), not in CAIS.
Gonad retention with surveillance is an option after counseling.

question: A 24-year-old man with urethral discharge and dysuria tests negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and is treated for nongonococcal urethritis with a complete course of doxycycline. His partner was treated at the same time. Three weeks later his symptoms persist and repeat gonococcal testing is negative. The next step is:
rationale: Persistent nongonococcal urethritis after adequate doxycycline therapy with partner treatment suggests infection with a doxycycline-resistant organism such as Ureaplasma urealyticum, which generally responds to azithromycin. Repeating doxycycline is unlikely to succeed against an organism that has already failed it. Ceftriaxone, penicillin, and amoxicillin-clavulanate are directed at gonococcal or other bacterial infections and are not effective for the organisms causing NGU.
learning_point: Nongonococcal urethritis that persists after a full course of doxycycline should be treated with azithromycin, which covers doxycycline-resistant Ureaplasma and other organisms; partners must also be treated.
key_facts: NGU is usually Chlamydia trachomatis or Ureaplasma; first-line therapy is doxycycline or single-dose azithromycin.
Failure after doxycycline suggests resistant Ureaplasma (or Mycoplasma genitalium); azithromycin is the recommended alternative in this item.
Newer CDC guidance favors testing for M. genitalium and using moxifloxacin for macrolide-resistant strains.
Cephalosporins, spectinomycin, and penicillins treat gonorrhea, not NGU.

question: A 42-year-old woman with recurrent stones has a 24-hour urine pH of 5.2 and uric acid excretion of 410 mg/day. She is started on potassium citrate, and a repeat collection six weeks later shows a pH of 6.4 and uric acid excretion of 950 mg/day with no change in diet. The most likely explanation for the change in uric acid excretion is:

options.C: reduced tubular reabsorption of urate caused by potassium citrate.
options.D: dissolution of uric acid crystals that had precipitated in the original collection.
options.E: laboratory error in the second collection.

rationale: At a urine pH of 5.2, well below the pKa of uric acid, much of the uric acid in the first collection precipitated as crystals and was not measured in the supernatant, giving a falsely low value. Raising the pH above 5.5 with potassium citrate redissolved the uric acid, so the second collection reflects her true excretion. Potassium citrate does not increase purine metabolism or alter renal urate handling in this way. Diet was unchanged, and the pattern is a known artifact rather than a laboratory error.
learning_point: When urine pH is below the pKa of uric acid (about 5.5), uric acid precipitates out of the 24-hour collection and the measured value is falsely low; alkalinization redissolves the crystals and reveals the true (higher) uric acid excretion.
key_facts: Uric acid pKa is about 5.5; below this it is largely insoluble and crystallizes in the collection container.
An apparent rise in urinary uric acid after potassium citrate reflects resuspension, not increased production.
True overproduction (Lesch-Nyhan, tumor lysis) is unrelated to alkali therapy.
Xanthine oxidase inhibition lowers, not raises, urinary uric acid.

question: A 61-year-old woman with refractory urgency incontinence had a sacral neuromodulation system implanted three years ago. Despite repeated reprogramming, her response has deteriorated. Plain films show the tined lead entering the S3 foramen far laterally and extending deep past the anterior sacral surface rather than following a medial-to-lateral course. After removal of the lead, the next step is:

options.A: place a new lead more laterally.
options.B: place a new lead at a deeper position.
options.C: place a new lead more medially using a curved stylet.
options.D: place a new lead in the S4 foramen.
options.E: explant the generator and begin onabotulinumtoxinA 100 units.

rationale: Optimal sacral neuromodulation depends on the lead running parallel to the S3 nerve, which courses from medial to lateral. A lead that is too lateral and too deep contacts the nerve poorly, and the correct revision is a more medial entry with a curved stylet so the electrodes lie along the nerve. Deeper placement risks leg stimulation and pain, and more lateral placement worsens contact. S4 is not a recommended target. Abandoning neuromodulation for botulinum toxin is premature when lead malposition explains the failure.
learning_point: Loss of sacral neuromodulation efficacy with a lead positioned too lateral and too deep in the S3 foramen is corrected by placing a new lead more medially with a curved stylet along the medial-to-lateral course of the S3 nerve.
key_facts: The S3 nerve runs medial to lateral through the foramen; the lead should follow this trajectory for maximal electrode contact.
Leads placed too deep stimulate leg muscles and cause adverse effects; lateral placement gives poor nerve contact.
S4 placement is not recommended.
If onabotulinumtoxinA is later used for OAB, the dose is 100 units, not 200.

question: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers traveling in the splanchnic nerves from T10 to L1 provide the nerve supply to the adrenal:

options.B: gland is not innervated; it is regulated only by circulating hormones.
options.D: cortex, with vagal parasympathetic fibers supplying the medulla.

rationale: The adrenal medulla is essentially a sympathetic ganglion: preganglionic cholinergic fibers from the thoracolumbar cord reach the chromaffin cells directly and trigger catecholamine release. The adrenal cortex is controlled by ACTH and the renin-angiotensin system and has no established neural supply. Parasympathetic innervation of either part of the adrenal has not been demonstrated.
learning_point: The adrenal gland receives only sympathetic innervation: preganglionic fibers from T10-L1 via the splanchnic nerves synapse directly on medullary chromaffin cells; the cortex has no demonstrated neural supply and there is no parasympathetic input.
key_facts: Chromaffin cells act as modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons releasing catecholamines.
Adrenal cortex is regulated hormonally (ACTH, angiotensin II), not neurally.
No parasympathetic innervation of the adrenal has been shown.

question: During fluoroscopic guidance for percutaneous nephrolithotomy, the largest contribution to the surgeon's radiation dose comes from:

options.A: leakage from the x-ray tube housing.
options.D: radiation reflected from the room walls and floor.

rationale: The operator does not stand in the primary beam, so direct beam exposure is not the main source of dose. Instead, Compton scatter generated when the beam interacts with the patient's tissue radiates in all directions and is the predominant source of staff exposure. This is why stepping back from the table and keeping the tube beneath the patient are effective protective measures. Tube leakage and scatter from instruments or room surfaces are comparatively negligible.
learning_point: During fluoroscopy, scatter radiation from the patient is the dominant source of operator exposure; distance from the patient and positioning the x-ray tube under the table minimize dose.
key_facts: The primary beam is collimated to the patient; the operator should never be in it.
Tube leakage and scatter from instruments, walls, or floor contribute minimally.
Dose falls with the inverse square of distance from the patient.
Under-table tube position directs scatter downward away from the operator's trunk and eyes.

question: A 31-year-old man reports inability to maintain erections with his partner for one year but has firm morning erections. After intracavernosal alprostadil 10 mcg he develops a fully rigid erection; duplex ultrasound shows bilateral cavernosal peak systolic velocities of 35 cm/sec. The most likely cause of his erectile dysfunction is:
rationale: A peak systolic velocity of 35 cm/sec is well above the threshold for arterial insufficiency, so arteriogenic ED is excluded. A fully rigid erection in response to injection indicates intact veno-occlusion, excluding venous leak and therefore any mixed vascular diagnosis. Duplex ultrasound does not evaluate neural pathways, and the history of preserved nocturnal erections also argues against an organic neurogenic cause. Situational ED with normal vascular testing in a young man is most consistent with psychogenic dysfunction.
learning_point: A normal cavernosal peak systolic velocity (>=25-30 cm/s) excludes arterial insufficiency, and achievement of a full rigid erection after intracavernosal injection excludes veno-occlusive dysfunction; in a young man with ED and these findings, psychogenic dysfunction is the most likely diagnosis.
key_facts: Penile duplex: PSV < 25-30 cm/s suggests arterial insufficiency; EDV > 5 cm/s or RI < 0.8 suggests venous leak.
A sustained full erection after injection argues against veno-occlusive dysfunction regardless of EDV.
Duplex ultrasound cannot assess neurogenic ED.
Clinical context overrides borderline vascular numbers.

question: A 33-year-old man with azoospermia and a low-volume ejaculate undergoes transurethral resection of the ejaculatory ducts for obstruction seen on TRUS. Six months later his ejaculate volume has increased from 0.6 mL to 2.4 mL but he remains azoospermic. Examination reveals a grade 2 right varicocele and normal-sized testes. The next step is:

options.D: repeat transurethral resection of the ejaculatory ducts.
options.E: scrotal exploration with testis biopsy and vasography.

rationale: Restoration of normal ejaculate volume proves that the ejaculatory ducts are now patent, so persistent azoospermia must arise from obstruction more proximally (epididymis or vas) or from failure of spermatogenesis. Scrotal exploration with testis biopsy and vasography distinguishes these and allows reconstruction or sperm retrieval. Further TRUS or repeat duct resection adds nothing once volume is normal. Varicocele repair is not indicated for obstructive azoospermia. Donor insemination is premature when the couple may achieve biologic paternity.
learning_point: If ejaculate volume normalizes after TUR of the ejaculatory ducts but azoospermia persists, the ejaculatory duct obstruction is relieved and the cause is either epididymal obstruction or testicular failure; scrotal exploration with testis biopsy (and vasography) is the next step.
key_facts: Normal post-TURED volume rules out persistent ejaculatory duct obstruction, so repeat TRUS or TURED is unnecessary.
Scrotal exploration distinguishes epididymal obstruction (reconstructable) from spermatogenic failure.
Varicocelectomy does not help obstructive azoospermia.
Donor insemination is premature when obstruction may be correctable or sperm retrievable.

question: A 64-year-old man with an orthotopic ileal neobladder requires adjuvant chemotherapy for node-positive urothelial carcinoma. The agent whose toxicity is increased by reabsorption from the intestinal reservoir is:
rationale: Methotrexate excreted into a bowel-based urinary reservoir is reabsorbed across the intestinal mucosa, prolonging systemic exposure and producing documented toxicity in patients with continent diversions. Preventive measures include draining the pouch with a catheter during infusion, vigorous hydration, urinary alkalinization, and liberal leucovorin rescue. Cisplatin, gemcitabine, doxorubicin, and vinblastine are not appreciably reabsorbed by ileal mucosa.
learning_point: Methotrexate is reabsorbed by the intestinal segment of a continent diversion or neobladder, increasing systemic toxicity; pouch drainage during administration, hydration, alkalinization, and leucovorin rescue reduce this risk.
key_facts: Intestinal mucosa in the urinary tract reabsorbs methotrexate excreted in urine.
Cisplatin, doxorubicin, vinblastine, and gemcitabine are not significantly reabsorbed.
Catheter drainage of the pouch during methotrexate infusion limits contact time.

question: A 46-year-old man with Crohn's disease who underwent ileal resection and has chronic watery diarrhea has formed six calcium oxalate stones in four years. In addition to hyperoxaluria, his 24-hour urine collection is most likely to show:
rationale: Chronic diarrhea causes loss of bicarbonate and fluid, producing systemic acidosis that drives renal citrate reabsorption and results in hypocitraturia along with low urine volume. Combined with enteric hyperoxaluria, this strongly favors calcium oxalate crystallization. Urinary calcium and magnesium are usually reduced because intestinal calcium is bound to fatty acids and magnesium is lost with malabsorption. The urine is acidic rather than alkaline, and uric acid excretion is not characteristically increased.
learning_point: Chronic diarrheal states (Crohn's disease, ileal resection) cause enteric hyperoxaluria together with hypocitraturia, low urine volume, acidic urine, and low urinary calcium and magnesium, leading to recurrent calcium oxalate stones.
key_facts: Fat malabsorption saponifies intraluminal calcium, leaving free oxalate for colonic absorption.
Bicarbonate and fluid loss in stool produce metabolic acidosis, hypocitraturia, and concentrated acidic urine.
Urinary calcium and magnesium are typically low, not high; uric acid excretion is unaffected.
Treatment: hydration, alkali citrate, oral calcium with meals to bind oxalate.

question: A 64-year-old man with metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma is being counseled about prognosis. Of the following metastatic sites, the one associated with the shortest median survival is:
rationale: Large multi-institutional data show that the organ involved by metastasis affects survival in clear cell RCC. Hepatic metastases confer the poorest outcome among the common sites, with median survival shorter than that for bone, nodal, pulmonary, or adrenal disease. Lung is the most frequent site but is relatively favorable, and adrenal metastases have the longest median survival among the listed options.
learning_point: Among metastatic sites in clear cell RCC, liver metastases carry the worst prognosis (shortest median survival), followed by bone, lymph node, lung, and adrenal; lung is the most common site but has relatively favorable survival.
key_facts: Frequency of metastasis: lung > lymph nodes > bone > liver > adrenal > brain > pancreas.
Median survival is shortest with liver (about 17-18 months) and brain metastases, longest with adrenal and lung.
Site of metastasis is an independent prognostic factor used in risk models.

question: A 68-year-old woman is about to begin a six-week course of intravesical mitomycin C for recurrent low-grade Ta urothelial carcinoma. She should be counseled that the two most frequent complications are:
rationale: Mitomycin C is a large molecule that is poorly absorbed across the urothelium, so its toxicity is mainly local: irritative chemical cystitis is common, and a contact dermatitis-type rash of the hands or genitalia occurs in roughly one in ten patients. Because systemic exposure is minimal, myelosuppression and alopecia are rare. Bladder contracture is an uncommon late effect. Fever, arthralgia, and flu-like symptoms are characteristic of BCG rather than intravesical chemotherapy.
learning_point: The most common adverse effects of intravesical mitomycin C are chemical cystitis and skin rash (contact dermatitis); its high molecular weight limits absorption, so myelosuppression is rare.
key_facts: Chemical cystitis occurs in a substantial fraction of patients receiving mitomycin C.
Rash, often palmar or genital contact dermatitis, occurs in roughly 9%.
Systemic absorption is minimal; myelosuppression and bladder contracture are rare.
Flu-like symptoms are typical of BCG, not intravesical chemotherapy.

question: A 29-year-old woman in a monogamous relationship who uses a copper intrauterine device has a thin, gray, fishy-smelling vaginal discharge. Vaginal pH is 5.0 and wet mount shows clue cells without trichomonads or yeast. The best management is:

options.A: oral metronidazole for the patient and her partner.
options.C: doxycycline for the patient and her partner.

rationale: The findings meet the clinical criteria for bacterial vaginosis, which is treated with metronidazole (orally or as vaginal gel) or clindamycin cream given to the patient only. Although BV is associated with sexual activity, treating male partners has not been shown to reduce recurrence and is not recommended. The IUD may be a risk factor but does not need to be removed. Fluconazole treats candidiasis, and doxycycline is used for chlamydia, neither of which fits this presentation.
learning_point: Bacterial vaginosis (malodorous thin discharge, pH > 4.5, clue cells) is treated with metronidazole (or clindamycin) for the patient alone; partner treatment and IUD removal are not indicated.
key_facts: BV results from replacement of lactobacilli by anaerobes; IUD use, douching, and new partners are risk factors.
Treatment: oral metronidazole 500 mg bid x 7 days, metronidazole gel, or clindamycin cream.
Routine partner therapy does not reduce recurrence and is not recommended.
Recurrence occurs in about one-third of patients.

question: During a left partial nephrectomy, the surgeon inadvertently ligates the first major branch arising from the main renal artery, a vessel that courses posterior to the renal pelvis. The renal segment most likely to become ischemic is the:
rationale: Before entering the hilum, the main renal artery gives off a small ureteral branch and then its first major division, the posterior (dorsal) segmental artery, which runs behind the renal pelvis to perfuse the posterior segment. The anterior division subsequently branches into apical, upper, middle, and lower segmental arteries. Because segmental arteries lack collateral supply, ligation of the posterior branch infarcts the posterior segment.
learning_point: The first major branch of the renal artery is the posterior (dorsal) segmental artery, which passes behind the renal pelvis and supplies the posterior segment; the anterior division supplies the apical, upper, middle, and lower segments.
key_facts: Renal artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions before the hilum; the posterior branch arises first.
Posterior segmental artery occasionally sends a branch to the apical segment.
Segmental arteries are end arteries; injury causes segmental infarction.

question: A 64-year-old man who underwent an Indiana pouch 12 years ago has recurrent urinary tract infections with Proteus mirabilis and urine pH of 7.8. He catheterizes without difficulty and is continent. CT shows a 4 cm stone and several 1-2 cm stones within the pouch, no hydronephrosis, and a thin abdominal wall with no bowel overlying the reservoir. The next step is:

options.A: endoscopic lithotripsy through the catheterizable channel.
options.C: percutaneous lithotripsy of the pouch stones.
options.E: open lithotomy with revision of the efferent limb.

rationale: These are infection-related struvite stones in a continent reservoir. The goal is complete stone clearance, because any retained fragment in an infected, mucus-producing pouch becomes a nidus for rapid recurrence. Open lithotomy accomplishes this most reliably, and a thin body habitus without intervening bowel makes access straightforward. Fragmentation by percutaneous or shock wave techniques leaves debris, and endoscopy through the catheterizable channel risks damaging the continence mechanism. Medical therapy cannot eliminate a stone burden of this size. Revision of the efferent limb is unnecessary in a continent patient with normal upper tracts.
learning_point: Large struvite stone burden in a continent cutaneous reservoir is best managed by open pouch lithotomy, which removes all stone intact and protects the continence mechanism; fragmentation techniques leave residual nidus and endoscopic access risks the efferent limb.
key_facts: Stones form in about 10% of continent cutaneous diversions; mucus, stasis, and urea-splitting organisms (Proteus) predispose.
Antibiotics and dissolution irrigation will not clear a large stone burden.
SWL and endoscopic or percutaneous lithotripsy leave fragments that re-form stones; transstomal access can injure the continence mechanism.
Pouch revision is only needed for incontinence or obstruction.

question: A 19-year-old man with recurrent hexagonal-crystal stones is diagnosed with cystinuria. In addition to cystine, his urine will contain excessive amounts of:
rationale: The defective transporter in cystinuria handles the dibasic amino acids, so cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine all appear in excess in the urine. Of these, only cystine is poorly soluble and forms stones; the others are clinically silent. Glycine and aspartic acid use different transport systems. Glycolate is elevated in primary hyperoxaluria type 1, not cystinuria, and methionine is a precursor of cystine but is not excreted in excess.
learning_point: Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive defect of the proximal tubular dibasic amino acid transporter causing excess urinary excretion of cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine (COLA); only cystine is insoluble and forms stones.
key_facts: Mnemonic COLA: cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine are all excreted in excess.
Ornithine, lysine, and arginine are soluble and do not form stones.
Glycine, glycolate, L-glycerate, and aspartate are unrelated to this transporter (glycolate and L-glycerate relate to primary hyperoxaluria).

question: A 61-year-old woman sustains a posterior bladder laceration during low anterior resection for locally advanced rectal adenocarcinoma; it is closed in two layers and a urethral catheter is left in place. Cystograms at four, seven, and ten weeks each show persistent extraperitoneal extravasation from the repair site. CT demonstrates no fluid collection, pelvic mass, or ureteral injury. The next step is:

options.C: cystoscopy with biopsy of the leak site.
options.E: continue catheter drainage and repeat cystogram in four weeks.

rationale: A bladder repair that has not sealed after ten weeks of adequate catheter drainage is unlikely to heal with more time, and in a patient operated on for advanced pelvic cancer, persistent or recurrent tumor at the repair site must be excluded. Cystoscopy with biopsy answers this question before committing to definitive treatment. Switching to suprapubic drainage offers no advantage if the urethral catheter is functioning. Fulguration or fibrin glue is appropriate only for very small tracts and still presupposes that malignancy has been excluded. Open re-repair should wait until biopsy results are known and roughly three months have elapsed since the original surgery.
learning_point: Persistent extravasation many weeks after primary repair of a bladder injury sustained during cancer surgery requires cystoscopy with biopsy to exclude recurrent or persistent malignancy before any definitive repair.
key_facts: Failure of a repaired bladder injury to heal after 6-9 weeks of catheter drainage suggests foreign body, poor drainage, or malignancy.
Further catheter drainage or a suprapubic tube is unlikely to succeed at this point.
Fulguration or fibrin glue is only for small (< 5 mm) tracts and only after cancer is excluded.
Definitive repair is delayed about three months after the index surgery to allow inflammation to settle.

question: A 34-year-old man being treated for prostatitis has a positive urine immunoassay screen for opiates at a pre-employment drug test, which he denies using. The antibiotic most likely responsible for a false-positive result is:
rationale: Quinolone antibiotics, including levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, and ofloxacin, are known to cross-react with urine opiate immunoassays and produce false-positive screens, which can be refuted with confirmatory mass spectrometry. Rifampin and poppy seed ingestion are other classic causes. Beta-lactams, tetracyclines, and nitrofurantoin do not interfere with opiate screening.
learning_point: Fluoroquinolone antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, ofloxacin, and others) can cause false-positive urine immunoassay screens for opiates; rifampin and poppy seeds do the same.
key_facts: Quinolones cross-react with opiate immunoassays; confirmatory GC/MS testing is negative.
Rifampin and poppy seed ingestion are other recognized causes.
Penicillins, cephalosporins, tetracyclines, and nitrofurantoin do not cause this interference.

question: A 22-year-old man sustains a complete spinal cord injury at T11. Once spinal shock has resolved, his most likely sexual function profile is:

options.A: both psychogenic and reflexogenic erections with impaired ejaculation.
options.B: no erections with preserved vibratory ejaculation.
options.E: reflexogenic erections with preserved vibratory ejaculation.

rationale: A complete lesion at T11 leaves the sacral reflex arc intact, so tactile stimulation produces reflexogenic erections, but it interrupts the descending pathways needed for psychogenic erections. The injury also involves the T12-L2 region that houses the spinal ejaculation generator and sympathetic outflow, so ejaculation, including vibratory-induced ejaculation, is impaired. Options describing preserved ejaculation or psychogenic erections are inconsistent with a complete lesion at this level.
learning_point: A complete suprasacral (thoracolumbar) spinal cord injury preserves reflexogenic erections via the intact S2-4 reflex arc but abolishes psychogenic erections and impairs ejaculation because the T12-L2 spinal ejaculation generator and sympathetic outflow are damaged.
key_facts: Reflexogenic erection: pudendal afferent to S2-4 parasympathetic efferent; preserved when the sacral cord is intact.
Psychogenic erections require supraspinal input through T10-L2 sympathetic pathways and are lost after complete lesions above this level.
Ejaculation is coordinated at T12-L2; lesions here impair both antegrade and vibratory ejaculation.
Sensation of orgasm is lost with complete lesions.

question: A 77-year-old confused man with congestive heart failure is found in urinary retention. He has pedal edema, jugular venous distension, blood pressure of 190/110 mmHg, and creatinine of 3.6 mg/dL with normal electrolytes. A catheter drains 2.5 L, and he produces 600 mL of urine over the following two hours. The next step is:

options.A: replace urine output milliliter for milliliter with normal saline.
options.B: check urine osmolality, sodium, and potassium.
options.C: measure creatinine daily until it normalizes.
options.D: restrict fluids and give intravenous furosemide.
options.E: record fluid intake and output every eight hours.

rationale: This patient has post-obstructive diuresis and multiple high-risk features: chronic obstruction with azotemia, volume overload, hypertension, and impaired cognition. Spot urine osmolality and electrolytes reveal whether the kidney is appropriately excreting retained salt and water or has lost concentrating ability, and they direct the composition and rate of replacement. Replacing output volume for volume prolongs the diuresis; replacement at about half of hourly output with hypotonic fluid is used when oral intake is not possible. Diuretics are inappropriate during a physiologic diuresis. Eight-hourly monitoring and daily creatinine are too infrequent for a high-risk patient who needs hourly vitals and output.
learning_point: In a high-risk patient with post-obstructive diuresis (edema, hypertension, azotemia, altered mental status), spot urine osmolality and electrolytes guide the type and rate of fluid replacement; fluids are replaced at about half of hourly output, not milliliter for milliliter.
key_facts: Post-obstructive diuresis: > 200 mL/hour for two hours or > 3 L/day after relief of obstruction.
High-risk features: chronic obstruction, volume overload, CHF, hypertension, azotemia, inability to drink.
Monitor vitals and output hourly; replace with D5 half-normal saline at half the prior hour's output if oral intake is inadequate.
Equal-volume replacement perpetuates the diuresis.

question: A 30-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has severe left flank pain unrelieved by analgesics. She is afebrile. Catheterized urinalysis shows 10 WBC/hpf. Renal ultrasound shows moderate left hydroureteronephrosis without a visible calculus and an absent left ureteral jet; the right kidney is normal. She declines CT. Empiric antibiotics are started. The next step is:

options.D: cystoscopy and left ureteral stent placement.

rationale: Left-sided hydronephrosis with an absent ureteral jet during pregnancy is unlikely to be physiologic and suggests ureteral obstruction, most commonly from a stone; pyuria adds urgency because an infected obstructed system may develop. A definitive diagnostic study is required, and with CT declined, non-contrast MRI avoids ionizing radiation and can demonstrate the level and nature of obstruction. Medical expulsive therapy or observation is inappropriate without a diagnosis in a patient with intractable pain. Stent placement and retrograde pyelography are invasive and reserved for when imaging confirms a need for intervention or is inconclusive.
learning_point: Isolated left-sided hydronephrosis in pregnancy is atypical for physiologic dilation (which favors the right) and must be investigated for obstruction such as a stone; when CT is declined, non-contrast MRI is the diagnostic study of choice after empiric antibiotics.
key_facts: Physiologic hydronephrosis of pregnancy is 2-3 times more common on the right.
Pyuria plus possible obstruction raises concern for infected obstruction and mandates diagnosis.
Low-dose CT is acceptable in pregnancy but non-contrast MR urography is the alternative when CT is refused.
Stent, nephrostomy, or retrograde study are reserved for intervention after diagnosis.

question: A four-year-old girl who underwent posterior sagittal anorectoplasty in infancy for a high anorectal malformation remains unable to toilet train. VCUG shows a thick-walled trabeculated bladder with grade 2 right vesicoureteral reflux and a large post-void residual. Renal ultrasound is normal. The next step is:
rationale: The combination of a high anorectal malformation and a trabeculated, poorly emptying bladder with reflux strongly suggests neurogenic bladder from an associated spinal cord anomaly such as tethered cord or lipomeningocele. Spinal MRI is the appropriate study because the ossified spine of a four-year-old prevents adequate sonographic evaluation. Starting catheterization or anticholinergic therapy without defining the neurologic lesion and bladder dynamics is premature. Prophylaxis alone addresses infection risk but not the underlying cause.
learning_point: Children with high anorectal malformations have a 20-50% incidence of occult spinal dysraphism; a trabeculated bladder with reflux and incomplete emptying should prompt spinal MRI, since spinal ultrasound is unreliable after about three months of age.
key_facts: Tethered cord, fatty filum, and lipoma are common with imperforate anus; severity parallels the rectal lesion.
After vertebral ossification (about three months), spinal ultrasound cannot exclude tethered cord; MRI is required.
CIC, anticholinergics, or vesicostomy are premature before urodynamic confirmation of neurogenic bladder.

question: A 24-year-old man with sickle cell disease has had four emergency department visits for ischemic priapism in six months, each resolved with aspiration and irrigation. He is sexually active and wants to preserve erectile function. The best treatment to manage future episodes is:

options.A: placement of an inflatable penile prosthesis.

rationale: Teaching a patient with recurrent ischemic priapism to self-administer intracavernosal phenylephrine at the onset of an episode aborts the event early, avoids emergency visits, and preserves erectile function. GnRH agonist therapy suppresses testosterone and is poorly suited to a young man who wishes to remain sexually active. Oral baclofen and terbutaline have inconsistent and weak supporting evidence. A penile prosthesis is a salvage option for men who have developed fibrosis or failed other therapy, not first-line management.
learning_point: For recurrent (stuttering) ischemic priapism in a sexually active man, home self-injection of intracavernosal phenylephrine is the best option; hormonal suppression with GnRH agonists impairs sexual function, and oral agents have inconsistent efficacy.
key_facts: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist with minimal cardiovascular effect; patients can be trained for home use.
