GnRH agonists and antiandrogens reduce recurrences but cause hypogonadal side effects.
Terbutaline, baclofen, digoxin, and similar oral agents have weak, variable evidence.
Penile prosthesis is reserved for refractory cases or established fibrosis.

question: A 62-year-old woman develops fever to 38.9 C and dysuria after her second induction instillation of BCG. The fever continues for four days despite acetaminophen. Urine culture is negative, urinalysis shows microscopic hematuria, and chest radiograph and liver tests are normal. BCG is discontinued. The next step is:

options.C: isoniazid and rifampin for six months.
options.D: isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol for six months.
options.E: observation and resume BCG at one-third dose.

rationale: A high fever that persists for more than 48 hours after BCG instillation and fails antipyretics, with no bacterial infection identified, is treated as early systemic BCG infection. The recommended management is to stop BCG permanently and give isoniazid alone for approximately three months. Combination antituberculous regimens for six months are indicated only when there is organ involvement such as pneumonitis, hepatitis, or sepsis, none of which is present. A fluoroquinolone treats bacterial cystitis and is not primary therapy for a mycobacterial process. Resuming BCG at any dose is contraindicated.
learning_point: Persistent high fever (>= 38.5 C) after intravesical BCG that does not respond to antipyretics, without bacteriuria, indicates possible systemic BCG infection: stop BCG and begin isoniazid for about three months; multidrug regimens are reserved for pulmonary or hepatic involvement.
key_facts: Transient low-grade fever < 48 hours is common and benign after BCG.
Persistent fever >= 38.5 C beyond 48 hours with negative cultures warrants isoniazid monotherapy for 3 months and permanent BCG discontinuation.
Pneumonitis, hepatitis, or sepsis require isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol for 6 months (plus steroids if septic).
Fluoroquinolones treat bacterial cystitis, not mycobacterial infection, as primary therapy.

question: A 59-year-old man taking lisinopril for hypertension and sildenafil 25 mg as needed for erectile dysfunction has bothersome LUTS with an IPSS of 20 and a benign prostate on exam. He chooses to start an alpha-blocker. He should be instructed to:

options.A: reduce the lisinopril dose before starting tamsulosin.
options.B: take tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily without any timing restriction.
options.C: take tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily at least four hours apart from sildenafil.
options.D: switch from sildenafil to vardenafil before starting tamsulosin.
options.E: avoid alpha-blockers and use a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor instead.

rationale: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg combined with low-dose sildenafil produces no clinically significant hypotension, and current evidence shows little difference across sildenafil doses, so the former four-hour separation rule is obsolete. Switching to vardenafil does not reduce the theoretical interaction. There is no need to lower the ACE inhibitor dose. A 5-alpha reductase inhibitor would be a slower and less appropriate choice for symptom relief in a man with a benign-sized prostate who has selected alpha-blocker therapy.
learning_point: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg can be combined with sildenafil without dose timing restrictions or antihypertensive adjustment; the historical four-hour separation for higher sildenafil doses is no longer recommended.
key_facts: Tamsulosin 0.4 mg has minimal additive hypotensive effect with PDE5 inhibitors.
Tadalafil is labeled for use with tamsulosin 0.4 mg at any dose; studies show little hypotension with sildenafil at all doses plus alpha-blockers.
Vardenafil carries the same theoretical hypotension concern as sildenafil, so switching gains nothing.
No need to reduce background antihypertensives when adding tamsulosin to a low-dose PDE5 inhibitor.

question: A 31-year-old man with anosmia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism diagnosed in adolescence has been on testosterone gel for ten years. He and his partner wish to conceive. Semen analysis shows a volume of 2.0 mL with no sperm. Exogenous testosterone is discontinued. The next step is:
rationale: Kallmann syndrome patients lack endogenous gonadotropins, and exogenous testosterone further suppresses any residual axis, producing azoospermia. After stopping testosterone, gonadotropin replacement with hCG (LH activity) plus recombinant FSH reliably induces spermatogenesis in most men. Pulsatile GnRH is an alternative but is expensive and impractical. Clomiphene works only when the pituitary can respond, which is not the case here. Sperm retrieval should not be attempted before hormonal stimulation, and post-ejaculate urine is unnecessary with a normal ejaculate volume.
learning_point: In hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Kallmann syndrome) rendered azoospermic on exogenous testosterone, fertility is restored by stopping testosterone and giving hCG plus recombinant FSH to stimulate intratesticular testosterone and spermatogenesis.
key_facts: Exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotropins and intratesticular testosterone, worsening azoospermia.
hCG substitutes for LH; recombinant FSH is added to drive spermatogenesis; pulsatile GnRH is effective but costly and cumbersome.
Clomiphene is ineffective because the pituitary cannot respond.
Post-ejaculate urine is for low-volume ejaculate; hormone assays add nothing to an established diagnosis; TESE before hormonal stimulation is inappropriate.

question: A 63-year-old man with urgency and a sensation of incomplete emptying undergoes uroflowmetry, voiding 220 mL with a peak flow of 13 mL/sec in a smooth bell-shaped curve. His PVR is 90 mL. The most accurate interpretation is that:

options.A: a pressure-flow study would add no further information.
options.B: the flow rate alone cannot distinguish outlet obstruction from detrusor underactivity.
options.C: his IPSS is likely to be greater than 20.
options.D: the study must be repeated because the voided volume is inadequate.
options.E: he is at high risk of acute urinary retention within the next decade.

rationale: Uroflowmetry measures the net result of detrusor pressure working against outlet resistance, so a reduced or borderline peak flow may arise from obstruction, a weak detrusor, or both; only a pressure-flow urodynamic study can separate these. A voided volume of 220 mL is sufficient for interpretation, so repetition is not required. A peak flow of 13 mL/sec is close to the age-adjusted mean and does not predict future retention. Flow rate correlates poorly with symptom scores, so no inference about IPSS can be made.
learning_point: A low peak flow rate reflects the combined effect of outlet resistance and detrusor contractility, so uroflowmetry alone cannot distinguish obstruction from detrusor underactivity; flow rate correlates poorly with IPSS and does not predict future retention.
key_facts: Adequate uroflow requires a voided volume of at least about 125-150 mL.
Mean Qmax in men declines with age (about 12 mL/s at 46-65 years).
Qmax has minimal correlation with symptom score.
Men with Qmax > 15 mL/s have less symptomatic improvement after TURP than those with Qmax < 15 mL/s; pressure-flow study is needed to confirm obstruction.

question: A 69-year-old man who received low-dose-rate brachytherapy for intermediate-risk prostate cancer three years ago and remains on androgen deprivation develops obstructive voiding requiring TURP. Before brachytherapy his prostate volume was 35 mL, PSA was 6.1 ng/mL, and IPSS was 9. The factor most predictive of incontinence after TURP is:
rationale: TURP after brachytherapy carries a substantial incontinence rate, and the risk rises when the procedure is performed two or more years after implantation, reflecting progressive radiation-induced fibrosis of the sphincteric urethra. The presence of obstructive symptoms at the time of surgery is the other recognized association. Androgen deprivation, gland size, pre-treatment PSA, baseline IPSS, and radiation dose have not been shown to influence the likelihood of incontinence.
learning_point: Incontinence after TURP for obstruction following prostate brachytherapy is common (at least 18%) and correlates with a longer interval (two years or more) since brachytherapy and with obstructive symptoms at the time of TURP; ADT, prostate size, PSA, dose, and baseline IPSS do not predict it.
key_facts: Delayed radiation fibrosis of the sphincter and urethra increases over time, raising incontinence risk with later TURP.
Minimal resection techniques are recommended when TURP is unavoidable after brachytherapy.
Pre-treatment PSA, prostate volume, ADT use, and pre-treatment IPSS are not associated with post-TURP incontinence.

question: A 66-year-old man underwent two-stage sacral neuromodulation for refractory urgency incontinence ten weeks ago. He now has purulent drainage from the gluteal incision, surrounding erythema, and a temperature of 38.3 C. In addition to antibiotics, the best management is:

options.A: removal of the pulse generator only, leaving the tined lead capped.
options.B: removal of the pulse generator and immediate reimplantation in a new contralateral pocket.
options.C: incision, drainage, and pocket irrigation with the device left in place.
options.D: removal of both the pulse generator and the tined lead.
options.E: removal of the pulse generator and lead with placement of a new lead at the same operation.

rationale: Purulent drainage, erythema, and fever at the generator pocket indicate an infected implant. Because bacterial biofilm extends from the generator along the attached lead, the entire system must be explanted; leaving the lead behind risks persistent or recurrent infection. Irrigation with device retention does not clear biofilm on prosthetic material. Placing any new hardware (a new generator or a new lead) at the time of explant exposes it to the infected field and has a high failure rate. Once the patient has healed and the infection is treated, a repeat test stimulation can be considered.
learning_point: An infected sacral neuromodulation pulse generator requires removal of the entire system (generator and tined lead) because biofilm tracks along the lead; no new hardware should be placed until the infection has fully resolved.
key_facts: Infection rate after sacral neuromodulation is roughly 3-10%; purulent drainage, erythema, and fever at the generator pocket indicate device infection.
Biofilm contaminates the connected lead, so partial explant (generator only) leaves infected material behind.
Reimplantation or simultaneous lead placement at the time of explant carries an unacceptably high reinfection risk.
After healing and antibiotic treatment, a repeat staged test can be offered.

question: An 88-year-old nursing-home resident who is known to have chronic asymptomatic bacteriuria develops new dysuria, urgency, and new-onset urge incontinence over 48 hours. She is afebrile with a benign abdomen. Urine culture grows more than 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli susceptible to all tested agents. The best management is:

options.B: renal ultrasound and cystoscopy before any treatment.
options.C: no antibiotics, because bacteriuria is chronic in this patient.
options.D: a single oral dose of fosfomycin.
options.E: begin vaginal estrogen cream and reassess in four weeks.

rationale: The appearance of new lower urinary tract symptoms in a patient with previously asymptomatic bacteriuria represents acute cystitis and warrants antibiotic treatment for 3 to 7 days; a five-day course of nitrofurantoin is a guideline-endorsed first-line option. Observation is wrong because she is now symptomatic. Single-dose regimens are inadequate for this population. Cystoscopy and upper tract imaging are not indicated for uncomplicated cystitis or recurrent UTI in women without red flags. Vaginal estrogen reduces future recurrences in postmenopausal women but does not treat an active infection.
learning_point: An older patient with known asymptomatic bacteriuria who develops new urinary symptoms has a symptomatic UTI and should receive a short antibiotic course (3-7 days); single-dose therapy, observation, and imaging are not appropriate.
key_facts: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common in institutionalized elderly women and is not treated, but new lower tract symptoms change the diagnosis to cystitis.
First-line regimens: nitrofurantoin 5 days, TMP-SMX 3 days (if local E. coli resistance < 20%), or a beta-lactam for 7 days; fluoroquinolones are no longer first-line.
AUA guidelines do not recommend cystoscopy or upper tract imaging for uncomplicated recurrent UTI in women.
Vaginal estrogen is a preventive strategy in postmenopausal women, not treatment of an acute infection.

question: A 47-year-old woman reports constant vaginal leakage of urine beginning two weeks after a total laparoscopic hysterectomy for fibroids; she is now six weeks postoperative. CT urogram shows no ureteral injury. Cystoscopy shows a single 10 mm fistula on the posterior bladder wall just above the trigone, well away from the ureteral orifices, with healthy surrounding mucosa. The best management is:

options.A: cystoscopic fulguration of the tract and catheter drainage.
options.B: indwelling catheter for six more weeks, then reassess.
options.C: transabdominal repair with omental interposition now.
options.D: transabdominal repair deferred until three months after the hysterectomy.

rationale: A 1 cm fistula is too large to be expected to close with prolonged catheter drainage, so continued catheterization only delays definitive care. Modern data show that repair at six weeks, once the tissue is healthy, achieves results equivalent to waiting three months, so deferral is unnecessary. The fistula is accessible from the vagina and does not involve the ureters, so a transvaginal repair offers high success with less morbidity than an abdominal approach. Fulguration has weak evidence and is reserved for tiny tracts.
learning_point: A 1 cm post-hysterectomy vesicovaginal fistula diagnosed at about six weeks will not close with catheter drainage alone; prompt repair is appropriate, and a simple supratrigonal/subtrigonal fistula without ureteral involvement is best approached transvaginally.
key_facts: Small (< 5 mm) early fistulas may close with catheter drainage; a 1 cm fistula will not.
Early repair (once tissues are healthy and non-inflamed) yields outcomes equal to delayed repair; waiting three months is no longer required.
Transvaginal repair has high success with lower morbidity than abdominal repair for accessible fistulas; tissue interposition (Martius or peritoneal flap) is often added.
Endoscopic fulguration has limited supporting data and is reserved for tiny tracts.

question: A 68-year-old man with a five-year history of Parkinson's disease reports urgency, nocturia four times nightly, occasional urgency incontinence, and a slow stream. Urodynamics demonstrate phasic involuntary detrusor contractions during filling, a cystometric capacity of 240 mL, a voiding detrusor pressure of 95 cm H2O with a maximum flow of 6 mL/sec, and a post-void residual of 180 mL. Sphincter EMG is quiet during voiding. The best initial treatment is:
rationale: The pressure-flow data (high detrusor pressure with very low flow) establish bladder outlet obstruction, most likely from prostatic enlargement, superimposed on the detrusor overactivity expected in Parkinson's disease. An alpha-blocker addresses the obstruction and should be tried first. Antimuscarinics or botulinum toxin would treat the overactivity but risk worsening emptying while the outlet remains obstructed. Baclofen targets striated sphincter spasticity, which is not present here; relaxed EMG during voiding confirms no dyssynergia, which in any case is not a feature of Parkinson's disease. CIC and outlet surgery are reserved for failure of medical therapy.
learning_point: In a man with Parkinson's disease whose urodynamics show detrusor overactivity together with high-pressure, low-flow voiding (bladder outlet obstruction), an alpha-blocker trial is the first step; antimuscarinics may worsen emptying and baclofen is irrelevant because sphincter dyssynergia does not occur in Parkinson's disease.
key_facts: Parkinson's disease causes detrusor overactivity; true detrusor-external sphincter dyssynergia is not a feature (unlike spinal cord injury).
High voiding pressure with low Qmax indicates outlet obstruction, typically from BPH in older men.
Treat the obstruction first (alpha-blocker) before adding antimuscarinics that could precipitate retention.
Outlet surgery in Parkinson's disease carries acceptable continence outcomes, unlike multiple system atrophy, but a medication trial comes first.

question: A 29-year-old man and his partner have 18 months of infertility. He has had recurrent sinus infections and productive cough since childhood. Semen analysis on two occasions shows volume 2.8 mL, concentration 41 million/mL, normal pH, and 0% motile sperm; no leukocytes are seen. Testes are normal in size and both vasa are palpable. The next step is:
rationale: The combination of lifelong sinopulmonary infections, a normal sperm count, and complete absence of motility points to primary ciliary dyskinesia, in which structural flagellar defects leave the sperm alive but immotile. A viability stain or hypo-osmotic swelling test confirms this and guides use of the sperm for ICSI. CFTR testing is relevant for absent vasa and azoospermia, not for this picture with palpable vasa and normal counts. Endocrine testing addresses low concentration rather than isolated motility loss. TRUS is invasive and is reserved for suspected ejaculatory duct obstruction, and the absence of pyospermia makes infection unlikely.
learning_point: Normal sperm concentration with total asthenozoospermia in a man with chronic sinopulmonary disease suggests primary ciliary dyskinesia; a sperm viability test is the next step and will show that the immotile sperm are alive.
key_facts: Primary ciliary dyskinesia (immotile cilia syndrome; Kartagener's when with situs inversus) produces normal counts with absent motility from axonemal defects.
Viability testing (eosin or hypo-osmotic swelling) distinguishes live-but-immotile sperm from dead sperm; viable immotile sperm can be used for ICSI.
CBAVD/cystic fibrosis and Young's syndrome also feature respiratory disease but cause azoospermia, not isolated asthenozoospermia.
Hormonal deficiency reduces concentration, not motility alone; TRUS is more invasive and reserved for suspected ductal obstruction.

question: A 68-year-old woman who underwent a retropubic midurethral sling seven weeks ago reports straining to void, a feeling of incomplete emptying, and urgency with leakage. Catheterized residual is 280 mL. Urinalysis shows 30-50 RBC/hpf and 20-40 WBC/hpf; culture is pending. She is started on intermittent catheterization. The next step is:
rationale: This patient has iatrogenic obstruction after a midurethral sling, and sling incision will eventually be needed regardless of urodynamic findings. However, the combination of hematuria and pyuria raises the possibility that the mesh has perforated or eroded into the urethra or bladder, which must be excluded endoscopically before choosing the operation. If erosion is found, excision rather than simple incision is required. Urodynamics add little when symptoms clearly began after surgery. An alpha-blocker will not correct a fixed mechanical obstruction.
learning_point: New voiding difficulty and elevated residual after a midurethral sling indicate obstruction, but hematuria and pyuria mandate cystoscopy to rule out urethral or bladder perforation/erosion before planning sling incision.
key_facts: Post-sling retention with symptoms beginning immediately after surgery is treated by sling incision (loosening); urodynamics rarely change this decision.
Microscopic hematuria plus pyuria after sling raises concern for mesh erosion or perforation, which requires cystoscopic evaluation.
Sling excision (full removal) is reserved for erosion; simple incision preserves more continence.
Alpha-blockers do not relieve fixed iatrogenic anatomic obstruction.

question: A 59-year-old man taking tadalafil 20 mg on demand reports effective erections but develops aching low back and thigh pain for about a day after each dose. The off-target enzyme most responsible for this adverse effect is:
rationale: Tadalafil is relatively selective for PDE5 but has meaningful activity against PDE11, an isoform expressed in skeletal muscle and testis; this cross-reactivity is the accepted explanation for the myalgia and back pain seen more often with tadalafil than with other agents. PDE6 inhibition causes visual color changes and is more characteristic of sildenafil and vardenafil. PDE1, PDE3, and PDE9 have not been linked to clinically important adverse effects of the approved PDE5 inhibitors. A patient with bothersome myalgia can be switched to sildenafil or avanafil.
learning_point: Tadalafil's cross-inhibition of phosphodiesterase type 11 is thought to cause its characteristic back pain and myalgia, whereas PDE6 cross-reactivity (greater with sildenafil and vardenafil) causes blue-green visual disturbance.
key_facts: All PDE5 inhibitors have some off-target activity; the profile differs by agent.
PDE6 in the retina: sildenafil and vardenafil bind it more than tadalafil or avanafil, producing color-vision changes.
PDE11 in skeletal muscle and testis: tadalafil has the greatest affinity, linked to myalgia and low back pain.
Switching agents can resolve a bothersome class-specific side effect.

question: A 44-year-old woman with a 2.5 cm left adrenal adenoma, elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol, and suppressed ACTH is scheduled for laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Her preoperative evaluation shows a hemoglobin A1c of 8.1%. The essential elements of her perioperative management are:

options.B: spironolactone, stress-dose hydrocortisone, and insulin infusion.
options.C: stress-dose hydrocortisone and tight glucose control.

rationale: An ACTH-independent cortisol-producing adenoma suppresses the normal contralateral adrenal, so removing the tumor leaves the patient acutely glucocorticoid deficient; stress-dose steroids with a prolonged taper are mandatory. Glucocorticoid excess also produces insulin resistance, reflected in her elevated A1c, so glucose must be monitored closely perioperatively. Alpha-blockade and volume loading are the preparation for pheochromocytoma, and beta-blockers are added there only after alpha-blockade. Mineralocorticoid antagonists and potassium replacement are for primary hyperaldosteronism, not for Cushing's syndrome.
learning_point: Patients undergoing adrenalectomy for cortisol-secreting tumors (Cushing's syndrome) need perioperative stress-dose glucocorticoids, because the contralateral gland is suppressed, plus close glycemic control; alpha-blockade is for pheochromocytoma and potassium repletion/spironolactone for aldosteronoma.
key_facts: Chronic cortisol excess suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary axis and the contralateral adrenal; adrenal insufficiency follows resection unless steroids are given.
Cushing's patients are often diabetic, obese, and hypertensive; perioperative hyperglycemia requires management.
Pheochromocytoma: preoperative alpha-blockade, volume expansion, then beta-blockade if tachycardic.
Aldosteronoma: correct hypokalemia, often with spironolactone or eplerenone.

question: A urologist comparing shock-wave lithotripters notes that one design is historically associated with the highest stone-free rates in part because its broad focal zone keeps a moving stone within the treatment volume. This generator type is:
rationale: Spark-gap, or electrohydraulic, generators create a relatively wide focal zone, so stones that shift with respiration remain within the high-pressure region; the unmodified HM3 remains the benchmark for efficacy largely for this reason. Piezoelectric arrays use a wide aperture that reduces skin discomfort but produce a very small focal zone and lower success rates. Electromagnetic machines produce higher peak pressures with a smaller focal zone than spark-gap units. Microexplosive and electroconductive designs are of historical interest only.
learning_point: Electrohydraulic (spark-gap) lithotripters such as the original Dornier HM3 have the largest focal zone, which eases targeting and contributes to high stone-free rates; piezoelectric devices have the smallest focal zone and electromagnetic devices are intermediate with higher peak pressures.
key_facts: Larger focal zone tolerates respiratory stone movement and improves fragmentation efficiency.
Piezoelectric: wide aperture, small focal zone, less pain, lower stone-free rates.
Electromagnetic: smaller focal zone, higher peak pressures, more consistent output than spark gap.
Microexplosive and electroconductive generators are not in general use.

question: A 39-year-old man undergoes left radical orchiectomy for a 5 cm pure seminoma with lymphovascular invasion. Postoperative AFP, hCG, and LDH are normal. Staging CT shows a single 1.6 cm left para-aortic lymph node just below the renal hilum and no thoracic disease. His estimated GFR is 38 mL/min from longstanding IgA nephropathy. The best treatment is:

options.B: 20 Gy to the para-aortic nodes alone.
options.C: left modified-template retroperitoneal lymph node dissection.
options.D: 30 Gy to the para-aortic and left pelvic nodes.
options.E: four cycles of etoposide and cisplatin.

rationale: A single sub-2 cm node in the primary landing zone of a left testis tumor with normal markers is clinical stage IIA seminoma. Standard options are radiotherapy of 30 Gy to a dog-leg field or cisplatin-based chemotherapy; because this patient's GFR is reduced, platinum chemotherapy is undesirable and radiotherapy is the choice. The 20 Gy para-aortic-only field and single-dose carboplatin are adjuvant regimens for stage I disease and are inadequate when nodal disease is visible. RPLND for stage II seminoma is investigational and, when performed, requires a full bilateral template rather than a modified one.
learning_point: Clinical stage IIA seminoma (retroperitoneal node 1-2 cm in the landing zone) is treated with radiotherapy of 30 Gy to the para-aortic and ipsilateral pelvic nodes or with BEP x3/EP x4; when renal impairment precludes cisplatin, radiotherapy is preferred. Adjuvant 20 Gy or single-agent carboplatin applies only to stage I.
key_facts: Right testis landing zone: interaortocaval nodes; left: para-aortic/preaortic nodes.
Stage IIA = nodes <= 2 cm; radiotherapy dose 30 Gy (36 Gy for IIB) to a dog-leg field.
Cisplatin-based chemotherapy is relatively contraindicated with reduced renal function.
RPLND for low-volume stage II seminoma (SEMS trial) is an emerging option but uses a bilateral full template, not a modified template.

question: A urology resident performing a high volume of fluoroscopic procedures asks about her dosimeter badge readings. According to National Council on Radiation Protection and Measurements recommendations, the maximum permissible annual whole-body occupational dose is:
rationale: The NCRP sets the annual occupational whole-body effective dose limit at 5 rem (50 mSv). The other figures correspond to different limits: 0.5 rem is the total allowed to the fetus of a declared pregnant worker, 15 rem is the annual limit to the lens of the eye, and 50 rem is the annual limit for an individual organ or the skin. One rem is the recommended ceiling for members of the general public from a licensed facility, not for occupational exposure. Practical dose reduction follows ALARA using shielding, distance, and minimized beam time.
learning_point: The NCRP occupational whole-body dose limit is 5 rem (50 mSv) per year; the fetal limit for a pregnant worker is 0.5 rem over the pregnancy and the limit to an individual organ is 50 rem per year.
key_facts: 5 rem = 5,000 mrem = 50 mSv annual whole-body occupational limit.
Fetus of a declared pregnant worker: 0.5 rem (5 mSv) total, 0.05 rem/month.
Single organ or skin: 50 rem/year; lens of eye: 15 rem/year.
ALARA principles: shielding (apron, thyroid collar, glasses), distance, under-table tube, minimizing fluoroscopy time.

question: During a clitoroplasty for congenital adrenal hyperplasia, the surgeon wishes to preserve glans sensation. At the mid-shaft of the clitoral body, the major nerve trunks that must be protected are located:

options.A: within the septum between the two corpora.
options.C: on the dorsal surface of the corpora.
options.D: along the lateral walls of each corpus.

rationale: The dorsal nerves of the clitoris, branches of the pudendal nerve, run on the dorsal surface of the clitoral body in a position homologous to the dorsal penile nerves. Although fine fibers encircle the shaft, no large trunks lie ventrally, laterally, or in the intercorporal septum, and the bulbospongiosus muscle carries no major sensory bundle to the glans. Surgical approaches that preserve or reflect the dorsal bundle are therefore essential to maintain erotic sensation.
learning_point: The main neurovascular bundles of the clitoris run along the dorsal aspect of the clitoral body, paralleling the dorsal nerves of the penis; this region must be protected during clitoral and gender-affirming surgery to preserve sensation.
key_facts: Clitoral innervation mirrors the penis: paired dorsal nerves from the pudendal nerve travel on the dorsum of the corporal bodies.
Small fibers encircle the corpora, but the ventral, lateral, and intercorporal regions lack major trunks.
Dorsal nerves fan out over the glans, so dissection near the 11 and 1 o'clock positions is highest risk.
Preservation of the dorsal bundle is key in clitoroplasty and gender-affirming genital surgery.

question: A 17-year-old girl with normal breast development has never menstruated. She has scant pubic hair, a female external phenotype, and a firm nodule in the left groin. Karyotype is 46,XY and serum testosterone is in the adult male range. Examination of the introitus is most likely to show:

options.A: a normal cervix with a transverse septum in the upper vagina.
options.B: a bifid clitoris with a widened pubic symphysis.
options.C: a bulging bluish membrane at the introitus.
options.E: a longitudinal vaginal septum with two cervices.

rationale: Normal breast development (from aromatization of testosterone), absent menses, scant pubic hair, a 46,XY karyotype, male-range testosterone, and an inguinal gonad together define complete androgen insensitivity syndrome. The testes secrete anti-Mullerian hormone, so the uterus, cervix, and upper vagina regress, leaving only a short blind vaginal pouch derived from the urogenital sinus. A bulging bluish membrane indicates imperforate hymen and a transverse septum indicates a Mullerian fusion defect, both occurring in 46,XX individuals with a uterus present. Duplicated Mullerian structures require a uterus, which is absent here. Bifid clitoris occurs with bladder exstrophy.
learning_point: A phenotypic female with primary amenorrhea, 46,XY karyotype, and male-range testosterone has complete androgen insensitivity syndrome; because functioning testes produce anti-Mullerian hormone, the uterus and upper vagina are absent and examination shows a short, blind-ending vagina.
key_facts: CAIS: androgen receptor defect; testes present (often inguinal), testosterone and LH elevated, no Mullerian structures.
Vagina is short and blind-ending; no cervix or uterus; sparse pubic and axillary hair.
Imperforate hymen and transverse vaginal septum cause amenorrhea with normal 46,XX karyotype and present with hematocolpos.
Bifid clitoris is a feature of bladder exstrophy, not disorders of sex development.

question: A 61-year-old man with muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma is counseled about urinary diversion before radical cystectomy. He asks for an orthotopic neobladder. Which finding in his history or workup would make an ileal neobladder inappropriate?

options.A: tumor extending onto the bladder neck.
options.B: external beam radiation for prostate cancer eight years ago.
options.D: a 1.5 cm obturator lymph node on CT.
options.E: multifocal carcinoma in situ in the bladder.

rationale: An orthotopic neobladder is built from a long segment of terminal ileum; active or prior inflammatory bowel disease of the small intestine jeopardizes the reservoir and risks fistula, stricture, and malabsorption, so Crohn's disease is a contraindication. Carcinoma in situ and bladder neck tumor do not preclude a neobladder in a man as long as the intraoperative urethral margin is negative. Lymph node metastases do not change the type of diversion. Prior pelvic irradiation raises complication rates but neobladders can still be constructed when the bowel appears healthy, so it is a relative rather than absolute contraindication.
learning_point: Inflammatory small bowel disease such as Crohn's disease (along with short bowel syndrome) is a contraindication to using ileum for an orthotopic neobladder; carcinoma in situ, bladder neck tumor in men, positive pelvic nodes, and prior pelvic radiation are not absolute contraindications.
key_facts: Absolute contraindications to orthotopic diversion: positive urethral margin, inability to self-catheterize or impaired cognition, severe renal insufficiency, Crohn's disease or short bowel.
Prior pelvic radiation increases complication and incontinence risk but is a relative contraindication only.
Node-positive disease is not a contraindication; it does not change the diversion choice.
Bladder neck or prostatic urethral involvement in men mandates frozen-section urethral margin, but a negative margin permits neobladder.

question: A 36-year-old woman with a RET mutation and a 4 cm right adrenal pheochromocytoma has been on phenoxybenzamine titrated to the maximum tolerated dose for three weeks, yet she continues to have paroxysms of blood pressure above 200/110 mm Hg with palpitations. The next step is:
rationale: Persistent hypertensive paroxysms despite full-dose alpha-blockade indicate inadequate preoperative preparation; the recommended addition is metyrosine, which inhibits tyrosine hydroxylase and reduces catecholamine production, thereby improving control before anesthesia. Operating now risks intraoperative crisis and cardiovascular collapse. Adding a beta-blocker while alpha-blockade is incomplete can provoke unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction and worsen hypertension. Switching to a selective alpha-1 blocker such as doxazosin is unlikely to improve on maximal phenoxybenzamine. Metyrapone inhibits cortisol synthesis and is irrelevant to pheochromocytoma.
learning_point: When pheochromocytoma remains poorly controlled despite maximal phenoxybenzamine, add metyrosine (a tyrosine hydroxylase inhibitor that lowers catecholamine synthesis) before surgery; surgery without adequate blockade is dangerous, and beta-blockers without full alpha-blockade can worsen hypertension.
key_facts: Preoperative preparation: nonselective alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine) for 1-2 weeks with volume repletion.
Metyrosine depletes catecholamine stores and is added when alpha-blockade alone fails or in very high-secreting tumors.
Beta-blockers are added only after alpha-blockade, for reflex tachycardia; given alone they cause unopposed alpha stimulation.
Selective alpha-1 agents (prazosin, doxazosin) are alternatives but are less effective at preventing intraoperative crises; clonidine and metyrapone have no role.

question: A 70-year-old man with chronic retention and a creatinine of 6.2 mg/dL is catheterized and drains 2 L of urine, after which output continues at 400 mL/hr for 18 hours despite oral intake; urine osmolality remains near 250 mOsm/kg and his serum sodium begins to fall. The mechanism that distinguishes this pathologic diuresis from a physiologic one is:

options.A: excretion of retained urea and sodium.
options.D: impaired tubular concentrating and sodium-reabsorbing capacity.

rationale: After relief of prolonged obstruction, most patients have an appropriate (physiologic) diuresis that eliminates the sodium, urea, and water accumulated during obstruction and stops once euvolemia is restored. When the diuresis persists beyond that point and the kidney cannot concentrate urine or retain sodium, the cause is tubular damage with a nephrogenic concentrating defect and salt wasting; this pathologic form threatens volume depletion and electrolyte derangement and requires intravenous replacement. Options A and E describe the physiologic variety. Prostaglandin and angiotensin changes are not the basis of pathologic post-obstructive diuresis.
learning_point: Physiologic post-obstructive diuresis is the appropriate excretion of retained sodium, urea, and water and resolves on its own; pathologic post-obstructive diuresis stems from tubular injury with impaired concentrating ability or sodium reabsorption and requires active fluid and electrolyte replacement.
key_facts: Expect diuresis > 200 mL/hr after relief of bilateral obstruction or obstruction of a solitary kidney.
Physiologic: driven by volume overload and retained solutes; patients can usually self-regulate with oral intake.
Pathologic: nephrogenic diabetes insipidus-like concentrating defect or salt-wasting from medullary and tubular damage; replace roughly half of urine output with IV fluids and monitor electrolytes.
Prostaglandins, angiotensin II, and free water clearance are not the mechanism of the pathologic form.

question: A 68-year-old man develops C. difficile colitis after perioperative antibiotics for a radical cystectomy and is started on oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily. Two days later he has ten liquid stools per day, a temperature of 39 C, abdominal distension, and a white blood cell count of 28,000/microL. The next step is:

options.C: add oral fidaxomicin and continue observation.

rationale: Worsening diarrhea with high fever, marked leukocytosis, and distension on standard oral vancomycin represents fulminant C. difficile colitis that is failing medical therapy; such patients are at risk of toxic megacolon and perforation and need early surgical evaluation, since subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy improves survival. Oral metronidazole is less effective than vancomycin and is a step backward. Intravenous vancomycin is not excreted into the colon and does not treat CDI. Fluoroquinolones are a major risk factor for hypervirulent C. difficile and are never a treatment. Substituting another oral agent and waiting delays life-saving intervention.
learning_point: Clostridioides difficile colitis that progresses to fever, leukocytosis, and worsening diarrhea despite oral vancomycin is fulminant disease; prompt surgical consultation for possible subtotal colectomy is indicated, as IV vancomycin and fluoroquinolones have no role.
key_facts: Oral vancomycin (or fidaxomicin) is first-line; oral metronidazole is inferior.
IV vancomycin does not reach the colonic lumen and is ineffective; IV metronidazole may be added in fulminant disease but does not replace surgery when the patient is deteriorating.
Markers of fulminant disease: WBC > 15,000, creatinine rise, hypotension, ileus, megacolon.
Subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy improves survival in fulminant, medically refractory CDI; fluoroquinolones promote the hypervirulent NAP1 strain.

question: A 63-year-old man with moderate LUTS asks whether he should take an over-the-counter saw palmetto extract instead of a prescription drug. Based on randomized placebo-controlled trials, you tell him that compared with placebo, saw palmetto alone is expected to produce:

options.B: a measurable decrease in prostate volume.
options.D: a modest increase in peak flow rate.
options.E: a reduced need for future BPH surgery.

rationale: Well-designed placebo-controlled trials, including dose-escalation studies, have found that saw palmetto is no better than placebo for symptom scores, peak flow, prostate size, PSA, or progression endpoints such as retention or surgery. The one respect in which it matches placebo is safety: adverse effects are mild and occur at similar rates. Thus, the honest counsel is that the supplement is safe but ineffective, and guidelines do not recommend it.
learning_point: In placebo-controlled trials, saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) monotherapy for BPH-related LUTS does not improve symptom scores, flow rates, prostate volume, or retention risk; its only similarity to placebo is a comparable, mild adverse-event profile.
key_facts: High-quality trials (STEP, CAMUS) showed no benefit over placebo even at escalating doses.
No effect on IPSS, Qmax, PSA, prostate volume, or progression to retention.
Adverse events are mild and equivalent to placebo.
AUA guidelines do not recommend saw palmetto for LUTS/BPH.

question: A 10-year-old boy is brought in because of blood drops appearing at the end of his urine stream and spots in his underwear over the past month. He has no pain, fever, or trauma, and his genital and abdominal examinations are normal. Urinalysis shows 2-4 RBC/hpf without protein, and urine culture is sterile. The next step is:

options.E: non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis.

rationale: Bleeding confined to the end of voiding with minimal microscopic hematuria, normal examination, and a sterile culture in a school-aged boy is characteristic of benign urethrorrhagia, an idiopathic self-limited inflammation of the bulbar urethra. Management is reassurance and follow-up; ultrasound and uroflow may be added but are typically normal. Cystoscopy and VCUG require urethral instrumentation, which can aggravate the inflamed urethra and is associated with later strictures. CT exposes the child to radiation for a condition that does not involve the upper tract, and metabolic stone testing is irrelevant to terminal hematuria.
learning_point: Terminal gross hematuria or blood spotting in an otherwise healthy prepubertal or adolescent boy with normal examination and negative culture is benign urethrorrhagia, which is self-limited; observation is appropriate, and cystoscopy or VCUG should be avoided because instrumentation can worsen urethral inflammation and strictures.
key_facts: Urethrorrhagia: blood at the end of voiding or in the underwear, often with mild dysuria, in boys aged 5-15.
Noninvasive evaluation (renal/bladder ultrasound, uroflow, PVR) is optional and usually normal.
Resolution typically occurs within months to a couple of years; strictures are an occasional late finding.
Calcium:creatinine ratio and CT are for suspected stone disease or hypercalciuria, not terminal bleeding.

question: During holmium laser enucleation of a 140 g prostate, the entire adenoma has been enucleated into the bladder when the surgeon notices a sizeable capsular defect with saline extravasating into the extraperitoneal space. The patient is hemodynamically stable with normal airway pressures. The best management is:

options.A: complete morcellation and remove the catheter the next morning.
options.B: stop, place a catheter, and return for morcellation in several days.
options.C: complete morcellation and keep the catheter for about three days.
options.E: place a suprapubic tube and leave the adenoma in the bladder.

rationale: Capsular perforation during HoLEP is managed conservatively when the patient is stable: the already-enucleated adenoma should be morcellated and removed in the same session, and the catheter is left in place for a few days to allow the defect to seal rather than being removed the next day. Aborting the procedure forces a second anesthetic without benefit. Open exploration is reserved for large intraperitoneal injuries or massive extravasation with hemodynamic compromise. Leaving the adenoma in the bladder is not acceptable, and routine next-day catheter removal risks ongoing extravasation.
learning_point: A capsular perforation with extraperitoneal extravasation recognized after complete adenoma enucleation during HoLEP does not require aborting or open conversion in a stable patient; finish morcellation and leave the urethral catheter for several days rather than overnight.
key_facts: Routine HoLEP: catheter removed the next morning if no perforation.
Significant capsular perforation: complete the case, prolong catheter drainage (about 3 days), monitor for TUR-like fluid absorption.
Open exploration is reserved for large intraperitoneal bladder injuries or massive extravasation with instability.
The mushroom technique is an alternative enucleation strategy, not a remedy for perforation.

question: A 42-year-old man undergoes right ureteroscopic laser lithotripsy of a 2 cm lower-pole stone with a stent placed afterward. Ten days after stent removal he reports intermittent mild right flank discomfort controlled with ibuprofen. He is afebrile with a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL. Low-dose CT shows a 3 cm column of 1-3 mm fragments in the distal ureter with mild hydronephrosis. The next step is:

options.C: shock wave lithotripsy to the distal fragments.
options.E: analgesia and repeat imaging in one to two weeks.

rationale: A column of small fragments in the distal ureter is a steinstrasse. When the patient is afebrile, has controlled pain, and has normal renal function, conservative management is appropriate because most such columns pass spontaneously, but close imaging follow-up is required to detect persistent obstruction. Stenting or nephrostomy is indicated for infection, intractable pain, or renal deterioration, none of which is present. Ureteroscopy is highly effective and becomes the definitive treatment if the fragments fail to clear, and SWL of a leading fragment is a secondary option in the same circumstance.
learning_point: Steinstrasse after stone surgery in a patient with mild symptoms, no fever, and normal renal function can be observed with serial imaging because 50-60% clear spontaneously; decompression or ureteroscopy is reserved for persistent obstruction, infection, or intolerable pain.
key_facts: Steinstrasse: column of fragments in the ureter, usually distal, after SWL or ureteroscopy for large stones.
Conservative management acceptable when afebrile, pain controlled, and no renal impairment; follow with imaging.
Fever or sepsis mandates urgent stent or nephrostomy.
Ureteroscopy is definitive when intervention is needed; SWL of a leading fragment is an alternative.

question: A 34-year-old man with lifelong premature ejaculation begins daily paroxetine. At follow-up his ejaculatory latency has improved. Which adverse effect is he most likely to report as a direct consequence of ongoing therapy?
rationale: Erectile dysfunction and reduced sexual desire are among the most frequent adverse effects of serotonergic antidepressants when used for premature ejaculation, along with yawning, nausea, excessive sweating, and fatigue. Libido falls rather than rises, and sweating increases rather than decreases. SSRIs treat rather than cause depression in this context. Insomnia is typically part of the discontinuation syndrome after abrupt cessation, not a dominant effect of continuing therapy.
learning_point: SSRIs used off-label for premature ejaculation commonly cause erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, yawning, nausea, sweating, and fatigue; insomnia is a feature of discontinuation syndrome rather than ongoing therapy.
key_facts: Daily paroxetine, sertraline, fluoxetine, or on-demand dapoxetine delay ejaculation via serotonergic effect.
Sexual side effects: erectile dysfunction, reduced desire, anorgasmia.
Abrupt cessation causes discontinuation syndrome: dizziness, nausea, headache, anxiety, insomnia.
Combining serotonergic agents can produce serotonin syndrome.

question: A 31-year-old woman with a complete T6 spinal cord injury performs CIC five times daily. Over the past ten days she has noticed markedly increased leg spasms and a vague sense of malaise, without fever or change in catheterization volumes. Urine culture grows 10,000 CFU/mL of Klebsiella pneumoniae. The next step is:

options.A: treat only if urinalysis shows pyuria.
options.B: repeat the culture in two weeks.

rationale: Patients with complete cord injuries lack bladder sensation and do not report dysuria or urgency; instead, infection manifests as increased spasticity, malaise, new incontinence, or dysreflexia. New spasticity plus a positive culture (well above the 100 CFU/mL threshold used in CIC patients) therefore represents symptomatic UTI and should be treated. Pyuria is unreliable in catheterizing patients and should not gate treatment. Escalating antispasmodics treats the symptom without addressing the cause. Urodynamics are reserved for recurrent symptomatic infections to look for high storage pressures.
learning_point: In a patient with complete spinal cord injury on CIC, new increased spasticity (or incontinence between catheterizations, malaise, cloudy urine) is a symptom of UTI; a culture with >= 100 CFU/mL in a symptomatic patient should be treated with antibiotics rather than observed.
key_facts: Bacteriuria is nearly universal on CIC and pyuria may reflect catheter irritation, so neither alone defines infection.
Symptomatic UTI in SCI: fever, increased spasticity, autonomic dysreflexia, new leakage, flank or abdominal discomfort.
Threshold for significant bacteriuria on CIC is >= 100 CFU/mL in a symptomatic patient.
If spasticity persists after treatment, search for other noxious stimuli (pressure sore, constipation, ingrown nail, syrinx) before adding baclofen.

question: A 61-year-old woman with stage 3 anterior and apical prolapse reports leakage she cannot characterize. During multichannel urodynamics at a capacity of 450 mL, repeated coughs and Valsalva with the prolapse reduced by a speculum blade produce no urethral leakage. Before finalizing surgical plans, the next step is:

options.A: infuse an additional 100 mL and repeat the stress maneuvers.
options.B: schedule prolapse repair with a concomitant midurethral sling.
options.C: remove the urethral catheter and repeat the stress maneuvers with prolapse reduced.
options.D: schedule prolapse repair alone with no anti-incontinence procedure.
options.E: repeat the study using a pessary for reduction.

rationale: A urodynamic catheter can obstruct the urethra enough to prevent demonstration of stress incontinence, so guidelines recommend repeating cough and Valsalva testing after the catheter is removed, with the prolapse still reduced, in patients suspected of SUI who did not leak with the catheter in place. Only after this complete evaluation can one rationally decide whether to add a sling or proceed with prolapse repair alone. Filling beyond capacity is unphysiologic and not recommended. Switching the reduction device is not expected to change the result since no method is standardized.
learning_point: When a woman with high-grade prolapse suspected of having stress incontinence fails to leak during urodynamic stress testing with prolapse reduced, the AUA/SUFU guideline directs repeating stress maneuvers after removing the urethral catheter before deciding on a concomitant sling.
key_facts: A urethral catheter can mask stress incontinence by partially obstructing the urethra.
Advanced prolapse kinks the urethra and may hide occult SUI, which can appear after prolapse repair.
There is no standardized method of prolapse reduction during UDS; changing the reduction method is not expected to alter findings.
Overfilling beyond capacity is not recommended.

question: A 63-year-old man has a 3 cm pruritic, well-demarcated erythematous plaque on the scrotum extending onto the penile shaft that has failed topical antifungals. Biopsy shows Paget cells within the epidermis. In addition to surgical excision, his evaluation should include:

options.B: peripheral blood flow cytometry for T-cell clonality.

rationale: Paget cells in genital skin define extramammary Paget's disease, which in men is linked to a synchronous or subsequent carcinoma of the urethra, bladder, prostate, or rectum in up to one-third of cases; endoscopic evaluation of the lower urinary tract (along with colorectal screening) is therefore an essential part of the workup. The disease shares only a name with Paget's disease of bone, so skeletal imaging is unnecessary. HPV is associated with verrucous and squamous carcinoma and HIV with Kaposi sarcoma, not with EMPD. T-cell lymphoma would be evident on histology and is not linked to Paget's disease.
learning_point: Extramammary Paget's disease of the penis or scrotum is associated with an underlying visceral malignancy (urethral, bladder, rectal) in 10-30% of cases, so excision must be accompanied by screening for these, including cystourethroscopy.
key_facts: EMPD: intraepithelial adenocarcinoma of apocrine-bearing skin; presents as erythematous, sharply demarcated, often pruritic plaque.
Treatment is wide excision or Mohs surgery; margins are often positive microscopically.
Screen for associated GU and GI cancers: cystourethroscopy, colonoscopy, PSA as appropriate.
No association with HPV, HIV, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, or Paget's disease of bone.

question: A 58-year-old woman has a left kidney obstructed for an estimated four months by an impacted ureteral stone; after nephrostomy placement, the surgeon wants to know whether the kidney will regain enough function to justify reconstruction rather than nephrectomy. The imaging study that most accurately predicts recovery is:
rationale: Recovery after prolonged obstruction depends on the amount of viable cortical tissue, which is most directly measured by a cortical agent; DMSA uptake by functioning tubular cells correlates better with eventual recovered function than do the tubular tracers. MAG-3 and DTPA are excellent for drainage curves and differential function in the acute setting but tend to underestimate the salvageable function of a chronically obstructed kidney. Doppler indices reflect vascular resistance rather than nephron mass, and CT parenchymal thickness has not been validated for this purpose.
learning_point: DMSA, a cortical-binding agent, best predicts the recoverable renal function after relief of prolonged obstruction, outperforming the tubular agents MAG-3 and DTPA; ultrasound and CT parenchymal thickness are not reliable predictors.
key_facts: DMSA binds proximal tubular cells and images functioning cortical mass.
MAG-3 (tubular secretion) and DTPA (glomerular filtration) assess drainage and differential function but underestimate recovery in obstructed kidneys.
Doppler ultrasound evaluates arterial inflow and resistive index, not functional reserve.
CT cortical thickness remains investigational for predicting recovery.

question: A 49-year-old woman notices vaginal urine leakage 12 days after a total vaginal hysterectomy. Cystoscopy shows a 3 mm fistula on the posterior bladder wall above the trigone, and CT urogram shows normal ureters without extravasation. After a Foley catheter is placed she is completely dry. The next step is:

options.B: continue catheter drainage and add an antimuscarinic.
options.C: tampon dye test to confirm the diagnosis.

rationale: A tiny fistula recognized early that renders the patient dry when the bladder is decompressed has a real chance of healing spontaneously, so a period of continuous catheter drainage, commonly with an antimuscarinic to suppress bladder spasms, is the appropriate first step. The diagnosis is already established by cystoscopy and the ureters are already cleared by CT urogram, so dye tests and retrograde studies are redundant. Surgical repair, by whichever route, is reserved for fistulas that persist after two to three weeks or more of conservative management, or for larger fistulas unlikely to close.
learning_point: A small vesicovaginal fistula diagnosed within the first few weeks after hysterectomy that leaves the patient dry with an indwelling catheter should be managed by continued catheter drainage (often with an antimuscarinic), because spontaneous closure is possible; repair is considered only if it persists after several weeks.
key_facts: Early small fistulas may close spontaneously with 2-6 weeks of bladder decompression.
Dryness with the catheter in place is a favorable sign; continued leakage despite catheter predicts failure of conservative therapy.
Once the diagnosis is confirmed cystoscopically and upper tracts are cleared by CT, additional dye tests or retrograde pyelograms add nothing.
Persistent fistula after conservative trial is repaired transvaginally or abdominally depending on location.

question: A 34-year-old woman with a complete C6 spinal cord injury managed by CIC has had three episodes in the past week of pounding headache, facial flushing, and sweating above the shoulders, each with a blood pressure near 190/100 mm Hg. Non-contrast CT shows a 10 mm stone at the left ureteropelvic junction with hydronephrosis; the stone measures 350 Hounsfield units. Urinalysis shows pH 5.0, moderate blood, few leukocytes, and no bacteria. The next step is:

options.B: potassium citrate to dissolve the stone.

rationale: Her paroxysms of hypertension with headache and sweating above the lesion are autonomic dysreflexia triggered by the obstructing stone; this condition can cause stroke or seizure and demands immediate elimination of the stimulus. A ureteral stent relieves the obstruction reliably and quickly. Although the low-density stone is probably uric acid, alkalinization takes weeks and is inappropriate in a symptomatic obstructed patient, and medical expulsive therapy is futile for a 10 mm stone at the UPJ. SWL does not promptly relieve obstruction. Definitive stone clearance by ureteroscopy or PCNL is reasonable later once she is stable.
learning_point: An obstructing stone in a patient with spinal cord injury above T6 that provokes autonomic dysreflexia (headache, sweating, hypertension) is an emergency requiring prompt decompression with a ureteral stent; medical dissolution or expulsive therapy and SWL do not reliably relieve the obstruction.
key_facts: Autonomic dysreflexia: lesion at or above T6, noxious stimulus below the lesion causes unopposed sympathetic surge with severe hypertension and headache.
Urologic triggers include bladder distension, obstruction, stones, and instrumentation.
Immediate goal is removal of the stimulus; stent or nephrostomy relieves obstruction promptly.
Definitive stone treatment (URS or PCNL) follows once stable and uninfected; alkalinization is for asymptomatic uric acid stones.

question: A 28-year-old man living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy presents with three days of left scrotal pain and swelling; examination shows a tender, indurated epididymis with normal testis and no abscess on ultrasound. Along with urine nucleic acid testing for gonorrhea and chlamydia and empiric ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, he should undergo:
rationale: Acute epididymitis in a sexually active young man is presumed to be a sexually transmitted infection, and the diagnosis of one STI is an indication to screen for others; syphilis is especially important in men with HIV, in whom its incidence is many times that of the general population. A nontreponemal test (RPR or VDRL) followed by treponemal confirmation is the standard approach. Hepatitis B and C screening is not part of the epididymitis algorithm. Prostatic secretion culture is reserved for suspected chronic prostatitis, and tissue sampling of the epididymis is unnecessary when there is no abscess or suspicion of tumor or tuberculosis.
learning_point: A sexually active man under 35 with acute epididymitis is evaluated for gonorrhea and chlamydia, treated empirically with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, and screened for other STIs including syphilis (and HIV if status unknown); hepatitis serologies, prostatic secretion cultures, and biopsy are not part of the evaluation.
key_facts: CDC: urethral Gram stain, NAAT for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis, first-void urine leukocytes.
Empiric therapy: ceftriaxone IM plus doxycycline for 10 days (add fluoroquinolone coverage for enteric organisms if insertive anal sex).
Syphilis incidence is dramatically elevated in men with HIV; screen with RPR/VDRL and confirm with treponemal test.
HIV testing is also recommended for anyone with a new STI.

question: A 64-year-old woman who underwent cystectomy with ileal conduit three years ago has an incidental 9 mm calculus seen within the conduit on a plain film obtained for back pain. She has no fever, flank pain, or change in stomal output, the stoma appears healthy, and renal ultrasound shows no hydronephrosis. The next step is:

options.A: flexible endoscopy through the stoma with basket extraction.
options.B: holmium laser lithotripsy via the stoma.
options.D: contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis.

rationale: Stones within the lumen of an ileal conduit typically result from urinary stasis, but a conduit that drains freely allows most such stones to pass on their own; in an asymptomatic patient with a healthy stoma and no hydronephrosis, observation with periodic imaging is appropriate. A loopogram evaluates for stomal or ureteroileal stenosis, which would be expected to produce upper tract dilation that is absent here. CT adds little once the stone is identified and the kidneys are normal. Endoscopic extraction or lithotripsy is effective but is reserved for stones that cause symptoms or fail to pass.
learning_point: An asymptomatic small stone within an ileal conduit, without hydronephrosis or stomal stenosis, can be observed because most conduit stones pass spontaneously; intervention is reserved for symptoms or failure to pass, and loopogram or CT is unnecessary when the upper tracts are normal.
key_facts: Conduit lumen stones are uncommon (< 10%) and relate to stasis, often from stomal or conduit stenosis.
Unlike continent reservoirs, conduits drain freely so small stones usually pass.
Normal renal ultrasound argues against outflow obstruction, so loopogram is not needed.
Endoscopic retrieval or laser fragmentation is reserved for symptomatic or retained stones.

question: A 57-year-old man with Peyronie's disease and medication-refractory erectile dysfunction undergoes placement of a three-piece inflatable prosthesis. With the cylinders inflated, a 95-degree dorsolateral curvature is seen; after two rounds of manual modeling it measures 65 degrees. The next step is:

options.A: perform additional modeling until the curve is less than 30 degrees.
options.B: remove the cylinders and place a malleable device.
options.C: remove the cylinders, perform grafting, and stage the prosthesis for six months later.
options.E: leave the inflatable device and correct the residual curve with plication or incision and grafting.

rationale: A residual curve of 65 degrees would still interfere with intercourse and should be corrected during the same operation. With the inflatable cylinders in place and inflated, the surgeon can straighten the penis by plication on the convex side or by incising the plaque and grafting the defect; both are accepted adjuncts and neither is clearly superior. Repeated modeling after two attempts rarely produces further gain and increases the risk of urethral or corporal injury. Switching to a malleable prosthesis does not address the deformity, and staging the prosthesis is unnecessary since the device can be protected during the straightening maneuver.
learning_point: During inflatable penile prosthesis placement for erectile dysfunction with Peyronie's disease, residual curvature greater than about 30 degrees after manual modeling should be corrected at the same operation with plication or incision/grafting rather than accepting the curvature or switching to a malleable device.
key_facts: Manual modeling over the inflated cylinders corrects most curvature; repeat modeling of a severe curve seldom achieves much more.
Residual curvature < 30 degrees is functionally acceptable; curvature > 60 degrees impairs penetration.
Plication and incision with grafting are both appropriate adjuncts with the IPP in place.
Changing to a malleable or two-piece device does not straighten the penis.

question: A 61-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has two days of worsening scrotal pain. His temperature is 37.4 C. The scrotal skin is edematous, dusky, and tender, and crepitus is felt on the left hemiscrotum. Ultrasound shows marked scrotal wall thickening with multiple hyperechoic foci producing dirty posterior shadowing; both testes are normal and a 1 cm epididymal cyst is noted. The best management is:

options.A: emergent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics.
options.E: incision and drainage of the scrotal wall at the bedside.

rationale: Crepitus and ultrasonographic gas within a thickened scrotal wall in a diabetic patient establish necrotizing fasciitis (Fournier's gangrene) even in the absence of fever. This is a surgical emergency: all necrotic skin and fascia must be excised promptly, often in repeated sessions, with broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms. Antibiotics with supportive care or a limited incision and drainage leave necrotic tissue behind and carry high mortality. The testes have an independent blood supply and are typically spared, so orchiectomy is not routinely required, and the incidental epididymal cyst is irrelevant.
learning_point: Scrotal cellulitis in a diabetic man with subcutaneous gas on imaging (hyperechoic foci with dirty shadowing on ultrasound) is Fournier's gangrene; treatment is emergent wide debridement of all necrotic tissue plus broad-spectrum antibiotics, regardless of the absence of fever.
key_facts: Fournier's gangrene: polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis of perineum/genitalia; diabetes, obesity, alcoholism, and immunosuppression are risk factors.
Ultrasound sign: hyperechoic subcutaneous foci with reverberation or dirty shadowing indicate gas; CT also shows gas and fascial thickening.
Testes are usually spared because of their separate blood supply.
Antibiotics alone, NSAIDs, or simple incision and drainage are inadequate; repeated debridement is often required.

question: A 45-year-old recurrent calcium oxalate stone former begins a ketogenic diet heavy in meat and eggs for weight loss. On repeat 24-hour urine collection, the parameter expected to decrease compared with his prior study is:
rationale: Diets rich in animal protein and poor in carbohydrates deliver a substantial acid load; the kidney responds by reabsorbing more citrate in the proximal tubule, so urinary citrate falls along with urine pH. At the same time, calcium excretion rises as bone buffers the acid and tubular calcium reabsorption decreases, uric acid excretion rises from the purine content of meat, and sulfate rises as a marker of sulfur-containing amino acid metabolism. Urinary oxalate is not reduced by protein intake and may rise. The net effect is hypocitraturia with hypercalciuria and hyperuricosuria, all favoring stones.
learning_point: A high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet imposes an acid load that lowers urinary citrate and pH while increasing urinary calcium, uric acid, and sulfate, thereby raising stone risk.
key_facts: Animal protein metabolism generates sulfuric acid; urinary sulfate is a marker of animal protein intake.
Acid load promotes bone calcium release and reduces tubular calcium reabsorption, increasing calciuria.
Acidosis increases proximal tubular citrate reabsorption, lowering urinary citrate.
Purine load raises uric acid excretion; low urine pH favors uric acid crystallization.

question: During robotic partial nephrectomy, the surgeon uses the argon beam coagulator on the resection bed. Within a minute the anesthesiologist reports a sharp rise in peak airway pressures and falling tidal volumes; oxygen saturation and blood pressure are unchanged, and the abdomen appears tense. The next step is:

options.A: lower the argon generator power and continue coagulation.
options.B: reduce the CO2 insufflator flow rate.
options.C: give a bolus of neuromuscular blocker.
options.D: increase FiO2 to 100% and place the patient in left lateral decubitus.
options.E: open a trocar valve to release intra-abdominal gas.

rationale: The argon beam coagulator delivers a continuous jet of argon that accumulates in the closed peritoneal cavity; without venting, intra-abdominal pressure climbs quickly, splinting the diaphragm and producing exactly this pattern of high airway pressures with low tidal volumes and a tense abdomen. Releasing gas through a port restores ventilation at once. Lowering the generator power still adds gas, and reducing CO2 insufflator flow does not evacuate what is already present. Hyperoxygenation with positional change and central aspiration is the treatment for gas embolism, which would present with hypotension and desaturation rather than isolated ventilatory compromise. Additional paralysis does not address the mechanical cause.
learning_point: During laparoscopy, the argon beam coagulator adds gas to the abdomen and can rapidly raise intraperitoneal pressure, causing decreased tidal volumes; the immediate response is to vent or release the pneumoperitoneum rather than adjust ventilation or lower the generator power.
key_facts: Argon gas flow (several L/min) rapidly increases intra-abdominal pressure if a port is not vented.
High intra-abdominal pressure impairs diaphragmatic excursion and reduces tidal volume and venous return.
Gas embolism presents differently (sudden hypotension, hypoxia, end-tidal CO2 drop) and is treated with FiO2 100%, left lateral decubitus/Trendelenburg, and aspiration via central line.
Lowering insufflator flow does not remove gas already delivered.

question: A nine-year-old girl is thrown from a horse and lands on a fence post, striking her right flank. In the emergency department she is alert with a heart rate of 96 and blood pressure of 108/66 mm Hg; there is a large flank contusion with tenderness. Urinalysis shows no blood, and chest and pelvic radiographs show no fractures. The next step is:

options.B: admission for observation and serial hematocrits without imaging.
options.C: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis.

rationale: A direct high-energy blow to the flank from a fixed object is itself an indication for renal imaging in a child, because the degree of hematuria does not predict renal injury in children and their vigorous sympathetic response preserves blood pressure even with substantial bleeding. Contrast CT with delayed images is the study of choice to detect and grade parenchymal and collecting system injury. Ultrasound lacks sensitivity for grading and for detecting urinary extravasation. Observation or discharge without imaging risks missing a significant laceration or vascular injury. There is no pelvic fracture or gross hematuria to suggest bladder injury, so cystography is not needed.
learning_point: In children, hematuria correlates poorly with renal injury and blood pressure is maintained despite blood loss, so imaging criteria are broader than in adults; a significant mechanism such as a direct high-velocity flank blow mandates contrast CT of the abdomen even with normal urinalysis and stable vitals.
key_facts: Pediatric imaging indications: gross hematuria; microhematuria with shock; significant deceleration/high-velocity mechanism or direct flank blow; associated major injuries (rib, spine, pelvic, femur fractures, intra-abdominal injury).
Children compensate hemodynamically with high sympathetic tone, masking hemorrhage.
Ultrasound cannot reliably grade renal injury or detect urinary extravasation.
Cystogram is reserved for pelvic fracture or gross hematuria suggesting bladder injury.

question: A 41-year-old man with a BMI of 44 kg/m2 is found to have a morning total testosterone of 235 ng/dL on two occasions; his calculated free testosterone is within the normal range. The remainder of his hormone profile is most likely to show:

options.A: normal LH, low estradiol, and elevated SHBG.
options.B: low LH, low estradiol, and low SHBG.
options.C: normal LH, elevated estradiol, and low SHBG.
options.D: elevated LH, low estradiol, and elevated SHBG.
options.E: elevated LH, elevated estradiol, and elevated SHBG.

rationale: In morbid obesity, insulin resistance suppresses hepatic production of SHBG, so total testosterone falls while the free fraction is relatively maintained, exactly as in this patient. Abundant aromatase in visceral fat converts testosterone to estradiol, raising estradiol levels. Because estradiol exerts negative feedback on the pituitary while testosterone is low, the two influences roughly cancel and LH is typically normal rather than frankly elevated or suppressed. Patterns with high SHBG or low estradiol are inconsistent with obesity-related hypogonadism; elevated LH would indicate primary testicular failure.
learning_point: Obesity lowers total testosterone chiefly by reducing hepatic SHBG and increasing aromatase conversion to estradiol; free testosterone is often preserved and LH is usually in the normal range because elevated estradiol feedback offsets the low testosterone.
key_facts: About 97-99% of testosterone circulates bound to SHBG and albumin; SHBG falls with obesity, insulin resistance, and nephrotic syndrome.
Visceral adipose aromatase raises estradiol, which suppresses gonadotropins.
Result: low total T, roughly normal free T, elevated estradiol, normal (not elevated) LH.
Weight loss raises SHBG and total testosterone; aromatase inhibitors or SERMs are treatment options when fertility matters.

question: An eight-year-old girl who underwent a left dismembered pyeloplasty at age 1 presents with colicky left flank pain and emesis. An ultrasound four months ago showed only mild residual pelviectasis. Current CT shows a 6 mm stone impacted at the left ureteropelvic junction with new moderate hydronephrosis and no other stones. The best management is:

options.A: two weeks of tamsulosin with repeat imaging.

rationale: A symptomatic, obstructing stone of this size lodged at the UPJ will not pass with medical expulsive therapy, particularly because it has not entered the ureter. Shock wave lithotripsy has markedly lower stone-free rates in children with prior reconstructive surgery, and PCNL is more invasive than needed for a single stone under 15 mm. Ureteroscopic laser fragmentation offers near-complete clearance with minimal morbidity and is the preferred option. The recent ultrasound showing minimal dilation demonstrates that the pyeloplasty remains patent, so the hydronephrosis is from the stone and revision pyeloplasty is unwarranted.
learning_point: A 7 mm symptomatic UPJ stone in a child with prior pyeloplasty and no evidence of recurrent obstruction is best treated by ureteroscopic laser lithotripsy; SWL performs poorly after reconstruction, medical expulsive therapy will not pass a stone of this size from the UPJ, and pyeloplasty revision is not indicated when the anastomosis is patent.
key_facts: Ureteroscopy achieves excellent stone-free rates for pediatric stones < 15 mm with low morbidity.
SWL is acceptable for pediatric stones up to about 15 mm but has reduced success in anatomically altered or reconstructed systems.
PCNL is reserved for larger burdens or when retrograde access fails.
Recent imaging showing minimal hydronephrosis indicates the prior pyeloplasty is functioning; hydronephrosis now is due to the stone.

question: A 24-year-old woman sustains an open-book pelvic fracture in a motorcycle crash. Rectal and vaginal examinations are normal. A urethral catheter cannot be advanced, so a 16 Fr suprapubic tube is placed and returns grossly bloody urine that drains poorly. CT urogram shows intact kidneys and ureters. Cystogram shows a bladder distended by a large filling defect with contrast rimming its periphery and no extravasation. The next step is:

options.A: maintain suprapubic drainage and perform delayed urethroplasty in three months.
options.B: laparotomy for repair of intraperitoneal bladder rupture.
options.C: operative clot evacuation with exploration and repair of the bladder neck and urethra.
options.D: exchange the suprapubic tube for a 24 Fr catheter.
options.E: continuous bladder irrigation through the suprapubic tube.

rationale: The cystogram pattern of contrast outlining a large clot without leakage indicates the bladder wall is intact, so the extensive bleeding must come from a bladder neck or urethral injury, consistent with the failed catheterization. In women with pelvic fracture, such injuries are repaired early because delayed repair leads to incontinence, fistula, and stricture, and the clot-filled bladder itself must be opened and evacuated since it will not drain. Irrigation or a larger tube does not treat the injury and will not clear organized clot. Bladder rupture is excluded by the cystogram. Delayed urethroplasty is a strategy for male posterior urethral distraction, not for female bladder neck injury.
learning_point: After pelvic fracture, failure to pass a urethral catheter with a bladder full of clot but no extravasation on cystogram implies a bladder neck or urethral injury; the bladder should be opened to evacuate clot and the bladder neck/urethral injury repaired primarily, because delayed repair of bladder neck injuries worsens continence.
key_facts: Pelvic fracture urethral injury: blood at meatus, inability to void, failed catheter; confirm with retrograde urethrogram.
A cystogram showing contrast outlining a large clot (rim sign) without extravasation excludes bladder rupture.
Massive hematuria without bladder or upper tract injury points to bladder neck or proximal urethra as the bleeding source.
Bladder neck injuries in women and children are repaired early; prolonged drainage alone leads to incontinence and stricture.

question: A 27-year-old man with poor-risk NSGCT (bulky retroperitoneal nodes, mediastinal and lung metastases) completes four cycles of BEP with normalization of AFP and hCG. Restaging shows a 2.5 cm residual retroperitoneal mass, a 1.2 cm right lung nodule, and a 1 cm residual mediastinal node. Post-chemotherapy RPLND is performed and the pathology shows only necrosis and fibrosis. The next step is:

options.A: surveillance with serial imaging and tumor markers.
options.B: thoracotomy to resect the lung nodule and mediastinal node.
options.C: two additional cycles of etoposide and cisplatin.
options.D: FDG-PET scan to assess the thoracic lesions.
options.E: CT-guided biopsy of the lung nodule.

rationale: The retroperitoneum is resected first because its histology is the best available predictor of what remains at other sites; when the RPLND specimen shows only necrosis, the chance that a small thoracic residual harbors teratoma or viable germ cell tumor is only about 10%, so surveillance is justified. Resecting every thoracic lesion would subject most patients to unnecessary thoracotomy. Biopsy of a 1 cm nodule is unreliable for excluding teratoma. FDG-PET is not validated for NSGCT residuals since teratoma is PET-negative. Additional chemotherapy is not indicated with normal markers and necrosis in the resected specimen.
learning_point: After chemotherapy for metastatic NSGCT with residual masses at multiple sites and normal markers, RPLND is performed first; if the retroperitoneal histology is fibrosis/necrosis, small residual masses elsewhere can be surveilled because they very rarely harbor teratoma or viable tumor.
