FDG-PET has no role in NSGCT.
key_facts: Post-chemo residual masses > 1 cm in the retroperitoneum with normal markers require RPLND.
Histologic discordance between sites exists, but necrosis in the RPLND specimen predicts necrosis elsewhere in about 90% of cases.
Extraretroperitoneal masses are more likely to be necrotic than retroperitoneal masses.
PET is useful only for post-chemotherapy seminoma residuals > 3 cm.

question: A 14-month-old girl followed since birth for left hydroureteronephrosis has a normal VCUG. Serial ultrasounds show a persistently dilated 15 mm distal ureter with worsening caliectasis. MAG-3 diuretic renography shows the left kidney contributing 33% of function with a drainage half-time of 35 minutes. She has had no infections while on prophylaxis. The next step is:

options.A: refluxing ureteroneocystostomy as a temporizing measure.
options.C: continue prophylaxis and repeat renography in 12 months.

rationale: A dilated distal ureter without reflux, delayed drainage on diuretic renography, and differential function that has fallen below 40% define a primary obstructive megaureter that is damaging the kidney, and continued observation would risk further loss of function. At 14 months the bladder and ureter are large enough for definitive reconstruction, so a tapered ureteral reimplant is the operation of choice. Cutaneous ureterostomy or a deliberately refluxing reimplant are temporizing strategies for neonates and young infants in whom a tapered reimplant is technically difficult. Nephrostomy drainage is reserved for a septic, obstructed infant failing antibiotics.
learning_point: A primary obstructive megaureter in an infant older than about 6-8 months with reduced differential renal function (< 40%) or symptoms warrants surgical correction, and the standard operation is excisional tapering with ureteral reimplantation; temporary diversions and refluxing reimplants are reserved for very young or very ill infants.
key_facts: Most primary megaureters improve spontaneously; observation with antibiotic prophylaxis is appropriate when function is preserved and the child is asymptomatic.
Indications for surgery: differential function < 40%, declining function, recurrent infection, or pain.
Tapered (excisional or folded) reimplant is the definitive repair in children beyond early infancy.
Cutaneous ureterostomy or refluxing reimplant is a temporizing option in very young infants; PCN is for infected, obstructed, septic infants.

question: A 29-year-old woman has hypertension of 172/104 mmHg despite maximal-dose amlodipine. Renal angiography shows a beaded, string-of-beads stenosis of the mid and distal portions of both main renal arteries; the segmental branches are normal. The next step is:
rationale: The angiographic picture of bilateral beaded mid-to-distal main renal artery stenosis in a young woman is fibromuscular dysplasia. When blood pressure cannot be controlled medically, the recommended intervention for main renal artery FMD without branch involvement is balloon angioplasty, which has excellent technical and clinical success and usually makes stenting unnecessary. Primary stenting is reserved for dissection or failed angioplasty, and surgical bypass is reserved for branch disease or lesions not amenable to percutaneous treatment. Adding an ACE inhibitor or ARB is not appropriate when a correctable lesion is causing refractory hypertension, and particularly with bilateral stenoses it risks renal function loss. Functional imaging adds nothing after angiography has already defined the lesions.
learning_point: Renovascular hypertension from fibromuscular dysplasia (young woman, bilateral, distal main renal artery, no branch disease) that is uncontrolled on medication is treated with percutaneous transluminal balloon angioplasty; stenting is reserved for angioplasty failure and surgery for branch disease or lesions not amenable to percutaneous therapy.
key_facts: FMD: predominantly young to middle-aged women, often bilateral, involves mid-to-distal main renal artery (beaded appearance), unlike proximal atherosclerotic lesions.
Balloon angioplasty alone has high success in FMD; primary stenting is not needed and surgical revascularization is for branch disease or percutaneous failure.
Poor BP control on medication is the indication to intervene rather than add another agent; angiography already establishes the diagnosis so no further imaging is needed.

question: A 61-year-old woman underwent radical cystectomy with an orthotopic ileal neobladder four years ago. She has bilateral 4 cm ureteroenteric strictures that have been managed with chronic indwelling ureteral stents exchanged every three months. Her creatinine has risen from 0.9 to 1.6 mg/dL over 18 months; bicarbonate and potassium are normal, and she voids to completion without incontinence. The next step is:

options.B: takedown of the neobladder and conversion to an ileal conduit.
options.C: endoscopic balloon dilation of both strictures.
options.D: open ureteral reconstruction using an interposed bowel segment.

rationale: Progressive renal decline despite chronic stenting indicates that the stents are not providing adequate drainage, and neither larger nor additional stents have been shown to preserve renal function. Lengthy strictures (here 4 cm) are poor candidates for balloon dilation because recurrence approaches certainty. The patient has a continent, well-emptying neobladder with normal electrolytes, so there is no indication to abandon the reservoir; the problem is the ureters, which should be definitively reconstructed and anastomosed to the neobladder, usually requiring an interposed bowel segment given the length of the strictures. Nephrostomy tubes trade one chronic tube for another and do not render the patient tube-free.
learning_point: Long (>1 cm) bilateral ureteroenteric strictures with declining renal function on chronic stents require definitive open reconstruction (often with bowel interposition because of stricture length); changing stent size or number, balloon dilation, and converting a well-functioning neobladder to a conduit do not solve the problem.
key_facts: Chronic indwelling stents are associated with pyelonephritis, incomplete drainage, and progressive renal deterioration; stent caliber or number does not improve renal preservation.
Endoscopic balloon dilation or incision has very high failure rates for strictures longer than about 1 cm.
A continent, well-emptying neobladder with normal electrolytes should be preserved; reconstruct the ureters rather than convert the diversion.

question: A 59-year-old man had a radical prostatectomy for Grade Group 4, pT3bN0 prostate cancer with a positive margin. Two years later his PSA has risen to 0.4 ng/mL on two consecutive measurements. The imaging study most sensitive for identifying a pelvic lymph node recurrence is:

options.C: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis with bone scan.

rationale: PSMA-targeted PET/CT has the highest detection rate for sites of recurrence at low PSA values after prostatectomy and is now the preferred imaging test for biochemical recurrence. Fluciclovine PET is better than choline and conventional imaging but was inferior to PSMA PET in direct comparison. FDG PET has low sensitivity for prostate adenocarcinoma, especially when PSA is below 1 ng/mL. Multiparametric MRI performs reasonably for local recurrence in the fossa but is less sensitive than PET for nodal disease, and CT with bone scan is rarely positive at this PSA level.
learning_point: For biochemical recurrence after radical prostatectomy at a low PSA (around 0.5 ng/mL), PSMA PET/CT is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting nodal and distant recurrence, outperforming fluciclovine, choline, FDG PET, and conventional CT/MRI.
key_facts: PSMA PET detects recurrence at lower PSA values than fluciclovine or choline PET; in head-to-head comparison PSMA outperformed fluciclovine.
FDG PET has poor sensitivity for prostate cancer recurrence, particularly at low PSA levels.
Multiparametric MRI is useful for local recurrence in the prostate bed but is inferior to PET for nodal and distant disease.

question: A 66-year-old man with urgency, frequency, and a weak stream undergoes pressure-flow urodynamics. During filling there are several involuntary detrusor contractions, each accompanied by a burst of increased external sphincter EMG activity, without leakage. When he is asked to void, EMG activity falls silent, detrusor pressure at maximum flow is 68 cm H2O, and Qmax is 9 mL/s with no residual urine. The most likely cause of his symptoms is:

options.B: benign prostatic enlargement with secondary detrusor overactivity.
options.C: primary bladder neck obstruction from a neurologic lesion.

rationale: The tracing shows detrusor overactivity with a normal guarding response: sphincter EMG increases during involuntary contractions to prevent leakage, then appropriately relaxes when the patient is given permission to void. High detrusor pressure with low flow during a voiding phase with a silent EMG meets urodynamic criteria for bladder outlet obstruction, which in a man this age is most commonly prostatic enlargement, with secondary detrusor overactivity explaining the storage symptoms. Dyssynergia and dysfunctional voiding (Hinman syndrome) are defined by sphincter activity persisting during the voiding contraction, which is absent here. Detrusor underactivity would show low pressure, not a Pdet at Qmax of 68 cm H2O.
learning_point: Urodynamic detrusor overactivity accompanied by increased EMG activity during involuntary contractions (a normal guarding reflex) that appropriately quiets during voluntary voiding, together with high-pressure/low-flow voiding, indicates bladder outlet obstruction from benign prostatic enlargement with secondary detrusor overactivity, not neurogenic dyssynergia or dysfunctional voiding.
key_facts: Guarding reflex: sphincter EMG rises with involuntary detrusor contractions to prevent urgency incontinence; this is normal and differs from dyssynergia.
DESD and dysfunctional voiding (Hinman) show sphincter activity during the voiding phase itself; in BPE-related obstruction the EMG is silent during voiding.
BOO criteria: Qmax below about 12 mL/s, Pdet at Qmax above 50 cm H2O, and elevated urethral resistance; secondary DO is common with obstruction.

question: A 47-year-old woman with severe intellectual disability presents with an infected, obstructing proximal ureteral stone and needs urgent decompression. Her husband, her mother, her 22-year-old daughter, and a friend who holds a health care proxy she signed years earlier are all present, and a court appointed her brother as her legal guardian last year. Consent for the procedure should be obtained from her:

options.D: friend holding the health care proxy.

rationale: A court-appointed guardian or decision maker sits at the top of the surrogate hierarchy and supersedes all other parties. A health care proxy designated by the patient while she had capacity ranks next, followed by the spouse, adult children, parents, and siblings in that order. Although the spouse is the highest-ranking family member, the existence of a court-appointed guardian makes him the appropriate consenting party. Note that the brother's authority derives from the court appointment, not from being a sibling, which otherwise would rank below spouse, child, and parent.
learning_point: When a patient lacks decision-making capacity, the surrogate hierarchy places a court-appointed guardian first, then a health care proxy designated by the patient while competent, then spouse, adult child, parent, sibling, and other relatives or close friends.
key_facts: The treating physician determines capacity and identifies the appropriate surrogate.
Court-appointed decision maker outranks a patient-designated proxy, who in turn outranks family members.
Among family, the usual order is spouse or domestic partner, adult child, parent, adult sibling, then other relatives or close friends.

question: A three-month-old boy born at term is seen for a left hemiscrotum that appears underdeveloped. The left testis cannot be palpated in the scrotum or inguinal canal; the right testis is normal and the penis is normal without hypospadias. The next step is:

options.B: re-examination at six months of age.

rationale: Spontaneous testicular descent can still occur during the first six months of life, so an infant with a unilateral nonpalpable testis and otherwise normal genitalia is observed and re-examined; if the testis has not descended by six months corrected age, orchiopexy (or laparoscopy for a nonpalpable gonad) is planned within the next year. Imaging does not reliably localize a nonpalpable testis or alter the decision to operate and is specifically discouraged. Karyotyping and hormonal studies are indicated for bilateral nonpalpable testes or when hypospadias coexists, because of concern for a disorder of sex development, not for isolated unilateral cryptorchidism. Laparoscopy is premature at three months.
learning_point: A unilateral undescended or nonpalpable testis in an infant under six months (corrected age) should be observed for spontaneous descent; surgery is performed between 6 and 18 months, imaging is not recommended, and karyotype is reserved for bilateral nonpalpable testes or associated hypospadias.
key_facts: AUA guideline: no spontaneous descent by 6 months corrected age warrants surgery within the following year.
Ultrasound and other imaging rarely change management in cryptorchidism and should not be ordered.
Karyotype and hormonal evaluation are for bilateral nonpalpable testes or cryptorchidism with hypospadias (possible DSD).

question: A 63-year-old man has Grade Group 2 prostate cancer in 3 of 12 cores with PSA 6.8 ng/mL and clinical stage T1c. He is interested in active surveillance but asks whether a molecular test of his tumor could help predict whether his cancer is likely to behave aggressively. The most appropriate test is:
rationale: Prolaris, like Decipher and Oncotype DX GPS, is a tissue-based genomic assay performed on biopsy tissue that adds independent prognostic information beyond grade, stage, and PSA and is appropriate for men with favorable-risk disease weighing surveillance against treatment. ExoDx and 4Kscore are pre-biopsy tests used to decide whether to biopsy, and ConfirmMDx evaluates benign biopsy tissue to estimate the chance that a repeat biopsy will find cancer. Germline BRCA2 testing informs cancer predisposition and family counseling, and although BRCA2 carriers tend to have worse outcomes, it is not the tool used for post-diagnosis risk stratification of a specific tumor in this setting.
learning_point: Tissue-based genomic classifiers (Decipher, Prolaris, Oncotype DX GPS) provide independent prognostic information in newly diagnosed localized prostate cancer and can help select men deciding between active surveillance and treatment; urine screening tests, ConfirmMDx, germline BRCA testing, and polygenic risk scores do not serve this purpose.
key_facts: Decipher, Prolaris, and Oncotype DX are run on biopsy or prostatectomy tissue and predict adverse pathology, metastasis, or mortality.
ConfirmMDx is an epigenetic test on negative biopsy tissue to assess need for repeat biopsy; ExoDx, PCA3, SelectMDx, and 4Kscore are pre-biopsy risk tests.
BRCA germline status and polygenic risk scores relate to the risk of developing prostate cancer, not to aggressiveness of an established tumor.

question: A 66-year-old man who had hypospadias repair in childhood has a 7 cm penile urethral stricture that has recurred after two urethrotomies and a failed staged graft urethroplasty. He has no interest in further reconstruction of the penile urethra and wants the option least likely to fail. The best treatment is:
rationale: A long penile stricture in a patient with a hypospadias history and multiple failed repairs has little remaining healthy urethral plate or skin, so the probability of durable success with further penile reconstruction is limited; staged repairs succeed in roughly 80% of such cases, whereas perineal urethrostomy achieves patency in over 90% and is specifically recommended by guidelines for patients with long strictures who are unwilling to undergo further urethroplasty. Urethrotomy and dilation have no realistic chance of cure after prior failures and only postpone the next procedure. A single-stage graft requires a viable bed, which is lacking here.
learning_point: For a long-segment penile urethral stricture after multiple failed repairs in a hypospadias cripple with little healthy local tissue, perineal urethrostomy offers the highest long-term success (over 90%) and should be offered; dilation and urethrotomy have essentially no durable success and staged urethroplasty succeeds in about 80%.
key_facts: AUA guideline: offer perineal urethrostomy to patients with long-segment strictures who cannot or do not wish to undergo urethroplasty, or after multiple failures.
Direct vision internal urethrotomy and dilation are ineffective for long or recurrent strictures; self-dilation only delays further surgery.
Two-stage urethroplasty is feasible but has lower success than perineal urethrostomy; single-stage grafting requires a healthy graft bed.

question: A 58-year-old woman reports leakage both with coughing and with sudden urgency. Six months of mirabegron and behavioral therapy have reduced her urgency only slightly. On examination she demonstrates urine loss with Valsalva, there is no prolapse, and her post-void residual is 110 mL. Urinalysis is unremarkable. The next step is:
rationale: She has mixed incontinence with an inadequate response to conservative OAB therapy and a borderline residual, so the appropriate step before any procedure is urodynamic testing to determine whether stress or urgency incontinence predominates, whether detrusor overactivity is present, and how well the detrusor empties. Those findings determine whether a sling, bulking, or third-line OAB therapy such as botulinum toxin or neuromodulation is appropriate. Jumping to a sling or to onabotulinumtoxinA without this information risks treating the wrong component or precipitating retention. Cystoscopy does not clarify the mechanism of her leakage.
learning_point: In a woman with mixed urinary incontinence refractory to OAB medication, urodynamics should be obtained to clarify the dominant component and detrusor function before committing to invasive therapy such as a sling or third-line OAB treatment.
key_facts: AUA/SUFU SUI guideline: urodynamics are appropriate in mixed incontinence and other complicated cases before invasive therapy.
UDS defines stress versus urgency components, demonstrates detrusor overactivity, and assesses emptying when the PVR is borderline.
Cystoscopy is not diagnostic for the cause of incontinence in the absence of hematuria, pain, or suspicion of a fistula or foreign body.

question: A 29-year-old man being evaluated for a low sperm count has a scrotal ultrasound that reveals a 1.2 cm sharply marginated, avascular intratesticular lesion with concentric alternating hyperechoic and hypoechoic rings. Serum AFP, beta-hCG, and LDH are normal. The next step is:

options.D: CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis.

rationale: A lamellated, avascular, well-circumscribed intratesticular mass with normal markers is the classic appearance of an epidermoid cyst, a benign keratin-filled lesion. Because it is not a germ cell tumor, there is no indication for staging imaging or radical orchiectomy, which would needlessly compromise fertility in a man already being evaluated for infertility. Observation (or testis-sparing enucleation if the diagnosis is uncertain or the patient prefers) is appropriate. Percutaneous biopsy of a testicular mass is not standard practice because of the risk of seeding if the lesion were malignant.
learning_point: A testicular epidermoid cyst has a characteristic lamellated onion-ring sonographic appearance with normal tumor markers; it is benign, requires no staging or radical orchiectomy, and can be observed (or managed with testis-sparing excision), preserving fertility.
key_facts: Epidermoid cyst: well-circumscribed, avascular intratesticular lesion with alternating hyper- and hypoechoic concentric rings (onion-skin or target appearance).
Serum AFP and hCG are normal; it is not a germ cell tumor and does not metastasize.
Radical orchiectomy and staging CT are unnecessary; MRI adds little when the ultrasound appearance is classic.

question: A 74-year-old man on chronic warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve is restarting anticoagulation after a HoLEP. He develops a lower urinary tract infection with a pan-sensitive E. coli. The antimicrobial most likely to produce a supratherapeutic INR if prescribed is:
rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is among the antibiotics most strongly associated with potentiation of warfarin; it inhibits CYP2C9 metabolism of warfarin and displaces it from protein binding, and like other broad-spectrum agents reduces vitamin K-producing gut flora, so INR can rise sharply within days. Fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, macrolides, and azole antifungals carry a similar warning. Nitrofurantoin has no clinically meaningful interaction with warfarin and is a reasonable choice for uncomplicated cystitis, as is fosfomycin. Beta-lactams such as cephalexin and amoxicillin have only minor and inconsistent effects on INR.
learning_point: Antibiotics such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, and erythromycin, and azole antifungals, potentiate warfarin and raise the INR; nitrofurantoin, oral iron, and orange juice have no meaningful interaction.
key_facts: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, reducing factors II, VII, IX, and X; effect fluctuates with vitamin K intake and drug interactions.
TMP-SMX, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, and macrolides raise INR by displacing warfarin, inhibiting its metabolism, or reducing gut flora vitamin K synthesis.
Azole antifungals inhibit CYP enzymes and reduce warfarin clearance; binge alcohol can also affect warfarin metabolism.
Nitrofurantoin and iron supplements do not significantly interact; the goal is steady, moderate vitamin K intake rather than elimination.

question: A 29-year-old man with primary infertility has a non-palpable left vas deferens and a palpable right vas; testes are 24 mL bilaterally. Two semen analyses show volume 0.6 mL, pH 6.5, and no sperm. FSH is 3.8 IU/L. Transrectal ultrasound shows absence of the left seminal vesicle and a small atretic right seminal vesicle without cysts or ductal dilation. CFTR mutation panel and 5T allele testing are negative. The next step is:
rationale: This man has a variant of congenital absence of the vas deferens: one vas is absent in the scrotum and the other is present in the scrotum but its seminal vesicle is hypoplastic, producing low-volume acidic azoospermia. When CFTR testing is negative, the etiology is attributed to a mesonephric (Wolffian) duct developmental defect rather than cystic fibrosis, and these men have an appreciable incidence of unilateral renal agenesis, so renal imaging is recommended. A sweat test adds nothing in an asymptomatic man with negative genetic testing. Vasography and seminal vesicle aspiration are for suspected ejaculatory duct obstruction, which the TRUS findings exclude, and testis biopsy is unnecessary with normal FSH and testicular volume since spermatogenesis is expected to be intact.
learning_point: Congenital absence of the vas deferens (including unilateral variants with contralateral seminal vesicle abnormality) in a man with negative cystic fibrosis gene testing should prompt renal ultrasound, because such cases arise from mesonephric duct maldevelopment and carry a risk of ipsilateral renal agenesis.
key_facts: Low-volume, acidic, azoospermic semen indicates absent seminal vesicle contribution: CBAVD or ejaculatory duct obstruction; TRUS distinguishes them (agenesis/hypoplasia vs cysts and dilated ducts).
All men with vasal agenesis need CFTR mutation testing; up to 15% have no identifiable mutation.
CFTR-negative vasal agenesis is associated with unilateral renal agenesis in a meaningful minority, whereas CFTR-related CBAVD is not.
Testis biopsy is unnecessary with normal FSH and testicular volume; treatment is sperm retrieval with IVF/ICSI.

question: A 71-year-old woman underwent anterior exenteration with an ileal conduit three years ago for BCG-unresponsive carcinoma in situ. At routine follow-up her urethral wash cytology is read as positive for high-grade urothelial carcinoma. She has no symptoms; CT urogram of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis shows no abnormality, and flexible urethroscopy demonstrates a normal-appearing urethra. The next step is:

options.A: repeat urethral wash in three months.

rationale: A positive urethral wash after cystectomy for CIS correlates strongly with recurrent urothelial carcinoma, and a normal endoscopic appearance points toward carcinoma in situ, which may reside in periurethral glands that random biopsies sample poorly, so a negative biopsy cannot be trusted to defer treatment. Because the urethra is defunctionalized with a conduit, removing it eliminates the risk at little functional cost, and treating surveillance-detected disease before it becomes symptomatic substantially reduces cancer mortality. Observation or repeat cytology delays treatment of a likely cancer; topical intraurethral chemotherapy is reserved for low-grade disease when preserving a functioning urethra matters, and MRI will not add to a normal CT and endoscopy.
learning_point: After cystectomy with a non-orthotopic diversion for high-risk disease such as BCG-refractory CIS, a suspicious or positive urethral wash cytology with no other site of disease warrants urethrectomy, even when urethroscopy is normal, because occult CIS in the retained urethra and periurethral glands is likely and biopsy has inadequate negative predictive value.
key_facts: Cystectomy for CIS, especially BCG-refractory, carries elevated risk of urethral and upper tract recurrence; surveillance includes urethral wash cytology.
Asymptomatic recurrences detected by surveillance have better survival than symptomatic recurrences, about 40% of which are fatal.
Intraurethral topical therapy is considered only when urethral preservation matters (neobladder) and disease is low grade; a defunctionalized urethra should simply be removed.

question: Six days after a laparoscopic hysterectomy, a 48-year-old woman notices continuous watery vaginal drainage. Cystoscopy shows an intact bladder, and a left retrograde ureterogram reveals extravasation into the vagina about 3 cm above the ureterovesical junction with mild proximal dilation. A guidewire cannot be advanced across the defect in either retrograde or antegrade fashion. She is otherwise healthy. The most appropriate management is:

options.A: percutaneous nephrostomy with repair in three months.
options.B: indwelling urethral catheter for four weeks.

rationale: A ureterovaginal fistula identified within the first week or so after surgery in a healthy patient can be repaired immediately once stenting has failed; waiting three months with a nephrostomy is the approach for late-recognized injuries with established inflammation. The injury is in the distal ureter, so excision of the injured segment and reimplantation into the bladder is straightforward and preferred over a distal ureteroureterostomy, which risks stricture from compromised blood supply. A Boari flap is unnecessary for a defect only a few centimeters above the bladder. A urethral catheter can help a small vesicovaginal fistula close but has no effect on a ureteral fistula.
learning_point: A ureterovaginal fistula recognized within the first 7-10 days after hysterectomy that cannot be stented should undergo early surgical repair; for a distal ureteral injury, ureteroneocystostomy is preferred over ureteroureterostomy, and a Boari flap or psoas hitch is needed only for longer defects.
key_facts: Ureterovaginal fistula: continuous vaginal leakage with normal bladder; retrograde ureterogram or CT urogram localizes the injury.
First step is attempted stenting; if successful, many fistulas heal without surgery. Catheter drainage alone does not heal a ureteral fistula.
Early repair is appropriate if diagnosed within about 7-10 days; later diagnosis typically means nephrostomy drainage and delayed repair at about 3 months.
Distal ureter: reimplant into the bladder; ureteroureterostomy of the distal ureter has higher stricture risk because of tenuous blood supply.

question: A 73-year-old man with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer started abiraterone acetate two months ago in addition to leuprolide. He now has ankle swelling and blood pressure of 162/94 mmHg, which was previously normal. Laboratory studies show potassium 3.1 mEq/L and normal creatinine and liver enzymes. The next step is:
rationale: New hypertension, edema, and hypokalemia in a patient recently started on abiraterone indicate mineralocorticoid excess from accumulation of CYP17 precursors driven by elevated ACTH. Low-dose prednisone replaces glucocorticoid activity, suppresses ACTH, and reverses the syndrome; this is why abiraterone is prescribed with a corticosteroid. A thiazide would worsen the hypokalemia and amlodipine may worsen edema, and neither addresses the cause. Spironolactone is avoided in prostate cancer because it has androgen receptor agonist activity (eplerenone is the preferred mineralocorticoid antagonist if one is needed). Leuprolide is not responsible for these findings.
learning_point: Abiraterone blocks CYP17, lowering cortisol, raising ACTH, and causing accumulation of mineralocorticoid precursors that produce hypertension, fluid retention, and hypokalemia; the treatment is co-administration of low-dose prednisone to restore cortisol feedback, not antihypertensives or diuretics.
key_facts: CYP17 inhibition reduces cortisol and androgens; compensatory ACTH rise drives corticosterone and deoxycorticosterone excess (mineralocorticoid effect).
Classic triad: hypertension, hypokalemia, edema; monitor BP, potassium, and liver tests on abiraterone.
Low-dose prednisone (e.g., 5 mg daily or twice daily) suppresses ACTH and corrects the syndrome; eplerenone can be used if needed (spironolactone avoided because of androgenic activity).
Thiazides worsen hypokalemia and calcium channel blockers can worsen edema; neither treats the underlying mechanism.

question: A 47-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis and prior banding of esophageal varices has an ileal conduit. Over three months he has had recurrent brisk bleeding from the peristomal skin and bowel mucosa that stops with pressure. The stoma shows a bluish discoloration with a surrounding caput medusae-like venous pattern. The next step is:

options.A: suture ligation of the bleeding stomal vessels.
options.C: MRI or contrast CT of the abdomen to map peristomal collateral veins.
options.E: topical silver nitrate and barrier appliance change.

rationale: Recurrent stomal bleeding in a patient with portal hypertension is almost always due to stomal varices, in which collaterals form between the portal-draining mesenteric veins of the bowel segment and the systemic veins of the abdominal wall. Imaging confirms the collaterals and guides treatment, which is portal decompression with TIPS; local approaches such as ligation, fulguration, or stoma revision are temporizing at best and risk hemorrhage because the underlying pressure gradient persists. Revision may be required later but only after decompression. Topical measures are inadequate for variceal bleeding.
learning_point: Recurrent bleeding from a catheterizable stoma or conduit in a patient with cirrhosis and portal hypertension is from stomal varices (portosystemic collaterals); the next step is cross-sectional imaging (MRI or CT) to define the collaterals, with definitive treatment by portal decompression (TIPS) rather than local stoma manipulation.
key_facts: Portal hypertension creates collaterals between the mesenteric venous drainage of the bowel segment and the systemic abdominal wall veins at the stoma.
Stomal variceal bleeding can be life threatening; local measures (smaller catheter, prolonged catheter, revision) risk further trauma and do not treat the cause.
TIPS decompresses the portal system; stomal revision, if needed, follows portal decompression.

question: A 57-year-old woman underwent robotic partial nephrectomy for a 2.8 cm clear cell RCC, pT1a, with negative margins. Surveillance CT at seven months shows a 2 cm round lesion in the resection bed that enhances intensely to the same degree as the aorta in the arterial phase and washes out on delayed images; she has no hematuria. The next step is:
rationale: A lesion at the resection site that enhances like the arterial blood pool and washes out promptly is characteristic of a pseudoaneurysm, a recognized complication of partial nephrectomy that can appear in delayed fashion even without hematuria. Early recurrence after a small, low-grade, margin-negative tumor is improbable. Doppler ultrasound is a noninvasive way to demonstrate turbulent arterial flow within the lesion and distinguish it from tumor; if confirmed, selective angioembolization is the treatment. Biopsy or ablation of a pseudoaneurysm could precipitate hemorrhage, and partial or radical nephrectomy would be unnecessary and sacrifice renal function.
learning_point: A new avidly enhancing lesion with rapid washout at a partial nephrectomy site on follow-up CT most likely represents a pseudoaneurysm rather than recurrence; confirm noninvasively with Doppler ultrasound (or CT angiography) and treat with selective embolization, not biopsy, ablation, or surgery.
key_facts: Renal artery pseudoaneurysm after partial nephrectomy usually presents early with gross hematuria but may be found incidentally or rupture late.
Imaging clue: enhancement that parallels the arterial blood pool with prompt washout, unlike a tumor which retains contrast.
Local recurrence within 6 months after a small, low-stage, margin-negative tumor is unlikely.
Management of confirmed pseudoaneurysm is angioembolization; radical nephrectomy is overtreatment.

question: A 27-year-old man completes chemotherapy for a stage II seminoma of the right testis after radical orchiectomy. His pretreatment ultrasound described a normal-volume left testis containing numerous punctate echogenic foci consistent with microlithiasis and no mass. Regarding the remaining testis, the recommended approach is:

options.A: ultrasound-guided biopsy to exclude germ cell neoplasia in situ.
options.B: prophylactic left orchiectomy with testosterone replacement.

rationale: Microlithiasis by itself does not raise the risk of testicular cancer, and even when a risk factor such as a prior germ cell tumor is present, the recommended management is to inform the patient of the modestly elevated risk and have him perform regular self-examination with periodic clinical follow-up. Serial screening ultrasounds and biopsy have not been shown to improve outcomes and are not recommended. Radiation of a solitary testis is reserved for proven GCNIS on biopsy, and prophylactic orchiectomy of a normal testis would render the patient hypogonadal and infertile without a demonstrated benefit.
learning_point: Testicular microlithiasis in the contralateral testis of a man with a personal history of germ cell tumor warrants counseling and regular self-examination with clinical follow-up; routine screening ultrasounds, biopsy, orchiectomy, and radiation are not indicated.
key_facts: Microlithiasis: five or more small nonshadowing echogenic foci per testis; prevalence about 5% in asymptomatic men with no increased cancer rate on follow-up.
Isolated incidental microlithiasis needs no further evaluation; risk is increased only with another risk factor (prior GCT, cryptorchidism, GCNIS, family history).
With risk factors, AUA guidance is counseling and periodic self-examination with physician follow-up, not imaging surveillance or biopsy.
Testicular radiation is for GCNIS found on biopsy after partial orchiectomy, not for microlithiasis.

question: A 54-year-old woman with a BMI of 41 and a history of prior stone passage has an incidental 1.2 cm non-obstructing interpolar renal calculus on CT with a mean attenuation of 420 Hounsfield units. She has no symptoms. The next step is:
rationale: A stone of about 400 HU in a recurrent stone former is suspicious for uric acid composition, and the simplest confirmatory step is a urinalysis: a persistently acidic urine (pH 5.5 or lower) together with low attenuation predicts uric acid with about 90% accuracy and justifies a trial of alkalinization. Starting potassium citrate empirically without this information is premature, and a plain film is unreliable in a patient with severe obesity. Because the stone is asymptomatic and non-obstructing, ureteroscopy or SWL is not needed until it is determined whether a noninvasive dissolution option exists.
learning_point: A radiolucent-range (about 300-500 HU) asymptomatic non-obstructing renal stone should first be characterized with urinalysis for pH; low urine pH with HU 500 or less strongly predicts uric acid composition and allows a trial of dissolution with alkalinization instead of surgery.
key_facts: Uric acid stones typically measure roughly 300-500 HU on CT; calcium stones are usually above 800-1000 HU.
Urine pH 5.5 or below plus HU 500 or below has about 90% positive predictive value for uric acid stones.
KUB is poorly sensitive in obese patients; uric acid stones are radiolucent.
Asymptomatic non-obstructing stones do not require immediate ureteroscopy or PCNL; confirm composition before choosing dissolution therapy.

question: A 63-year-old woman reports a gradual loss of sexual desire, diminished arousal, difficulty reaching orgasm, and reduced genital sensation over the past decade. These changes are most directly linked to an age-related decline in:
rationale: Although menopause produces an abrupt fall in estrogen and progesterone, the specific constellation of reduced libido, arousal, orgasmic capacity, and genital sensation in aging women tracks with the gradual decline of ovarian and adrenal androgens. Testosterone therapy has improved these domains in trials, although it remains off-label. Estrogen deficiency contributes to vaginal atrophy and dyspareunia but does not directly explain loss of desire and sensation, and exogenous estrogen can worsen the problem by increasing sex hormone-binding globulin and lowering free testosterone. Prolactin elevation, not decline, impairs sexual function, and oxytocin is not implicated in age-related change.
learning_point: Age-related decline in female libido, arousal, orgasm, and genital sensation is associated with falling androgen (testosterone) levels; estrogen and progesterone decline more abruptly at menopause but do not directly account for these changes, and estrogen can further lower free testosterone by raising SHBG.
key_facts: Androgens decline gradually with age in women and correlate with desire, arousal, orgasm, and genital sensitivity.
Testosterone supplementation improves these domains in studies but is off-label for women.
Oral estrogens raise SHBG and suppress gonadotropins, reducing bioavailable testosterone.
Serotonin influences orgasm but is not linked to age-related decline in sexual function.

question: During a transobturator midurethral sling for stress incontinence in a 49-year-old woman, intraoperative cystourethroscopy reveals the left helical trocar passing through the lateral wall of the midurethra. After the trocar is removed and the urethral defect is closed, the surgeon should:

options.A: harvest rectus fascia and place an autologous sling.
options.C: end the procedure and leave an indwelling urethral catheter.
options.D: convert to a retropubic mesh sling.
options.E: proceed with placement of the transobturator mesh sling.

rationale: A urethral perforation during sling surgery is managed differently from a bladder perforation: synthetic mesh placed adjacent to a fresh urethral injury carries a high risk of erosion and fistula, so guideline principle is not to place a mesh sling of any type once the urethra has been injured. The urethrotomy is repaired, a catheter is left for healing, and anti-incontinence surgery is deferred and readdressed later after counseling. Simply changing the route of the mesh does not eliminate the risk. Bulking agents into a freshly injured urethra are inappropriate, and although an autologous sling is sometimes considered, it has a different risk profile and requires specific consent, so aborting is the correct answer.
learning_point: If the urethra is perforated by a trocar during midurethral sling placement, the urethra should be repaired, mesh must not be placed, and the procedure is aborted with catheter drainage; in contrast, a bladder perforation can be managed by re-passing the trocar and continuing.
key_facts: Bladder trocar perforation (2-25% of retropubic slings) is managed by withdrawing and re-passing the trocar and proceeding with catheter drainage.
AUA/SUFU SUI guideline clinical principle: do not place a mesh sling if the urethra is injured during the planned procedure.
Urethral injury requires repair when feasible and postoperative catheter drainage; a Martius flap is unnecessary for a small fresh urethrotomy.
An autologous fascial sling at the same sitting is theoretically possible but requires separate counseling and is not the standard answer.

question: A 31-year-old man and his partner have 14 months of infertility. Two semen analyses obtained four weeks ago, each with normal ejaculate volume, showed no sperm on centrifuged specimens. Ten weeks before the analyses he was hospitalized for three days with COVID-19 pneumonia and fevers to 39.5 C. Examination shows 18 mL testes with palpable vasa; FSH is 11 IU/L and testosterone is normal. The next step is:

options.C: repeat semen analysis in two to three months.

rationale: A high fever disrupts spermatogenesis and may cause transient azoospermia with a reactive rise in FSH; because a full spermatogenic cycle takes roughly three months, semen collected within that window after a febrile illness does not reflect baseline function. Semen analysis should therefore be repeated after recovery before labeling him azoospermic. Normal ejaculate volume makes ejaculatory duct obstruction unlikely, so TRUS is not indicated, and vasography is not performed until obstructive azoospermia is established. Genetic testing and micro-TESE are appropriate only if azoospermia with elevated FSH persists.
learning_point: A recent febrile systemic illness can transiently suppress spermatogenesis, producing azoospermia with a mildly elevated FSH; semen analysis should be repeated about three months after recovery before pursuing obstruction work-up or sperm retrieval.
key_facts: Spermatogenesis takes about 72-90 days, so fever within the prior three months can affect current semen quality.
Normal-volume azoospermia with elevated FSH suggests a testicular cause; low-volume azoospermia prompts post-ejaculate urine and TRUS.
Prior bilateral hernia repair raises the possibility of vasal injury, but obstruction evaluation is deferred until persistence is confirmed.
Micro-TESE is considered only after persistent nonobstructive azoospermia is established.

question: After a left supracostal upper-pole PCNL, a 45-year-old woman has a postoperative CT showing the nephrostomy tube passing through the inferior pole of the spleen before entering the kidney. There is a small perisplenic hematoma. Her heart rate is 82, blood pressure is 124/76 mmHg, and hemoglobin is 12.1 g/dL. The next step is:

options.B: immediate removal of the nephrostomy tube.
options.C: exchange the nephrostomy for a ureteral stent.
options.E: bed rest with serial hemoglobin measurements and delayed tube removal.

rationale: A trans-splenic nephrostomy tract in a stable patient should be observed: the tube tamponades the tract, and the patient is monitored with serial hemoglobin while the tube is left in place for several days before cautious removal, with interventional radiology available. Pulling or exchanging the tube acutely removes the tamponade and may provoke bleeding. Angiography and splenectomy or laparotomy are reserved for hemodynamic instability or evidence of ongoing hemorrhage. Converting to a ureteral stent is the approach for a retrorenal colon injury, not a splenic traversal.
learning_point: A nephrostomy tract that has traversed the spleen (typically with supracostal upper pole access) in a hemodynamically stable patient is managed conservatively with bed rest, serial hemoglobin, and delayed tube removal; immediate repositioning, angiography, or exploration is not indicated.
key_facts: Splenic and hepatic injury during PCNL occur almost exclusively with supracostal (above 11th/12th rib) upper pole access; risk rises with splenomegaly.
Obesity does not increase trans-splenic puncture risk; CT-guided access is advised when organomegaly is present.
Stable patient: observe with serial hematocrit, leave the tube to tamponade the tract, remove later (often over a wire with angiographic readiness).
Angiography or surgery is reserved for hemodynamic instability or ongoing bleeding; a retrorenal colon injury is handled differently (reposition tube, stent, conservative).

question: A 70-year-old man with Lynch syndrome and a prior colectomy and pelvic radiation for rectal cancer has a 2.5 cm high-grade urothelial carcinoma of the proximal-to-mid right ureter confirmed by ureteroscopic biopsy. He has chemotherapy-related peripheral neuropathy. Staging CT shows no nodal or distant disease, and eGFR is 68 mL/min/1.73 m2. The next step is:

options.A: ureteroscopic laser ablation with adjuvant mitomycin.
options.B: right radical nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff excision.
options.E: distal ureterectomy with psoas hitch reimplantation.

rationale: High-grade upper tract urothelial carcinoma, especially a sizable lesion, is not suitable for endoscopic ablation because of high rates of recurrence and progression. Ureteral-sparing segmental resection is an option in select patients, but prior pelvic surgery and radiation sharply increase the risk of anastomotic breakdown and stricture, and with good renal function there is no compelling reason to accept that risk. Cisplatin is contraindicated by his neuropathy and neoadjuvant chemotherapy has not demonstrated a survival advantage in UTUC. Although Lynch syndrome may raise concern for future contralateral disease, the evidence for increased bilaterality is limited, and nephroureterectomy offers the best oncologic outcome.
learning_point: A large high-grade ureteral urothelial carcinoma in a patient with Lynch syndrome and adequate renal function, whose prior pelvic surgery and radiation and neuropathy make segmental reconstruction and cisplatin unattractive, is best treated with radical nephroureterectomy; endoscopic ablation is inappropriate for high-grade bulky disease.
key_facts: Lynch syndrome raises the risk of upper tract urothelial carcinoma, but data do not clearly show higher bilaterality than sporadic cases.
Endoscopic management is reserved for low-grade, small, low-volume tumors; high-grade disease has high recurrence and progression rates.
Segmental or distal ureterectomy is feasible for select ureteral tumors but prior pelvic surgery and radiation markedly raise anastomotic complication rates.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for UTUC lacks proven survival benefit and cisplatin is contraindicated with peripheral neuropathy.

question: Among the following neurologic conditions, bladder emptying by suprapubic manual compression (Crede maneuver) is most likely to be effective in a patient with:

options.A: a complete T12-L1 spinal cord injury.
options.B: a complete C6 spinal cord injury.
options.C: a complete T4 spinal cord injury.
options.E: a right middle cerebral artery stroke.

rationale: Manual compression empties the bladder only when the detrusor is acontractile and the outlet offers little resistance, because the Valsalva-type pressure rise otherwise provokes the same guarding response that prevents stress incontinence. Injury at the thoracolumbar junction (roughly T11-L2) damages the sympathetic outflow to the bladder neck and often produces an areflexic bladder with a denervated, incompetent outlet, so compression can overcome what little resistance remains. Cervical and upper thoracic cord injuries, multiple sclerosis, and stroke generally leave the sphincter mechanism intact or dyssynergic, so compression is ineffective and may generate dangerous intravesical pressures.
learning_point: The Crede maneuver (manual suprapubic compression) works best when the bladder is areflexic and the outlet is denervated with low resistance, which is typical of lesions at the thoracolumbar (T11-L2) sympathetic outflow or after sphincter ablation; suprasacral lesions with an intact outlet respond poorly because compression triggers reflex outlet closure.
key_facts: Crede is nonphysiologic: rising abdominal pressure does not trigger reflex sphincter opening and may provoke reflex increase in outlet resistance.
Best candidates have detrusor acontractility plus decreased outlet resistance (T11-L2 injury damaging sympathetic supply, prior sphincterotomy, or sphincter botulinum toxin).
Patients with stroke, MS, or cervical/upper thoracic SCI typically have an intact or hyperactive outlet and are poor candidates.

question: A 44-year-old man with chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome refractory to alpha-blockers, pelvic floor physical therapy, and neuromodulating agents begins a two-week trial of oral oxycodone with agreed functional goals. At follow-up he reports no meaningful change in pain or activity level. The next step is:

options.A: convert to a long-acting opioid formulation.
options.C: taper and discontinue the opioid and pursue non-opioid strategies.

rationale: Opioids are continued only when a trial produces clinically meaningful improvement in pain and function; if a time-limited trial fails, the drug should be discontinued and the treatment plan redirected, as should have been agreed when the trial began. Escalating the dose or switching to a long-acting preparation increases risk without evidence of benefit when the initial trial has not worked. Co-prescribing a benzodiazepine with an opioid raises the risk of respiratory depression and death and is discouraged in all cases. A urine screen is used to assess for misuse or diversion and does not address the problem of an ineffective therapy.
learning_point: In chronic pelvic pain syndrome, an opioid trial that fails to produce clinically meaningful improvement in pain and function should be discontinued and alternative therapy pursued; dose escalation and benzodiazepine co-prescription are inappropriate.
key_facts: Set functional and pain goals before starting opioids and plan in advance how to taper if benefits do not outweigh harms.
Lack of meaningful benefit means stop, not escalate; CDC and pain guidelines emphasize reassessing within 1-4 weeks of initiation.
Opioid-benzodiazepine combinations increase overdose and death risk and should be avoided.
Urine drug screening is for monitoring misuse risk and would not change management when the trial has simply failed.

question: The parents of a healthy five-year-old boy are frustrated that he wets the bed five nights a week. He has been dry during the day for two years, has no urgency or frequency, and has a normal examination and urinalysis. After counseling on timed voiding and management of mild constipation, the next step is:

options.B: reassurance and reassessment after age six.

rationale: This is monosymptomatic enuresis, which is common and resolves spontaneously in a substantial proportion of children each year. Guidelines advise general measures (regular voiding, fluid timing, bowel management) for all children, but active treatment is not usually initiated before six years of age because of the high natural resolution rate and limited motivation in younger children. Once the child is older and motivated, the alarm or oral desmopressin are first-line options. Oxybutynin is used when daytime symptoms or standard therapy failure suggest detrusor overactivity, and imipramine is a third-line agent because of cardiac toxicity.
learning_point: Monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis in a child under six years old is managed with reassurance, regular voiding, and treatment of constipation; active therapy (enuresis alarm or desmopressin) is deferred until at least age six.
key_facts: Monosymptomatic enuresis: nighttime wetting without daytime symptoms; spontaneous resolution rate about 15% per year.
First-line active treatments after age six are the enuresis alarm and oral desmopressin; nasal desmopressin is avoided because of hyponatremia risk.
Anticholinergics are added for failures or non-monosymptomatic enuresis; imipramine is third line because of cardiotoxicity.

question: A 66-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2) is being evaluated for prostate cancer screening. Compared with men with normal renal function, his renal impairment is expected to raise his serum level of:
rationale: Free PSA is a relatively small, unbound protein that depends in part on renal clearance, so its absolute level and the free-to-total ratio rise in advanced CKD. Total and complexed PSA are not meaningfully affected, and proPSA isoforms are likewise unchanged. Because a higher percent free PSA is interpreted as lower cancer risk, derived tests such as the prostate health index and 4Kscore may underestimate the probability of clinically significant cancer in men with severe renal dysfunction, and results should be interpreted with caution.
learning_point: Severe chronic kidney disease elevates serum free PSA and percent free PSA (not total PSA or proPSA), which can falsely lower cancer risk estimates from tests that incorporate free PSA such as the prostate health index and 4Kscore.
key_facts: Free PSA is a small molecule cleared partly by the kidney; total PSA (mostly complexed) is not significantly affected by renal function.
Higher percent free PSA in CKD suggests a lower probability of cancer, so phi and 4Kscore may underestimate risk.
proPSA and total PSA are not altered by renal dysfunction.

question: A 58-year-old postmenopausal woman has had three culture-proven episodes of cystitis in 12 months, each treated successfully. CT urogram shows no stones or hydronephrosis on the unenhanced phase; the excretory phase demonstrates bilateral smooth, cobra-head dilations of the intravesical ureters measuring about 1.5 cm with prompt drainage. Her post-void residual is 20 mL. The next step is:

options.E: address other UTI risk factors; no treatment of the ureteroceles.

rationale: The imaging shows bilateral simple orthotopic ureteroceles, which are a benign incidental finding in adults and are not recognized as a cause of recurrent cystitis when there is no obstruction or stone. Incising them would not reduce her infections and could create reflux. VCUG and retrograde studies are unlikely to alter management, and a renal scan is unnecessary with prompt drainage and no hydronephrosis. Her evaluation should focus on modifiable contributors such as postmenopausal vaginal atrophy (vaginal estrogen), sexual activity (post-coital prophylaxis), and other strategies such as self-start therapy or low-dose antimicrobial prophylaxis.
learning_point: Bilateral simple (orthotopic) ureteroceles found incidentally in an adult with recurrent UTIs are not a cause of infection and need no intervention; management should focus on identifying and treating other risk factors for recurrent UTI.
key_facts: Adult orthotopic ureteroceles appear as cobra-head intravesical dilations on the excretory phase; without obstruction or stones they are incidental.
Evaluate recurrent UTI for residual urine, diabetes, sexual activity, and menopausal status; options include post-coital or low-dose prophylaxis, self-start therapy, and vaginal estrogen.
VCUG, retrograde pyelography, and ureterocele incision do not change management in the absence of obstruction or reflux-related pathology.

question: A ten-week-old girl has ultrasound showing a duplex left kidney with marked upper pole hydroureteronephrosis. To determine whether the upper pole ureter ends in a ureterocele or inserts ectopically, the sonographic feature to focus on is:

options.B: degree of tortuosity of the dilated ureter.
options.C: presence of a thin-walled cystic structure protruding into the bladder lumen.
options.D: thickness of the upper pole parenchyma.
options.E: severity of the upper pole caliectasis.

rationale: The kidney and ureter look essentially the same in both conditions: a dilated, tortuous upper pole ureter with thinned upper pole parenchyma. The distinction is made at the bladder. A ureterocele is a cystic dilation of the intravesical ureter that bulges into the bladder lumen with a thin wall, whereas an ectopic ureter remains outside the bladder, and the normal bladder wall thickness is preserved between the dilated ureter and the lumen even when the ureter indents the bladder base. A very full bladder can compress a ureterocele, so imaging with a partially filled bladder helps. Lower pole hydronephrosis relates to reflux into the lower moiety rather than to the upper pole ureteral termination.
learning_point: In an infant with upper pole hydroureteronephrosis of a duplex kidney, the bladder images on ultrasound distinguish a ureterocele (thin-walled cystic structure within the bladder lumen) from an ectopic ureter (dilated ureter behind the bladder with preserved bladder wall between them); the renal findings do not differentiate the two.
key_facts: Both anomalies affect the upper pole moiety of a duplex system and produce similar upper pole hydronephrosis and ureteral tortuosity.
Ureterocele: thin-walled cystic dilation projecting into the bladder lumen; it may be flattened and missed when the bladder is very full.
Ectopic ureter: dilated distal ureter extends beyond the bladder base, with the bladder wall intact and visible separating the two lumens.

question: A 58-year-old healthy man has a 4 cm high-grade T1 urothelial carcinoma with micropapillary and sarcomatoid differentiation. Repeat transurethral resection two months later again shows high-grade T1 disease with muscularis propria present and uninvolved. CT urogram and chest imaging are negative. The next step is:
rationale: Persistent high-grade T1 disease on restaging resection combined with aggressive variant histology places this patient in the highest-risk category of non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer, for whom guidelines advise offering immediate radical cystectomy because the risk of progression with intravesical therapy is high and patients who progress fare worse than those presenting with muscle-invasive disease. Intravesical BCG or gemcitabine/docetaxel would be reasonable for standard high-risk NMIBC but are inadequate here, especially in a young, fit patient. Pembrolizumab is indicated only for BCG-unresponsive carcinoma in situ, and chemoradiation is a treatment for muscle-invasive cancer and performs poorly with variant histology.
learning_point: High-grade T1 bladder cancer that persists on repeat resection and shows variant histology (e.g., sarcomatoid) represents very high-risk NMIBC; guidelines recommend considering upfront radical cystectomy rather than BCG, since progression after intravesical therapy carries worse outcomes than primary muscle-invasive disease.
key_facts: Repeat TURBT is required for HG T1; persistent T1 on re-resection and variant histology (micropapillary, sarcomatoid, plasmacytoid, etc.) predict progression.
AUA/SUO: offer initial radical cystectomy to high-risk NMIBC with these adverse features, especially in fit patients.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy and chemoradiation are for muscle-invasive disease; pembrolizumab is approved only for BCG-unresponsive CIS in patients ineligible for or declining cystectomy.

question: A five-month-old boy has had episodic wetness at the umbilicus since birth; the fluid is clear and odorless and the surrounding skin is not inflamed. He is afebrile and otherwise healthy. The next step is:

options.A: ultrasound of the bladder and anterior abdominal wall.
options.B: cystoscopy with retrograde injection of the tract.
options.D: silver nitrate cautery of the umbilicus.
options.E: reassurance and follow-up at one year.

rationale: Clear fluid leaking from the umbilicus in an infant is most consistent with a patent urachus communicating with the bladder. Ultrasound is noninvasive and typically shows a fluid-filled tubular structure extending from the bladder dome to the umbilicus, confirming the diagnosis and excluding an associated cyst; if the study is equivocal a VCUG can demonstrate contrast reaching the umbilicus. A patent urachus does not usually close on its own, so observation is not appropriate, and cystoscopy is not used for initial diagnosis. Culture is unnecessary without signs of infection, and silver nitrate is used for umbilical granulomas and should be avoided when a urachal anomaly is suspected.
learning_point: Intermittent clear fluid draining from the umbilicus in an infant suggests a patent urachus; the initial study is ultrasound of the bladder and umbilical region to show the fluid-filled tract, with VCUG reserved for equivocal cases; observation is not appropriate because it rarely closes spontaneously.
key_facts: Patent urachus presents with continuous or intermittent urine drainage from the umbilicus; other urachal anomalies include cyst, sinus, and diverticulum.
Ultrasound (longitudinal midline view) demonstrates the tubular connection between bladder dome and umbilicus and is the best first test.
VCUG confirms the tract if ultrasound is indeterminate; cystoscopy is not part of the initial evaluation.
Fluid culture is only needed when infection is suspected; avoid silver nitrate if urachal anomaly is possible.

question: A 72-year-old man scheduled for radical cystectomy and ileal conduit has lost about 6 pounds over the preceding three months; his albumin is 3.5 g/dL and he is eating normally. His surgeon admits him for a week of central venous total parenteral nutrition before the operation. This intervention places him at increased risk of postoperative:
rationale: Preoperative parenteral nutrition improves outcomes only in severely malnourished patients whose gastrointestinal tract cannot be used; this man has mild weight loss, a near-normal albumin, and a functioning gut, so TPN offers no benefit. In such patients, TPN exposes them to central line infections and hyperglycemia, and randomized data show higher rates of infectious complications and sepsis without reductions in other surgical morbidity. Ileus, anastomotic leak, dehiscence, and reoperation are recognized cystectomy complications but their frequency is not increased by preoperative TPN.
learning_point: Preoperative total parenteral nutrition benefits only severely malnourished patients who cannot be fed enterally; giving TPN to a mildly undernourished patient before cystectomy provides no outcome benefit and increases the risk of catheter-related sepsis and other infectious complications.
key_facts: Severe malnutrition markers: loss of about 20 lb or more over 3 months, albumin well below 3.0 g/dL, low lymphocyte count.
Seven to ten days of preoperative TPN improves outcomes in severe malnutrition with a nonfunctional GI tract.
In well-nourished or mildly malnourished patients TPN does not reduce ileus, anastomotic leak, or dehiscence and raises septic complication rates.
Enteral or oral supplementation is preferred when the gut works.

question: A 58-year-old uncircumcised man reports a thin, spraying urinary stream and pruritus of the glans. Examination shows atrophic white plaques encircling the glans and prepuce, a pinpoint meatus, and a 1 cm indurated ulcer on the glans that has not healed over two months of over-the-counter antifungal cream. The next step is:

options.B: meatal dilation and biopsy of the ulcer.

rationale: The white sclerotic plaques with meatal stenosis are characteristic of lichen sclerosus, a condition that predisposes to penile squamous cell carcinoma; a persistent indurated ulcer in this setting must be assumed to be possibly malignant until a biopsy proves otherwise. At the same time, his obstructive symptoms warrant relief of the meatal stenosis, which can be accomplished by dilation at the same visit. Topical steroids treat the dermatosis but neither diagnose the ulcer nor correct the stenosis, and antifungal therapy has already failed and is not indicated for LS. Circumcision or meatoplasty may form part of later management but would leave a possible cancer undiagnosed.
learning_point: In a man with features of lichen sclerosus (white sclerotic glans changes, meatal stenosis) and a non-healing glans ulcer, the ulcer must be biopsied to exclude squamous cell carcinoma while the obstructive meatal stenosis is simultaneously relieved by dilation; topical steroids alone do not address either problem.
key_facts: Lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans) causes ivory-white plaques, phimosis, meatal stenosis, and urethral stricture; diagnosis is clinical or by biopsy.
LS is associated with penile squamous cell carcinoma; any non-healing ulcer or indurated lesion requires biopsy.
Potent topical steroids (clobetasol) treat cutaneous LS but do not relieve established stenosis or diagnose malignancy.
Meatotomy or meatoplasty may ultimately be needed, but only after the ulcer has been biopsied.

question: A 24-year-old man is struck in the left flank in a motorcycle crash. CT with delayed images shows a deep left renal laceration extending into the collecting system with a moderate amount of contrast extravasation in the perinephric space; contrast opacifies the distal left ureter and the renal pelvis is intact. Eighteen hours later he has a temperature of 38.1 C, a heart rate of 88, stable blood pressure, and stable hemoglobin. The next step is:

options.A: immediate repeat CT with delayed images.
options.B: percutaneous drainage of the perinephric collection.

rationale: A stable patient with a grade IV laceration and urinary extravasation but intact renal pelvis and contrast reaching the distal ureter can be managed expectantly, because the majority of such collecting system injuries heal without intervention. A low-grade fever within the first day is most often due to atelectasis or the injury itself rather than an infected urinoma. Repeat CT is indicated if fever persists beyond 48-72 hours or if there is ileus, worsening flank pain, or continued hematuria; stenting or drainage is then considered for persistent extravasation or symptomatic urinoma. Exploration is not warranted in a hemodynamically stable patient without expanding hematoma.
learning_point: A hemodynamically stable patient with a renal laceration and urinary extravasation (grade IV) on CT, with contrast seen in the distal ureter and no pelvic or ureteropelvic junction disruption, is managed with observation; an early low-grade fever does not mandate intervention, and repeat CT is reserved for persistent fever, ileus, worsening pain, or ongoing hematuria at 48-72 hours.
key_facts: Most parenchymal collecting system injuries with extravasation seal spontaneously; intervention (stent or nephrostomy) is for persistent extravasation, urinoma with sepsis, or UPJ/pelvic injury.
Presence of contrast in the distal ureter indicates ureteral continuity.
Fever on postinjury day 1 is commonly atelectasis; repeat imaging at 48-72 hours if fever persists or for grade IV-V injuries per protocol.
Perinephric drain, retrograde pyelogram, and exploration are premature in the stable patient.

question: A 27-year-old healthy sexually active woman has had four episodes of culture-confirmed uncomplicated cystitis over the past year, each responding to a short antibiotic course. Her pelvic examination is normal and she drinks about one liter of fluid daily. She asks for a nonantibiotic preventive strategy supported by evidence. The best recommendation is:

options.E: increase water intake by about 1.5 liters per day.

rationale: A randomized controlled trial in premenopausal women with recurrent cystitis and low fluid intake showed that adding about 1.5 liters of water per day reduced cystitis episodes by roughly half, and the AUA recurrent UTI guideline supports increased hydration as a preventive measure. The guideline does not recommend D-mannose, probiotics, or methenamine because of insufficient evidence. Vaginal estrogen is an effective strategy but is indicated for peri- and postmenopausal women, not a 27-year-old with normal estrogen status.
learning_point: For a healthy premenopausal woman with recurrent uncomplicated cystitis, increasing daily water intake (about 1.5 L additional) is supported by randomized data for prevention; cranberry, D-mannose, lactobacillus, and methenamine are not recommended by the AUA guideline, and vaginal estrogen is for peri- and postmenopausal women.
key_facts: AUA rUTI guideline (2019): offer increased fluid intake; vaginal estrogen for peri/postmenopausal women; may offer cranberry; D-mannose, lactobacillus, and methenamine not recommended.
A randomized trial of 1.5 L extra water daily roughly halved cystitis episodes in premenopausal women with low baseline intake.
Antibiotic prophylaxis (continuous or post-coital) and self-start therapy are also guideline options after risks are discussed.

question: A 33-year-old man who had bilateral orchiopexy as an infant has been unable to conceive with his 30-year-old partner for 18 months. Semen analyses show volume 2.0 mL, concentration 0.1 million/mL, and 25% motility. Testes are 10 mL bilaterally. FSH is 24 mIU/mL and total testosterone is 410 ng/dL. Karyotype is 46,XY and Y-chromosome microdeletion assay is negative. The next step is:
rationale: A history of bilateral cryptorchidism, small testes, severe oligospermia, and markedly elevated FSH together indicate primary spermatogenic failure. His ejaculate volume is normal, so retrograde ejaculation and ejaculatory duct obstruction are not plausible and post-ejaculate urine and TRUS add nothing. Hormonal manipulation with clomiphene or aromatase inhibitors is unlikely to improve sperm production when testosterone is already normal and FSH is high, and exogenous testosterone would suppress gonadotropins and worsen or abolish sperm production. Since sperm are present in the ejaculate, IVF with ICSI is the most effective route to pregnancy, with success rates comparable to couples without male factor.
learning_point: Severe oligospermia with elevated FSH and a history of bilateral cryptorchidism indicates primary testicular failure; with normal karyotype and Y-microdeletion testing, the appropriate next step is IVF with ICSI using ejaculated sperm, not obstruction work-up or hormonal therapy.
key_facts: Elevated FSH with small or damaged testes signifies impaired spermatogenesis (nonobstructive); normal ejaculate volume argues against ejaculatory duct obstruction or retrograde ejaculation.
Clomiphene is not useful when testosterone is already normal and FSH is high; exogenous testosterone suppresses spermatogenesis further.
Severe oligospermia (under about 5 million/mL) warrants karyotype and Y-microdeletion testing; once done, ICSI offers pregnancy rates comparable to couples without male factor.
Post-ejaculate urinalysis is for low-volume ejaculate suggesting retrograde ejaculation.

question: A 30-year-old woman at 20 weeks gestation requires urgent laparoscopic management of a symptomatic adrenal lesion that cannot be deferred until after delivery. The safest site for initial Veress needle entry is:

options.D: left anterior axillary line at the level of the umbilicus.

rationale: In pregnancy the enlarging uterus displaces bowel and occupies the lower and mid abdomen, so blind entry at or below the umbilicus or in the suprapubic region risks uterine injury. Palmer's point in the left upper quadrant, just below the costal margin in the midclavicular line, is reliably remote from the uterus and avoids the liver, making it the preferred Veress site; the right subcostal position risks hepatic puncture. Lateral sites along the anterior axillary line are not standard because entry into the peritoneal cavity there is unreliable. The second trimester, after organogenesis and before the uterus becomes very large, is the optimal time for surgery that cannot wait.
learning_point: During pregnancy, initial laparoscopic access should be obtained as far from the gravid uterus as possible, at Palmer's point in the left upper quadrant (midclavicular line below the costal margin); supraumbilical and right upper quadrant entry risk the uterus and liver, respectively.
key_facts: Palmer's point: 3 cm below the left costal margin in the midclavicular line; avoids the uterus and the liver.
Right upper quadrant entry risks hepatic injury; supraumbilical entry risks the uterine fundus as the uterus enlarges.
Open (Hasson) technique at a site adjusted for fundal height is an alternative; second trimester is the preferred time for unavoidable surgery.
Anterior axillary line sites make peritoneal entry difficult and are not standard.

question: A 59-year-old man with cT3N0M0 muscle-invasive bladder cancer involving the dome and posterior wall has pathology showing urothelial carcinoma with approximately 30% glandular differentiation. Creatinine clearance is 85 mL/min, hearing and neurologic function are normal, and metastatic evaluation is negative. The next step is:

options.A: partial cystectomy with en bloc resection of the urachus and umbilicus.
options.C: neoadjuvant gemcitabine and cisplatin followed by radical cystoprostatectomy.
options.E: colonoscopy to exclude a colorectal primary.

rationale: Urothelial carcinoma with glandular differentiation is still urothelial carcinoma and behaves, stage for stage, like the pure form; patients with muscle-invasive disease who are cisplatin-eligible should receive neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy (gemcitabine-cisplatin or dose-dense MVAC) before radical cystectomy, and tumors with squamous or glandular components appear to respond well. Proceeding directly to cystectomy forgoes the proven survival benefit of neoadjuvant therapy in a fit patient. Colonoscopy and FOLFOX apply to primary bladder adenocarcinoma where a GI source must be excluded, and partial cystectomy with urachal excision is the operation for urachal adenocarcinoma, not for cT3 urothelial cancer of the dome.
learning_point: Urothelial carcinoma with glandular (or squamous) divergent differentiation is treated like pure urothelial carcinoma: cisplatin-eligible patients with muscle-invasive disease receive neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy (ddMVAC or gemcitabine-cisplatin) followed by radical cystectomy; colonoscopy, GI regimens, and partial cystectomy with urachal excision apply to primary or urachal adenocarcinoma, not to this entity.
key_facts: Divergent differentiation (squamous, glandular) is common and, stage for stage, carries prognosis similar to pure urothelial carcinoma; these tumors respond well to neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
Pure bladder adenocarcinoma requires colonoscopy to exclude a GI primary; urachal adenocarcinoma is treated by partial cystectomy with en bloc urachus and umbilicus.
AUA guideline: partial cystectomy is not recommended as primary curative therapy for fit MIBC patients who will accept radical cystectomy.
FOLFOX-type regimens are for adenocarcinoma, not urothelial carcinoma.

question: A 48-year-old woman with recurrent Proteus urinary infections has a 1.8 cm filling defect in the right renal pelvis causing mild hydronephrosis. The lesion is invisible on plain radiograph and measures 40 Hounsfield units on noncontrast CT with a faint peripheral rim of calcification; urine culture again grows Proteus mirabilis. After antibiotic treatment, definitive management of the calculus is best achieved with:

options.C: observation with repeat imaging in six months.

rationale: A radiolucent, very low-attenuation renal pelvic stone with a thin calcific rim in a patient with chronic urea-splitting infection is a matrix calculus composed mostly of mucoprotein. Its gelatinous texture makes shock wave lithotripsy ineffective, and because it molds to and obstructs the collecting system, it should be removed; PCNL permits complete evacuation of the soft material with the highest success and lowest recurrence rates, whereas ureteroscopy is less reliable for this volume of soft stone. Alkalinization dissolves uric acid stones only, acetohydroxamic acid is a urease inhibitor adjunct for struvite disease in patients unfit for surgery, and observation is inappropriate for an obstructing infected stone.
learning_point: Matrix calculi are soft, radiolucent mucoprotein stones that form in the setting of chronic urea-splitting infection; they are poorly fragmented by shock wave lithotripsy and are best treated by percutaneous nephrolithotomy, with ureteroscopy a less successful alternative and medical dissolution ineffective.
key_facts: Matrix stones: gelatinous, radiolucent on plain film, low attenuation on CT, often with a faint calcific rim; associated with Proteus or E. coli infection and commonly obstructing.
SWL fails because of minimal mineral content; PCNL allows complete evacuation and has high success and low recurrence.
Acetohydroxamic acid is a urease inhibitor used for struvite stones in nonoperative candidates; alkalinization dissolves uric acid stones, not matrix.
Antibiotic treatment of the associated infection is adjunctive.

question: A 28-year-old woman undergoes laparotomy for a stab wound to the left flank. She is hemodynamically stable with no other major injuries. The general surgeon identifies a complete transection of the left ureter at the level of the lower pole of the kidney, and the urologist is called. After debriding devitalized edges, the next step is:

options.A: exteriorization of both ureteral ends as cutaneous ureterostomies.
options.B: ligation of the proximal ureter and percutaneous nephrostomy.
options.C: ureteral stent placement alone with reassessment at six weeks.
options.D: spatulated ureteroureterostomy over a stent at this operation.
options.E: drain placement with planned repair in 48 to 72 hours.

rationale: In a stable patient, a ureteral transection recognized at the time of laparotomy is best managed by immediate debridement and tension-free, spatulated anastomosis over a stent. Delayed repair, stent-only management, ligation with nephrostomy diversion, or exteriorizing the ends are damage-control strategies appropriate only when the patient is unstable and the operation must be abbreviated. Deferring definitive repair in a stable patient adds a second operation and risks urinoma and stricture without benefit.
learning_point: A ureteral transection found intraoperatively in a hemodynamically stable trauma patient should be debrided and repaired primarily (spatulated ureteroureterostomy over a stent) under the same anesthetic.
