Staged or temporizing approaches (stent/nephrostomy, ligation, exteriorization) are reserved for unstable patients.
key_facts: Stable patient + intraoperative ureteral injury = immediate repair at the index operation.
Midureteral transection: debride, spatulate, tension-free anastomosis over a stent with a drain.
Ligation with nephrostomy or stent-only with delayed repair is for damage-control settings (unstable patient).
Cutaneous ureterostomy of the ends is unnecessary when primary repair is feasible.

question: A surgeon performing robotic-assisted radical cystectomy in a 61-year-old man plans a nerve-sparing approach to preserve erectile function. Compared with a non-nerve-sparing cystectomy, the step that requires a deliberately different, more extensive dissection is the:

options.A: development of the space of Retzius.
options.D: lateral aspect of the seminal vesicles.

rationale: Nerve sparing hinges on completely dissecting the seminal vesicles, especially their lateral tips, so the lateral pedicle of the prostate can be thinned, ligated high and divided, allowing the neurovascular bundle to be released laterally. This extra seminal vesicle dissection is not performed in a non-nerve-sparing cystectomy. Mobilizing the bladder off the anterior abdominal wall, dividing the anterior and posterior bladder pedicles, and the endopelvic fascia incision are performed similarly regardless of nerve preservation.
learning_point: In nerve-sparing robotic radical cystectomy, the distinguishing step is meticulous dissection of the lateral extent of the seminal vesicles, which thins the lateral prostatic pedicle so the neurovascular bundle can be released; the Retzius, anterior and posterior bladder pedicle dissections are the same in both approaches.
key_facts: Nerve sparing requires full release of the seminal vesicles laterally to define the prostatic pedicle.
Neurovascular bundles are released from the prostate after high ligation of the lateral prostatic pedicle.
Dropping the bladder (space of Retzius) and dividing bladder pedicles do not differ between techniques.

question: A 31-year-old sexually active woman has had four culture-proven E. coli cystitis episodes in the past year, each beginning within two days of vaginal intercourse. Post-void residual is 10 mL and pelvic examination is normal. The best preventive recommendation is:

options.A: cephalexin 500 mg as a single dose after intercourse.
options.B: wipe front to back and increase daily water intake.
options.C: nitrofurantoin 50 mg as a single dose after intercourse.
options.D: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole DS twice daily for three days after each exposure.
options.E: void immediately before and after intercourse.

rationale: Infections clustered after intercourse are best prevented with single-dose post-coital antibiotic prophylaxis; nitrofurantoin 50-100 mg is one of the guideline-endorsed regimens. Cephalexin 500 mg exceeds the recommended prophylactic dose of 250 mg. A three-day TMP-SMX DS course after each exposure is a treatment regimen, not prophylaxis, and promotes resistance. Behavioral measures such as timed voiding and wiping technique have not been shown to lower recurrence rates.
learning_point: For recurrent post-coital UTIs, a single prophylactic antibiotic dose around intercourse is recommended (e.g., nitrofurantoin 50-100 mg, TMP-SMX single or double strength, cephalexin 250 mg); behavioral measures such as voiding around intercourse or wiping technique have not been shown to reduce recurrence.
key_facts: AUA recurrent UTI guideline: post-coital single-dose prophylaxis is appropriate when infections are temporally related to intercourse.
Acceptable doses: nitrofurantoin 50-100 mg, TMP-SMX SS or DS, cephalexin 250 mg; timing before or after intercourse does not matter.
Cephalexin 500 mg is a treatment dose, not the prophylactic dose.
Hygiene changes and pre- or post-coital voiding are not evidence-based preventive measures.

question: A 38-year-old man felt a sharp bend of his erect penis during intercourse 14 hours ago. He did not hear a snap, and the erection subsided gradually over several minutes. He now has shaft pain and a modest area of ecchymosis along the ventral shaft without a palpable defect. He voids normally without blood at the meatus. The next step is:

options.A: analgesics, ice and follow-up in one week.

rationale: The history lacks the classic features of penile fracture (audible snap, immediate detumescence, large hematoma), so the diagnosis is uncertain. In equivocal cases the recommended first study is penile ultrasound, which can demonstrate a tunica albuginea defect quickly and inexpensively. MRI is appropriate only if ultrasound is unavailable or nondiagnostic. Supportive care is reasonable only after a fracture has been excluded, and surgical exploration without confirmation risks an unnecessary operation; a urethrogram is indicated for blood at the meatus or voiding difficulty, which are absent.
learning_point: When penile fracture is suspected but the history is equivocal (no audible snap, no immediate detumescence, limited hematoma), penile ultrasound is the first-line study to confirm or exclude a tunical tear; MRI is reserved for when ultrasound is unavailable or nondiagnostic.
key_facts: Classic fracture: snap, immediate detumescence, eggplant deformity; these may be managed with direct surgical exploration.
Equivocal presentation: ultrasound first because it is fast, cheap and widely available.
MRI is the second-line imaging if ultrasound is unavailable or inconclusive.
Supportive care is appropriate only once a fracture has been excluded.

question: A 15-year-old girl with a BMI of 36 kg/m2 has her third uric acid stone and two prior afebrile E. coli cystitis episodes. A 24-hour urine shows pH 5.2, volume 2.3 L, calcium 165 mg (normal < 200), uric acid 1.1 g (normal < 0.75), elevated sodium, and normal sulfate, urea nitrogen and magnesium. Serum uric acid is normal. The factor most responsible for her stone formation is:
rationale: Obesity and insulin resistance reduce renal ammonium excretion, producing persistently low urine pH, and are associated with increased uric acid excretion; together these are the dominant risk factors for uric acid lithiasis and fit the hyperuricosuria and pH 5.2 here. E. coli does not split urea, and infection stones occur in alkaline urine. High sodium raises urinary calcium, but her calcium is normal. Excess protein would be reflected by elevated urinary sulfate and urea nitrogen, which are normal, and gout is exceedingly rare in adolescents.
learning_point: In an obese adolescent with uric acid stones, hyperuricosuria combined with low urine pH is most likely driven by obesity (insulin resistance causes impaired ammoniagenesis and acidic urine plus increased uric acid excretion). Non-urease UTIs, high sodium (with normal calcium), high protein (normal sulfate/urea nitrogen) and gout (rare in children) are excluded by the data.
key_facts: Uric acid stones form in persistently acidic urine (pH < 5.5); obesity/metabolic syndrome lowers urine pH and raises uric acid excretion.
Infection stones require urease-producing organisms (Proteus, Klebsiella, etc.) and alkaline urine; E. coli does not produce urease.
High animal protein intake would raise urinary sulfate and urea nitrogen.
Sodium excess drives hypercalciuria, not uric acid stones, and gout is very rare in children.

question: A 31-year-old woman with a T6 complete spinal cord injury performs CIC every four hours and remains incontinent between catheterizations despite solifenacin and mirabegron. Urodynamics show phasic detrusor overactivity to 70 cm H2O with incontinence at 220 mL and no stress leakage. Five weeks ago she received 300 units of onabotulinumtoxinA into her hamstrings for spasticity. The next step is:

options.B: increase CIC to every two hours.
options.C: 200 units of intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA in about two months.

rationale: Her urodynamics show neurogenic detrusor overactivity refractory to oral therapy, so intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA at 200 units is the appropriate next treatment. Because she received 300 units for spasticity five weeks ago, adding 200 units now would exceed the recommended cumulative ceiling (around 400 units per 12 weeks) and raise the risk of generalized weakness; the bladder injection should be scheduled roughly two months out and coordinated with her physiatrist. Sacral neuromodulation lacks an indication for neurogenic bladder, more frequent CIC will not stop reflex incontinence at 220 mL, and bulking agents address sphincteric, not detrusor, incontinence.
learning_point: For neurogenic detrusor overactivity refractory to CIC and oral therapy, intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (200 units) is the next step, but cumulative dosing should not exceed about 400 units in a 12-week window; recent injection for spasticity means the bladder injection should be deferred and coordinated with the physiatrist.
key_facts: OnabotulinumtoxinA 200 units is the labeled starting dose for neurogenic detrusor overactivity; 300 units for refractory cases.
Total body dose should stay below ~400 units per 12 weeks to limit generalized weakness.
Sacral neuromodulation is not FDA-approved for neurogenic bladder.
Artificial sphincter or bulking treats sphincteric incontinence, not detrusor overactivity.

question: A 74-year-old man with oxygen-dependent COPD and ischemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 20%) has a PSA of 24 ng/mL. Biopsy shows Grade Group 5 adenocarcinoma in 4 of 12 cores; DRE shows a firm left lobe without extension. PSMA PET-CT shows no metastases. He has no urinary symptoms, and his cardiologist estimates survival of two to three years. The next step is:

options.E: external beam radiation with 24 months of ADT.

rationale: With a life expectancy well under five years and no local symptoms, this man will not live long enough to benefit from any treatment of his localized prostate cancer, and guidelines recommend observation. Radiation with ADT or surgery would add toxicity without survival gain. ADT alone, continuous or intermittent, is reserved for men with limited life expectancy who have local symptoms, which he lacks.
learning_point: An asymptomatic man with clinically localized prostate cancer and life expectancy under five years should be offered observation regardless of risk group; ADT alone is reserved for those with local symptoms, and definitive local therapy is not warranted.
key_facts: AUA guideline: observation for asymptomatic localized disease when life expectancy is < 5 years.
ADT alone may be considered for high-risk localized disease only when local symptoms are present and life expectancy is limited.
Radiation, surgery and combination therapy offer no survival benefit in this setting and add morbidity.

question: A 59-year-old man with ESRD from IgA nephropathy has a compatible living kidney donor. Pre-transplant evaluation reveals PSA 4.8 ng/mL and biopsy with Grade Group 1 adenocarcinoma in 2 of 12 cores, and he has elected active surveillance. Regarding timing of transplantation, he should:

options.A: complete five years of surveillance before listing.
options.B: complete one year of surveillance with a stable confirmatory biopsy first.
options.C: proceed to transplantation without delay and continue surveillance.
options.D: undergo radical prostatectomy and transplant six months later if PSA is undetectable.
options.E: undergo brachytherapy and wait two years without recurrence.

rationale: Grade Group 1 prostate cancer on active surveillance has negligible short-term risk and does not justify delaying a living-donor transplant; surveillance can simply continue after transplantation. Treating low-risk disease before transplant exposes him to unnecessary morbidity and postpones the kidney. Arbitrary waiting periods of one, two or five years are not supported for surveillance-eligible disease; waiting intervals apply only after treatment of higher-risk cancer.
learning_point: Low-risk prostate cancer eligible for active surveillance is not a contraindication to kidney transplantation; the patient can proceed to transplant without delay and continue surveillance afterward. Only treated higher-risk disease requires a recovery interval (about six months).
key_facts: Active surveillance candidates should not have transplantation postponed.
Surveillance can continue after transplant despite immunosuppression.
Men treated for high-risk disease with surgery or radiation can proceed once recovered, typically around six months.

question: A 4-year-old boy who completed therapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia 18 months ago has painless enlargement of the right testis noted by his parents. Ultrasound shows a diffusely enlarged hypoechoic testis with increased flow. Serum AFP and beta-hCG are normal. The next step is:
rationale: In a boy with a history of leukemia, a new testicular mass most likely represents leukemic infiltration, and biopsy establishes the diagnosis so that systemic salvage therapy can be planned by oncology. Orchiectomy or radiation treats only the local site of a disease that is systemic and often heralds marrow relapse. Starting chemotherapy without histologic confirmation is inappropriate, and testis-sparing excision with frozen section is the approach for a presumed benign tumor in a child without a leukemia history.
learning_point: A testicular mass in a boy previously treated for acute lymphoblastic leukemia should be biopsied to confirm leukemic relapse; testicular leukemia is a systemic disease treated with salvage chemotherapy, not orchiectomy or radiation.
key_facts: Isolated testicular relapse of ALL is now rare (0-2%) but still occurs; marrow relapse often follows within months.
Diagnosis is by biopsy; local therapy (orchiectomy, scrotal radiation) is not the treatment.
Without a leukemia history, most prepubertal testis masses are benign and testis-sparing excision with frozen section is appropriate.

question: A 6-year-old girl undergoes transperitoneal laparoscopic pyeloplasty through three 5 mm ports. At the end of the case, the port sites should be managed with:

options.A: no fascial closure, as in adults.

rationale: Children have a thinner, more compliant abdominal wall and smaller-caliber bowel, so even 5 mm trocar defects can herniate; the fascia should therefore be closed with absorbable suture. Skin adhesive or subcuticular closure alone leaves the fascial defect open and raises hernia risk. Non-absorbable suture is not recommended for pediatric port closure, and the adult practice of leaving 5 mm sites unclosed does not apply to children.
learning_point: Unlike adults, children should have 5 mm laparoscopic port sites closed at the fascial level with absorbable suture because of a thin, pliable abdominal wall and small bowel caliber that predispose to port-site hernia; skin-only closure or non-absorbable suture is not appropriate.
key_facts: Adult 5 mm ports generally need no fascial closure except in special circumstances (ascites, prior hernia, connective tissue disorders).
Pediatric 5 mm ports: close fascia with absorbable suture.
Glue or subcuticular closure alone increases hernia risk in children; non-absorbable fascial suture is not recommended.

question: A 22-year-old woman with myelomeningocele who had an ileocystoplasty at age 9 reports that her period is six weeks late and a home urine pregnancy test was positive. She catheterizes per urethra and has no urinary symptoms. The next step is:

options.D: repeat urine pregnancy test in one week.

rationale: Urine from an augmented bladder contains intestinal secretions that frequently produce false-positive urine hCG results, so pregnancy must be confirmed with a serum hCG. Repeating the urine test does not solve the problem. Urine culture and prophylaxis become relevant once pregnancy is confirmed, and ultrasound is used later to document an intrauterine gestation rather than to establish pregnancy itself.
learning_point: In a woman with bowel incorporated into the urinary tract (augmentation cystoplasty), urine pregnancy tests have a high false-positive rate, so suspected pregnancy must be confirmed with a serum hCG before further steps such as culture, prophylaxis or imaging.
key_facts: Intestinal mucus and bowel segments cause false-positive urine hCG in over half of augmented patients.
Serum hCG is the confirmatory test.
Once pregnancy is confirmed, urine culture and often prophylactic antibiotics follow; ultrasound comes later to confirm intrauterine pregnancy.

question: A 58-year-old man undergoing non-contrast CT for a 4 mm right distal ureteral stone is incidentally found to have a well-circumscribed 4 cm right adrenal mass that contains large regions measuring -70 Hounsfield units interspersed with soft tissue density. He has no hypertension or cushingoid features. Regarding the adrenal lesion, the next step is:

options.B: surveillance imaging in a few years.

rationale: Macroscopic fat within an adrenal mass is pathognomonic for myelolipoma, a benign tumor of fat and hematopoietic elements. Because the diagnosis is secure on the non-contrast study, washout CT, MRI or biopsy would not change management, and functional workup is unnecessary since these lesions are rarely hormonally active in older adults. Asymptomatic myelolipomas are observed with interval imaging every few years because they can slowly enlarge; adrenalectomy is reserved for symptomatic or very large tumors.
learning_point: An adrenal mass containing macroscopic fat on non-contrast CT is a myelolipoma, a benign tumor that requires no further characterization, biopsy or hormonal workup; asymptomatic lesions are observed with imaging every few years to monitor growth.
key_facts: Macroscopic fat (negative Hounsfield units) within an adrenal mass is diagnostic of myelolipoma.
Washout CT, MRI and biopsy add nothing once fat is demonstrated.
Hormonal activity is rare in older adults with myelolipoma; surgery is reserved for large or symptomatic lesions.

question: A 50-year-old man with chronic irritative voiding symptoms undergoes cystoscopy for microscopic hematuria, revealing a 2 cm polypoid lesion at the dome. Transurethral resection shows cystitis cystica et glandularis without dysplasia or malignancy. The next step is:

options.B: repeat transurethral resection in four to six weeks.

rationale: Cystitis cystica et glandularis is benign but is sometimes found alongside or preceding adenocarcinoma, so most experts recommend periodic surveillance with cystoscopy or urinalysis every one to two years rather than discharging the patient. Because no cancer or dysplasia is present, repeat resection or partial cystectomy would be overtreatment, and BCG is used only for urothelial carcinoma. Antibiotic prophylaxis does not alter the natural history of these lesions.
learning_point: Cystitis cystica et glandularis is a benign proliferative lesion with a low, debated risk of transformation to adenocarcinoma; after resection it warrants periodic cystoscopic surveillance every one to two years rather than re-resection, partial cystectomy, or antibiotic prophylaxis.
key_facts: Red polypoid lesions with von Brunn's nests and columnar/cuboidal metaplasia on histology.
Not clearly premalignant, but surveillance cystoscopy or urinalysis every 1-2 years is prudent.
No indication for repeat TUR or partial cystectomy in the absence of carcinoma; antibiotics do not prevent recurrence.

question: Two days after robotic-assisted radical cystectomy with ileal conduit, a 58-year-old woman develops loose stools and localized left lower quadrant tenderness. Temperature is 37.4 C, WBC is 2.8 x 10^9/L with 82% neutrophils, and she is hemodynamically normal. CT with oral contrast shows wall thickening and pericolonic stranding of the sigmoid colon, a small amount of free air, and no extraluminal contrast. The next step is:

options.D: repeat CT scan in six to eight hours.
options.E: stool C. difficile testing and empiric oral vancomycin.

rationale: Leukopenia with a left shift, diarrhea and focal pain two days after robotic pelvic surgery is the classic, understated presentation of an occult bowel injury, and the sigmoid inflammation on CT heightens that concern. Because she is stable and the scan shows no definite leak (free air is expected at this stage), a short-interval repeat CT is appropriate to detect an evolving perforation, with prompt laparotomy if she worsens. Endoscopy could extend a thermal injury, and treating presumptively for C. difficile or bile-salt diarrhea would delay recognition of a surgical complication.
learning_point: Early after minimally invasive abdominal surgery, leukopenia with left shift, diarrhea and focal abdominal pain should raise suspicion for an unrecognized bowel injury; when CT shows bowel inflammation without definite leak in a stable patient, short-interval repeat CT (6-8 hours) is the next step, with laparotomy if the patient deteriorates.
key_facts: Unrecognized bowel injury after laparoscopy presents atypically: low WBC with neutrophilia, diarrhea, focal pain, low-grade fever, distension.
Postoperative free air is normal for up to a week and does not confirm perforation.
Colonoscopy may worsen a thermal injury; empiric C. difficile therapy or cholestyramine does not address the concern.
Clinical deterioration mandates exploration rather than more imaging.

question: A 35-year-old woman is brought in after a high-speed collision with an unstable pelvic ring fracture and gross hematuria. A urethral catheter passes easily. A plain-film cystogram is obtained with 200 mL of contrast; end-fill and post-drainage images show no extravasation. The next step is:

options.B: CT scan with delayed excretory-phase images.
options.C: remove the catheter and allow spontaneous voiding.
options.D: leave the catheter for 10 days and repeat the cystogram.
options.E: repeat the cystogram with at least 300 to 350 mL of contrast.

rationale: A cystogram excludes bladder rupture only when the bladder is distended enough to force contrast through a tear; 200 mL is insufficient and false negatives are well documented at low volumes, so the study must be repeated with adequate filling. Removing the catheter before rupture is excluded is unsafe. Prolonged catheter drainage is the treatment for a confirmed extraperitoneal rupture, not a diagnostic step. Urethrography is reserved for blood at the meatus or difficult catheterization, and excretory-phase CT images evaluate the upper tracts rather than reliably distending the bladder.
learning_point: A cystogram for suspected bladder rupture is only valid when the bladder is adequately distended (at least 300-350 mL) with end-fill and post-drainage images; a negative study at a lower volume may be falsely negative and must be repeated with adequate filling before the patient is allowed to void.
key_facts: Pelvic fracture with gross hematuria carries roughly a 30% risk of bladder rupture and mandates cystography.
Required images: scout, full bladder (>= 300 mL), and post-drainage film.
Underfilled studies miss small ruptures.
Retrograde urethrogram is indicated for blood at the meatus or difficult catheter passage, not for this presentation.

question: A 9-year-old girl who underwent allogeneic stem cell transplant six weeks ago develops gross hematuria with dysuria. She voids without difficulty, has no clots, and her hemoglobin is unchanged from baseline. Urine PCR is positive for BK virus. The next step is:

options.E: three-way catheter with continuous bladder irrigation.

rationale: BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis is usually self-limited in a child who is voiding freely without clots and has a stable hemoglobin, so supportive care with hydration and pain control is the appropriate first-line management. Continuous irrigation requires a catheter and is reserved for clot retention, and cystoscopy is reserved for intractable bleeding requiring clot evacuation. Cidofovir has only case-series support and carries nephrotoxicity and neutropenia risk in a transplant recipient, while acyclovir does not treat polyomavirus.
learning_point: BK virus hemorrhagic cystitis after hematopoietic stem cell transplant is managed supportively with hydration and analgesia when the patient is voiding, without clot retention, and hemodynamically stable; catheter irrigation, cystoscopy and antivirals such as cidofovir are reserved for refractory or complicated cases.
key_facts: BK polyomavirus is the most common cause of post-transplant viral hemorrhagic cystitis.
First-line therapy is supportive: hydration, analgesics, platelet/coagulation support as needed.
Catheter with irrigation only for clot retention; cystoscopy only for intractable bleeding.
Cidofovir is nephrotoxic and myelosuppressive and is not first-line; acyclovir has no activity against BK virus.

question: A urologist performs a transperineal pudendal nerve block for analgesia before a perineal urethroplasty. Using the ischial spine as the landmark, the needle is directed toward the nerve where it:

options.A: exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen.
options.E: re-enters the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen.

rationale: The pudendal nerve hooks around the sacrospinous ligament at the ischial spine and re-enters the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen; the ischial spine is palpable and makes this the classic site for a pudendal block. The greater sciatic foramen is where the nerve leaves the pelvis and is not accessible for the block. The nerve runs in Alcock's canal within the obturator internus fascia and never passes through the obturator foramen. Passage through the perineal membrane and deep to Buck's fascia describes the dorsal nerve of the penis, the target of a distal dorsal penile block rather than a pudendal block.
learning_point: The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) leaves the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen, wraps around the ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen into Alcock's canal; a pudendal block is directed at the nerve near the ischial spine as it enters the lesser sciatic foramen.
key_facts: Landmark for pudendal block: ischial spine, where the nerve enters the lesser sciatic foramen.
The nerve travels in Alcock's (pudendal) canal within the obturator internus fascia, not through the obturator foramen.
Its terminal branch, the dorsal nerve of the penis/clitoris, passes through the perineal membrane and under Buck's fascia, the target of a dorsal penile block.

question: A 61-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes has had five days of right flank pain, lethargy and poor appetite. Temperature is 38.6 C and heart rate is 112/min. Non-contrast CT shows a 1.2 cm obstructing proximal right ureteral stone with gas in the right renal collecting system and parenchyma. After resuscitation and intravenous antibiotics, the next step is:

options.A: oral antibiotics and outpatient metabolic stone evaluation.

rationale: Gas within the renal parenchyma and collecting system behind an obstructing stone represents emphysematous pyelonephritis, a surgical emergency in which the obstructed infected kidney must be drained immediately, most commonly with a percutaneous nephrostomy, alongside antibiotics and glycemic control. Attempting lithotripsy or PCNL in an infected obstructed system risks overwhelming sepsis and is deferred until the infection clears. A renal scan would be both delayed and inaccurate in the setting of obstruction, and outpatient management with a metabolic evaluation ignores a life-threatening infection.
learning_point: Emphysematous pyelonephritis with an obstructing stone requires emergent decompression (percutaneous nephrostomy) plus broad-spectrum antibiotics and resuscitation; definitive stone surgery and metabolic or functional studies are deferred until the infection has resolved.
key_facts: Gas in the renal parenchyma or collecting system on CT defines emphysematous pyelonephritis, typically in diabetics.
Obstruction plus infection mandates urgent drainage; nephrostomy is favored for a gas-forming infected kidney.
PCNL or ureteroscopy in an infected obstructed system risks sepsis; renal scans are inaccurate during obstruction.
Urine culture is appropriate, but metabolic stone evaluation is not an acute-phase step.

question: During robotic prostatectomy, the surgeon dissects the seminal vesicles and vasa deferentia and is mindful of the nearby ureter. In its pelvic course, the ureter passes:

options.A: anterior to the renal vein at the ureteropelvic junction.
options.B: lateral to the medial umbilical ligament.
options.E: anterior to the uterine artery in women.

rationale: As the vas deferens travels medially from the internal inguinal ring toward the seminal vesicle, it crosses anterior to the ureter, so the ureter lies posterior to the vas; this is why the ureter can be injured during seminal vesicle dissection. The ureter runs posterior, not anterior, to the gonadal vessels, and passes medial and deep to the medial umbilical ligament rather than lateral to it. It begins posterior to the renal vessels at the UPJ and, in women, passes posterior to the uterine artery.
learning_point: In the male pelvis the ureter passes posterior to the vas deferens as the vas courses from the internal ring to the seminal vesicle; it also runs posterior to the gonadal vessels and medial/deep to the medial umbilical ligament, and in women posterior to the uterine artery.
key_facts: Ureter lies posterior to the gonadal vessels on the psoas and crosses anterior to the iliac vessels.
It passes medial and deep to the medial umbilical ligament (obliterated umbilical artery).
Water under the bridge: ureter posterior to the uterine artery and posterior to the vas deferens.
The vas can injure or kink the ureter during seminal vesicle dissection, reimplantation or cutaneous ureterostomy.

question: A 36-year-old man with von Hippel-Lindau disease and prior right partial nephrectomy has three new enhancing masses in the left kidney, the largest 3.2 cm and abutting the hilum. Metastatic workup is negative and serum creatinine is 1.5 mg/dL. To reduce tumor size before attempting nephron-sparing surgery, the most appropriate systemic agent is:
rationale: Belzutifan directly targets HIF-2alpha, the transcription factor that drives tumor growth when VHL is lost, and is the only agent approved for non-metastatic VHL-associated renal tumors, with response rates near 50% that can downsize lesions and make partial nephrectomy more feasible or allow it to be deferred. Sunitinib, cabozantinib and checkpoint inhibitor regimens are approved for advanced or metastatic RCC and have no indication for localized hereditary tumors.
learning_point: Belzutifan, an oral HIF-2alpha inhibitor, is FDA-approved for VHL-associated non-metastatic RCC (and CNS hemangioblastomas and pancreatic NETs) not requiring immediate surgery, and can shrink tumors to facilitate or delay nephron-sparing surgery; TKIs and checkpoint inhibitors are approved only for metastatic RCC.
key_facts: Belzutifan approved August 2021 for VHL-related tumors; objective response about 49% in VHL RCC.
Mechanism: inhibits HIF-2alpha, the pathway constitutively active with VHL loss.
Axitinib, pazopanib, cabozantinib, sunitinib and immunotherapy combinations are indicated for advanced/metastatic disease, not localized VHL tumors.

question: A 6-year-old boy who underwent posterior urethral valve ablation as a neonate has progressive bilateral hydroureteronephrosis on serial ultrasounds. He makes large urine volumes, performs CIC four times daily and takes oxybutynin. VCUG shows bilateral grade 3 reflux and a widely patent urethra. The next step is:

options.C: addition of overnight indwelling catheter drainage.

rationale: This boy has valve bladder syndrome: obligate polyuria from tubular concentrating defects combined with a remodeled bladder that cannot handle the volume, producing persistent upper tract dilation and reflux even on daytime CIC. Overnight continuous drainage provides a prolonged low-pressure period that halts further bladder deterioration and improves hydronephrosis, and it is the standard next step after CIC and anticholinergics. Reimplantation or bulking agents have poor results until the bladder is optimized, botulinum toxin is not established for valve bladders, and augmentation is deferred because many valve bladders become more compliant with growth.
learning_point: In valve bladder syndrome (post-PUV polyuria with a poorly compliant bladder causing persistent hydroureteronephrosis and reflux despite CIC and anticholinergics), the next step is adding overnight continuous catheter drainage; anti-reflux surgery, botulinum toxin and augmentation are deferred until bladder function is optimized.
key_facts: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus after PUV produces high urine volumes that overwhelm bladder emptying.
Nocturnal indwelling drainage decompresses the bladder for long periods and protects the upper tracts.
Anti-reflux procedures have lower success in valve bladders; augmentation is uncommon because valve bladders often become more compliant with time.
Intradetrusor botulinum toxin is described for neurogenic bladder, not valve bladder.

question: A 27-year-old woman with sickle cell trait presents with gross hematuria and right flank pain. She is afebrile, blood pressure is normal, and creatinine is 0.9 mg/dL. Renal ultrasound shows moderate right hydroureteronephrosis without a visible stone. In addition to intravenous hydration, the next step is:

options.C: CT scan with and without intravenous contrast including excretory phase.

rationale: In a patient with sickle hemoglobinopathy, hematuria with new unilateral obstruction points to papillary necrosis with a sloughed papilla or clot, and the excretory phase of a contrast CT is the preferred study to demonstrate papillary defects, filling defects and any mass such as renal medullary carcinoma. Retrograde pyelography is a second-line test when CT is inconclusive. A renal scan can confirm obstruction but not its cause. Aminocaproic acid can precipitate obstructing clots in the upper tract, and empiric tamsulosin is inappropriate before the etiology is defined.
learning_point: Gross hematuria with unilateral obstruction in a patient with sickle cell trait suggests renal papillary necrosis with a sloughed papilla (or, less commonly, renal medullary carcinoma); after hydration, CT with and without contrast including an excretory phase is the gold-standard diagnostic test and should precede other interventions.
key_facts: Sickling causes medullary ischemia, papillary necrosis and sloughing that can obstruct the ureter.
Excretory-phase CT shows papillary defects and filling defects; retrograde pyelography is reserved for inconclusive CT.
Renal medullary carcinoma must be considered in young patients with sickle cell trait and hematuria.
Aminocaproic acid risks intrarenal clot obstruction; tamsulosin is premature before the cause of obstruction is known.

question: A 71-year-old frail man on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve, with two prior deep venous thromboses and no reliable transportation, is found to have castration-sensitive prostate cancer metastatic to multiple thoracic vertebrae without neurologic symptoms. The preferred agent for initial and ongoing testosterone suppression is:
rationale: Vertebral metastases make an unopposed GnRH agonist like leuprolide hazardous because the initial testosterone flare can precipitate cord compression. A GnRH antagonist avoids flare; between the two available, relugolix is oral, achieves castration within days, and spares a frail man with transportation barriers the recurring injection visits that degarelix requires, with a lower rate of major cardiovascular events in the HERO trial. Orchiectomy is a surgical procedure in a patient on therapeutic anticoagulation with thrombotic history. Abiraterone is combined with ADT rather than used as sole castration and would aggravate hypertension and fluid retention.
learning_point: For metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer with vertebral metastases, GnRH agonists risk a testosterone flare and cord compromise unless covered by an antiandrogen; a GnRH antagonist or orchiectomy avoids flare. In a frail, anticoagulated patient with poor access to clinic visits, oral relugolix is the preferred ADT backbone.
key_facts: GnRH agonists (leuprolide) cause an initial testosterone surge; avoid unopposed use with spinal metastases.
Degarelix is an injectable antagonist requiring monthly visits; relugolix is an oral daily antagonist with faster castration and fewer major cardiovascular events (HERO trial).
Orchiectomy avoids flare but is surgery in an anticoagulated, frail patient.
Abiraterone is an add-on to ADT, not a standalone castration therapy, and worsens edema and hypertension.

question: A 70-year-old man is three years out from radical prostatectomy followed by salvage radiation. He leaks with standing and exertion, using three pads daily, but has no urgency, no nocturia and stays dry overnight. Urinalysis is normal and PVR is 10 mL. Four months of supervised pelvic floor muscle training produced no change. The next step is:

options.E: an additional three months of pelvic floor therapy.

rationale: His symptoms are classic sphincteric stress incontinence without any storage features, so he has reached the point of surgical management and further pelvic floor therapy is unlikely to help. Because of prior radiation, an artificial urinary sphincter rather than a sling is the appropriate device, but before implantation the urethra and bladder neck must be inspected cystoscopically to exclude a contracture or stricture that would compromise the outcome. Urodynamics would add little in a man without urgency, nocturia or nighttime leakage.
learning_point: A man with persistent pure stress incontinence years after prostatectomy and radiation who has failed pelvic floor therapy is a surgical candidate (artificial urinary sphincter, since slings are discouraged after radiation), but cystoscopy to exclude bladder neck contracture or urethral pathology is required before implantation; UDS is not needed without storage symptoms.
key_facts: Pelvic floor therapy benefits plateau after about three months.
Prior radiation favors AUS over male sling.
Cystoscopy before anti-incontinence surgery rules out stricture, contracture or bladder pathology.
UDS is reserved for men with urgency, nocturia or nocturnal leakage suggesting detrusor dysfunction.

question: A 34-year-old man with a gunshot wound to the right lower abdomen is hypotensive and is taken immediately to laparotomy without imaging. The trauma team finds a large right-sided pelvic retroperitoneal hematoma overlying the iliac vessels, and a right common iliac vein injury is repaired. The best method to assess the right ureter is:

options.A: cystotomy with retrograde passage of a ureteral catheter.
options.B: intravenous methylene blue with observation for extravasation.
options.D: CT urogram after stabilization at 48 hours.
options.E: direct exploration and inspection of the right ureter.

rationale: A penetrating injury to the iliac vessels lies directly in the ureter's path, and since the retroperitoneum is already being explored, the ureter should be exposed and inspected along its course; this is the most reliable way to detect transection, contusion or devascularization that could necrose later. Retrograde pyelography or catheterization delays the operation and is reserved for when the ureter cannot be identified. Intravenous dye may show frank leaks but will miss an intact-wall contusion, and deferring CT by two days risks a missed injury with urinoma and sepsis.
learning_point: When a penetrating injury tracks near the ureter and the patient has gone to laparotomy without imaging, the ureter should be evaluated by direct surgical exploration; one-shot IVP is unreliable in hypotension, retrograde studies waste time, and delayed imaging misses contusions that later necrose.
key_facts: Iliac vessel injury from penetrating trauma should prompt suspicion of adjacent ureteral injury.
Direct inspection detects contusion and devascularization that can necrose days later, especially after gunshot.
One-shot IVP is unreliable when the patient is hypotensive.
Retrograde ureteral catheterization via cystotomy is an adjunct when the ureter cannot be located, not the first step.

question: A 79-year-old man on alfuzosin for three years develops urinary retention and fails a trial of voiding after one week of catheter drainage. Digital rectal examination reveals a smooth 50 g prostate, PSA is 3.8 ng/mL, and urinalysis is normal. He is otherwise healthy and wishes to be free of a catheter. The next step is:

options.B: add dutasteride and repeat the voiding trial in three months.
options.C: long-term indwelling catheter with monthly exchanges.

rationale: Retention despite an alpha-blocker, with a failed voiding trial, is a clear indication for surgical relief of outlet obstruction, and TURP is appropriate for a 50 g gland after sizing by imaging or cystoscopy. A 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor acts slowly and is preventive rather than therapeutic for established retention, and bethanechol has not been shown to restore voiding. A mildly elevated PSA with a benign exam in a 79-year-old does not warrant biopsy, and a permanent catheter is a fallback for men who decline or cannot tolerate surgery.
learning_point: Urinary retention that develops despite long-term alpha-blocker therapy is an indication for surgical outlet treatment such as TURP; adding a 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor or bethanechol will not resolve established retention, and a prostate biopsy is not indicated in an elderly man with a mildly elevated PSA and benign exam.
key_facts: Retention on an alpha-blocker is a failure of medical therapy and a surgical indication.
5-alpha-reductase inhibitors reduce the future risk of retention but do not treat acute retention.
Bethanechol has no proven efficacy for retention.
Prostate size should be assessed (imaging or cystoscopy) before choosing the outlet procedure.

question: A 78-year-old woman has taken oxybutynin for urgency urinary incontinence for two years. Her family reports new forgetfulness, and her blood pressure today is 172/94 mmHg despite two antihypertensives. Examination shows vaginal atrophy; urinalysis is normal and PVR is 25 mL. Oxybutynin is stopped. The best next medication is:
rationale: Her cognitive change warrants moving off antimuscarinics entirely, so substituting another agent of the same class such as solifenacin is not advisable. Beta-3 agonists lack cognitive effects, but mirabegron can elevate blood pressure and should not be started when hypertension is uncontrolled, leaving vibegron as the appropriate choice. Vaginal estrogen helps atrophic symptoms but does not treat urgency incontinence by itself, and tibial nerve stimulation is a third-line option reserved for medication failure.
learning_point: In an older woman with cognitive decline on an antimuscarinic for urgency incontinence, switch to a beta-3 agonist; because mirabegron is contraindicated with uncontrolled hypertension, vibegron (no blood pressure effect in EMPOWUR) is the appropriate choice.
key_facts: Antimuscarinics are associated with cognitive impairment and dementia risk in the elderly.
Mirabegron can raise blood pressure and is contraindicated in severe uncontrolled hypertension.
Vibegron showed no meaningful blood pressure effect in its pivotal trial.
Vaginal estrogen treats GSM but not urgency incontinence; third-line therapies follow failure of medications.

question: During robotic radical cystectomy with extended pelvic lymphadenectomy in a 66-year-old woman, bipolar cautery is inadvertently applied to a short segment of the left obturator nerve, which is blanched but remains in continuity. The next step is:

options.A: obtain intraoperative neurology consultation for nerve conduction testing.
options.B: resect the injured segment and perform primary epineural repair.
options.C: complete the operation and arrange postoperative physical therapy.
options.D: resect the segment and bridge with a sural nerve graft.
options.E: wrap the nerve with pedicled omentum.

rationale: A cautery injury to an intact obturator nerve is managed expectantly: no intraoperative intervention improves outcome, the case is completed, and the patient receives physical therapy for any adductor weakness, which typically recovers. Resection with anastomosis or grafting converts a recoverable injury into a transection and is only appropriate when the nerve has actually been cut. Omental or amniotic wraps and debridement have no supporting evidence, and intraoperative conduction testing would not change management.
learning_point: An obturator nerve cautery injury during pelvic lymphadenectomy with the nerve still in continuity requires no intraoperative repair; the operation is completed and the patient is treated with physical therapy. Suture repair is reserved for partial or complete transection, and clips should be removed.
key_facts: Thermal injury to an in-continuity obturator nerve: no repair, complete surgery, postoperative physiotherapy; function usually recovers.
Transection: primary epineural repair with fine non-absorbable suture.
Misplaced clip: remove it.
No evidence supports amniotic wrap, omental wrap, debridement or nerve grafting for cautery injuries.

question: A 3-year-old girl underwent right ureteral reimplantation for grade 4 reflux with mild preoperative hydronephrosis. At her six-week visit she is asymptomatic and remains on prophylactic antibiotics. Renal ultrasound shows moderate right hydroureteronephrosis, increased from the preoperative study. The next step is:

options.D: repeat renal ultrasound in four to six weeks.

rationale: Early after reimplantation, worsening hydronephrosis in a well child most often represents edema at the new tunnel rather than true obstruction, particularly when the ureter was already dilated preoperatively, so continued prophylaxis and a repeat ultrasound in a month or so is appropriate. If dilation persists on follow-up, a diuretic renogram is then obtained to assess for obstruction; it is not needed yet in an asymptomatic patient. Stenting or nephrostomy is reserved for symptomatic or confirmed obstruction, and a VCUG evaluates residual reflux rather than drainage.
learning_point: New or increased hydronephrosis on the first ultrasound after ureteral reimplantation in an asymptomatic child usually reflects transient anastomotic edema; management is continued prophylaxis and a repeat ultrasound in four to six weeks, with diuretic renography only if dilation persists or symptoms develop.
key_facts: Postoperative edema at the reimplanted ureter is common at one month and resolves spontaneously.
Pre-existing dilation (dilating reflux) predicts more postoperative hydronephrosis.
Symptoms (pain, vomiting, infection) prompt expedited renogram and possible stent or nephrostomy.
VCUG assesses residual reflux and does not evaluate obstruction.

question: A 16-year-old girl with cystinuria forms a new 8 mm left renal stone despite drinking 3 L daily, restricting sodium to under 2 g per day, and taking potassium citrate with a documented urine pH of 7.3. After the stone is cleared, the next step is:

options.E: increase potassium citrate to target urine pH of 8.0.

rationale: She has recurred despite optimal hydration, sodium restriction and alkalinization, so a cystine-binding thiol drug should be added; tiopronin is the preferred agent because it is markedly better tolerated than D-penicillamine, which frequently causes rash, gastrointestinal upset, cytopenias and nephrotic syndrome. Captopril has weak, inconsistent evidence and is not a first-line thiol. Pushing urine pH toward 8 risks calcium phosphate precipitation, and thiazides treat hypercalciuria, not cystinuria.
learning_point: For cystinuria with recurrent stones despite high fluid intake, sodium restriction and adequate urinary alkalinization, add a thiol-binding agent; tiopronin (alpha-mercaptopropionylglycine) is preferred over D-penicillamine because of better tolerability.
key_facts: Conservative therapy: fluids (2-2.5 L/day in adolescents), sodium 2-3 g/day, potassium citrate to urine pH > 7.
Thiol drugs cleave the cystine disulfide bond into more soluble cysteine-drug complexes.
D-penicillamine causes more GI, dermatologic, hematologic and renal toxicity than tiopronin.
Thiazides are for hypercalciuria and allopurinol for hyperuricosuria; neither helps cystinuria.

question: A 61-year-old man with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m2) has a 3.5 cm solid left interpolar renal mass on ultrasound performed for hematuria. To characterize the mass, the best study is:

options.C: MRI scan with a group II gadolinium-based contrast agent.
options.D: CT scan with iodinated contrast after prehydration and N-acetylcysteine.
options.E: MRI scan with a group I gadolinium-based contrast agent.

rationale: A renal mass must be shown to enhance and be anatomically defined before treatment planning, and in severe CKD the safest way to do that is MRI with a group II gadolinium agent, for which large series show no cases of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis even with eGFR under 30. Group I agents carry the historical NSF risk and are avoided. Iodinated contrast risks contrast nephropathy in a patient close to dialysis, and neither dose reduction nor N-acetylcysteine has proven protective. Non-contrast CT cannot evaluate enhancement, and biopsy without cross-sectional characterization is poor practice.
learning_point: To characterize a solid renal mass in a patient with stage 4 CKD, use MRI with a group II gadolinium-based contrast agent, which carries essentially no risk of nephrogenic systemic fibrosis; iodinated contrast (even half-dose or with N-acetylcysteine) risks contrast nephropathy and non-contrast CT cannot assess enhancement.
key_facts: Group II GBCAs (gadobutrol, gadoterate, gadobenate, gadoteridol) have very low, if any, NSF risk even at eGFR < 30.
Group I agents (e.g., gadodiamide) are associated with NSF and are avoided in advanced CKD.
Half-dose iodinated contrast and NAC do not reliably prevent contrast-induced nephropathy.
Enhancement is required to characterize a renal mass; non-contrast CT is insufficient.

question: A 68-year-old woman with a prior hysterectomy reports leakage with coughing and exercise and a sense of vaginal fullness, but denies seeing or feeling a bulge. Standing POP-Q shows Aa -2, Ba -1, Ap -2, Bp -2 and C -7. Cough stress test is positive, vaginal atrophy is present, urinalysis is normal and PVR is 20 mL. She is scheduled for a midurethral sling. The appropriate concomitant procedure is:
rationale: Her stress incontinence is demonstrated and warrants a sling, but her POP-Q shows only mild anterior and posterior descent that does not reach the hymen and a well-supported apex, with no bulge symptoms, so no prolapse repair is indicated. Anterior or posterior colporrhaphy would treat an asymptomatic finding, and apical procedures such as sacrocolpopexy or uterosacral suspension are inappropriate when point C is at -7. Her vaginal fullness is more plausibly explained by genitourinary syndrome of menopause and may improve with vaginal estrogen.
learning_point: Concomitant prolapse repair at the time of midurethral sling is indicated only for symptomatic prolapse (bulge) or prolapse at or beyond the hymen; mild asymptomatic anterior/posterior descent with good apical support on POP-Q does not warrant repair, and vaginal pressure symptoms may reflect genitourinary syndrome of menopause.
key_facts: Vaginal bulge sensation is the most sensitive symptom of clinically significant prolapse.
POP-Q points at -1 or -2 with point C well supported indicate no prolapse to the hymen and no apical descent.
Demonstrable SUI justifies a midurethral sling on its own.
Vaginal atrophy with pressure symptoms may respond to vaginal estrogen.

question: A 56-year-old woman has received the same first-line combination regimen for clear cell metastatic RCC for 14 months with a good response and no immune-related toxicity. Cytoreductive nephrectomy is planned. The drug in her regimen that must be discontinued at least four weeks before surgery is:
rationale: Cabozantinib has a half-life of roughly four days and anti-VEGF effects that impair wound healing, so it should be withheld for at least four weeks before a major operation. Axitinib clears within hours and can be stopped one to two days preoperatively; lenvatinib has an intermediate half-life requiring about a week. Checkpoint inhibitors such as nivolumab and pembrolizumab have no effect on wound healing and are typically held only in the two weeks before surgery, particularly in a patient who has tolerated them for over a year.
learning_point: Before cytoreductive nephrectomy in a patient on combination therapy for metastatic RCC, cabozantinib (half-life about 99 hours, impairs wound healing) should be stopped at least four weeks preoperatively; axitinib's short half-life allows stopping one to two days before, and checkpoint inhibitors can be held within about two weeks since they do not affect wound healing.
key_facts: Cabozantinib: long half-life (~99 h), hold >= 4 weeks before surgery.
Axitinib: half-life 2-5 h, hold 1-2 days; lenvatinib has an intermediate (~28 h) half-life.
PD-1/CTLA-4 antibodies (nivolumab, pembrolizumab, ipilimumab) do not impair wound healing; most irAEs occur in the first 1-5 months.
Patients tolerating therapy for a year are at low risk of new immune-related toxicity.

question: A 15-year-old girl with an ileocystoplasty, bladder neck closure and appendicovesicostomy has been unable to catheterize for ten hours and has a tense, painful suprapubic mass. In the emergency department, a 12 Fr catheter passes 5 cm and stops at a firm point well below the skin without draining urine; a 10 Fr catheter does the same. Flexible cystoscopy through the stoma is unavailable. The next step is:

options.A: dilate the channel with sequential sounds.
options.C: urgent open revision of the channel.
options.D: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis.
options.E: percutaneous suprapubic needle drainage of the bladder.

rationale: With the bladder neck closed, the catheterizable channel is her only outlet, so an undrainable, distended augmented bladder must be decompressed immediately by percutaneous puncture; relieving the distension frequently straightens a kinked channel and permits catheterization, and the puncture can be converted to a suprapubic tube if not. Blind dilation of an obstruction deep to the skin risks perforating the appendix or creating a false passage. Imaging will not drain the bladder, nephrostomies do not address the full bladder, and open revision is an elective operation after the acute problem is controlled.
learning_point: Inability to catheterize a continent catheterizable channel in a patient with bladder neck closure and a distended bladder is an emergency; after gentle attempts with a smaller catheter fail, the bladder should be drained percutaneously (needle, convertible to a suprapubic tube), which often relieves channel kinking and allows catheterization; dilation of deep stenosis, imaging or nephrostomies do not solve the problem.
key_facts: Resistance deep to the skin may be fascial tightness, a kink from overdistension, or a false passage.
Try the usual or smaller catheter, then flexible endoscopy over a wire; if unsuccessful, decompress the bladder percutaneously.
Sound dilation below skin level risks perforation of the channel.
Bilateral nephrostomies do not empty the already distended bladder; formal revision is elective.

question: A urology department wants to reduce the quantity of opioids prescribed at discharge after outpatient procedures. The intervention with the strongest evidence for reducing opioid prescribing is:

options.A: routing all discharge prescriptions through advanced practice providers.
options.B: electronic prescribing with lower default pill quantities.
options.D: having patients fill their opioid prescription before surgery.
options.E: postoperative messaging about pain through the patient portal.

rationale: Electronic prescribing, especially when the system defaults to smaller pill counts, has repeatedly been shown to reduce opioid quantities, and state e-prescribing mandates have decreased prescribing substantially. Preoperative (not postoperative) counseling about pain expectations is the other proven strategy. Filling prescriptions before surgery is associated with worse outcomes, portal communication has not changed prescribing, and whether APPs prescribe more or less than physicians is unsettled.
learning_point: Electronic prescribing systems, particularly with default settings that lower the number of pills dispensed, and preoperative expectation-setting are evidence-based ways to reduce postoperative opioid prescribing; patient portal messaging, APP prescribing and preoperative filling of prescriptions are not.
key_facts: Electronic prescribing mandates have cut opioid prescribing by up to half; lower default quantities are especially effective.
Preoperative education about expected pain reduces opioid prescribing without increasing dissatisfaction.
Preoperative opioid fills are associated with more complications.
Portal communication has no demonstrated effect; APP versus physician prescribing data are mixed.

question: A 58-year-old man with a PSA of 5.1 ng/mL and a benign exam is considering a secondary blood test before biopsy. In addition to total PSA, the serum analyte measured by both the Prostate Health Index and the 4Kscore is:
rationale: Free PSA, together with total PSA, is a component of both assays. [-2]proPSA is unique to phi, whereas intact PSA and human kallikrein 2 are unique to the 4Kscore. PCA3 is a urinary RNA marker rather than a serum analyte and is part of neither test.
learning_point: Both the Prostate Health Index (total PSA, free PSA, [-2]proPSA) and the 4Kscore (total PSA, free PSA, intact PSA, hK2) are serum tests that share total and free PSA; IsoPSA is a separate serum isoform assay and PCA3 is a urine test.
key_facts: phi = total PSA, free PSA, [-2]proPSA.
4Kscore = total PSA, free PSA, intact PSA, human kallikrein 2 plus clinical variables.
Shared analytes are total and free PSA.
PCA3 is urine-based; IsoPSA is a structure-based serum PSA isoform test.

question: A 60-year-old transgender woman who underwent vaginoplasty eight years ago and takes estradiol reports two years of progressive hesitancy and straining to void. Urinalysis is normal, PVR is 35 mL, and flexible cystoscopy shows a patent neourethra without stricture and an enlarged prostate. She is bothered by her symptoms. The next step is:
rationale: Her prostate remains in place and the findings point to benign prostatic obstruction, for which an alpha-blocker is the first-line therapy once urinalysis is normal and stricture has been excluded. Uroflowmetry and urodynamics are not routinely needed before starting medical therapy for uncomplicated LUTS. Bethanechol lacks efficacy for impaired emptying, and urethral dilation is pointless when no stricture is present.
learning_point: Transgender women retain the prostate after gender-affirming surgery and remain at risk for BPH-related obstruction; with obstructive LUTS, normal urinalysis and no stricture on cystoscopy, first-line treatment is an alpha-blocker, and uroflowmetry or UDS is not required initially.
key_facts: Vaginoplasty does not remove the prostate; feminizing hormones do not eliminate BPH risk.
Initial evaluation of LUTS requires urinalysis; PVR is recommended but uroflow/UDS are optional.
Alpha-blockers are first-line for bothersome obstructive LUTS.
Bethanechol is not recommended for underactive bladder.

question: A 29-year-old woman has incidental bilateral enhancing renal masses (3.4 cm right lower pole, 1.8 cm left mid-kidney) and a 2.5 cm left adrenal nodule measuring 32 HU on non-contrast CT without appreciable enhancement. Blood pressure is 128/80 mmHg and she is asymptomatic. Creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL and chest CT is normal. The next step is:

options.C: percutaneous biopsy of the largest renal mass.
options.D: bilateral partial nephrectomies with left adrenalectomy.
options.E: percutaneous biopsy of the adrenal nodule.

rationale: Multifocal renal tumors in a young adult together with an adrenal mass that is too dense to be a lipid-rich adenoma raises strong suspicion of VHL with a pheochromocytoma, which can be silent and normotensive. Biochemical screening with plasma free metanephrines must be completed before any needle biopsy or operation, because manipulating an unrecognized pheochromocytoma risks a hypertensive crisis. MRI will not reliably separate a pheochromocytoma from other adrenal lesions, and adrenal biopsy is particularly hazardous in this setting.
learning_point: A young patient with multifocal enhancing renal masses and an indeterminate adrenal mass (non-contrast density >10 HU) should be suspected of a hereditary syndrome such as VHL with pheochromocytoma; biochemical testing (plasma free metanephrines) must precede any biopsy or surgery so that a pheochromocytoma can be medically prepared.
key_facts: Multifocal bilateral RCC at a young age suggests VHL or another hereditary syndrome.
Adrenal lesion > 10 HU on non-contrast CT is not a lipid-rich adenoma; small renal tumors rarely metastasize to the adrenal.
Unrecognized pheochromocytoma can cause a hypertensive crisis during biopsy or surgery.
Alpha blockade before adrenalectomy and partial nephrectomy if metanephrines are elevated.

question: Investigators develop a questionnaire to quantify symptom burden in patients with ureteral stents. As their validation step, they ask a panel of endourologists to review the questions and indicate whether the items seem to address the problems stented patients experience. This process is best described as assessing:
rationale: An informal expert judgment that the items appear reasonable on their face is face validity; it is qualitative and considered the weakest form of validity evidence. Content validity sounds similar but requires a structured demonstration that the items comprehensively sample every domain of the construct. Criterion validity compares the instrument against an external gold standard, construct validity tests whether results behave as the underlying theory predicts, and test-retest reliability measures reproducibility rather than validity.
learning_point: Having experts simply read an instrument and judge whether it appears to cover the condition is face validity, a qualitative, lowest-credibility form of validation; content validity requires systematic demonstration that all facets of the construct are covered, and criterion/predictive validity compare the instrument against a gold standard or future outcome.
key_facts: Face validity: subjective expert impression that the items look appropriate.
Content validity: systematic assessment that items represent all domains of the construct.
Criterion validity: agreement with a gold standard; predictive validity is its forward-looking subtype.
Construct validity: performance consistent with the theoretical model of the condition.

question: During excision of a bulky retroperitoneal sarcoma in a 4-year-old girl, the left ureter is divided just below the ureteropelvic junction and again near the iliac vessels, leaving a long devascularized segment. Her preoperative creatinine was 0.9 mg/dL, and she will require adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation. The next step is:

options.B: ligation of the proximal ureter and percutaneous nephrostomy.

rationale: A long proximal ureteral defect in a small child with impaired renal function and impending radiation and chemotherapy is not suited to immediate complex reconstruction; ligating the proximal stump and placing a nephrostomy protects the kidney and allows a deliberate, multidisciplinary plan that accounts for the radiation field. Bowel or appendiceal interposition is prone to mucus-related and radiation-induced stricture, and transureteroureterostomy generally cannot bridge a defect that begins near the UPJ. Nephrectomy discards nephrons she will need during nephrotoxic chemotherapy, and autotransplantation may be considered later but is not an emergent step.
learning_point: A complex proximal ureteral injury with long segment loss in a child who has reduced renal function and will need chemotherapy and radiation should be temporized with proximal ureteral ligation and percutaneous nephrostomy; definitive reconstruction is deferred to a planned, multidisciplinary setting rather than attempted immediately.
key_facts: Pediatric iatrogenic ureteral injuries follow adult principles, but oncologic treatment plans and renal function shape reconstruction.
Ligation plus nephrostomy preserves the kidney and buys time for planning around radiation fields.
Bowel/appendiceal interposition strictures from mucus and radiation; TUU rarely reaches for proximal injuries.
Nephrectomy sacrifices nephrons in a child with elevated creatinine facing nephrotoxic chemotherapy; autotransplant is a later option.

question: A 67-year-old woman reports spotting of blood on her underwear. Examination shows a 1 cm mobile, exophytic mass at the urethral meatus; biopsy reveals invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Cystourethroscopy shows no additional lesions, there are no palpable inguinal nodes, and CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is unremarkable. The best treatment is:
rationale: A small, mobile squamous cell carcinoma at the meatus with a normal bladder and negative staging is localized distal urethral cancer, which is well treated by distal urethrectomy; the distal third of the female urethra can be resected while maintaining continence. Inguinal lymphadenectomy is performed only for clinically positive nodes because prophylactic dissection has not improved survival in urethral cancer. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy and chemoradiation are reserved for locally advanced or proximal tumors. Anterior exenteration is far more surgery than this distal lesion requires, and random bladder biopsies add nothing when cystoscopy is normal and the histology is squamous rather than urothelial.
learning_point: A small, mobile squamous cell carcinoma confined to the distal female urethra (meatus) is treated with distal urethrectomy, which can be curative while preserving continence. Prophylactic inguinal node dissection, bladder biopsies, neoadjuvant chemotherapy, and cystectomy are not indicated for localized distal disease.
key_facts: Distal urethral carcinoma in women has a better prognosis than proximal disease and is amenable to local excision.
Lymphadenectomy in urethral cancer is reserved for clinically or radiographically positive nodes; prophylactic dissection has no proven survival benefit.
Dynamic sentinel node biopsy is a penile cancer tool, not a urethral cancer tool.
Multimodal chemoradiation or chemotherapy is used for locally advanced or proximal urethral tumors, not for small distal lesions.

question: A 58-year-old woman with a 12 cm right renal cell carcinoma has tumor thrombus extending through the intrahepatic vena cava into the right atrium. She undergoes radical nephrectomy and thrombectomy on cardiopulmonary bypass with deep hypothermic circulatory arrest. The complication she is most likely to experience is:

options.D: acute kidney injury of the remaining kidney.

rationale: Deep hypothermia, systemic heparinization, and the bypass circuit all impair platelet function and deplete clotting factors, so bleeding related to coagulopathy is the most common serious complication of nephrectomy with atrial thrombectomy under circulatory arrest. Neurologic injury and hepatic dysfunction are recognized hazards of circulatory arrest but occur less often. Tumor embolization is uncommon in this setting precisely because bypass allows the thrombus to be extracted under direct vision. Contralateral acute kidney injury can occur with any major vascular surgery but is not the characteristic complication of this technique.
learning_point: When a renal tumor thrombus extends into the right atrium and cardiopulmonary bypass with deep hypothermic circulatory arrest is used, the most frequent major complication is coagulopathy with hemorrhage from platelet and clotting factor dysfunction; neurologic and hepatic injury and tumor embolization occur but are less common.
key_facts: Level IV (supradiaphragmatic/atrial) thrombus generally requires cardiopulmonary bypass, often with hypothermic circulatory arrest.
Hypothermia, bypass circuitry, and heparinization impair platelet function and consume clotting factors, so bleeding is the leading complication.
Bypass reduces the risk of tumor embolization by allowing controlled extraction under direct vision.
CNS injury and hepatic dysfunction are recognized but less frequent complications of circulatory arrest.

question: A 69-year-old man with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer progressing on abiraterone is found on germline testing to carry a pathogenic BRCA2 mutation and is started on olaparib. The antitumor activity of this drug depends on a tumor deficiency in:
rationale: PARP inhibitors block repair of single-strand DNA breaks; in cells that already lack functional homologous recombination because of BRCA1/2 or similar mutations, the resulting double-strand breaks cannot be repaired and the cell dies (synthetic lethality). This is why olaparib and rucaparib are approved for mCRPC harboring DNA repair gene alterations. Androgen receptor signaling is the target of abiraterone and the newer antiandrogens, not PARP inhibitors. VEGF angiogenesis and tyrosine kinase pathways are targeted by sunitinib and related agents in kidney cancer, mTOR by everolimus and temsirolimus, and microtubules by docetaxel and cabazitaxel.
learning_point: PARP inhibitors (olaparib, rucaparib) exploit synthetic lethality in tumors with defective homologous recombination DNA repair (BRCA1/2, ATM, CHEK2, PALB2, etc.); in prostate cancer they are approved for metastatic castration-resistant disease with these alterations.
key_facts: PARP repairs single-strand DNA breaks; blocking it in homologous-recombination-deficient cells causes lethal double-strand break accumulation.
Olaparib (PROfound) and rucaparib are approved for mCRPC with HRR gene mutations, especially BRCA2.
Abiraterone/enzalutamide/apalutamide target androgen receptor signaling; taxanes target microtubules.
mTOR inhibitors (everolimus, temsirolimus) and VEGF tyrosine kinase inhibitors are kidney cancer agents.

question: A 27-year-old man undergoes a bilateral full-template RPLND for clinical stage IIA nonseminoma and afterward reports orgasm without any ejaculate. The sympathetic nerves responsible for this complication were most likely injured at the:

options.A: celiac plexus at the origin of the superior mesenteric artery.
options.B: superior hypogastric plexus anterior to the aortic bifurcation.
options.C: lumbar sympathetic chain posterior to the inferior vena cava.
options.D: pelvic plexus lateral to the rectum.
options.E: aortorenal ganglion at the renal hilum.

rationale: Anejaculation after RPLND results from loss of sympathetic input needed for seminal emission and bladder neck closure. The postganglionic fibers from the lumbar sympathetic chains converge into the superior hypogastric plexus, which crosses directly anterior to the aorta at its bifurcation; because that tissue sits squarely in the surgical field of a full bilateral template, this is the most common site of injury. The lumbar chains behind the cava and the aortorenal ganglia are more lateral or cephalad and are less often disrupted. The celiac plexus is well above the dissection and does not mediate ejaculation, and the pelvic plexus lies below the standard RPLND field.
learning_point: During RPLND the sympathetic fibers responsible for emission and ejaculation are most vulnerable where the hypogastric plexus crosses anterior to the aortic bifurcation; this is why the bifurcation region is excluded from modified templates and why dissection there must be meticulous during nerve-sparing procedures.
key_facts: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers (L1-L4) run from the lumbar sympathetic chains through the aortic plexus to converge in the superior hypogastric plexus anterior to the aortic bifurcation.
Injury to these fibers causes loss of emission (anejaculation or retrograde ejaculation), not erectile dysfunction.
Modified RPLND templates omit the contralateral and infra-bifurcation tissue to protect these nerves; nerve-sparing techniques prospectively identify and preserve the fibers.
Ejaculation is preserved in over 90% of patients with modified template or nerve-sparing RPLND.

question: A 70-year-old man undergoes complete TURBT of a solitary 2.5 cm papillary tumor; pathology is high-grade Ta without carcinoma in situ and muscle is present in the specimen. The hospital pharmacy has no BCG available because of a national shortage. The next step is:
rationale: A solitary high-grade Ta tumor of 3 cm or less is intermediate-risk disease with a meaningful recurrence risk and a small progression risk, so adjuvant intravesical induction therapy is indicated rather than cystoscopic observation alone. With BCG unavailable, a six-week induction course of intravesical chemotherapy such as gemcitabine or mitomycin is the recommended alternative and has efficacy similar to BCG in intermediate-risk patients with fewer side effects. Radical cystectomy is reserved for high-risk or BCG-unresponsive disease. Nadofaragene firadenovec and pembrolizumab are approved only for BCG-unresponsive NMIBC and are not first-line agents.
learning_point: A solitary high-grade Ta tumor 3 cm or smaller is intermediate-risk NMIBC; after resection, induction intravesical therapy is indicated, and when BCG is unavailable, induction intravesical chemotherapy (e.g., gemcitabine or mitomycin) is the appropriate first-line substitute. Observation undertreats, and cystectomy or salvage agents are not appropriate for treatment-naive intermediate-risk disease.
key_facts: AUA/SUO intermediate risk includes high-grade Ta <=3 cm, solitary, and recurrence within one year of low-grade Ta, multifocal or >3 cm low-grade Ta.
Induction BCG and induction intravesical chemotherapy have comparable efficacy in intermediate-risk disease, with less toxicity from chemotherapy.
During BCG shortage, the AUA recommended intravesical chemotherapy as first-line for intermediate-risk NMIBC.
Nadofaragene firadenovec and pembrolizumab are reserved for BCG-unresponsive disease.

question: A 12-year-old boy has intermittent scrotal aching after soccer that resolves without treatment. Scrotal ultrasound shows normal-sized testes with innumerable tiny nonshadowing echogenic foci scattered diffusely through both testes, no focal mass, and normal blood flow. He has no history of undescended testis. The most appropriate management is:
rationale: The ultrasound findings are classic for bilateral testicular microlithiasis, a common incidental finding in healthy boys and young men. In the absence of a mass or additional risk factors it is not considered premalignant, so no treatment or formal surveillance is required; the key is to teach the patient (and parents of younger children) to perform regular self-examination and return for any palpable change. Tumor markers and serial ultrasound are not recommended for isolated microlithiasis. Biopsy and orchiectomy are unwarranted in a child with no mass.
learning_point: Isolated testicular microlithiasis in a child or young man with no mass and no other risk factors is not a premalignant condition and requires no imaging surveillance, tumor markers, biopsy, or surgery; management is reassurance with instruction in regular self-examination (or parental examination in younger children).
key_facts: Classic microlithiasis: five or more punctate nonshadowing echogenic foci per image, often bilateral.
Present in more than 5% of healthy young men; not an independent risk factor for germ cell tumor without other risk factors (cryptorchidism, atrophy, prior tumor, infertility).
No serial ultrasound or tumor marker surveillance is recommended for isolated microlithiasis.
Biopsy and orchiectomy have no role.

question: A 49-year-old sexually active man has a cT2 urothelial carcinoma at the bladder neck with diffuse carcinoma in situ on mapping biopsies. After four cycles of dose-dense MVAC, restaging cystoscopy with biopsies, CT, and examination under anesthesia show no residual disease. He asks for the treatment most likely to preserve his erections. The next step is:

options.A: prostate-capsule-sparing cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection.
options.B: two additional cycles of chemotherapy and repeat TURBT.
options.C: surveillance cystoscopy and imaging every three months.
options.D: nerve-sparing radical cystectomy with pelvic lymph node dissection.

rationale: A clinical complete response after neoadjuvant chemotherapy does not reliably indicate pathologic complete response; a substantial minority harbor residual disease and up to half of those who defer surgery recur in the bladder, so radical cystectomy remains the standard. For a young man who wants to preserve erectile function, sparing the neurovascular bundles is the accepted way to do so when there is no locally advanced disease. Prostate-sparing cystectomy is contraindicated here because the tumor involves the bladder neck and CIS is present, both of which predict prostatic urethral involvement. Diffuse CIS also makes partial cystectomy and trimodal chemoradiation unfavorable, and simply extending chemotherapy with surveillance is not guideline-supported.
learning_point: After neoadjuvant chemotherapy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer, radical cystectomy is still indicated even with a clinical complete response; when sexual function is a priority, nerve-sparing (neurovascular bundle preservation) radical cystectomy is appropriate, whereas prostate-sparing cystectomy is contraindicated with bladder neck/prostatic urethral tumor or CIS, and partial cystectomy or trimodal therapy are poor choices with CIS.
key_facts: Residual disease is found at cystectomy in 25-30% of clinical complete responders to NAC; bladder recurrence occurs in up to 50% of those who skip cystectomy.
Contraindications to prostate-sparing cystectomy: bladder neck or prostatic urethral involvement, CIS, and concomitant prostate cancer.
CIS is a relative contraindication to partial cystectomy (multifocality) and to trimodal bladder preservation (worse outcomes).
Nerve-sparing cystectomy preserves erectile function without compromising oncologic principles in non-locally-advanced disease.

question: A 58-year-old man with a body mass index of 41 undergoes partial penectomy for squamous cell carcinoma; pathology shows invasion into the corpus spongiosum with negative margins. No inguinal nodes are palpable, but pelvic CT shows a 1.2 cm left inguinal lymph node. CT of the chest and abdomen is negative. The next step is:

options.D: percutaneous biopsy of the left inguinal node.
